The energy giant is hoping to install 91 turbines at 335-metres in height or 144 280-metre turbines in waters to the north-west of Islay and to the west of Colonsay on Scotland’s west coast.

records.bodyText:
CONSERVATIONISTS have delivered postcards to every MSP at Holyrood warning them that a planned offshore wind farm could kill 4,000 seabirds every year.
The Scottish Seabird Centre in North Berwick is warning that the Berwick Bank development could threaten thousands of seabirds each year.
The charity has delivered 129 handwritten postcards, one for every MSP, to the Scottish Parliament.
Fanny Royanez, policy and campaigns officer at the Seabird Centre, said: "These postcards and the sand art they display will be a powerful reminder to MSPs, as they come back from their summer recess, of the public opposition to Berwick Bank.

records.title: The ever increasing cost of ideology. Please read the full article 🙏
records.bodyText:
The ever increasing cost of ideology. Please read the full article 🙏
#AffordableEnergy #climatechange #Hopetosaveourcountryside
This did not happen by accident.
For nearly two decades, successive governments have pushed the same energy ideology: legally binding carbon targets, mass electrification, weather-dependent generation and a vast rebuild of the electricity grid — all sold to us on the promise of cheaper energy, green jobs and greater security.
Now look at the results.
Household energy debt is approaching £5 billion. Food prices are almost 40% higher than in 2020. Britain has some of the highest industrial electricity prices in the developed world. Energy-intensive industrial output has fallen by a third. Historic factories are closing, investment has gone overseas, and more of the goods we once made ourselves are being imported.
At the same time, the grid needed to support this transformation is running years behind the political timetable. Scotland is already showing what happens when renewable generation outruns transmission capacity: wind farms are being constrained because the electricity cannot always be moved to where it is needed, while consumers pick up the cost.
And after all this investment, Britain still needs tens of gigawatts of gas-fired generation to keep the system secure when the weather does not cooperate.
This is the story behind the montage.
Different politicians. Different governments. The same direction of travel.
The target came first. Engineering, affordability and industrial competitiveness came afterwards.
Now Britain is paying the price.
Read the full investigation here:
A MONTAGE OF FAILED IDEOLOGY — Britain was promised a green industrial revolution. What we got was higher bills, lost industry and a grid struggling to keep up.

records.title: SC Charollais
records.bodyText:
SC Charollais
Just look at the map....a bit OTT  !! Scotland been properly succored  !!
Wind Energy's Absurd
The National Audit Office has now published its examination of Britain's grid upgrade programme.
And there is rather more to it than the headlines about a £70bn upgrade and rising constraint payments.
The NAO's starting point is remarkably clear: renewable generation was allowed to expand faster than the transmission network, with successive governments' 'connect and manage' policy allowing generation to connect before the network was ready.  (How many times we've mentioned SCAM - Stop Connect And Manage!
But the report also asks some much more uncomfortable questions.
Why were opportunities to upgrade the grid earlier missed?
Why did Ofgem reject some proposed upgrades when they were first put forward, only for them subsequently to be approved at higher cost?
Why has there been no full whole-system business case or options appraisal for the grid upgrade programme, despite the costs ultimately being borne through consumers' bills?
And who, exactly, is accountable for the £70bn programme as a whole?
The NAO says there is currently no single person or organisation accountable for the overall progress and value for money of the portfolio.
Perhaps the most revealing illustration of how much the electricity system has changed is the NAO's own map comparing generation sites in 2000 with those operating in 2025.
In 2000 there were 179 major generation sites.
By 2025 there were 1,317.
The geography of electricity generation has been transformed.
The question is not whether the grid has to change with it.
The question is whether government, regulators and the industry planned that transformation properly - and whether consumers are now paying for the consequences of getting the sequencing wrong.

What are your thoughts on affordable energy vs. preserving the countryside?

NET ZERO The Government’s control
Which would you prefer?
#AffordableEnergy #climatechange #Hopetosaveourcountryside
NET ZERO The Government’s control
THE GREAT NET ZERO LAND CONTRADICTION
Why are we industrialising the countryside before we have exhausted the land we have already developed?
Britain has vast areas of warehouse roofs, factories, supermarkets, public buildings and car parks where solar power could be generated without sacrificing another field or transforming another rural community.
Yet enormous countryside developments—complete with fencing, access roads, inverter stations, substations, cables and battery compounds—continue to be presented as a national necessity.
If rooftop and car-park solar costs more, takes longer or is less attractive to investors, the Government should be honest about it. Communities should not be told there is no alternative simply because hundreds of acres of countryside are easier and more profitable to develop than thousands of separate roofs.
The cheapest project for a developer may become one of the costliest decisions Britain makes—for our countryside, food security and the communities left surrounded by industrial infrastructure for decades.
My latest article asks the simple question Ed Miliband and DESNZ must answer:
Why is inconvenience allowed to protect an already-developed car park, while “national necessity” is used to justify sacrificing the countryside?

CWP Energy has warned that £60bn of private investment could be at risk due to restrictions on onshore wind development around the Eskdalemuir seismic array in Scotland.
The developer suggested £10bn could be unlocked by onshore wind farms if government and Ministry of Defence rules were to be relaxed, claiming a further £50bn could be attracted through capital investments from AI and data centre companies.
The opportunity could support more than 10,000 jobs across the energy and technology sectors and enable around 6GW of new renewable-energy capacity, with shovel-ready projects that have grid connections and finance in place ready to be delivered by 2030, according to CWP.
The UK government is currently assessing industry feedback to a consultation earlier this year on a new approach to managing interference from wind turbines on the Eskdalemuir array.
The facility in the Scottish Borders monitors for seismic activity as part of the Comprehensive Nuclear Test Ban Treaty and is safeguarded by the Ministry of Defence.
Wind farms are excluded from a 10km zone around the station and are subject to a noise budget – currently full – if seeking to be built within a 50km consultation zone, to avoid impacting its monitoring capabilities.
CWP said the MoD's existing approach to managing interference has acted as a barrier to investment in southern Scotland and northern England for the last 20 years.

Vineyard Wind: 800 MW doesn’t mean 800 MW 24/7.
Vineyard Wind is often described as an 800 MW project capable of powering around 400,000 homes. But there is an important distinction between nameplate capacity and actual electricity production.
Wind turbines only generate electricity when wind conditions allow, and output can also be affected by maintenance and other operating factors. So an 800 MW nameplate capacity does not mean 800 MW is continuously available around the clock.
The real question is: how much electricity will the project actually deliver over an entire year, and how does that compare with the “400,000 homes” figure? 
Are capacity figures sometimes misunderstood as actual, continuous power production?
#VineyardWind #WindPower #RenewableEnergy #EnergyDebate

BLOCK ISLAND WIND TURBINES HALF-MILE SPACING
SEPTEMBER 26, 2026
https://www.windtaskforce.org/.../block-island-wind...
The commercial fishing vessel F/V Mistress sank in rough weather near Block Island, Rhode Island, shortly after midnight on January 1, 2019, resulting in the tragic deaths of two crew members.
In a "targeted" dive, seven years after it sank, a shipwreck believed to be the commercial fishing vessel F/V Mistress was discovered in September 2026, resting just 50 feet from the base of turbine No. 1 at the Block Island Wind Farm.
Coast Guard records confirm that an MH-60 Jayhawk helicopter abandoned its aerial search for the commercial fishing vessel F/V Mistress on January 1, 2019, due to the proximity to the Block Island wind turbines. The MH-60 is fully instrument-rated, leveraging a digital glass cockpit with advanced GPS (RNAV), TACAN, and Instrument Landing Systems (ILS) to navigate safely through dense clouds and zero-visibility conditions.
The community and local maritime groups had long-standing radar concerns that 500-foot commercial wind turbines—spaced just a half-mile apart—create clutter and "ghost readings" that severely hinder search and rescue (SAR) electronics during heavy storms.
The approval and environmental assessment of the Block Island Wind Farm—including the layouts, navigation pathways, and the specific 1/2 mile spacing between turbines—involved a collaborative review by federal and state agencies
The primary regulatory bodies responsible for reviewing and approving the project layouts and spacing were:
Federal Agencies:
U.S. Army Corps of Engineers (USACE): environment
US Coast Guard: safety, radar, vessel transit zones
Bureau of Ocean Energy Management BOEM ): transmission right-of-way
National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA): adverse impacts, spacing turbines
Federal Aviation Administration (FAA): Aviation safety
Rhode Island State Agencies:
Rhode Island Coastal Resources Management Council (CRMC): lead permitting agency
Rhode Island Department of Environmental Management RIDEM: Local coast impacts
Note: # Long before construction of the Block Island wind project, on October 7, 2008, a meeting was held at the Hyannis Marina in Massachusetts regarding Cape Wind. The meeting involved the fishing industry addressing marine radar interference and the need for turbine spacing of two to three nautical miles. The Block Island turbines were in operation by 2016.
Offshore wind submarine cables can sell for up to $1000.00 per foot. Wind turbine advocates, politicians, and construction companies wanted the project to proceed with 1/2 mile spacing rather than two or more nautical miles.
#Follow the money

The South Planning Applications Committee (SPAC) of the Highland Council will consider the Glen Earrach Energy (GEE) application at their meeting next Wednesday (7th Oct).
This may surprise some of you, as we are still in an active consultation period, following the 4th submission of further information by GEE. in September.  
For those you who don't read the Environmental Impact Assessment (Scotland) Regulations 2017, at bedtime - the consultation period for additional or supplementary information for an EIA is a minimum of 30 days. The consultation period remains open until the 5th Oct (next Monday).
Sound planning practice should mean that the Officer would wait until the end of that consultation period and ensure all relevant information is reviewed before completing the report on an application of this nature.
The Highland Council have opted to arbitrarily truncate the statutory minimum consultation period and the Officers report was issued a week prior to consultation deadline.
Clearly the Highland Council don't wish to consider any more responses and/or they are under pressure to get the application to committee.
This has potential ramifications for the outcome of the SPAC meeting, as matters of 'material consideration' may be overlooked!
The decision to unilaterally stop the consultation clock prior to the published deadline could prejudice any decision made next week.

records.bodyText:
Rural residents close to a proposed wind farm in Caithness will face “unacceptable” levels of shadow flicker if the development goes ahead . Campaign group Scotland Against Spin says shadow flicker – a visual effect caused when rotating turbines cut through sunlight – should not exceed 30 hours a year.
However, research carried out by a retired engineer who lives near the Olrig Mains Wind Farm site indicates that some properties could experience over 100 hours of the phenomenon and, “in the worst case”, over 180 hours.
Renewable energy company Green Switch Capital announced this month that it was lowering the maximum tip height of the four turbines from 200m to 180m following environmental assessments and feedback from the community.
It insists the Olrig scheme “has been designed to minimise potential effects of shadow flicker through careful turbine placement”.
Scotland Against Spin spokesperson Aileen Jackson, who lives in East Renfrewshire, said: “The standard planning benchmark used across the UK is that shadow flicker from wind turbines at neighbouring dwellings should not exceed 30 minutes per day or 30 hours per year, so this level of flicker is unacceptable.
“While the general rule of thumb suggests shadow flicker is only an issue within 10 rotor diameters of a turbine, evidence proves this is inadequate. Scotland Against Spin has received numerous complaints over the years of flicker well beyond this threshold.
“Personally, I have experienced severe flicker from turbines with a 90m rotor diameter at a distance of 1 km.
“We were advised by environmental health to make videos and keep a diary for a year. This proved that it breached the 30 hours a year guidance and the operator agreed to apply a software fix to shut down the turbines any time flicker occurred, i.e. on clear winter days when the sun was low in the sky.
“But we were very fortunate as often environmental health officers are reluctant to intervene, and operators are unwilling to apply software fixes due to the financial impact of forced downtime.
“We also have problems with flicker at night caused by the blades passing in front of the turbine aviation lights. There is nothing that can be done about this and our environmental health officer told us it was not a statutory nuisance because the frequency was not fast enough to induce an epileptic fit. He advised us to buy blackout curtains!”
https://www.johnogroat-journal.co.uk/.../campaign-group.../

Scotsman letters
We have one of the lowest world reserves of diesel fuel upon which most lorries transporting goods depend. Canada has 1,320 days’ (import) reserves, the UK has 42 days. Just over a month and that is without panic buying. And the SNP and UK governments allowed refineries to shut because of high energy costs in the over zealous pursuit of net-zero.
Our gas storage reserves are among the lowest in the world – yet we have the capacity and capability to store, but we do not do so and therefore lose our buffer against a sharp increase in gas prices (as is the case just now), as well as risking shortages if we cannot import.
We don’t use our own North Sea gas, in the over zealous pursuit of net-zero, and are not opening up energy fields in the North Sea – unlike Norway – losing jobs and tax revenue in the process.
We have not invested in water storage, and so farmers in times of unusually hot and dry weather have been unable to water their crops, resulting in low harvest yields on potatoes, barley and other grains, which will undoubtedly increase food inflation.
Meanwhile, we spend enormous sums of money paying wind turbine owners to shut down because the electricity grid cannot transfer power from where it is being generated to where it is required, largely because of years of under investment.
Successive governments have massively under invested in our armed services, placing the country at risk from those who would wish to do harm. Some RAF bases have been protected by a simple wire fence which activists have penetrated, causing millions of pounds worth of damage to aircraft.
These are all long-term issues demanding strategic action. Meanwhile our new Prime Minister obsesses about alcohol at football matches and bus fare caps, and strengthening our relationship with Europe where all the major economies have grown less than the UK economy has since Brexit.
What on earth happened to strategic thinking in the UK? The Conservatives failed us, Labour has failed us and the SNP has failed us. It’s enough to make one weep.
Mind you, if enough of us do, Labour and the SNP will find a way to tax weeping as well.
Brian Barbour Haddington, East Lothian 
Before allowing agreements for data centre builds to proceed in Scotland, the Scottish government should commission independent expert Aidriven studies on the design and operation of such proposed industrial hubs.
For example, on the subject of the energy and water demands of data centres, proven changes in technical assessment methods such as the use of Deepmind Applied could be instituted. In 2016 the use of this AI methodology allowed a reduction of 40 per cent in the energy demand for the cooling of Google temperature-sensitive data centres.
The future substantial demands of both energy and water must surely now be scientifically evaluated using these AI techniques to optimise energy and water efficient designs well in advance of locating new data centres in Scotland if we are to optimise the protection of our natural environment.
Elizabeth Marshall
Edinburgh

It is time for a seismic shift in our latest blog, where we get the perspective of a systems engineer, sharing his thoughts on electricity generation and geology.  See our blog for the full letter - https://savelochness.co.uk/a-seismic-shift-a-systems.../
'The planned and existing Pumped Storage Hydro Electricity schemes on Loch Ness piqued my curiosity a little while ago. Comrie is located on the Highland Fault was famous for earth tremors which peaked in the 1830s. Loch Ness is in the Great Glen another geological fault line which runs across Scotland south west to north east. This is a major fault with other smaller associated faults around it. There have been tremors in the area in the recent past. A 5.1 magnitude tremor in 1816, 4.0 in 1888, 4.5 in 1890, 5.0 in 1901 amongst the biggest and most recent are 3.1 magnitude near Drumnadrochit in 2025 and one of 2.5 in July 2026. So, although the fault is said to be stable it is not tremor free. 
There are several reasons to be concerned about building pumped storage power stations in an area like this. Large reservoirs in areas where there are faults can force water into the cracks changing the structure and causing movement along the fault line. Moving large volumes of water, potentially twice or more times a day, will cause the land to sink and rise as the mass of water moves. This has been known to trigger tremors in other locations globally and is known as Reservoir Induced Seismicity or RIS. Excavation of huge underground chambers redistribute stresses in the surrounding rocks this can take time to stabilise. The water in the reservoir can potentially enter existing faults and cause movement by reducing friction between the rocks. Work can be undertaken to mitigate this at the head reservoir but it is not guaranteed to be 100% successful and nothing can really be done to Loch Ness itself. Tremors of between 1 and 2 and stronger on the Richter Scale are known from other schemes around the world. Much stronger tremors although claimed to be unlikely are possible.
The limit for tremors induced by fracking for gas in the UK is set at 0.5 magnitude, a political choice. A tremor of 2.5 is, due to the way the scale works, is roughly 1000 times stronger than the fracking limit. There is no limit on tremor strength for Pumped Hydro electricity generation as far as I am aware. The reason for the difference would appear, for a cynic, to be that Pumped Hydro is green renewable supporting other green renewable electricity generation. So, residents near shale gas deposits are protected from earth tremors whereas those near renewable energy are not.'

Consequences of the Triumph of the Elitist Climate Agenda of CO2 Reduction:
An Analysis from the Skeptical Perspective
Abstract
From the skeptical climate perspective, the claim that CO2 is a pollutant that must be eliminated at any cost is scientifically weak and politically instrumentalized. CO2 is the gas of life, the basis of photosynthesis and of the planetary greening observed over the last four decades. Imposing sanctions, carbon taxes, consumption limits, and Net Zero targets through coercion would not save the planet but would trigger a cascade of negative consequences of economic, energetic, food-related, social, geopolitical, and cultural nature. This essay develops, in depth, all the bad things that would happen if that agenda were to triumph completely.
Introduction
The official narrative presents decarbonization as inevitable and morally superior. However, climate science is far more uncertain than admitted: climate sensitivity is lower than modeled, models have systematically overestimated warming, and there is no empirical evidence of an ongoing climate crisis attributable to anthropogenic CO2 (Koonin, 2021; Lomborg, 2020). CO2 has risen from 280 ppm to 420 ppm and, far from being a poison, has fertilized the planet, increasing agricultural productivity by more than 15% (Idso, 2022; CO2 Coalition, 2023). The agenda that seeks to sanction its emission starts from a categorical error: confusing an essential trace gas with pollution.
1. ECONOMIC CONSEQUENCES: DEINDUSTRIALIZATION AND IMPOVERISHMENT
The first effect of the total triumph of the agenda would be accelerated deindustrialization in the West. The evidence is already visible: more than 40,000 industrial jobs lost in Canada, closure of steel mills in Germany and the UK, and flight of investment to China and India (Energy News Beat, 2024). By artificially making reliable energy more expensive through carbon taxes, emissions trading, and subsidies for intermittent renewables, competitiveness is destroyed. The GDP of the most decarbonized economies shows structural deceleration: the UK went from 2.6% to 1.4% growth and Germany from 2.8% to 0.9% between 1985-1994 and 2015-2024 (BusinessWorld, 2024).
Sanctions and consumption restrictions would generate persistent inflation and stagflation. Energy is a universal input; if it rises, everything rises. The forced transition is top-down Keynesian climate socialism that adds scarcity, inflation, and impoverishment (Lacalle, 2023, cited in Tomorrow's Affairs, 2023). SMEs, unable to absorb regulatory costs and carbon audits, would go bankrupt, concentrating the market in mega-corporations that can afford ESG consultancies. It is green crony capitalism.
The final result is a massive transfer of wealth from the common citizen and the middle class to financial elites who control green funds, carbon credits, and patents for so-called clean technologies.
2. ENERGY CONSEQUENCES: ENERGY POVERTY AND GRID FRAGILITY
Imposing Net Zero means replacing dense, cheap, and dispatchable sources (gas, coal, nuclear) with diffuse and intermittent sources (solar and wind). That does not effectively reduce emissions, but it destroys reliability. Germany and California already experience blackouts and electricity prices 3 to 4 times higher than the U.S. average (Epstein, 2022).
Energy poverty would skyrocket. When electricity goes from $0.08/kWh to $0.35/kWh, poor families must choose between eating or heating. Studies on energy poverty show direct correlation with lower agricultural productivity, school dropout, and health deterioration (Gonzalez-Eguino, 2015; MDPI, 2023). The elitist agenda turns energy, once an abundant good, into a rationed luxury.
Moreover, the grid becomes fragile: overdemand in winter, weather dependence, need for backup with lithium batteries whose mining is highly polluting and controlled by China. Paradoxically, to “save the planet” ecosystems in Africa and Latin America are devastated to extract cobalt, lithium, and nickel.
3. SOCIAL CONSEQUENCES: CONTROL, INEQUALITY, AND LOSS OF FREEDOMS
Reducing consumption by force requires measuring and punishing consumption. Hence the systems of personal carbon footprint, climate passports, coercive 15-minute cities, restrictions on flights, meat, and private cars. What is sold as “sustainability” is, in practice, a digital rationing system managed by unelected elites (World Economic Forum, central banks, Big Tech).
Two classes would be created: a hyper-mobile elite that buys carbon offsets and continues to fly in private jets, and an immobilized mass that must ask permission to travel, eat meat, or turn on heating. The discourse of climate justice produces climate injustice: the poorest in the Global South are condemned to remain without cheap energy, without fertilizers and without mechanization, perpetuating their underdevelopment (CO2 Coalition, 2023).
Collective mental health also suffers. Eco-anxiety induced in children and young people, telling them the world is ending, generates paralysis, guilt, and rejection of having children. It is a profoundly anti-human agenda.
4. FOOD AND AGRICULTURAL CONSEQUENCES: LESS CO2, LESS FOOD
This is the most ignored and most serious consequence. CO2 is aerial fertilizer. Greenhouse enrichment experiments show yield increases of 20-40% in wheat, rice, and tomato at 800 ppm (Idso, 2022). NASA confirms global greening of the planet over the last 35 years precisely because of extra CO2 (Zhu et al., 2016). Reducing CO2 to 280 ppm would condemn agriculture to lose productivity.
Nitrogen reduction policies, as imposed in the Netherlands and Sri Lanka, already caused agricultural collapse and massive protests. Banning nitrogen fertilizers derived from natural gas and sanctioning livestock reduces food supply, makes animal protein more expensive, and pushes hundreds of millions into food insecurity. It is not accidental: less meat consumption is an explicit goal of the agenda.
If the agenda triumphs, eating meat will be a privilege for the rich, the diet will be based on lab ultra-processed foods patented by the same corporations that finance climate alarmism, and food sovereignty will disappear.
5. GEOPOLITICAL CONSEQUENCES: HANDING POWER TO CHINA AND LOSS OF SOVEREIGNTY
The West cannot manufacture solar panels, turbines, batteries, or semiconductors without China. China controls 80% of polysilicon refining, 75% of lithium battery manufacturing, and 60% of wind turbine production (International Energy Agency, 2023). Imposing forced decarbonization is deindustrializing Europe and the U.S. to reindustrialize China. It is geopolitical suicide.
Furthermore, national sovereignty is eroded. Climate targets are imposed via treaties, IMF and World Bank conditionalities, and ESG metrics that dictate from outside what a country can produce. Mexico and Latin America would be pressured not to exploit their own hydrocarbons, remaining as reserves of “environmental services” so Europe can clean its conscience, while buying U.S. gas at a premium price.
6. PARADOXICAL ENVIRONMENTAL CONSEQUENCES: A MORE FRAGILE PLANET
Paradoxically, the “green” agenda is environmentally destructive. A wind farm requires 300 times more materials than an equivalent gas plant (Epstein, 2014). Millions of tons of concrete, steel, non-recyclable fiberglass, and rare earths are needed. Forests in Germany are cut down to install wind turbines. Deserts are covered with panels that alter albedo and kill migratory birds.
Reducing CO2 would not cool the climate in a measurable way — even if the U.S. reached zero emissions tomorrow, the effect on temperature in 2100 would be 0.1°C according to the IPCC’s own models (Lomborg, 2020) — but it would impoverish the planet and make it more vulnerable to extreme cold, which kills 10 times more people than heat.
7. CONCLUSION: THE HUMAN COST OF A FALSE VIRTUE
If the elitist agenda of sanctions and CO2 reduction were to triumph completely, we would not get a cooler planet. We would get a poorer, hungrier, more unequal, more controlled, and more China-dependent planet. We would get blackouts, inflation, industrial unemployment, agricultural collapse, loss of basic freedoms, and a climate priestly caste that decides who can consume and who cannot, while it remains exempt.
Climate skepticism does not deny climate change — climate has always changed — it denies that CO2 is the climate control knob and that impoverishing humanity is the solution. History shows that human prosperity has always depended on cheap, dense, and abundant energy. Replacing it with expensive, diffuse, and rationed energy is a return to pre-modernism, but with carbon-tracking apps.
True progress is not Net Zero. It is more energy for more people, more food thanks to more CO2, more wealth to adapt to any climate, as humanity has always done.

The 52-foot vessel F/V Mistress sank during a winter storm on New Year's Day in 2019 near Block Island, Rhode Island. The US Coast Guard closed its initial investigation without finding the hull, officially declaring the wreck "lost".
The Coast Guard dispatched an all-weather MH-60 Jayhawk helicopter from Cape Cod. Despite the aircraft's advanced capabilities, the aerial rescue mission was aborted after just 37 minutes.
Wind turbines' 500-foot spinning blades in a half-mile space create significant radar clutter, reflecting and distorting the radar signals of a helicopter crew. This severely compromises a pilot's situational awareness, navigation tools, and ability to track small targets (like a fishing boat).
The wreck may have been recently found 50 feet from Block Island wind turbine #1.
A privately funded dive team organized by Green Oceans conducted a "targeted" dive and located the wreck along with apparent human remains. Rumors from the local marine community say they knew the wreck may have been sighted over the last seven years but never reported it.
During the original installation planning for the Block Island wind farm, an argument ensued over 1/2-mile safety spacing for ocean wind turbines versus 2 nautical miles. State and federal agencies approved the 1/2 mile spacing. Wind farm operators or federal agencies may have known about or overlooked the wreck to avoid negative publicity.
The argument over the 1/2 mile spacing and 2 nautical mile safety spacing comes down to the cost of submarine cables between turbines at $1000.00 per foot.
Since 2019, subsea maintenance has been conducted by jack-up barges parked on top of the wreck.
Federal and state authorities are being actively pressed to reopen the marine-casualty investigation and identify remains.

Federal Survey Mapped “Potential Marine Debris” at Turbine 1 Years Before Mistress Discovery
Thy Back Door September 28, 2026
https://thybackdoor.substack.com/.../federal-survey...
BLOCK ISLAND — A federally funded survey mapped the seabed around Block Island Wind Farm Turbine 1 in 2021, more than five years before divers documented what is now believed to be the wreck of the F/V Mistress roughly 50 feet from the turbine.
Public records show sophisticated sonar equipment surveyed the area years earlier, produced detailed images of the bottom, and was capable of detecting vessel debris. That raises an important question: whether the wreck may have already appeared in federal survey data before Green Oceans located it in 2026.
The Mistress sank Jan. 1, 2019, with three people aboard. One survived, while Captain Oscar Diaz and John Ansay Jr. were lost. Green Oceans announced this week that scientific divers had documented a wreck in about 92 feet of water approximately 50 feet from Turbine 1. Photographed equipment and other features are consistent with the Mistress, although authorities have not yet officially confirmed the vessel’s identity.
From Aug. 25 through Sept. 1, 2021, CSA Ocean Sciences conducted a hydrographic survey of the Block Island Wind Farm for the federal Bureau of Ocean Energy Management. The survey covered approximately 1,957 acres using a high resolution multibeam echo sounder. Survey lines were run in parallel with approximately 20 percent overlap where practical to provide enough coverage to identify seabed features, disturbances and scour.
The resulting data were processed into detailed maps and examined using geographic information system software. Researchers also created shaded relief models designed to make objects and changes on the ocean floor easier to identify. According to the BOEM report, the bathymetric data showed features including gravel, boulders and vessel debris.
Turbine 1 received its own detailed analysis. Researchers identified 15 seafloor disturbances around the turbine in the 2021 data, including four remaining depressions from jackup vessel legs and 11 areas of scour. One location southwest of the turbine was described as containing cobble and boulders or potentially marine debris, with hard material protruding roughly one half to 1.5 meters above the bottom.
There is currently no evidence establishing that this material was the Mistress. The wreck’s exact coordinates have not been publicly released, preventing a reliable comparison between the object described in the 2021 report and the wreck located by Green Oceans. The report also does not identify the material as a vessel or indicate that researchers suspected the missing Mistress.
Detecting an unidentified object on the seabed is not the same as recognizing it as a missing fishing vessel. Still, the public records show that the area surrounding Turbine 1 was surveyed in considerable detail more than two years after the Mistress sank.
BOEM says five rounds of earlier bathymetric surveys had also been conducted within the Block Island Wind Farm construction area, followed by the 2021 survey. Separate federal research between 2016 and 2019 included sampling at Turbines 1, 3 and 5, diver work, video transects and cameras observing portions of the seabed near the turbine foundations.
None of the public reports reviewed by Thy Back Door identifies the Mistress by name or states that investigators had located a previously unknown shipwreck beside Turbine 1. What the records do establish is that the seabed around the turbine was repeatedly examined and that the technology being used was capable of identifying marine debris and vessel related features.
Green Oceans has called for greater transparency concerning monitoring and maintenance activity around the turbine since the sinking. Its July 2026 side scan sonar image reportedly shows the wreck close to Turbine 1 while a jackup barge was also operating in the area.
The question now is whether the wreck had already appeared in years of seabed data and, if it did, whether anyone recognized what they were looking at.

Amazon has agreed a power purchase agreement (PPA) with developer Statkraft for the Mossy Hill wind farm on the outskirts of Lerwick.
Amazon has agreed to take the generation of 36MW of renewable electricity from the wind farm, which is expected to become operational in 2030.
The company said the agreement builds on its long-term investment in renewable energy projects in Scotland, and its wider carbon-free energy portfolio across the UK.
Located just outside Lerwick, Mossy Hill will be an eight turbine onshore wind farm – with the turbines expected to be delivered in 2029.
Amazon said it has now invested in more than 50 carbon-free energy projects across the UK, including wind farms and solar installations, representing more than 1 gigawatt (GW) of capacity.
It said this was enough to power the equivalent of more than 1.3 million households per year.
Last year Amazon announced their plan to invest £40 billion in the UK by 2027, and the transition to a lower-carbon economy is a part of how we’re putting that commitment to work.
The agreement gives Statkraft the certainty to move the project forward.— in Lerwick.

records.bodyText:
The £1bn Orkney link project is connecting the archipelago to the UK transmission network for the first time. 
SSEN Transmission’s link project is connecting the archipelago to the electricity transmission network for the first time, with the remote project shaping the construction of two substations.
Orkney’s exposed location off the north coast of mainland Scotland has given it access to abundant renewable energy resources, in particular wind, wave and tidal.
Over the years, it has also become a hub for renewable energy innovation, as it hosted the UK’s first grid-connected wind turbine in 1951 and became home to the European Marine Energy Centre in 2003. The islands now have an established onshore wind presence and are also an important location for the next generation of renewable marine energy technologies.
However, until now, Orkney’s ability to export electricity has been constrained by limited transmission grid capacity. The under-construction Orkney-Caithness 220kV link is expected to change this.
The electricity transmission scheme involves a new high-voltage alternating current link between Finstown in Orkney and Dounreay in Caithness. It is also part of SSEN Transmission’s wider infrastructure investment programme in electricity transmission upgrades across the north of Scotland, representing around £29bn of investment.
The transmission link will enable the connection of 220MW of new renewable energy, and importantly, extend the electricity transmission network to Orkney for the first time, making it the last of Scotland’s three main island groups to be connected to the grid.
The full scheme consists of a new-build substation at Finstown; approximately 14km of underground onshore cable from Finstown to the landfall site at Warebeth; approximately 53km of subsea cable crossing the Pentland Firth to Dounreay; and around 800m of underground cable from the Dounreay landfall to a second new-build substation at Dounreay West, alongside modifications to the existing Dounreay substation.
Ofgem confirmed the project’s Final Needs Case in July 2023, and by 2024, all planning consents were secured.
Contract specifics
In 2024, under a disaggregated contracting model, the Siemens Energy and Bam UK & Ireland joint venture (JV) was chosen to design and build the two substations, with support from various in-house design functions as well as BT Bell as a civil design partner.
RJ McLeod is responsible for the underground cable civil works and horizontal directional drilling landfall works, supported by fellow OCU Group firm McCormack Drilling, while Nexans is manufacturing and installing the cable system.
Orcadian businesses, including BDS, R S Merriman, Orkney Aggregates, Orkney Research Centre for Archaeology, Aquatera, Orkney Builders, Casey Construction and Leask Marine have been employed to help deliver crucial services to the project. At Dounreay, Global Infrastructure is leading the delivery of the civil engineering works, working with a range of local supply chain partners, including John Gunn & Sons and G&A Barnie.
On the substation side, the Siemens Energy and Bam JV is working under two separate contracts – one for Finstown and one for Dounreay – structured around a pre-construction phase (Part A) and a delivery phase (Part 
A long-standing joint venture with Bam and partnership with SSEN Transmission, dating back to 2013. The close relationship with SSEN Transmission, allows for some early  early contractor involvement (ECI). 
Part A is effectively the ECI, where the design is developed and support SSEN Transmission with planning-related deliverables, with a view to an early and successful start to Part B in terms of the construction phase. It’s all about landing in Part B with as much of the design in place as possible, as well as a whole host of project deliverables ranging from construction phase plans through to environmental plans.
The Orkney-Caithness link is also one of largest substation contracts globally and is a “showpiece project” in the UK, drawing international attention.
The scheme consists of two new-build substations at Finstown and Dounreay West, alongside modifications to the existing Dounreay substation
Construction complexity
The Siemens Energy and Bam JV began main construction works on the substation sites in September 2024 at Dounreay and in October 2024 at Finstown.
Both new substations are designed for a C5 coastal environment, classified as highly corrosive under ISO 12944, which sets out standards for corrosion protection. As a result, and to fit in with the existing agricultural structures in the area, the high voltage mechanical and electrical equipment supplied by Siemens Energy will be housed in a number of new buildings – eight at Finstown and five at the Dounreay West site, plus one at the existing Dounreay substation site.
That’s quite different from a standard substation build, where a lot of this equipment would be outside. The buildings cover a lot of space and constrain the way contractors are allowed to build the substations, so it’s a more complex job.
On Orkney, the ground engineering on the project has turned into quite a success story.
To accommodate the 250m-by-250m level substation platform at Finstown, the project team undertook significant earthworks, with drilling and blasting carried out by Bam Ground Engineering. To reduce the visual impact of the substation, excavated and blasted material is being used to create additional landscaping and landform around the site.
At Finstown, approximately 260,000m³ of material was generated from the site, of which 85,000m³ comprised drilled and blasted rock. Around 92% of the blasted material has been reprocessed for reuse on site.
In addition to sustainability benefits, the reuse of material at Finstown has helped address local concerns. The team recognised that the island’s road network would face pressure from transporting large volumes of imported material, which could also have caused concerns during the public consultation process.
The same approach could not be replicated at Dounreay West, where the ground contained argillaceous material.
At Dounreay, we’ve reused where we can in terms of landscaping bunds and tried to minimise the amount of that material going off-site, but it just unfortunately was not suitable for reuse.
The project team also tackled some initial issues with limited concrete supply capacity on Orkney and worked closely with Orkney Aggregates to overcome these prior to commencement of works on site.
The Siemens Energy and Bam JV considered lower-carbon concrete options, but the remote location made it difficult to secure and transport an alternative product. The team therefore opted for a standard ordinary Portland cement mix for the in-situ reinforced concrete foundations supporting most of the equipment and buildings. Some of the smaller bases, including those for CCTV and lighting columns, are built on precast concrete foundations.
From a design perspective, Siemens Energy confirmed the building foundations required careful coordination.
Be casting ground-bearing ring beams directly on the rockhead which are deep enough to allow access for the numerous site services we have running across site, plus all of the HV cable entries. Making all those below-ground foundations and services work together has been a bit of a challenge within the design.
Some of the project’s most complex foundations are those for the two synchronous condensers (syncons) to be installed at Finstown, which have strict temperature-control requirements.
The syncons will play an important role in enhancing grid stability and represent a first for both the Siemens Energy and Bam JV and the SSEN Transmission system.
Workforce logistics
Orkney has a population of only around 22,000 people. At peak we could accommodate up to 300 people on the Finstown substation site. For a single project, that’s a notable increase relative to the local population.
The project has therefore invested in high-standard temporary accommodation and welfare facilities, which required significant planning and close collaboration with Orkney Islands Council before they could be installed. The resulting accommodation camp was a major undertaking during the early stages of the project. It includes a subsidised canteen, gym, reading room, recreational area, pool and games room, and even a cinema room.
By creating a village on site, around 200 people staying there at the moment and it’s fully catered, designed to almost hotel standards in terms of the regulations applied.
Travel has also required careful coordination with Loganair, which meant the project team did not need to charter dedicated aircraft.
The high voltage mechanical and electrical equipment will be housed in a number of new buildings – eight at Finstown and five at the Dounreay West site, plus one at the existing Dounreay substation site
Orkney’s changeable weather conditions, while a boon from a renewable energy generation perspective, have also had an impact on the construction works.
The buildings are up now and clad in their entirety, and finishing off the last of the FRC [formwork, reinforcement and concrete] works inside. 
Environmental and heritage constraints have also shaped the project. Finstown is located close to the Heart of Neolithic Orkney World Heritage Site, which includes the Ring of Brodgar. Lowering the substation into the landscape and creating substantial landscape bunds were key considerations.
At the Dounreay substation, cable route and landfall sites, proximity to the Dounreay nuclear power station, which is in the process of being decommissioned, added regulatory complexity.
Working collaboratively with the Scottish Environment Protection Agency and other stakeholders, to secure the necessary permits for the project.
At the end of August 2026, earthworks are complete at both sites, building frames are up, with structural foundations nearing completion, and internal reinforced concrete structures are largely in place.
Progress at the existing Dounreay site is slightly behind the two new-build sites due to the additional constraints of working within a live substation environment. This has also included the demolition of part of an existing building.
The emphasis is very much on getting the buildings up, because the critical path revolves around allowing Siemens Energy to start with the installation of its equipment.
Siemens Energy is starting to ramp up activities on the sites. Once the civil works are completed by around April 2027, Bam is expected to effectively hand over running of the sites to Siemens Energy, and the focus will then shift predominantly to HV primary works.
The project is currently on track to energise in 2028— in Orkney Islands.

RWE has confirmed completion of construction of its latest Scottish onshore wind farm, Enoch Hill, located near New Cumnock in East Ayrshire. Farrans were the main civil engineering contractor on the project.
Commissioning of the turbines was completed in May this year, when Enoch Hill became the second new onshore wind farm to be constructed by RWE in Scotland in 2026 – it followed hot on the heels of Camster II in Caithness, which was completed in April also by Farrans. 
Together, both projects add 106 MWs of new, clean and secure generation capacity to RWE’s existing operational portfolio in Scotland – the company currently operates nine onshore wind farms with a combined maximum installed capacity of 229 MWs.
The 70 MW Enoch Hill project was consented in September 2019, with construction starting in June 2023 and first electricity generated in April 2026. The project consists of a mix of Nordex’s N133/4.8 turbines and its N117/3600 Delta4000 turbines. The wind farm will be capable of providing enough electricity to power around 68,000 typical UK homes.
Throughout the construction of the project, RWE, Farrans and Nordex, placed a strong emphasis on using the local supply chain. Over 38% of Farrans’ construction spend was directed towards suppliers located within 20 miles of the site, and a further 23% of spend went to suppliers within 50 miles. 68% of all subcontracts were awarded to local suppliers, with more than 26% of all subcontracted spend retained in the region.— at Enoch Hill (berg i Storbritannien).

Nant Hydro Power Station is a conventional station  constructed as a detached element within the Cruachan pumped storage project. First commissioned in 1963, it is of 15MW capacity and has a fall of 564ft (172m). Council Argyll And Bute Parish Kilchrenan And Dalavich
Nant is a relatively small station with an operating capacity of 15MW and was one of the last stations commissioned by NoSHEB. The station uses water from Loch Nant, which comes through a tunnel to a surge shaft above the station where additional water from other catchments is also piped in. Water then enters a pressure tunnel to reach the turbine. Nant power station is a relatively small underground station, with the powerhouse blasted from solid bedrock. It is amongst the deepest of the under ground stations in Scotland. The interior of the station is predominantly standard for this type as is the large arched access tunnel portal. 
The Nant reservoir is also topped up from the Sior lochs via a burn with an additional pipeline above the Sior lochs from the Muasdale side into Loch Nant (comment from Snus )
Loch Awe
A loch and reservoir in Argyll and Bute to the southeast of Oban, Loch Awe stretches for 23 miles (37 km) from northeast to southwest and is the longest freshwater loch in Scotland. It receives the Orchy and Strae rivers in the northeast as well as numerous short streams which flow in from all sides. The loch drains through the Pass of Brander, via a northwestern arm and the River Awe, into Loch Etive, operating a hydro-electric power station en route, while its waters also serve the pumped-storage power station at Cruachan to the north. In addition to numerous ancient crannogs there are the remains of Inishail Chapel and the two former Campbell strongholds of Kilchurn and Finharn. Close to the shores of Loch Awe are a number small settlements including Lochawe, Port Sonachan, Ford, Dalavich, Inverinan and Taychreggan
Nant is a small station, capacity 15MW. The Nant dam, 1220ft long and 93ft high, considerably enlarged loch Nant. From an intake tower on the South shore of Loch Nant, water is led by tunnel to the underground Nant power station, operating under a head of 535ft. The Fionain aqueduct and tunnel system, 5 miles long, captures water from the slopes above Loch Awe and leads it into the surge shaft, providing additional water for the turbine..
The dam and water intake lie a long way up a private road behind a locked gate which I have yet to successfully pentrate! Thus, the only image of this part of the scheme is from archival material.

Nant is a small station, capacity 15MW. The Nant dam, 1220ft long and 93ft high, considerably enlarged Loch Nant. From an intake tower on the South shore of Loch Nant, water is led by tunnel to the underground Nant power station, operating under a head of 535ft. The Fionain aqueduct and tunnel system, 5 miles long, captures water from the slopes above Loch Awe and leads it into the surge shaft, providing additional water for the turbine.
Nant dam provides the required storage capacity for the conventional high head hydro section of the Awe scheme. The dam is of mass gravity type with a fixed spillway. The dam is designed to prevent the loss of water out of the catchment over a separate watershed. The associated intake gatehouse is located further up the loch. Water from the dam is used in a cascade running through Nant and Inverawe Power Stations. Nant Dam is a reasonably standard example of a mass concrete gravity dam. Hydrogen is often described using colour labels that indicate its production pathway and, broadly, its associated carbon emissions. These colours are industry conventions rather than different forms of the hydrogen molecule itself—the product is still H₂.
1. 
 Grey hydrogen
Produced mainly from natural gas through steam methane reforming (SMR) without capturing the resulting CO₂.
Engineering point: Mature and widely used, but the process has significant direct and indirect CO₂ emissions.
2. 
 Blue hydrogen
Produced from natural gas, commonly through SMR or autothermal reforming (ATR), with carbon capture applied to part of the resulting CO₂.
Engineering point: Its emissions depend strongly on capture rate, methane leakage, energy requirements, and how captured CO₂ is handled.
3. 
 Green hydrogen
Produced by electrolysis of water using renewable electricity, such as solar or wind power.
Engineering point: Operational emissions can be very low when the electricity supply is genuinely renewable.
4. 
 Brown hydrogen
Traditionally refers to hydrogen produced through coal gasification, particularly from lignite/brown coal.
Engineering point: Coal gasification produces syngas containing mainly H₂ and CO, followed by processing such as water-gas shift and purification.
5. 
 Black hydrogen
Produced through coal gasification, traditionally associated with bituminous or other higher-rank coal.
Engineering point: Without carbon capture, substantial CO₂ emissions are associated with the process.
6. 
 Turquoise hydrogen
Produced through methane pyrolysis, where natural gas is thermally decomposed into hydrogen and solid carbon.
Engineering point: Unlike SMR, carbon is produced primarily as a solid rather than directly as CO₂. The overall emissions depend on the energy source and process efficiency.
7. 
 Pink hydrogen
Produced through water electrolysis powered by nuclear electricity.
Engineering point: The electricity source is nuclear rather than renewable, so its lifecycle emissions depend on the nuclear power system.
8. 
 Yellow hydrogen
Usually refers to hydrogen produced through electrolysis using grid electricity.
Engineering point: Its carbon intensity depends on the electricity mix supplying the electrolyzer.
9. 
 White hydrogen
Refers to naturally occurring geological hydrogen found underground.
Engineering point: Unlike manufactured hydrogen, the hydrogen occurs naturally and may potentially be extracted from geological formations where economically and technically feasible.
 Main production pathways
Natural gas → SMR/ATR → H₂
 Grey | 
 Blue
Natural gas → Methane pyrolysis → H₂ + solid carbon
 Turquoise
Coal → Gasification → Syngas → H₂
 Brown | 
 Black
Water → Electrolysis → H₂ + O₂
 Green | 
 Pink | 
 Yellow
Geological formations → Natural H₂
 White
 Engineering takeaway
The colour does not describe a different type of hydrogen molecule. It describes the production route and energy/carbon characteristics associated with producing H₂. For engineering comparisons, the important parameters are the feedstock, energy source, process efficiency, CO₂ capture, methane leakage, lifecycle emissions, water consumption, and hydrogen purity.

A significant milestone has been ticked off in the development of a major offshore wind farm.
A second 85km offshore export cable has been installed at Inch Cape Offshore Wind Farm in the North Sea.
Energy from the development, which will feature 74 turbines off the coast of Angus, will be brought onshore via a substation on part of the former Cockenzie Power Station site in East Lothian.
The second of two 220kV three-phase export cables was installed in three 28-kilometre sections by Enshore Subsea.
It required two offshore joints which were carried out by jointing specialists and was buried in the seabed using hybrid trenching vehicle ENS1100, with some final rock placement to come.
The two parallel cables will transmit power from the 1.1 GW substation platform to its new onshore substation at Cockenzie then onto the national grid. 
The cables will be energised over the coming weeks in advance of first power toward the end of this year.
The completion of this crucial  link between the offshore and onshore supstations is another major achievement for the project and testament to the excellent collaboration between the Inch Cape team and contractors, particularly Orient Cable and Enshore Subsea.
The successful finalisation of this scope builds on the solid progress as they enter the next phases of offshore construction.
Inch Cape recently completed its monopile and transition piece installation and current offshore activity, includes array cable laying and jacket foundation pin pile installation.
The components for the project's 15 MW turbines are being delivered to the Port of Dundee in advance of tower assembly and offshore installation.
The project remains on track for full commercial operations next year— at Cockenzie.

A scaled-back application for a 13 turbine, 93.6 MW energy development, 14km southeast of Aberfeldy, has been submitted collaboratively between Lanarkshire-based Muirhall Energy Ltd and Scone Estates.
The North Logiealmond Wind Farm proposal has been reduced in scope from an initial 20 turbine plan, with 6 turbines also scaled back to 180m in size following opposition to the original vision.
Now applicants have pledged a potential stake of up to 10% for community groups to share in the financial benefits of the energy project, should planners give the green light.
An economic report by Biggar Economics on behalf of the scheme outlined potential gains to the Perthshire economy of £11.9m during the development and construction phase, with a further £1.3m a year when operational.
Non-domestic rates income has been estimated at £1.2m per year while Muirhall Energy has pledged an inflated £7000 per MW investment into a local community fund, netting £655 000 annually for local projects, if the windfarm proceeds.
However, it is the offer of a share in ownership, prior to construction, which is relatively novel, ‘creating sustainable income streams that can be used to support community development.’
In the supporting documentation, Muirhall say it has already completed a successful ownership arrangement (5%) at the 10-turbine Crossdykes Wind Farm in Dumfries and Galloway. The local beneficiary group chose to offload their 5% stake when the wind farm was sold in 2022.
Representations can be made to Scottish Government until 22nd November, with previous objections raised by Amulree and Glen Quaich residents and NatureScot, who voiced concerns for ‘potential effects on the River Tay National Scenic Area’.
The Dunkeld and Birnam Community Council voiced its concerns over the cumulative impact of energy schemes earmarked for the local area.
The project, should it go ahead will create 20 jobs, with 10 being local and businesses in the surrounding area will be given a tendering advantage when applying for construction contracts. Scone Estates are partners and want to see local economic benefits.
Overall, it is estimated the project will save 119 000 tonnes of carbon per year over its lifespan but the decision by Scottish Government is still to be confirmed.
A previous application for a similar number of smaller turbines in the area was rejected in 2008, on landscape and visual grounds.
The new plans can be viewed at Bankfoot Church Centre, Birnam Arts and Chapelhill Hall.— in Aberfeldy.

The delivery of a 505km electricity transmission connection between Scotland and England, contains hidden challenges - but it also offers valuable lessons for future projects engaged in enhancing the UK's clean energy transmission capacity.
Labelled as the largest ever single investment in the UK transmission system, at £4.3bn Eastern Green Link 2 (EGL2) is part of a portfolio of projects that will support the country's energy transition by providing additional capacity to transmit renewable energy produced in Scottish wind farms, hydro stations and solar farms. It will also make an important contribution to energy security across the UK.
EGL2 will connect Peterhead on the northeast coast of Scotland to Wren Hall in Drax, North Yorkshire, using 505km of 2GW, high voltage direct current (HVDC) cable - with 436km of the cable to be laid offshore and the remainder onshore.
It is being delivered by the first joint venture between National Grid Electricity Transmission – which owns and manages the electricity transmission network in England and Wales – and SSEN Transmission, which does the same in the North of Scotland.
The project also involves the construction of a 525kV bi- pole converter station at each end of the electrical transmission connection, which will convert electricity between alternating current (AC) and direct current (DC).
The electricity generated by renewable sources will be sent through the AC network to the Peterhead Converter Station, where it will be converted to DC and transmitted via the HVDC subsea and onshore cables.
Once it reaches the converter station at Wren Hall, it will be converted back to AC and introduced into the wider transmission network.
The use of HVDC is that there are minimal electrical transmission losses, between Peterhead and Drax compared to an equivalent AC connection. For long distance routes, a DC connection is particularly efficient.
The bi-pole technology provides advantages compared to more traditional converter stations (Hitachi Energy –  provided the technology). It offers better redundancy and resilience. If there is an issue on one side of the converter stations, they can still operate at 50% capacity.
The project started in earnest in 2019, alongside EGL1.
High level development work, identified the efficient options to provide additional capacity at appropriate points on the electricity network in Scotland and England.
System design studies, identified Peterhead and Drax connection points for the EGL2 project. More detailed system studies and a significant amount of development studies,
Identified potential cable routes and locations for the converter stations.
In terms of the subsea cable routes, the project team initially carried out a desktop study to gather information on the geological conditions of the seabed. This identified a broad route corridor that was then surveyed in 2020, and used that to finesse the final route selection.
This work was carried out simultaneously with the EGL1 project, driving efficiencies and ensuring the same information at the same time. Survey data which identified a route corridor was used to inform the overall cable contract, tender specification and marine cable contract.
In early 2024, a consortium between Bam UK & Ireland and Hitachi Energy was awarded the contract to carry out engineering works and supply technology for the two for stations with Mott MacDonald providing design services.
The Prysmian Group was appointed to design, manufacture and install the HVDC cable, while Balfour Beatty was subcontracted by Prysmian to install the onshore underground cable. With the Peterhead converter station being near the coast, only 1km of onshore cables needs to be installed to Sandford Bay where the subsea cable's journey will commence. In England, 68km of onshore cable will be installed between Bridlington in Yorkshire – the southernmost location of the subsea cable – and the Wren Hall converter station site.
Converter stations
Bam contractor has been working with SSEN Transmission on the construction of substations for over a decade. On this project, it is responsible for the buildings and surrounding infrastructure, as well as the installation of the specialist HVDC equipment.
Despite Bam's experience in the sector, this project has challenges because of the major influence of the electrical design on the civil works. In addition, the converter stations' designs are not identical, as each client has specified desired outcomes, leading to nuances in the design.
Hitachi Energy has offered the technology in other projects before, for example the Dogger Bank Wind Farm, however each project is unique because of the grid connections as well as client requirements. 
As the size of equipment impacts the size of the buildings, electrical design had to precede civil works design. Even number of years into the project, the finalised design, is  getting more and more mature.
Carrying out construction works while design is still not finalised is challenging, highlighting the need for collaboration between the teams to ensure that construction works can be carried out in a timely manner.
Bam's team was mobilised on the two sites in September 2024, with earthworks carried out until April 2025. The earthworks had to be really well thought through in terms of water run-off and coping with that, especially during the winter.
Peterhead was a conventional cut and fill. Wren Hall is in a flood plain, so the first thing to do was@ a 4m-high platform that will provide the base for the converter station and remove any risk of future flooding.
He says that for the rest of 2025, the team focused primarily on piling, drainage and foundations, with Mott MacDonald assisting in the rationalisation of various design elements.
Slipform construction of both transformer buildings has been completed, with continuous concrete pours which took up to 12 days. At one point over 100 people on each shift for this element of the works. Getting these elements completed was really good start to 2026.
The works for the rest of the year focus on structural steel and cladding for the buildings, which are up to 28m high. By the second quarter of 2027 to the site will welcome the first of Hitachi Energy's equipment.
Offshore work
More surveys were carried out over the years to verify the desktop study's results of the marine cable route and refine it. In addition to Unexploded Ordnance surveys, further surveys were commissioned to gather more detail about the seabed, for example the existence of boulder fields.
Geotechinal surveys at the bottom of the ocean to determine the integrity of the ground. The trench to lay the cable into the seabed, will be approx 1.2m deep.
In very soft ground conditions, you'll use either a plough or blowout technology to blow the sand away when you bury the cable. In harder conditions, particularly in boulder areas, you may actually have to lay the cable on the surface and then place rock protection on top to shield that cable from any form of damage.
The installation of the offshore cable in 2028 will be one of the project's most challenging works. Working in the North Sea throughout the winter of 27/28 will be a challenge.
The project team is currently finalising the horizontal directional drill in Sandford Bay near the Peterhead Converter Station, which will extend 1.2km into the ocean. In preparation for the drilling, sheet piling was carried out to allow the entry pit to be excavated, and two steel casings were installed.
Once completed, the process will be repeated in Bridlington. On the English side of the project, there will also be a number of small horizontal drills to take the cable under roads, canals and railways.
EGL2 is expected to be operational in 2029. EGL1 a joint venture project being delivered by National Grid and Scottish Power – is a 196km electricity link that will run from the Torness area in East Lothian to Hawthorn Pit in County Durham, and is also currently in construction.

BERNACCHI-1 UPDATE DEVELOPMENT APPLICATION EXPECTED “SHORTLY”, BUT SUBCO’S TIMELINE RAISES SERIOUS QUESTIONS 
SUBCO has confirmed that a project briefing has taken place with George Town Council and that a development application for 122 Bellbuoy Beach Road is expected to be submitted shortly.
As of 30 September 2026, I have not located a publicly advertised application for the proposed cable landing on George Town Council’s planning page.
Let’s be absolutely clear:
 A project briefing is not a development application.
 A development application is not planning approval.
 An indicative company timetable is not government authorisation to begin work.
SUBCO’S PUBLISHED TIMELINE
PHASE 1 PLANNING
June–September 2026
- Initial route selection
- Agency consultation and project briefings
- Planning assessment and desktop studies completed
PHASE 2 FINAL SURVEY AND DESIGN
October–November 2026
- Marine route surveys to determine the final cable route
- Site and ground-condition investigations at the proposed HDD and cable-shelter locations
- Survey approvals
PHASE 3 CABLE-INSTALLATION APPROVALS
November 2026–January 2027
* George Town Council development consent
* Crown Lands consent
* NRE and Parks consent
* Cultural-heritage consent
PHASE 4 INSTALLATION
November 2026–February 2027
- Construction of the beach manhole and horizontal directional drilling out to sea
- HDD and beach-manhole installation
- Street-conduit works
- Cable-landing shelter construction
MARCH 2027
- Subsea cable installation
- Street cable-hauling works
PHASE 5 NETWORK COMMISSIONING
February–March 2027
- Equipment installation
- System testing and commissioning
THE TIMELINE OVERLAPS
SUBCO’s own timetable shows the installation phase beginning in November 2026, while its approvals phase runs from November 2026 until January 2027.
That does not prove construction will begin without approval but it creates an obvious and legitimate question:
How can installation be scheduled to begin while the listed approvals may still be under consideration?
The community deserves to know exactly:
* Which activities SUBCO intends to undertake before January 2027
* Which activities require Council or government approval
* Whether site investigations involve drilling, excavation or vegetation disturbance
* Whether Crown Lands and Parks approvals have already been sought
* Whether an EPBC Act referral has been lodged
* Whether an ACMA submarine-cable installation permit has been applied for
* When the community will be able to inspect the complete application and make submissions
* What alternative landing sites were properly assessed, including Four Mile Bluff and Five Mile Bluff, where major infrastructure already exists
George Town Council confirmed on 18 September 2026 that no development application had been lodged and no planning approval had been granted at that time.
SUBCO subsequently stated that a Council briefing had occurred and that the development application for 122 Bellbuoy Beach Road would be submitted shortly.
Bellbuoy Beach residents should not discover that surveys, investigations or works have started before the necessary approvals and conditions are publicly explained.
This is not simply about a cable approximately the diameter of a 50-cent piece.
It is about horizontal directional drilling beneath a sensitive coastal area, a beach manhole, construction machinery, street-conduit works, a cable shelter and the future industrial use of a residential beachfront block.
NO CONSTRUCTION SHOULD BEGIN UNTIL EVERY REQUIRED APPROVAL IS IN PLACE AND PUBLICLY ACCOUNTED FOR.
A PROJECT BRIEFING IS NOT PUBLIC CONSULTATION.
DIRECT LINKS
SUBCO Bernacchi-1 community information and project timeline:
https://sub.co/bernacchi-1/community
George Town Council current development applications:
https://georgetown.tas.gov.au/planning
Report confirming that no Council application had been lodged as of 18 September:
https://www.heraldsun.com.au/.../16852407d805ac4eed4f1077...
Report quoting SUBCO saying the application would be submitted shortly:
https://www.themercury.com.au/.../fae9e5b6ea63cbc5ce0beb6...
Commonwealth EPBC Act public portal:
https://epbcpublicportal.environment.gov.au/all-referrals/
ACMA submarine cables and installation permits:
https://www.acma.gov.au/submarine-cables
Tasmania Parks and Wildlife Service proposed works and developments on Crown land:
https://parks.tas.gov.au/.../works-developments-and-events
HOW DOES THE BROADER COMMUNITY FEEL ABOUT THIS?
This proposal will not affect only the residents living beside 122 Bellbuoy Beach Road. It concerns everyone who values Bellbuoy Beach, our coastline, our environment and transparent decision-making.
If you have concerns, questions or information, now is the time to speak up because once the approvals are granted, the machinery arrives and drilling begins, it may be much harder to change the outcome.
I CAN’T READ YOUR MIND PLEASE SPEAK UP. 
SPEAK NOW BEFORE THE COMMUNITY IS LEFT TO FOREVER HOLD ITS PEACE.
THIS IS THE PEOPLE’S BEACH AND THE PEOPLE DESERVE A VOICE.

The New Bedford Light
Opinion: Reopen the investigation of the F/V Mistress
by Constance Gee September 30, 2026
https://newbedfordlight.org/opinion-reopen-the.../
A recent discovery does not, by itself, establish that Block Island Wind Farm Turbine 1 caused the sinking or prevented a rescue. It does demand answers.
The fishing vessel Mistress sank in the early hours of Jan. 1, 2019. Two of its three crew members were lost. More than seven years later, a private dive team documented a wreck believed to be the Mistress, roughly 50 feet from Turbine 1 at the Block Island Wind Farm.
That location deserves attention. In its mayday call, the crew said the vessel was “right below the Block Island Wind Farm.” A Coast Guard helicopter searched near the coordinates of the final distress signal but then abandoned a hover search after about half an hour amid poor visibility, low clouds, “windmills,” and high winds.
The team making the recent discovery used the mayday coordinates, the Coast Guard’s investigative report, and rumored accounts from mariners and divers to narrow its search. Side-scan sonar revealed wreckage just east of Turbine 1.
Divers documented features and equipment that match photographs of the Mistress in the Coast Guard report. They also found what appear to be human remains among the wheelhouse debris.
The wreck was not the first indication of boat debris near the turbine. A BOEM-sponsored survey reported seeing “partial boat debris (e.g., paneling from a small boat hull)” around Turbine 1 in 2019, although it claims no footage was obtained. Why was that observation apparently never connected to the loss of the Mistress?
The new sonar image also shows a maintenance barge beside the turbine, with its legs or “spuds” planted close to the wreckage. Given the recurring maintenance activity at Turbine 1 since 2019, investigators should determine what seabed checks were performed, what operators observed, and whether earlier work disturbed the site.
Confusion over the wreck’s location may have hindered scrutiny. On Jan. 28, 2019, the Martha’s Vineyard Times reported that a private search had found the Mistress “well to the east” of the wind farm. That account was never publicly reconciled with the Coast Guard’s investigative record or the crew’s mayday call. NOAA searched for wreckage twice in 2019. Both efforts were curtailed by weather and had gaps in sonar coverage. After the second search, NOAA recommended no further investigation in the area.
At the same time, BOEM was a year into its permitting reviews for Vineyard Wind and South Fork Wind. Permitting for Revolution Wind began in March 2020, with New England Wind, Sunrise Wind, and SouthCoast Wind following in 2021.
Federal agencies were assessing how vessels and rescue crews would operate among a growing number of offshore turbines. Fishermen called for wider spacing and dedicated transit corridors. Developers favored tighter layouts to reduce seafloor cable costs and maximize development of the lease areas.
In its Massachusetts and Rhode Island Port Access Route Study, the Coast Guard recommended a uniform grid of turbines spaced one nautical mile apart. Its discussion of helicopters being able to execute turns within the grid layout assumed “using normal flight procedures in visual conditions” — crucial qualifications for anyone considering what happened on the night the Mistress sank.
BOEM later relied on that grid in its navigation and search-and-rescue assessments for offshore wind projects. But a planned route through an array cannot guarantee access in darkness, poor visibility, and high winds.
Turbine 1 sits at the north end of the Block Island Wind Farm’s five-turbine line, with open water on three sides. Even there, a helicopter crew could not complete its hover search or intervene to rescue the fishermen of Mistress.
The recent discovery does not, by itself, establish that the turbine caused the sinking or prevented a rescue. It does demand answers about a search that failed to find a vessel so close to a known structure, boat debris seen on the nearby seafloor soon after, and the assumptions used to assess future rescue operations.
It also calls for a hard look at how industry priorities and political imperatives overrode the safety concerns of fishermen at every turn. Imagine how confirmation of the grave site at Turbine 1 might have given empirical credibility to fishermen’s warnings.
With new evidence provided to the Coast Guard and other authorities, the Coast Guard investigation must be reopened, and Turbine 1 secured for a proper forensic site investigation. BOEM and the Coast Guard should then revisit their search-and-rescue assessments using what this case reveals about real conditions at sea.
The families of the lost fishermen —and everyone who works offshore — deserve that much.
Constance Gee, a member of Westport’s Offshore Wind Advisory Committee, is the founder of Protect Our Westport Waters (POWW!)
