Luichart Hydro Power Station (Commissioned 1954) installed Capacity 34MW. Luichart Power Station, part of the Conon Hydro- Electric Scheme, was  constructed in the 1950s
There are six dams and power stations, 20 miles of tunnels and 15 miles of aqueducts in the Conon Hydro Electric scheme. It involved raising the water level of Loch Fannich using a series of aqueducts, tunnels and a rock fill dam. A large plug of rock then had to be blasted from the side of Loch Fannich to complete a tunnel to Grudie Power Station in what became known as 'Operation Bathplug'.
Dams at Loch Droma and Strath Vaich send water to Glascarnoch Power Station and then on to Mossford Power Station and into Loch Luichart.
Luichart Power Station is the largest in the Scheme and was commissioned in 1954. Several of the power stations, including Luichart, Grudie Bridge and Mossford, were designed by the same man, James Shearer, and look very similar to each other. Shearer was also responsible for the Pictish carvings in some of the Power Stations.
The stations turbine hall houses two turbines. Additional workshop and office accommodation is contained to the East end and in the lower single storey block. A transformer station lies across the minor road which bisects the site. Loch Luichart power station receives water from Luichart dam via tunnel from a short distance upstream. 
This station is characteristic of a medium power station forming part of a broader scheme. The station has the characteristic design features of the period including large two-storey glazed windows to the turbine hall and large teak access doors. The station is constructed from local Torrodail sandstone characteristic of James Shearer’s desire that all projects use local stone as far as possible for their construction. 
Loch Luichart Power Station is located around 25 miles north-west of Inverness. The rivers Meig and Conon flow into the loch.
The station generates power by using flowing water to spin a turbine which turns a shaft that's connected to an electric generator. The Loch Luichart Power Station has two turbines which are turned by water received via a system of tunnels. 
CONON HYDRO SCHEME
The Conon scheme lies within the northwest Highlands, broadly between Inverness and Ullapool. Electricity generation started here when the Ross-shire Electricity Supply Company built the small Falls of Conon hydro electric power station in the 1920s.
1946 Operating Hydro Stations listed Loch Luichant with a capacity of 2035Kw, new site commissioned 1954 had capacity of 34Mw.— at Loch Luichart.

THIS has to be one of the biggest (and cruellest) jokes perpetrated on the population of Great Britain in recent times.
Our country’s landscape and seascape have been desecrated by the construction of increasingly massive wind turbines, many of which do not operate for anything other than a fraction of the time they could be operational.

Clatteringshaws Dam was built in the early 1930s as part of the Galloway Hydro-Electric Scheme. Its main job was to hold back water from the River Dee and send it through a tunnel nearly two miles long to Glenlee Power Station, where it drops almost 380 feet before driving the turbines. The dam is made of solid concrete and curves gently across the valley, designed not just for strength but to sit well in the landscape. It was built from the upstream side using steam cranes on rails, with concrete mixed on site.
The work was carried out by James Williamson, with Sir Alexander Gibb as consulting engineer and Merz and McLellan handling the electrical design. Around 1,500 men were employed across the whole scheme during peak construction. The total cost of the entire Galloway Hydro-Electric Scheme was about £3M, which made it one of the most cost-effective hydro projects in Britain at the time.
Before the loch was formed, the area now under water was known as Raploch Moss, a deep, peaty moor where the River Dee wandered through deep channels. It was quiet land, rich in natural history and memory. In 1307, Robert the Bruce fought and won a battle here against English forces. The original Bruce’s Stone, marking the spot where he is said to have rested after the fight, stood on the moss itself. When the dam was built and the loch rose, the stone was submerged. A new memorial was placed on the shore near the visitor centre, where it still stands today.
Clatteringshaws is the largest dam in the scheme and holds back millions of gallons of water. Its foundations were driven twenty feet into solid granite, and the control tower still stands watch over the loch. Though the visitor centre is now closed, the path to Bruce’s Stone remains, leading through a landscape shaped by both legend and engineering.— at Clatteringshaws Dam.

Orrin power station receives water via tunnel and pipe from Orrin dam some 5KM to the South East. The station houses a single 18MW turbine. It is located on a steeply sloping site, the turbine hall oversails the tailrace and is built into the hillside with a single storey section to the rear adjacent to a large transformer station connecting the station to the grid. A good example of a smaller power station forming a component of a larger scheme.
The design of the station is characteristic of this period with large windows to the turbine hall and relatively limited architectural detailing. The site is narrow and steeply sloping which has resulted in some changes from the characteristic design features. The turbine hall is very tall and narrow and has a shallow pitched roof with a recessed ashlar panel and small windows to the centre of the gable end over a large teak vehicular access door. The advanced flat roofed block built into the hillside to the rear of the turbine hall has a panel of ashlar with relief carving.
The construction of Orrin dam marked the last phase in the development of the Conon Hydro Electric scheme and brought in a further catchment on the Orrin River. 
The dam is of a mass gravity type and is some 300 meters long. Water from the outlet is transferred by a 5km lined tunnel and steel pipeway through to Orrin power station (see separate item). The dam includes a particularly unusual fish pass housed in the central buttressed section of the dam. The pass is composed of four adjacent Borland lift type passes which all exit into the dam at different levels. This is to accommodate the large fluctuations in water level which characterise this dam. A small subsidiary dam is located to the East of the main section, separated by a small hill and is rubble fill with a turfed downstream face. This is a large-scale dam which occupies a dominant position at the top of a large valley in an upland area. The prominent walkway
spans the fixed spillway on large concrete piers. The large central buttress flanked by concrete gate control towers is a dramatic feature and houses an unusual four level fish pass. 
The last stage of development involved the construction of two dams separated by a small hill, to create Loch Orrin which feeds the Orrin Power Station on the south shore of Loch Achonachie in Strath Conon. 
Fish ladders are found on several of the dams, with one of particular sophistication at Orrin. The stations are run by Scottish & Southern Energy Plc.
The Conon scheme total electricity generating capacity is 116 MW.— at Orrin Dam.

Alba Energy is the representative organisation for independent hydro-electric producers in Scotland. Founded in 1998 to support the development of so-called "Small Hydro" (100kW - 5MW) schemes in the Scottish uplands, the number of sites has increased from 36 to more than 400, with an overall capacity of 222 MW (of which Alba represents 180MW). 85% of all hydropower in the UK is generated in Scotland: engineered, built and financed by Scots. It represents rural enterprise at its most innovative: the longest lasting, most efficient, least intermittent, least obtrusive and most ecologically beneficial renewable energy source of them all.
Once construction is complete, a hydro scheme has an average 80-100 year lifespan, requiring replacement only of machine parts. Alba members provide various examples of both run-of-river and storage schemes. One example of a 500kW storage hydro scheme, capable of producing the electricity required by 800 average households, makes the landholding in which it is built carbon negative in the long-term. Predominantly constructed in upland and wetland areas, such schemes complement wider peatland and nature recovery projects better than any other renewable energy source. Buckny Hydro in Perthshire, operated by Riemore Estate in partnership with CRF Hydro, is currently underway with a £2 million storage development that will hold back 315,000 cubic metres of water in a depleted wetland. As a condition of the development the surrounding peatland is being restored. This will form part of a wetland-moorland-woodland plan that would not have been possible without the hydro development. The new storage capacity will also act as flood mitigation for the village of Butterstone below, able to hold back water in a naturally-formed glacial reservoir at the onset of a red precipitation warning. The combination of clean, long-duration electricity generation with biodiversity uplift and carbon capture renders Small Hydro – proportionately – the most successful, all-round, local, carbon-footprint reducing technology. Although developed and built locally, producing just a modest share of the national energy mix, hydro schemes at this scale nevertheless represent an estimated offset in Scotland of between 1.5-2 million tonnes of carbon every decade.
In order to deliver the environmental and economic benefits of hydropower, it is essential to fight the corner of a small industry. Alba Energy connects members with each other to share information, experience and advice to cover operational issues: from grid connections to energy markets to spare parts. But the key challenges have been those of public policy. Alba has provided the advice and inspiration to transform the development of run-of-river schemes into storage schemes – as described in the case of Buckny Hydro – or has pioneered local energy security and pricing, in the case of Inver's hydro-solar colocation scheme in Jura. Three policy battles Alba has fought have been with SEPA, SSE and the Scottish Assessor. SEPA's attempt to impose unjustified charges on hydro schemes was significantly ameliorated by dogged engagement with the agency; SSE's habit of imposing arbitrary outages was rationalised through engagement with Scottish Government and SSE; but most significant of all has been Alba's 13-year legal challenge to the Scottish Assessor's imposition of extraordinary increases to Rateable Values for hydro schemes in the 2010, 2017, 2023 and 2026 valuations. This required no fewer than three committee hearings (all successful) and two verdicts at the Lands Valuation Court, culminating in a final hearing last year at the Upper Tribunal before Lord Young. Now the biggest case in ratings history, a successful verdict could save the sector more than £100 million of punitive and unjustified taxation over the course of a decade.Success in battles against irrational public policy does not merely save money; it paves the way to new development. Failure at the Upper Tribunal will mean hundreds of schemes shutting down, but success will mean the continuation of the small hydro sector beyond the life of the Feed-in-Tariff system. 
Over the last 13 years, Alba has been able to raise a million pounds for the legal case, thanks to the enterprise and solidarity of its membership. By fighting this battle against a regressive Scottish Assessor, Alba – if successful – will have paved the way for future innovations, such as storage developments (allowing for controlled export during peak demand), colocation of hydro and solar (allowing for continuous generation in both hot and wet conditions) and local energy pricing to provide residents and nearby businesses with cheaper electricity prices. There is also the potential for the development of new schemes through a modification of the UK Government's Contracts for Difference (CfD) system. CfD is currently prejudiced against hydro, but that problem may be resolved through targeted lobbying. To this end, Alba is working with our partners at the British Hydropower Association to advocate for the policy shifts that will allow both new development and local pricing. The great goal of locally produced energy is to produce local pricing – to make the political case that the environmental benefits of renewable energy can also be benefits to the consumer, driving the argument beyond the current crisis in Net Zero policies.
Buckny Hydro System, Butterstone Village
Planning Ref. No: 12/01087/FLL. The planning application for the formation of a run of river hydro scheme, powerhouse and associated works at Buckny Burn by Butterstone. 
The project is a run of river scheme that would operate without storage and according to the flow of the burn. Water is abstracted via a weir structure downstream of Dubh Loch into the pipeline before being passed through a 500Kw capacity turbine which generates over 1750 MW hours of energy per year. The abstracted water is returned into the burn at Butterstone Village.
Access to the site for construction traffic was along the A923 into Butterstone village before entering the existing estate road network. The element of development to the west of the Buckny Burn was accessed via the road to Riemore and Riechip, while the eastern side was accessed via the road to Craigton.
Permanent tracks were proposed to allow long-term maintenance to the intake and turbine house. A turning area is located at the header tank, which allows access for maintenance. The proposal did not require permanent access to the pipe bridge in the Den of Riechip as there is an existing logging track to this location at low level alongside the burn. However, a temporary access track to enable construction traffic to enter this area wax installed. Following construction the temporary access was removed and the land reinstated.
The intake weir consists of a low concrete weir spanning the river below the Dubh Loch. The intake is predominantly buried and constructed using reinforced concrete. The right bank (when looking downstream) rises steeply from the channel, while the left bank is shallower and requires the formation of a new 1.5m high flood bund to tie the top of the wing walls of the intake weir to the natural ground level further upstream thereby reducing the extent of pasture that would be flooded. The bund was constructed using earth recycled from elsewhere on site, and would contain an impermeable membrane to prevent seepage.
The abstracted water would flow through the unpressurised intake (feeder) pipe for approximately 450m towards the header tank. From the header tank, a pressurised pipeline (penstock), would route water towards the turbine house. The gravity pipe and penstock have nominal diameters of 900mm and 850mm respectively and buried in a trench between 1650mm and 2500mm deep by 1000mm wide, providing capacity to backfill using locally excavated materials to a depth of 800mm or more. The pipe material selected is continuously welded High Performance Polyethylene (HPPE). The pipe has flexibility which allows this to be routed round obstacles. The use of concrete thrust blocks will secure the pipeline where it cannot be anchored to the bedrock. Due to the undulation of the pipe route valves are required at high points and washout valves will be required at low points, this means manhole covers will be visible at these points. A pipe bridge is constructed to enable the penstock to cross the valley. The pipe is  self-supporting ductile iron in this section with concrete abutments partially submerged on either side of the river bank resulting in the pipe being suspended over the watercourse.
The turbine house is located on the eastern bank of the watercourse. It is located within the valley floor and has a steep embankment to the rear (eastern elevation) of the turbine house. The building has a concrete foundation to support the turbine while the exterior will be clad in larch with mineral fibre panels to the roof. The closest dwelling is around 45 metres to the south of the Turbine House.
The tailrace returns water to the watercourse from the turbine house. Water flows from the turbine house through 30m of buried pipe before being discharged through a concrete headwall into an open channel spillway within the left bank of the Buckny Burn. The outfall structure is contained within a treated timber post and rail fence for safety. Locked screening will be positioned on the headwall to prevent fish and small mammals from travelling up the tailrace and into the turbine house.
Scottish and Southern Energy (SSE) has provided a grid connection point. The connection is on the opposite side of the river where there is an existing overhead line. This will be reached by burying the cable using directional drilling.
Buckny Hydro Limited operates a 500Kw run-of- river hydropower scheme in Riemore Estate, Perthshire, Scotland, which was commissioned in 2014. The project employs  a Newmills turbine with a vertically installed twin-jet Pelton wheel, designed for high-head efficiency. The site is focused on sustainable energy generation and local habitat restoration.
Key details regarding the project include:
Location: Riemore Estate, Dunkeld, Perthshire, Scotland.
Capacity: 500 kW.
Technology: Vertically installed twin-jet Pelton turbine (Newmills).
Operator/Owner: Buckny Hydro Limited.
Status: Operational (commissioned 2014).
A 2024 planning application to add a storage capability to the hydro scheme through the expansion of Dubh Loch. This would allow the ability for the scheme to generate on demand without the constraint of flow availability in the burn. The existing weir & penstock intake would be replaced with larger structure upstream. — in Butterstone, Perth and Kinross.— in Butterstone, Perth and Kinross.

Some photos of the Hydro scheme construction around Fort William & Lochaber. The dates on these are between 1925 & 1928......so they have been hidden in storage for nearly 100 years!!
The Lochaber hydroelectric scheme is a hydroelectric power generation project constructed in the Lochaber area of the western Scottish Highlands after the First World War. Like its predecessors at Kinlochleven and Foyers, it was designed to provide electricity for aluminium production, this time at Fort William.
Water is collected from the River Spean catchment, plus the headwaters of the River Spey and some smaller watercourses. It contains two main reservoirs Loch Treig and Laggan Reservoir, and 18 miles (29 km) of tunnels excavated through the hillside.
The scheme was originally built between 1924 and 1943 by the British Aluminium Company. This company was bought by Canadian-based Alcan in 1982 which was subsequently bought by Rio Tinto in 2008. Rio Tinto Alcan then sold the scheme to GFG Alliance in November 2016.
The hydro scheme has a catchment area of 303 square miles (780 km2), including the headwaters of the River Spey, the River Spean and River Treig, and the northern flanks of the Grey Corries and Ben Nevis. There are two principle reservoirs, Loch Treig and Loch Laggan (which was extended as Laggan Reservoir), both with a top water level of about 820 feet (250 m) above sea level. These reservoirs are linked by a 2¾ mile (4.4 km) long, 15 feet (4.6 m) diameter low pressure tunnel, which collects water from three intermediate streams.
From Loch Treig, a main pressure tunnel 15 miles (24 km) long was driven around the Ben Nevis massif. This has a horseshoe shaped cross-section, with an equivalent diameter of 15 feet 2 inches (4.6 m), and lined with concrete to reduce friction. This tunnel also collects water from a further eleven burns along the way. It was, until 1970, the longest water-carrying tunnel in the world. Steel penstocks then convey the water down the western flank of Ben Nevis to the power house below.
Turbines in the power house generate electricity to power the adjacent aluminium smelting plant. The power house and smelter are located to the northeast of Fort William, on the eastern bank of the River Lochy, into which the tailrace discharges.
The scheme was expanded to increase output to meet demand for aluminium in World War II. Floodwaters of the Spey are captured by Spey Dam and diverted via an open cut to Loch Crunachdan then through a tunnel to Loch Laggan. In addition, the River Mashie (a tributary of the Spey) is diverted via an aqueduct and tunnel into the River Pattack, which flows into Loch Laggan.
The scheme was initially designed by engineer Charles Meik but after his death in 1923, the scheme's realisation was left to William Halcrow, by then a partner in the firm founded by Meik's father Thomas Meik.
The project was finally sanctioned by Parliament in 1921, but construction did not start until 1924. Given the scale of construction, it was undertaken in three main phases:
• The works to the west of Loch Treig, including the pressure tunnel, intake, powerhouse, and smelter.
•’The Treig and Laggan dams, plus connecting tunnel and intakes.
• The Spey dam, Crunachdan cut and tunnel, plus the River Mashie diversion and Strathmashie tunnel.
Over 3,000 men were employed during the peak of construction.
A narrow-gauge railway was used in construction and subsequent maintenance of phases 1 and 2, see Lochaber Narrow Gauge Railway for details.
Stage 1 – downstream of Loch Treig
The first stage of construction took five years, from 1924 to 1930, and cost around £3m.
The main challenge was the pressure tunnel from Loch Treig under the Ben Nevis massif, which commenced in summer 1926. The tunnel was dug by hand through the solid rock, with compressed air drills used to bore holes for the explosive charges. Initially liquid oxygen based explosives were used, but despite being safer their use was complicated, so gelignite was used instead. The final stage of construction, was to connect the tunnel to Loch Treig, having dug to a point about 20 feet (6 m) from the bottom of the loch and 100 feet (30 m) below the surface. On 3 January 1930, a charge of 1.5 tons of specially prepared gelignite was detonated to blast out the remaining section of rock.
To facilitate construction, work progressed in both directions from 11 intermediate points: four vertical shafts and seven horizontal adits, giving a total of 23 working faces including the western portal above Fort William. These intermediate points were located close to watercourses, which were later captured by a series of dams and contributed around 16% of the total water for the scheme.
The power station and smelter were completed by the end of 1929, initially equipped with five 6,800 kW generators, connected to Pelton turbines. The turbines sat in a deep rock excavation, as close to sea level as possible to maximise the head of the scheme.
On 30 December 1929, the first aluminium was cast, powered only by the waters from the side streams.
Stage 2 – Treig and Laggan Dams
A Supplementary Act of Parliament was obtained in July 1930 extending the time to complete the second stage of the scheme. Work started early the following year and the civil engineering works on the Treig and Laggan dams plus connecting tunnel were completed by 1934.
Three years later, following a period of slack demand for aluminium, the power station was upgraded. Three additional pipes were installed on the hillside above the power station. These were 69 inches (1.8 m) in diameter, delivered in 30 feet (9.1 m) long sections, and welded together in-situ. Five additional Pelton turbines and generators were installed, each rated at 7,000 kW.
A dam was built approximately 1/4 mile (400 m) downstream of Loch Treig, raising the top water level by 35 feet (11 m) to 819 feet (250 m) OD. This significantly increased the storage available, with 7,838 million cubic feet (221.9 million m3) available above the lowest draw-down level of 695 feet (212 m) OD. The dam also increased the head of the hydro scheme, providing more power.
The dam is rock-filled with a central concrete core-wall keyed into the bedrock. The exposed part of the dam is 40 feet (12 m) high and 380 feet (120 m) wide, while the core wall has a crest length of 675 feet (206 m) and maximum depth of 122 feet (37 m). Both upstream and downstream faces have a slope of 3:1, with the spillway protected by reinforced concrete, cast in-situ.
Construction of the reservoir also necessitated diverting 1.5 miles (2.4 km) of the West Highland Line along the shores of Loch Treig.
Laggan Dam was constructed at a constriction in the valley approximately 4.5 miles (7 km) downstream of Loch Laggan creating Laggan Reservoir. This is linked to Loch Laggan by a short section of the River Spean, which was dredged to make use of the storage capacity in the loch. While the downstream dam site required a larger dam than an alternative location upstream it had several advantages:
A shorter tunnel to Loch Treig, with a smaller diameter for an equivalent capacity,
Increased storage capacity in Laggan Reservoir, including dead storage below the tunnel invert level for the accumulation of sediment, and
Removing the need for an aqueduct to divert the Roughburn.
The dam is a massive concrete gravity structure, 700 feet (210 m) long and 130 feet (40 m) high. In plan, the dam has a slight curve with a radius of 2,000 feet (610 m), although it does not function as an arched dam. The dam has a plain spillway along its length, together with six siphons to increase the flood flow capacity.
Laggan Reservoir has a usable storage of 1,480 million cubic feet (42 million m3), between a top water level of 820 feet (250 m) OD and maximum drawdown level of 804 feet (245 m). The level of Loch Laggan was not raised by the dam, as this would have required significant diversion of the adjacent A86 road and would have also inundated valuable property.
As with the main pressure tunnel downstream of Loch Treig, the tunnel between Laggan Reservoir was driven through rock and lined with concrete. Again, it was constructed from multiple faces with three intermediate adits, which were then used to collect water from streams. The tunnel is approximately 14 feet (4.3 m) in diameter with a flattened invert, and has a fall of 15 feet (4.6 m) over the 2.75 miles (4.4 km) length.
Stage 3 – Spey Dam and Mashie diversion
The third and final phase of the scheme was undertaken between 1941 and 1943, and further enlarged the catchment of Loch Laggan by harnessing the headwaters of the River Spey. The work was supervised by Syril Minchin Roberts, a partner in Sir William Halcrow and Partners. It was constructed by Balfour Beatty, with assistance from the 1st Tunnelling Company of the Canadian Army. Many of these Canadian soldiers were ex-miners from Kirkland Lake.
The Spey Dam was constructed in 1942–1943, just downstream of the confluence of the River Markie. The main structure is a concrete gravity dam, 943 feet (287 m) long and 57 feet (17 m) high. It has a spillway 93 metres (305 ft) long at a crest level of 268.2 metres (880 ft) OD, and a mass fill section to the north, approximately 2 metres (6.6 ft) higher. The dam incorporates a fish pass at the southern side.
Water impounded by the dam flows westwards through a cut into Loch Crunachdan, against the natural flow of water. It then passes through a tunnel approximately 2 miles (3 km) long which discharges into the eastern end of Loch Laggan. The maximum abstraction from the Spey is 776 cubic feet per second (22.0 m3/s), although the average for 2020–2022 was just 14 m3/s. The tunnel was constructed in 1941, completed at the end of December.
A smaller dam was constructed across the River Mashie, a tributary of the Spey, just upstream of the A86 road. Water is transferred via an aqueduct and two smaller tunnels to the River Pattack, the main inflow to Loch Laggan. The maximum abstraction is 11.3 m3/s (400 cu ft/s).
In 2008, Rio Tinto Alcan awarded a contract worth €30m for the upgrade of the hydroelectric turbines to Andritz Tech Hydro. This was to replace the original twelve turbines, which were horizontal-axis twin-jet Pelton wheel machines driving two DC generators with a total capacity of 72 MW. Five new horizontal-axis Francis turbines driving AC generators were installed by 2012, each rated at 17.3 MW giving a 20% increase in power output.
Following the closure of Rio Tinto/Alcan's other UK smelters at Invergordon (1981), Kinlochleven (2000), Anglesey (2009) and Lynemouth (2012) the hydro-electric scheme and smelter at Fort William was operated by Rio Tinto Alcan. Under threat of closure the smelter was put up for sale in 2016. GFG Alliance, which incorporates SIMEC and the Liberty House Group, as the successful bidder, bought the Lochaber Smelter for £330 million. It announced plans to expand the factory and produce car parts such as alloy wheels. This was later dropped, replaced by plans for an aluminium recycling facility announced in November 2020.
On 3 April 2021, it came to light that the Jahama Highland Estates (formerly the "Alcan Estate") had been purchased in 2016 as part of the Rio Tinto Mines deal for the Lochaber aluminium plant, because the furnace requires so much power that the smelter is located near a hydroelectric plant, which drains the basin of the 114,000 acre Estate. Alcan designed all their smelters that way. The Estate includes the north face of Ben Nevis. According to reports, the Scottish Government mandated that the Estate never be split from the hydro plant and aluminium smelter, but Gupta ignored them and placed ownership of the Estate in a company that is domiciled on the Isle of Man. The 2016 deal was worth £330 million and was guaranteed by the UK Chancellor of the Exchequer. Conservative finance spokesperson Murdo Fraser was critical about the alleged breach of the Scottish Government agreement and urged the Scottish Government to "take whatever steps are necessary to protect public funds".— at Lochaber Smelter.

Revera Energy's Hunterston battery storage project reached financial close on 24 September 2026 as a 400 MW/800 MWh non-recourse deal backed by four banks and anchored by bp and Danske Commodities, revealing the five-pillar financing template now defining bankable UK large-scale BESS.
The senior debt came from Santander, Barclays, Commonwealth Bank of Australia and NatWest, on a non-recourse basis, with bp and Danske Commodities underpinning the revenue side of the structure.
A close of this scale carries weight in the current UK energy picture. Scotland is deploying large-scale battery storage faster than almost anywhere else in Britain, driven by a grid that needs more flexibility as wind capacity climbs, and a 400 MW/800 MWh transmission-connected asset reaching close on structured offtake tells you something concrete about how far lender appetite for merchant storage has moved.
The Hunterston battery storage project in North Ayrshire, roughly 50 km south-west of Glasgow. At full output it can discharge for two hours, and it connects directly to the transmission network rather than the local distribution grid.
The final investment decision came in June 2026. Financial close followed three months later, and a notice to proceed went out immediately, meaning construction has already begun on site.
Construction now underway. Commercial operations targeted for Q3 2028.
The composition of that lending group is the read for anyone tracking the sector. When four separate institutional lenders will syndicate non-recourse debt against a single battery asset, it signals that structured storage has crossed from speculative bet into a financing class banks treat as genuinely bankable infrastructure. 
A non-recourse structure only works if the revenue risk has been dealt with elsewhere. 
On Hunterston, two commercial arrangements do that heavy lifting, and understanding them is the difference between reading this as an announcement and reading it as a template.
Start with bp. Under a long-term tolling structure, bp takes on responsibility for optimising the battery and carries the exposure to wholesale and ancillary-service prices. In effect, bp pays for the right to use the asset’s capacity while absorbing the volatility of the merchant market.
That shifts a large slice of price risk off the project company and onto a highly rated counterparty. Lenders can then size their debt against relatively stable contracted revenue rather than against income that swings with the power market.
Then comes Danske Commodities, which handles optimisation and trading under a long-term revenue-floor arrangement. A revenue floor guarantees a minimum level of income over a set period, with any upside shared between the project and the optimiser.
The floor narrows the range of possible cash-flow outcomes. That lets the banks model debt-service coverage with more confidence, because even if wholesale arbitrage underperforms, a contracted minimum still services the debt.
Grasping how battery storage earns money across Dynamic Containment, the Balancing Mechanism, wholesale arbitrage and Capacity Market payments is the foundation for reading why a revenue floor and tolling structure carry so much weight with lenders evaluating debt-service coverage.
Two more parties complete the picture. Sungrow supplies the battery units and provides long-term servicing, taking on technology and performance risk under warranty. OCU Group acts as balance-of-plant contractor and long-term operations and maintenance provider.
Danske Commodities Optimisation and trading, revenue-floor arrangement Downside revenue risk via contracted floor
Sungrow Battery supply and long-term servicing , Technology and performance risk
OCU Group Balance-of-plant contractor and O&M Construction and operational risk
The financing logic Each risk sits with the party best placed to manage it: market risk with the trader and the energy major, technology risk with the OEM, construction and operational risk with the contractor. The project does not depend on any single revenue channel being right.
That is the point for anyone assessing other BESS deals. If wholesale arbitrage disappoints, the floor holds the debt; the tolling-plus-floor combination is what moved four banks to lend. It gives you a checklist for judging whether the next project has the contractual architecture lenders actually require.
Hunterston does not stand alone. It is the second of Revera’s UK transmission-connected battery projects to reach financial close in 2026, following Windyhill, a 200 MW/400 MWh system at Bearsden near Glasgow that closed in February 2026.
A third project is already queued. Kincardine, a 400 MW/800 MWh system in Fife, is targeting construction start in Q1 2027.
Behind that cadence sits Carlyle Group, the institutional equity backer for the portfolio. Carlyle’s involvement is why the capital keeps flowing at this pace, and it explains how Revera can run multiple large projects through development, financing and construction in parallel rather than one at a time.
Platform-scale BESS investment is not unique to Scotland: France is deploying a comparable portfolio-aggregation model in 2026, with institutional equity backers funding multi-asset development programmes under a structure that shares several features with the Carlyle-backed Revera approach.— at Hunterston.

Herald letters
WE face the worst financial crisis ever, with energy costs forecast to rise a further 16% in January. On top of diesel rising to over £2 per litre, many more families will move into energy poverty status, unable to pay bills. Under these extreme circumstances, we should approve all gas and oil development applications in the North Sea, to increase our self-sufficiency.
Also, winter fuel payments should increase by at least 200%.
Dennis Forbes Grattan, Aberdeen.

A POWERFUL union boss has warned that the energy ministry is becoming ‘the department for P45s’ due to jobs being lost to Net Zero.
Gary Smith, the head of the GMB union, launched a scathing attack on the Government’s policy, which he said was closing factories and driving workingclass voters to Reform UK.
At Labour’s party conference he warned ‘economics, engineering and the electorate’ would ‘put paid to’ Labour’s energy agenda; and that renewables had to be backed up by gas when ‘the wind didn’t blow and the sun didn’t shine’.
In a withering critique of the Government’s energy policy, Mr Smith told a Tony Blair Institute event: ‘Our members who work in manufacturing in the Midlands are not against Net Zero or technology. But they are against what is happening to them with this energy policy because it is closing factories.

records.title: Wind Energy's Absurd
records.bodyText:
In 2016, the late John Curtis, an engineer, WEA contributor and friend to so many of us, looked at the various technologies being proposed to store electricity from intermittent renewable generation.
Much has changed since then. Battery storage has expanded enormously, and pumped-storage hydro is once again attracting major investment, particularly in the Scottish Highlands.
Interestingly, however, some of John's fundamental questions remain highly relevant.
In 2024 we reported Miliband's plans for giant flywheels to be installed around the UK to help stabilise a grid increasingly dominated by wind and solar. Some of those flywheels are now being used - but primarily to provide inertia and rapid grid stabilisation, rather than the hours or days of energy storage John was discussing.
John also considered batteries, hydrogen, compressed air, thermal storage and pumped hydro, asking whether any could provide the large-scale, long-duration, controllable electricity required to compensate for prolonged periods of low renewable output.
Ten years later, the technology and scale of deployment have changed considerably. But the distinction between power capacity (GW) and energy storage (GWh) remains fundamental.
We thought it was worth revisiting John's analysis and seeing what has changed - and what hasn't.
What is particularly interesting are John's comments on pumped hydro storage,  given the applications consented and in planning process currently.

CONON VALLEY HYDRO ELECTRIC SCHEME, VAICH DAM,
Williamson and Partners (engineers for North of Scotland Hydro Electric Board technical panel), 1957. Large turfed rubble dam with control tower to left (W) and 2 large spill towers near to upstream face. Mass rubble fill to downstream face with turf over; coursed random rubble to upstream face; concrete piers and walls to spill towers. Battered downstream face with concrete parapet to top. Additional concrete weirs and lined spillway channel adjacent to downstream face.
Vaich Dam is an excellent example of the innovation in dam design in response to local conditions and materials by the North of Scotland Hydro Electric Board (NoSHEB) during their development of hydro electric schemes in the Highlands. It provides key storage capacity for Conon Valley hydro electric scheme, which is one of the major post-war hydro electric developments by the North of Scotland Hydro Electric Board (NoSHEB). The dam is technically unusual, constructed predominantly from rubble fill, either side of a vertical concrete wall which is waterproof. As a consequence the dam cannot spill in the conventional manner as this would erode the downstream face, so large spill towers have been constructed adjacent to the upstream face, acting like large drains to allow water to spill into them and exit to the downstream side of the dam when water levels are high. The use of rubble fill instead of mass concrete saved a significant outlay in both time and money during the construction of the dam, which was consequently able to use tunnel spoil from the nearby shaft dug through to Glascarnoch Dam for the bulk of construction.
Conon Valley was one of a large number of schemes developed in Scotland by the North of Scotland Hydro Electric Board (NoSHEB), formed after 1943 as a nationalised body to oversee the development of Scotland's resources for water power. The scheme played a key role in the realisation of the social agenda of NoSHEB by providing power to a remote community. Power generated on schemes in the southern Highlands, such as Tummel was exported via the grid to the central belt, the profit from which subsidised the provision of power to remote north Highland communities and stimulated economic regeneration. Under the leadership of eminent chairman Sir Tom Johnston the board undertook developments throughout Highland Scotland and his aspirations saw the development of schemes in locations such as Loch Dubh near Ullapool and Storr Lochs on Skye. Johnstone's social aspirations and wider wishes to reinvigorate the economy of the Highlands ensured that schemes in remote areas formed a key part of the NoSHEB development plan.
All of the developments carried out by NoSHEB were subject to parliamentary approval and objections on the grounds of scenic amenity were common. In order to meet these objections the board appointed a panel of architectural advisers which included Reginald Fairlie (1883-1952), James Shearer (1881-1962) and Harold Ogle Tarbolton (1869-1947), appointed in 1943. Initially the role of the panel was to adjudicate on competition entries for designs, but by 1947 it had become one of designers. The panel had little control over the functional form of the buildings, as they left this to engineers, but they did influence the appearance and the style of the designs. The rigid views on the roles of engineers and architects during the design process resulted in the development of a style which can be characterised as vernacular modernism. This style is characteristic of many NoSHEB buildings and is a direct product of the strict role which engineers and architects played in the design process and of the increasing desire to harmonise buildings with the landscape.
The design of Vaich Dam is typical of Williamson and Partners approach, with an innovative solution designed specifically to suit the requirements of a particular site. Their design allowed for the use of local materials and minimised the need for concrete thus saving significant amounts of time and labour in building a concrete batching plant and bringing materials to site. Williamson was a prominent engineer who specialised in the design of dams following his work on the Galloway Hydro Electric scheme, in the 1930s. He acted as one of the chief engineering advisors to NoSHEB and was the lead engineer for a number of schemes. Following his death in 1953 Williamson and Partners continued in the role as engineering advisors to NoSHEB building on the expertise developed during their long association with the development of hydro power.
Vaich Power Station is located at the end of the tunnel feeding Loch Glascarnoch.

If the new UK Government wants to reform energy, then it should do it properly. Start from ground zero. Pause the current headless chicken rush of willy-nilly development and hold an independent inquiry into the entire energy question.
“We’ve likely missed 2030 targets, so let’s stop panicking and have a sober reassessment of the system, and an honest and fully transparent conversation about where we really want to go as a nation  - Dan Bailey
This is at the end of an article in The National entitled 'Highland activists hit out at Andy Burnham’s GB Grid plan'
https://www.thenational.scot/.../26599406.highland.../...
'ACTIVISTS battling massive pylon and transmission line developments across the Scottish Highlands – as well as expected huge incoming energy bills for homes and businesses – are challenging Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s new proposal for a UK Government-controlled energy system called GB Grid.
They demand a pause to projects and the launch of public inquiries.
“The devil will be in the details,” said Dan Bailey of Highland-based Better Cable Route on Burnham’s Labour Conference announcement to establish the new body alongside GB Energy in Aberdeen to speed up grid connections and increase competition among private sector operators.
“But we still hear far too little about the communities at the sharp end of the green transition,” Bailey added.
Better Cable Route relied on a September National Audit Office (NAO) report to describe what it termed “delays, chaos and secrecy”. This showed that some 64 of 88 grid projects won’t be delivered by the UK Government’s own 2030 clean power deadline. The National Electricity System Operator (Neso) dismissed such language as “misleading”.
The release also quoted an Ofgem publication claiming eight major grid projects being built in Scotland by Scottish and Southern Electricity (SSE) were forecasting average cost increases of 284% while a controversial super-pylon project between Loch Buidhe and Spittal is facing a 467% projected cost increase, according to an energy expert.
In pushback, the NAO report is one on which SSE published an online blog claiming that investing in the electricity transmission grid is essential to deliver energy security, support economic growth, and get costs down for consumers.
While there were costs associated with building and maintaining the grid, consumers would be better off overall, with grid upgrades planned for 2030 helping reduce a typical household bill by around £30.
The company is dismissive of Better Cable Route’s projected project costs, claiming early estimates were set in 2022, with prevailing supply chain costs.
A different cost narrative is presented by Better Cable Route. Network charges – the part of bills paying for pylons, cables and substations – are set to jump 65% between 2025 and 2030. That’s from £207 to £342 a year for the average home, citing tracking platform electricitybills.uk, with rises for businesses up to 90%.
The activist group called the findings “a national scandal in slow motion”, adding that the public deserved greater transparency.
Bailey doubled down (with backing from the recently formed convention of 200 community councils across Scotland), calling for an immediate pause on what he called “an unnecessarily expensive and complex energy system largely because of our over-deployment of wind in the north”.
The much-trumpeted GB Energy has yet to make a mark in the energy sector, so it remains to be seen whether its new powers “will amount to anything more than soundbites”, according to Bailey. GB Grid could reportedly claim some £4 billion from GB Energy’s £8.3bn budget after the latter’s formal opening in September.
“Speeding up the rollout under a piecemeal picture of part private, part public ownership would simply mean making the same mistake faster. The money still has to be found somehow, and whether it’s through bills or taxation, ultimately the public pay either way,” said Bailey.
He went on: “The UK Government should conduct a high-level inquiry into the entire grid project – and this needs to be fully transparent and collaborative. Given that planning is devolved, the Scottish Government cannot hide behind blaming Westminster and should urgently conduct its own inquiry into energy, a pan-Scotland Planning Inquiry Commission, as called for by ourselves and the CC convention.”
Meanwhile, political reaction to the Prime Minister’s GB Grid announcement has been generally muted, perhaps due to puzzlement over the implications.
While SNP Westminster energy spokesperson Graham Leadbitter was reportedly critical of GB Grid “as a new gimmick”, UK Energy Minister Michael Shanks acknowledged the NAO report on the grid.
He said: “As the National Audit Office recognises in its report, our once-in-a-generation reforms are finally building the infrastructure we need: reducing our dependence on the fossil fuels that leave households exposed to price spikes and helping lower people’s bills for good.”
Also, representing the body approving energy funding and regulating investment, an Ofgem spokesperson said: “We look forward to working with government and Great British Grid as these proposals develop, building on this progress to deliver faster connections and better value for consumers.”
Ofgem said it had taken major steps to overhaul the connections system, prioritising projects introducing clearer service standards, better information and stronger accountability for network companies.
On the proposed GB Grid and without mention of its aim for greater competition, SSE’s spokesperson said: “We’re in the process of delivering one of the most significant infrastructure build programmes Scotland and the UK have ever seen, rewiring the grid through our £29bn investment programme.
“This public-private partnership is already delivering lasting benefits for communities and the country. We look forward to working with governments and other stakeholders to continue that work into the 2030s and beyond.”
As an independent public spending watchdog, the NAO’s September report on upgrading the energy transmission network was closely examined by the organisations involved.
For example, under “programme governance”, it noted “no single point of accountability” as well as “limited management of projects as a portfolio” and “limited access to project information”. Under “strategic network planning”, national grid upgrades were funded by consumer bills and not subject to a full business case or options appraisal.
But the major players within the ambit of these findings see the report as not calling for network investment to be slowed, halted or re-considered as demanded by activists.
Indeed, a Neso spokesperson said: “The NAO report is clear that consumers are better off when electricity network infrastructure, built by Transmission Owners, is delivered on time. Delivering a new network is the single biggest lever to reduce the costs of balancing the electricity system and could halve these costs by the end of the decade.”
Activists, however, claim that new technologies could reduce the need for environment-wrecking pylons and cables in new projects, saving up to £75bn in bills. SSEN Transmission says new technologies, including dynamic line rating and modular substations, could reduce costs and site footprints.
However, activists are adamant on the way forward. Bailey said: “If the new UK Government wants to reform energy, then it should do it properly. Start from ground zero. Pause the current headless chicken rush of willy-nilly development and hold an independent inquiry into the entire energy question.
“We’ve likely missed 2030 targets, so let’s stop panicking and have a sober reassessment of the system, and an honest and fully transparent conversation about where we really want to go as a nation.”

Cruachan Power Station is pump storage hydro that’s uses electricity from the grid to pump water to the upper reservior from Loch Awe, during periods of low demand. The process is reversed to generate electricity at periods of high demand and the site is currently being updated to increase capacity to 480 MW.
Basically a giant water battery hidden in a Scottish mountain, and it's been doing it since the 1960s.
This form of long term storage is required to balance the electricity network going forward and plans have been submitted to add 8-10GW of pump storage capacity over the next 10 years. All the new proposed sites located in Scotland.— at Cruachan Dam.

Wind and solar save UK from gas imports worth £5.9bn during Middle East war. 
The UK has avoided the need for gas imports worth £5.9bn since the start of the Hormuz crisis as a result of record generation from wind and solar. 
While gas prices are surging to levels not seen since the 2022 energy crisis, the UK has been generating record amounts of power from wind and solar, up 14% year-on-year.
This unprecedented clean-power generation is directly cutting the need for gas-fired electricity, which is down by nearly 10% year-on-year in 2026 to date.
In total, wind and solar have generated a record 41% share of the UK’s electricity needs in 2026 to date, compared with 25% from gas.
The figure below shows that wind and solar has avoided the need for UK gas imports worth £5.9bn, since the outbreak of war between the US and Iran in February 2026.
These avoided gas imports would have required the UK to secure the equivalent of more than 100 additional tanker deliveries of liquefied natural gas (LNG).
The £1.3bn import saving in September 2026 to date is the result of record wind and solar output, at nearly 10 terawatt hours (TWh), combined with surging gas prices.
Wholesale gas prices in the UK have remained elevated ever since Russia cut off supplies to Europe in the wake of its invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
Gas averaged 90p per therm from 2023 until the start of this year, roughly three times above 2019 prices, before the Covid and Ukraine crises.
Since the outbreak of war in the Middle East in March, gas prices have climbed higher still, averaging 134p per therm or nearly four times the level seen in 2019.
In September 2026 to date, gas prices have averaged 189p per therm, reaching their highest level since the global energy crisis in 2022.

'Labour’s energy policy is “crazy” and the department overseeing net zero is “basically the ministry for P45s”, one of Britain’s most powerful union leaders has said, as he urged ministers to approve new North Sea oil and gas projects or lose out on billions in investment. 
Gary Smith, the GMB general secretary, accused the government of relying on “sticking-plaster politics” while companies struggled with high energy costs and warned that rising energy bills would create a raft of fresh strikes across the public and private sector.
Smith described the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero as “basically the ministry for P45s” and said: “We are [using] sticking-plaster politics all the time.” He added: “It’s not credible. Batshit crazy.”
He warned a fresh rise in bills could trigger a new wave of strikes. He said: “The last time we had the spike in inflation, we had a spike in industrial unrest. That wasn’t driven by ideology. All that was driven by pure economics, housing economics.”
Smith’s intervention came as ministers prepared to decide on whether to approve drilling in the Rosebank oilfield and Jackdaw gasfield, off the coast of Scotland. 
The decisions rest with Miatta Fahnbulleh, the energy secretary, and it is widely expected that Jackdaw will be approved while the fate of Rosebank is less certain. However, industry sources believe both will go ahead, although the announcements will be delayed for political reasons as the Holborn & St Pancras by-election takes place next week.
Andy Burnham, the prime minister, said in his speech to Labour Party conference in Liverpool this week that he would be “pragmatic” in relation to North Sea oil and gas “as we build a bridge to a clean energy future as we confront the climate crisis”. Michael Shanks, the energy minister, said a decision would be reached in the near future and the government was going through the evidence “piece by piece”.
In an interview with The Times, Smith warned rejecting either project would damage confidence in Britain as a place to invest.
He said: “If they do not do this, it will damage hugely the government’s credibility, and it will massively damage investment because that infrastructure, as I understand it, is ready to go — billions of investment. And if it does not now happen, who in their right mind is going to put money into this country?”
Smith went further and backed additional North Sea exploration beyond Rosebank and Jackdaw while Britain remained reliant on imported oil and gas.
The developments were previously approved under the Conservatives but consent was overturned by the courts in January last year, after judges ruled environmental assessments had failed to take account of the emissions created when the oil and gas was eventually burnt. Developers have since submitted fresh assessments and new government decisions are required before production can begin.
Asked whether ministers should permit more exploration, Smith said: “Yeah, absolutely. As long as we are importing, it is more energy-intensive and more carbon-intensive. It doesn’t make any sense in terms of environment and zero sense in terms of the economy.”
New figures this week showed domestic energy production fell by 5.8 per cent in the three months to June compared with the same period a year earlier. Total UK energy production in 2025 was at a record low and was 68 per cent below its 1999 peak.
Sharon Graham, the general secretary of Unite, backed the sites. She told The Times: “We shouldn’t be letting go of one rope before we have got hold of another. Jackdaw is gas. We are going to be able to consume that, we need it and I think we need to go ahead and it should be done.
“We will run out of what’s in the North Sea,  but there’s a lot of time still left in there. We need the time to transition into the industries that we should transition into. 
“For me, of course I’m going to be jobs, jobs, jobs. But equally it’s about the security of the country as well. Until we have got the industries in place, we need to look at what we need. We’re almost cutting our nose off to spite our face. We are literally saying we are cutting this out when we’ve got absolutely nothing to replace it with.”
Smith said it did not make sense to focus on electricity when Britain’s homes were overwhelmingly reliant on gas.
He said: “Four times as much energy goes down the gas pipes as the electricity cables because we heat our homes with gas. If you want to transfer that energy usage, you’ve got to dig the cables up and make them four times bigger. You’re going to have to rewire all the way back to the transmission line.”
Meanwhile, households and businesses face fresh energy bill spikes driven by the war in Iran. 
The household price cap rose by 4 per cent to £1,723 for a typical dual-fuel household on Thursday, while Cornwall Insight has forecast a further 16 per cent rise in January to £1,999, an increase of £276. The consultancy has also estimated that business energy costs have risen by about 25 per cent since February.
Smith said: “When they say it’s going to be cheaper, I keep saying two things: when and how? Because it’s not.”
The Department for Energy Security and Net Zero was contacted for comment.'

The Harker electrical substation south of Carlisle doesn’t look like much, but it is one of Britain’s most expensive wiring failures.
This unglamorous tangle of metalwork and cables should help take electricity from [Scottish wind farms](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/.../wind-farms-accused.../) to England’s cities.
Instead, it has become part of a “£1bn bottleneck”, so badly connected that only 60pc of Scotland’s renewable output reaches consumers.
That weakness forces thousands of Scottish turbines to sit uselessly in the wind – switched off because their electricity cannot reach customers – while owners claim millions in compensation for lost sales.
Further south, gas-fired power stations must ramp up to replace missing power, and they too must be paid.
These “constraint payments” added £1.9bn to energy bills last year, and will exceed £2bn this year. Such payments are a key part of the £47 added to the average annual domestic power bill in such “balancing payments”.  Full story can be read here https://archive.ph/RmMX6

What it really means...
Learning from experience: Northern Ireland was the test bed. Back in 2015, 11 "super-councils" were formed. The outcome?
1) less localised services such as social care; more travel and less availability
2) councillors and staff were making decisions in areas they knew nothing about
3) processes took longer
4) accessibility to officers/offices became more difficult
5) larger developments that should have been made by the government were taken by these councils 
6) local development plans were not updated when they transpired
7) Any information that was captured as environmental assessments became more difficult to access
 local tailored environmental assessments no longer took place and sites were categorised under sporadic and irrelevant data capturing
9) increase in rates
Most of us have experienced very poor standard of service from EDC and this move will not give us any improvement. Why are they doing this now? 
Because data centres are their focus for "growth". The huge investment (and even bigger return on investment nationally and through export of data and nuclear power) will be brought under Glasgow's budget. Less accountability for impacts and direct profiteering. In NI, the reason was to bury high grade nuclear waste in the council areas. (research Geological Disposal Facility white paper 2014).  So who is making decisions on where our money will go? It is the Trustees of the pension fund who have a fiduciary duty to get best returns for members, not to invest in Glasgow because Glasgow wants it. 
Please look up the word "fiduciary", it is important!
Who are the Trustees who are and will be making decisions on our behalf if we allow this extension?
It's not a private trust with trustees - it's a COUNCIL COMMITTEE

ROOFTOP SOLAR IS BOOMING
We keep being told that we need more and more large-scale solar developments because we need more renewable energy.
But while all the attention is on huge solar farms, something rather interesting is already happening on our rooftops.
In 2025, 269,000 new solar installations were completed in the UK, the highest annual total on record.
Around 255,000 of those were rooftop installations.
That's roughly 95%.
A new rooftop solar system was being installed around every two minutes.
Yes you read that right every 2 minutes! 
Every suitable roof that is used for solar is generating electricity without taking another acre of farmland.
Homes are doing it.
Businesses are doing it.
Warehouses, schools and public buildings can do it.
Maybe rooftop solar alone can't provide everything the country needs.
But surely, before we cover thousands more acres of productive farmland with industrial-scale solar developments, we should be asking whether we are making the best possible use of the enormous amount of roof space we already have?
And there is another part of this conversation that too often gets forgotten.
Our local distribution networks need investment anyway as electricity demand grows.
So why aren't we having a much bigger conversation about rooftop solar, local generation, battery storage and strengthening the distribution network alongside the billions being spent on new transmission infrastructure?
The argument is not about being anti solar. It's about putting it in the right places, at the right scale, and looking at the whole energy system rather than one project at a time.
Rooftop solar is already proving that people and businesses are willing to play their part.
Perhaps we should be making it easier for more of them to do exactly that.
Right energy. Right place. Right scale.
www.lincsland.co.uk
Source: Department for Energy Security and Net Zero, UK solar deployment figures.

The proposed AI data centre for Chapelcross, Dumfries (Scotsman, 6 October), about 0.2 square miles (or 80 football pitches) in area, apparently will require a power input of 1 gigawatt. That’s the average output of about 600 of the largest on-shore wind turbines covering some 60 square miles of our beautiful countryside – plus of course the necessary grid system. To me that is so horrendous that I’m almost glad that I very likely won't be here to witness it. Two of the latest generation of Rolls-Royce Small Modular Reactors would be a far better supply system and will have a lifetime of at least twice that of wind turbines.
Stephen Gethins’ claim of “Scotland’s remarkable renewable energy potential” and the usual referral to nuclear waste are both a bit nonsensical, so let’s hope that the Tory intention to impose the same law on energy provision on all parts of the UK (Scotsman, 5 October) comes to pass.
A McCormick, Terregles, Dumfries
Nuclear option
The Conservatives plan to legislate to override the SNP’s opposition to nuclear power, thus enabling Small Modular Reactors to be built in Scotland and located at places such as Hunterston, Torrness and Dounreay, all of which have or have had nuclear capability.
What a breath of fresh air that would be – a sensible policy that enhances our energy security, bringing tax revenue from the jobs that would follow. Maybe even helping to close the SNP’s £5 billion black hole. Strange how much of a fuss there was before the last election of the UK government’s supposed £22bn black hole, but so little is made of the SNP’s black hole, which is effectively more than double that in relative terms.
It’s a pity that the Conservatives are unlikely to win that election because at a UK level and a Scottish level we need a good doze of commonsense policies. We certainly are not going to get that with the current level of debate, and the lack of challenge to the SNP.
Maybe the Conservatives should go one stage further and propose a referendum on abolishing Holyrood? Now that would set the cat amongst the pigeons of our self-serving, overpaid, under-qualified MSPs.
Brian Barbour, Haddington, East Lothian

records.bodyText:
Hidden away in a remote part of East Lothian is one of Scottish Water's most environmentally friendly sites. The Castle Moffat Water Treatment Works uses water from the Whiteadder reservoir and is generating more energy than it uses.
Castle Moffat WTW is the only Scottish Water asset where pumped water is used to power a site. The water is pumped from the Hungry Snout Pumping Station at Whiteadder reservoir, over Friar's Nose Hill and then drops by gravity to the site inlet. Water enters the treatment works via the turbine and is clarified in three upward flow clarifiers, before it is filtered in 14 pressure filters.
The introduction of the Feed in Tariffs in 2010 has meant that typically, only gravity-fed hydro turbines have been promoted across Scotland, as pumped sites did not attract funding. However, because we offset nearly all the electricity generated at the treatment works, it is still significant energy cost saving. 
Currently, more than 70 of the company's water and wastewater treatment works are now either self-sufficient or partly sufficient in their power requirements. This is leading to lower operating costs and a more sustainable business. 
‘
The site provides on average 21 Ml/day of clean, fresh drinking water to approximately 47,000 customers across all of East Lothian. 
This self-sufficiency is a result of hydro power which is supplied by a new state of the art generator and control panel which were upgraded in a £200,000 investment last May. The original hydroturbine, which is more than 50 years old, was installed on the site in 1992 and was in need of refurbishment. 
It generates 750,000 kWh/annum – enough to power 2,416 homes. 
The site uses around 80 per cent of the electricity it generates from the turbine with the remaining 20% exported to National Grid. 
The original hydro scheme was designed in the 1990s by Prof Robin Wallace and name Jim Pearson using  raw water was pumped from the Whiteadder reservoir to a receiving chamber at the top of a hill.
The raw water then dropped about 70m to a potable water treatment plant. They inserted secondhand Gilkes turbine (built circa 1960) - was drove a 210kW generator. 
Prof Robin Wallace was working with Edinburgh University and Jim Pearson employed at by Scottish Water. Jim visited the site recently, which is still operational and providing Scottish Water had a very attractive financial benefit. 
Castle Moffat WTW near Garvald, Gifford, Haddington. The original turbine was sitting idle near Edinburgh - Alex McRostie came up with the idea to utilise it. The generator was Hertzinger manufacturer.
Thanks to Jim Pearson for the information and history of this power generation site.— at Castle Moffat Garvald.

Chapelcross Data Centre
This proposed 1GW (1000MW) data centre development, covering 57 hectares, is planned for land just north of the former Chapelcross nuclear site near Annan, Dumfries and Galloway. A Planning Application was validated 28th September 2026 and the deadline for comments and objections is 29th October. The developer is CX Power. The developer has undertaken an Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA).
The documents are available on the Dumfries and Galloway Planning Portal  26/1649/PIP
This data centre capacity, at 1000MW, is bigger than any data centre currently operating in the world (EpochAI.) The data centre with the highest IT power in the world in operation is Elon Musk’s Colossus II in Memphis with 946MW of capacity. 
The Chapelcross data centre would use 7 million MWh of energy a year, if operating at the estimated 80% capacity of AI data centres, which is equivalent to almost a third (32%) of all the electricity used in Scotland in 2024.
And the same as 2.2 million households, which is 88% of Scottish households.(references for calculations in the data centre calculator)
The Scottish Parliament recently voted for a pause in decision making while guidance and a strategic approach was put in place. 
The site is not on the old nuclear site and most is greenfield. The proposed data centre is at least half on green-fields used for grazing and not on brownfield land.
The 2024 prospectus for development at the site notes that the area which is now being proposed for the data centre (the larger purpose area in the map below) is outside the nuclear licenced site. 
Unlicensed NDA Landholding – this land is owned by NDA but is outside of Nuclear Licensed area and therefore potentially available for development in the short-medium term. It comprises a mix of brownfield land (former airfield) and greenfield land to the north, south and east of the former Power Station which is currently in low intensity agricultural use (grazing).
The brownfield land being referred to as brownfield comprises the old RAF airfield, this is species-rich grassland and the request for a scoping opinion from D&G council notes that The uncultivated areas at Chapelcross are known to be extremely valuable for biodiversity having been sympathetically managed since the 1940’s.— at Chapelcross nuclear power station.

Today is International Geodiversity Day!
A day that raises public awareness of how Geodiversity supports ecosystems, biodiversity, agriculture, water supplies and human societies and encourages the protection of geological heritage and landscapes. 
One of the key material considerations for the Glen Earrach Scheme should be regarding Geology given that the site lies in a Dynamic Fault Zone, but it appears to have been somewhat forgotten/buried. 
Other projects have engaged the British Geological Society (BGS) for detailed advice on geology, hydrogeology, engineering properties and seismic hazard. GEE have not. 
The Officers report has little to say on geology and does not consider seismic risk. I just contains meaningless statements such as:
‘The applicant considers the scale of the Great Glen Fault would not be affected’
Given the fact that only last August the epicentre of an Earthquake Mag 2.8 occurred near the site of another proposed scheme at Loch Quoich we should really be expecting more due diligence of survey and reporting to ensure that the proposal will not result in unacceptable risks. 
Currently multiple projects are being proposed on a major fault line and the issue of induced seismicity in relation to Reservoir-loading on faults should be being taken much more seriously.

BEFORE BUILDING 50 OFFSHORE WIND FARMS BY 2050, WE DEMAND ANSWERS.
Thousands of turbines, kilometres of underwater cables and billions invested—but have we fully understood the environmental and financial consequences of the parks already operating?
We need:
• Independent, public assessments of existing offshore wind farms.
• Long-term studies on marine biodiversity and cumulative environmental impacts.
• Honest assessments of landscape, heritage and tourism impacts.
• Transparent accounting of construction, connection, maintenance, grid and decommissioning costs.
• A clear answer to one crucial question: who ultimately pays—the State, developers, taxpayers or consumers?
• Independent oversight, with projects subject to review when costs or impacts exceed expectations.
The sea is not an open laboratory.
Marine biodiversity is not replaceable.
Consumers are not a cash register.
And transparency should not have to wait until 2050.
 Before expanding the scale, let’s make sure we have learned the lessons from what is already operating.

Referring to the Glen Earrach Energy proposal, the head of Ness District Salmon Fishery Board has warned of damage “beyond comprehension” should a hydro scheme on Loch Ness be granted planning permission.
The board plays a key role in protection and data gathering associated with populations of salmon and trout in Loch Ness and the surrounding area.
At a meeting of Highland Council’s South Planning Applications Committee this Wednesday members are being recommended to raise no objection to proposals for the Glen Earrach Pumped Storage Hydro (PSH) scheme which would be located between Drumnadrochit and Invermoriston and use water from Loch Ness.
Ahead of this, fishery board director Brian Shaw has issued a statement urging councillors to disregard the case officer’s recommendation and vote against the scheme.
“Combined with other consented or proposed pump storage schemes on the loch, the level of Loch Ness could rise and fall by up to 1.25 metres, turning Loch Ness into an inland tidal loch, with rapid and frequent changes in loch levels,” he said.
“This will have harmful impacts on the loch, including damage to the shoreline ecology, harming both the ecology and the vital tourism industry”.
“Jacobite Cruises object to the proposal, rightly stating that the impact on tourism has not been properly considered”.
“Glen Earrach intends to modify Dochfour Weir as part of the development. The proposal includes the construction of tilting gates along the top of Dochfour Weir and a technical fish pass”.
“The tilting gates would operate seasonally with no mitigation to protect the River Ness from rapidly changing flows during the autumn and winter months”.
“Flows in the River Ness are very stable at present but would become subject to hydro-peaking flows during the autumn and winter, in response to changing loch levels, with daily changes in river levels of over one meter likely”.
“The proposed new fish pass will create a predation hotspot for salmon smolts, increasing pressure on an endangered species, and it will be impassable for elvers (juvenile eels). Combined with the introduction of hydro-peaking flows environmental regulation and protection appears to be regressing not improving”.
“Pump storage hydro sites have been granted approval elsewhere and other proposals, in far less sensitive locations, are going through the planning process”.
“The iconic Loch Ness, and its surroundings, require protection from harmful developments. It could potentially be subject to permanent disfigurement and ecological damage on such a scale that is beyond the comprehension of most members of the public.”

COUNCILLORS today (October 5) objected to a proposed windfarm on a “jewel in the crown” Borders landscape - despite support from communities on its doorstep hoping for a share in its £17m benefits  
Peebles, Innerleithen and Eddleston community councils have written letters of support for the construction and operation of a wind farm comprising up to 13 turbines each with tips up to a maximum of 200m on land to the north of Glentress Forest in Innerleithen.
The proposal for Leithenwater Wind Energy Hub from Belltown Power UK would generate more than £17 million in community benefits over its 40-year operational lifespan.
But at a meeting of [Scottish Borders Council](https://www.bordertelegraph.com/.../scottish-borders.../...)’s Planning and Building Standards Committee on Monday (October 5), members formally objected to the application amid concerns over its impact on the Tweed Valley landscape and potential risk to the area’s golden eagle population.

Chleansaid Wind Farm is a 96MW onshore wind and battery storage project located on the Dalnessie Estate, approximately 13km north-east of Lairg in the Scottish Highlands. The 96 MW export capacity, paired with a 20 MW battery energy storage system (BESS).
A total of 16 GE Vernova wind turbines (6.1MW each); 12 with a 200m tip height and four with a 180m tip height. 
The project received Scottish Government consent in December 2023 and the Final Investment Decision was made in September 2026. Site  mobilisation is planned for autumn 2026 with commercial
operation targeted for late 2028.
Electrical Works will be managed by Kirby Group, including connection by SSEN Transmission to the Dalchork substation via a new 132kV overhead line.
Community Benefits are expected to provide a community fund of £5,000 per MW of installed capacity annually (approx. £480,000 per year) over its estimated 35-year operational lifespan
Farrans secured a contract with ESB on Chleansaid Wind Farm delivering the Civil Balance of Plant (CBoP).
This milestone marks the commencement of delivery of one of ESB's most strategically important renewable energy projects and represents the first ESB-developed onshore wind project in Scotland.
Chleansaid Wind Farm is a 100% ESB-owned project and will comprise 16 wind turbines with a total installed capacity of 96MW. The project secured planning consent in 2023 and successfully obtained a 15-year Contract for Difference (CfD), providing a long-term route to market for renewable electricity generation.
Construction is expected to commence later this year, with the project targeted to achieve commercial operation in 2028.
The project has been developed entirely by ESB's in-house team and is a flagship development ESB's broader onshore wind portfolio. Chlean the first project to advance into construction ESB's current pipeline of approximately 2GW.— at Dalnessie Estate.
