A battery unit capable of storing enough electricity to power 200 homes for four hours has been proposed in Straiton.
AMP Clean Energy has applied to South Ayrshire Council to install the unit on land north of Main Street.
Planning application 26/00624/APP seeks permission for a 200kW energy storage system with a storage capacity of 800kWh.
The proposed development, known as a Battery Box, would be built on an existing grass field used for livestock.
The equipment would occupy about 24 square metres, roughly the size of two car parking spaces. It would sit on a concrete plinth and be enclosed by a steel wire mesh fence.
Battery Boxes import electricity from the local network when demand is low or when renewable generation is high. They export stored power when demand rises, helping to balance the network.
The company says the electricity would be stored locally and returned to the local network. The unit would not connect directly to a wind or solar farm.
AMP Clean Energy expects each Battery Box to save 160 tonnes of carbon a year.
The statement estimates a potential saving of 4,800 tonnes over the project's lifetime, including construction, transport, operation, removal and recycling.
The company says the unit could provide power to 200 homes for four hours during a local supply disruption. It says battery storage may also help meet increased demand caused by electric vehicles and electric heating.
Construction is expected to take about two weeks. Equipment would be made off site, delivered and lifted into position on the concrete base before the electrical connection is completed.
The battery cabinets would be mild steel and white. The electrical cabinet and surrounding fence would be green.
South Ayrshire Council will consider the application in the coming months— in South Ayrshire.

A few years ago, solar grazing pretty much just meant sheep.
This summer, partnering with Nexamp on a cattle-grazing pilot at two solar sites in Fort Covington, New York. Five cattle rotated through the sites, grazed the vegetation down well, stayed comfortable around the equipment and gave us a much better sense of what's important when you start thinking beyond sheep.
It was found that breed mattered less than disposition (a surprise to us). Calm cattle that are used to rotational grazing, electric fence and frequent handling may have a real place in this model.
Sheep are still a flexible, adaptable fit for solar, and they'll always be a huge part of what we do. But there's room to keep experimenting with cattle, pigs, chickens and other forms of agricultural production under and around solar.
That's the beauty of agrivoltaics. It isn't one fixed system, and it's constantly evolving. It's also helping us figure out how to keep the land productive, support farmers, and make the agricultural use relevant and farmer-specific.

I had a version of this letter in the Scotsman and the Inverness Courier. Both cut my final two paragraphs. I don't know why. 


As I hadn't seen it anywhere I did a minor rewrite and 'softened' the slap at the end thinking that may be the problem and resubmitted.

Maybe someone somewhere will be brave enough to publish it in full. 


The copies aren't too clear so here is the text of my rejigged submission.

************************

How have the energy giants managed to dominate our politics? One word: Fear
Unless we pay increased taxes and more for energy, we and the world will boil. They sit on committees, advise governments, and help shape policies in order to boost their profits at the public’s expense. They simply don’t care about our environment or communities forced to live beside their developments.
Most people believe the climate is changing but nothing the UK does alone will alter its trajectory. The natural world is being trashed for so‑called “green” energy, instead of producing it reliably, affordably and cleanly as possible, while tackling issues like microplastics and sewage in waterways. How is destroying the environment and forcing citizens’ choices between heating and eating - sustainable?
Hand wringing politicians warn of a “climate emergency” without admitting the obvious: unless the entire world cripples its economy the way we are doing for the moving target of Net Zero nothing will change. How do we know if they did it would make a difference anyway?
They drag us down this ruinous path while enjoying lucrative salaries plus expenses and having their ears bent by the very industry causing the carnage.

Guaranteed public money pours into corporate coffers so the need to be competitive on the open market vanishes. Governments say Scotland and the UK can be “world leaders” in renewables and other nations will follow.
Will they say: “The UK is doing a great job impoverishing their own citizens while ripping up their environment for the profit of ruthless global investors— let’s copy that!”
The lunacy isn’t ours alone but we do have the highest energy bills.
Maybe it’s the: guaranteed public money payments to unreliable, weather‑dependent generators; reckless over‑deployment of wind turbines in remote regions far from the point of need; lack of grid capacity out of Scotland or guaranteed customers; new subsidy — constraints — where generators are paid handsomely to produce nothing. What political ‘genius’ thought that one up?
Indoctrination from early age has folk believing their own money must be handed over to corporations “to save the planet”. The very corporations destroying it.
Our politicians are shamefully complicit. The Green Party is now ironically demanding a moratorium on data centres — no doubt run on fickle wind energy — while backing ruthless wind and BESS developers that rural communities have begged them to help stop.
When the same parties are re-elected, they believe they are invincible — that we back their insanity and that they have a mandate to continue. The arrogance in Holyrood and Westminster is astonishing: corporate puppets dancing to whatever tune Big Green plays, insisting we can reverse global climate patterns.
King Canute comes to mind.
They should be hauled through the courts for cruelty to their own citizens, economic negligence and ecocide.
Has the political elite had a collective lobotomy? For the good of the country, perhaps they should be removed to secure units for the clinically incompetent so we can start again.

Lyndsey Ward
Communities B4 Power Companies

ENERGY BILLS ARE NOT ABOUT TO GET CHEAPER.
The October 2026 price cap is quoted as £1,723 — but Ofgem changed the “typical household” consumption benchmark.
Using the previous benchmark, the same cap is around £1,935.
And if current January forecasts are right, the comparable figure could rise to around £2,250.
That is before households fully absorb the cost of:
new pylons, substations and transmission lines, renewable support, network financing, carbon-related policy costs and the huge infrastructure programme now being built.
The promised savings may come later.
The costs are arriving now.
That is exactly why Parliament should be required to show the public the full bill.
How much will this transition really cost?
How high could household bills rise?
What will the grid cost?
And when are the promised savings actually supposed to arrive?
MAKE THEM SHOW THE EVIDENCE.

please see the following updates.
Drone Survey Update
You may notice drones operating within the area of the consented new Bingally Substation over the coming weeks. The project aims to improve the quality of environmental data collected while also reducing the amount of time survey teams need to spend working on the ground. The surveys are purely for data collection and do not involve any construction activity.

Phew - that was some kind of corporate waffle fest from $$EN.

Should we be grateful that they have decided to trash our environment in a slightly different way?

The facts remain. We don't want or need Fanellan substation.

You can fly your corporate junk in on the wings on unicorns and we'd still say NO!

P & J today

Do you feel involved in the grid upgrade projects progressing around the north and north-east?
Well in the case of communities in and around Kilmorack, Beauly and Kiltarlity, grid operator SSEN believes that thanks to local feedback, they have been sent back to the drawing board.
It comes over a replacement of the Black Bridge in Kilmorack, a key access point for SSEN’s high-voltage 400kV Fanellan substation plans.
The substation is currently under appeal with the Scottish Government.
Concerns were raised about construction traffic accessing the site, and the Black Bridge’s condition became one of several reasons the substation was initially refused.
The substation’s project director Laurence Kibblewhite, who is better known as Laurie, told us that a redesign of the bridge is a good example of SSEN putting community feedback into action.
However, local groups have called continuing progress on the substation while under appeal “self-serving” and an attempt to “bypass local democracy”.
The Press and Journal spoke exclusively with Laurie, the project director for both Fanellan substation and the Black Bridge replacement, about the new bridge’s journey so far.
Why does the Black Bridge need replaced?
As the 400kV Fanellan substation has been passing through the planning system, concerns were raised about site traffic accessing the site via narrow single track roads and villages like Kiltarlity.
The reason for this was the Black Bridge in Kilmorack, which after being assessed was deemed not in good enough condition to support all of the traffic required for Fanellan.
The original Black Bridge replacement design. Image: SSEN Transmission.
This concern over site access was one of several reasons given by Highland Council when they rejected planning permission for the substation earlier this year.
Laurie and his team at SSEN then went away and developed plans to build a replacement Black Bridge, “almost over the top” of the original, with two lanes, and pedestrian access alongside.
‘Black Bridge replacement another example of SSEN listening and changing plans’
However, at the first consultation event in December last year, Laurie explained: “There was a genuine sentiment of people with concerns around the duration of road closures that would have been associated with the initial development proposals.”
SSEN’s new plan is to relocate the bridge 10 metres downstream of the existing bridge, leaving it open to traffic for much longer.
“That’s the whole point in doing consultation events.
“The Black Bridge is one example of many times that we’ve gone out to consultation with the best intent and then people have gone, “oh, hold on, have you thought of X, Y and Z?”
“And we’ve come back and changed our plans.
What the new bridge could like after having been moved. Image: SSEN Transmission.
“There’s logic in keeping the bridge where it was originally located, in that you don’t have to amend existing road approaches, etc.
“But the feedback was pretty clear and fair with concerns around road closures associated with the construction period.”
At the second consultation event held last month on the revised designs, Laurie added he got the impression it alleviated “quite a few” concerns of the “vast majority” of the community that attended.
What level of work went into changing the design?
Laurie also told The P&J the Black Bridge proposals involve “tens of people” and making the changes came at a “substantial cost” to the grid operator.
They got to work as soon as they got the feedback from the first consultation event.
The new plans required further ground investigations and extra support from their structural engineers, as the bridge’s calculations had to be redone.
The current Black Bridge only allows one lane of traffic at a time. Image: Will Angus/DC Thomson.
Designers also had to work up new plans for the roadways leading to and from the bridge, and a whole host of new environmental impact work had to be completed.
The second consultation event was also held back, having a potential knock-on effect on the timing of the application itself.
And in SSEN’s case, they are pushed for time, as they aim to achieve their “pathway to 2030”, an ambitious target of completing the upgraded grid network in the Highlands.
What could the Black Bridge’s future look like?
SSEN is also intending for a 120-year design life of the bridge, and once completed will be handed over to Highland Council, if approved.
The bridge team are also assessing the state of the current bridge, and whether it has any future use as a bridleway or “green” bridge, or if it could be removed.
Laurie said: “It’s intended to be an asset for Highland Council and the community for many generations.
“Therefore, it’s really important that we get the feedback from those whose bridge it would become.”
SSEN are offering over £22 billion in investment in the Highlands alongside their infrastructure projects. Image: Will Angus/DC Thomson.
He believes that the new bridge shows SSEN’s commitment to the region, as projects across the north and north-east progress.
Laurie added: “For people like myself and others, that’s actually one of the main things that drives and motivates people in SSEN.
“We’re trying to deliver, responsibly, a network for the north of Scotland and deliver economic benefit for the communities of Scotland.
“I’ve got a team where about 60% live within the vicinity of the sites.
“They live in Inverness, on the edge of Loch Ness, Beauly, etc.
“Not only are we trying to deliver for a community, a lot of our team are part of that community.”
But do Black Bridge changes ease concerns for local groups?
The Press and Journal also asked local leaders what they thought of SSEN’s changes, ahead of the proposals applying for full planning permission.
Susan Ogston, chair of Kiltarlity community council, said: “We do not accept SSEN’s claim that these changes are an example of listening to community feedback.
“In our view, the revisions appear to be a self-serving attempt to help SSEN maintain its project timetable rather than address the fundamental concerns raised by residents.
Susan Ogston addressing a council meeting on Fanellan substation earlier this year. Image: Highland Council.
“The proposed replacement bridge remains out of keeping with its surroundings and would leave the community with a long-term legacy that is inappropriate for the area.
“More importantly, the community’s opposition has always been to the bridge replacement project itself and the disruption and impacts it would bring.
“These latest changes do not address those concerns.”

This was supported by local campaign group Communities B4 Power Companies.
Their spokesperson Lyndsey Ward told The P&J: “The reality is SSEN have tried to bypass local democracy entirely.
“They appealed Highland Council’s refusal of the Fanellan substation to the Scottish Government, ignoring over 2,000 objections from the very community they pretend to listen to.
“The only reason they are now looking at the Black Bridge option is because they have been forced to.”

THE COVER-UP OF THE SINKING OF THE F/V MISTRESS
The F/V Mistress, a 52-foot wooden trawler, sank on New Year’s Day 2019 near the Block Island wind turbines.
The Coast Guard dispatched an all-weather MH-60 helicopter, which abandoned the search after 37 minutes, likely because of radar clutter caused by the wind turbines.
Since the Cape Wind project, the fishing industry and maritime interests had advocated for a two-mile separation between wind turbines.
The federal and state governments ultimately determined that a one-mile separation represented an acceptable safety trade-off. Agencies had renewable energy goals to meet, and safety took a back seat.
Had it been determined in 2020 that the Block Island wind turbines interfered with the rescue attempt, the required setbacks would likely have been two miles.
Recently, divers from Green Oceans conducted a targeted dive at Turbine #1 and located the wreck.
The wreck location has been known by government officials the entire time.
In the September 2020 OCS Study BOEM 2020-044, on page 184, immediately preceding Figure 79, the report states:
“On the final day of the dive survey, partial boat debris (e.g., paneling from a small boat hull) was observed around Turbine 1, but no footage was obtained.”
They always knew the boat was there.
Green Oceans has asked federal officials to reopen the Coast Guard case.
See study: page 184 preceding Figure 79
https://espis.boem.gov/final%20reports/BOEM_2020-044.pdf

F/V Mistress
The F/V Mistress was a 52-foot commercial fishing boat that sank near the Block Island Wind Farm on January 1, 2019, during a winter storm, claiming the lives of two crew members while one was rescued.
The U.S. Coast Guard all-weather MH-60 Jayhawk helicopter abandoned its search after 37 minutes. The wind turbines were involved in the search area.
The Rhode Island State Police Marine Services Unit assisted, and the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration later conducted two sonar searches in 2019.
The Coast Guard's multiagency search never located the M/V Mistress; the inquiry never determined the cause of the sinking.
In August 2026, a private investigation in a "targeted" dive funded by Green Oceans located the F/V Mistress wreckage just 50 feet from Block Island wind turbine #1. The wreckage lies in 92 feet of water.
The discovery of apparent human remains near the wheelhouse has since sparked renewed calls to reopen federal investigations into the incident.
JFK Jr. Piper Saratoga Search Vs F/V Mistress
A Piper Saratoga carrying JFK Jr., his wife, and her sister crashed off the coast of Martha's Vineyard, Massachusetts, on the night of July 16, 1999.
The intensive joint operation involving the Coast Guard and the U.S. Navy continued until July 21, 1999, when Navy divers using a robotic camera and remote vehicle located the wreckage on the ocean floor and recovered the bodies.
Navy divers, rather than the Coast Guard, from the Navy's USS Grasp (ARS-51), a dedicated salvage ship, recovered the bodies at a depth of 116 feet from the plane crash because the operation had transitioned from a rescue mission to a deep-water salvage and recovery operation. The Grasp exceeded the standard Coast Guard diving limits.
Last
Information is available that a Bureau of Ocean Energy Management (BOEM)-sponsored survey conducted in 2019 explicitly documented seeing “partial boat debris (e.g., paneling from a small boat hull)” surrounding Turbine 1. OCS Study BOEM 2020-044

records.bodyText:
Further thoughts, as the mounts get impatient at the starting line.
We've been taking a closer look at NESO's guide as to how Scotland's first Regional Energy Strategic Plan will actually be governed.
And having read it,  it raises an interesting question.
This isn't simply a plan which NESO will write and then hand down. The Strategic Board will steer its development, consider the major choices and trade-offs, and has a formal role in approving it.
The Board will include representatives from the electricity and gas distribution networks, local government, wider energy interests and the Scottish Government, and will be chaired by NESO.
More importantly, NESO says that participants will help identify where infrastructure may be needed to enable economic growth, building a shared evidence base which will inform future network planning and investment decisions.
Which brings us back to SSEN and ScottishPower.
Both are currently making very substantial public cases for their infrastructure investment.
SSEN has been particularly prominent, with its £29bn northern programme, economic-impact material, community investment and a very substantial PR campaign which now reaches into our living rooms through television sponsorship.
ScottishPower is making a remarkably similar economic case, with Keith Anderson talking about £24bn of UK investment, £2.7bn already spent in its Scottish supply chain, jobs, apprenticeships and investment right across Scotland.
Perhaps this is simply good corporate communications.
But there is a rather obvious question to ask.
If the evidence being assembled now will help inform future network planning and investment decisions, how important is it for each network company to ensure that its view of Scotland's future energy needs is firmly established within that evidence base?

records.title: Wind Energy's Absurd
records.bodyText:
We believe that it was Matt Ridley and John Constable who first used the expression 'making out like bandits' - in 2017.  That piece is still current and we are putting the text at the bottom, so we've got it for our archives.
We were reminded of this by a piece in yesterday's Telegraph where the expression has been used again, as well as another comment by an industry executive - 'One energy executive claimed the situation was an “absolute p---take”.'
Silly us.  When the announcement came that developers would no longer be able to game the CfD system by delaying the start of contracts so that they would be able to rake in more dosh, we thought that it would apply retrospectively.  It doesn't!
So any developer who signed up before 2023 can still game, at consumer expense.
https://www.telegraph.co.uk/.../wind-farms-accused.../...
'Wind farm owners have been accused of pushing up household bills by exploiting a “loophole” in green energy subsidies.
The loophole involves contracts for difference (CfDs), the 15- or 20-year fixed-price deals that are handed to wind farms to give developers certainty about their future income.
These are used to underpin the finances of most renewable energy schemes and are ultimately funded through consumer bills.
Ministers have repeatedly described CfDs as good value because they lock in relatively low-priced supplies of power for consumers that can shield them from price increases during crises.
But some developers have repeatedly exploited a rule allowing them to delay the start of their contracts so they can sell power at higher market rates instead. This has allowed some to reap huge windfalls.
Ministers closed the loophole in 2023, but projects awarded CfDs before then can still use it.
One energy executive claimed the situation was an “absolute p---take”.
They accused some developers of “making out like bandits” from the arrangement at the expense of millions of households and businesses, at a time when the US-Iran war has sent power prices surging.
One wind farm, Seagreen, off the coast of Angus, Scotland, is thought to have made about £27m extra by exploiting the loophole in the past two years, according to an analysis of market data by The Telegraph.
The scheme’s first phase secured a CfD in 2019 and construction finished in 2023.
Its CfD had a target start date of March 2025, but this has been repeatedly pushed back, with owners SSE, TotalEnergies and PTTEP now saying that they expect to activate it in March 2027.
There is no suggestion of wrongdoing by the companies, which must activate the CfD by a “hard stop” deadline of September 2028.
Spot power prices in Britain have jumped about £75 per megawatt-hour (MWh) during 2026 and are currently sitting at around £156 per MWh.
This means a wind farm, such as Seagreen, which was awarded a fixed CfD price of about £55 per MWh in today’s prices, can currently reap substantial profits by selling electricity at market rates.
David Turver, an independent energy analyst, argued this went against the spirit of CfDs, which are meant to help support the business cases of wind farms.
He said: “The ability to delay the start of CfDs was originally intended to help developers manage the risk of construction delays.
“But in some cases, the wind farms have been built already and they are simply choosing not to activate the contracts so they can get higher merchant power prices. They are benefitting in that way from higher gas prices.”
The energy executive added: “The CfD bid they made was predicated on what they [would] earn over the period covering construction, plus operations, plus the cost of capital – so the extra earnings now are pure windfall.
“In these times of high energy prices, they make out like bandits before activating it at their discretion.”
The Government previously urged wind farms to “act fairly on this matter, recognising the public support they have received for development”, before closing the loophole in 2023.
A spokesman for Seagreen Wind Energy Limited said on Friday: “In August 2026, we updated the Low Carbon Contracts Company regarding the expected start date for the CfD for Seagreen Phase 1.
“This has been done in accordance with the terms and conditions of the contract.” '
Matt Ridley/John Constable, writing for CapX, in 2017 - they were talking about Renewable Obligations Certificates, as CfDs hadn't really started.
Imagine a sausage factory – the luckiest, most profitable sausage factory in the world. Its machines crank out their sausages, and lorries carry them to supermarkets. So far, so normal.
But this particular factory makes as many sausages as the management and staff choose. If they feel like taking the day off, the lorries and shelves stay empty. If they want to go a bit wild, they sometimes make so many sausages that there aren’t enough lorries to take them away. Or they carry on cranking out sausages even if the shelves are already full.
And here’s the really amazing thing: even when the lorries can’t cope or there is no demand for sausages, the factory gets paid. Indeed, they get paid more for not sending the sausages to the shops than for sending them. This is such great business that the factory is actually building an extension, so it can threaten to make even more unwanted sausages.
Does all that sound completely mad? Of course it does. But it’s what happens in the British electricity industry – where the blackmailing, money-printing sausage factory is a wind farm in Scotland.
There are currently about 750 wind farms north of the border, with roughly 3,000 wind turbines. Their total generating capacity amounts to 5,700 MW. The actual amount produced varies according to the weather. But at its maximum, that wind capacity is more than the 5.5 GW peak demand on the Scottish grid.
What this means, of course, is that the output from Scottish wind turbines is often more than the Scottish system can absorb. That requires the surplus energy to be exported to England and Wales. But that isn’t as easy as it sounds.
The wind farms are distributed across Scotland, sometimes in very remote regions, so there is a real problem in getting their energy down to the English border – let alone getting it across. For some years now, Scotland’s total export capacity has been only 3.5 GW, well under the peak output of the wind farm fleet.
So, reinforcements and new links are being introduced. These range from the hugely controversial, and to many environmentally unacceptable, £820 million Beauly-Denny upgrade, to the massive Western Link, a subsea connector from Hunterston to Deeside that is set to come online this year at a cost of more than £1 billion – and will entail a standing charge on energy bills across Britain of about £100 million a year for 35 years.
Yet in spite of the cost, these upgrades cannot completely address the problem: there is still more wind power in Scotland than can be reasonably and affordably absorbed into the system, or exported to its neighbours, partly because the wind fleet keeps growing.
Why has so much been built? Partly, it is because of income-support subsidies. This top-up of nearly 100 per cent over the wholesale price – funded, of course, from consumer bills – makes wind farms very attractive, at least until they wear out (by which time developers hope to have sold them on to naive pension funds and investment trusts).
There is also the political situation. In England and Wales, onshore wind is effectively dead, due primarily to the strong local resistance the turbines tend to attract, to which government eventually responded.
In Scotland, the story is different. The country is intensely urbanised, with most voters located in the cities. Rural objectors were simply too few in number to have much influence, no matter how strong their environmental or economic arguments.
Subsidies to onshore wind in the UK now cost a little under £600 million a year, with Scottish wind taking about half, yet the Scottish government continues to ignore the protests and consent to new wind farms as if they cost almost nothing at all.
Which as far as Holyrood is concerned, is in fact true. Part of the attraction for Scottish politicians is that the subsidies that pay for Scottish wind farms come from consumers all over Great Britain. Scottish consumption is about 10 per cent of the British total – so when the Scottish government grants planning permission to the wind industry, it is simply writing a cheque drawn overwhelmingly on English and Welsh accounts. Taxation without representation, in fact.
But a careless government and a lucrative subsidy system doesn’t explain the full flourishing of Scotland’s wind industry. Bizarre as it may seem, the fact that the Scottish grid cannot physically absorb all this wind power is also an attraction – because subsidised wind farms can actually earn more per unit generated when that unit is thrown away than when it is sold to consumers. In other words, they really do get paid more for not making sausages than they do when selling normally.
The explanation is simple. A wind farm receives roughly half of its income from the wholesale price and half from subsidy, the infamous Renewables Obligation Certificate (ROC). When the grid is either at or close to capacity, National Grid stops the wind farm from generating, in order to prevent damage to the overhead wires and, at worst, a major system disruption.
When this happens, the wind farm will keep its wholesale income – which is fair enough, since it was contracted in to the system. But it loses its ROCs, because those are only issued for electricity actually sold to consumers.
What happens then, however, is that the wind farm will ask for compensation for the lost ROCs.  The euphemism for “being paid for not producing sausages” is “constraint payment”. And often – and this is the crucial point – they will ask for more compensation than they are losing in income.
When one of us, John Constable, first exposed this problem back in 2011, the average compensation being paid was nearly four times the lost income. One wind farm, Crystal Rig, was asking for (and receiving) £991/MWh in compensation when it was losing about £50/MWh.
Naming and shaming worked, and prices fell. But they are still well above the income lost, with onshore wind farms regularly asking for between £60 and £90/MWh in compensation when they are only losing about £45/MWh.
The result is that wind farms in Scotland have a higher average income per unit of power generated, because local demand is low and the grid system is hopelessly congested – leaving National Grid no option but to buy them off at any price.
For National Grid, this is just a pass-through cost, so they don’t care much about it – they simply increase the amount they’re charging consumers. But for consumers, it’s a truly terrible deal. Since 2010, we’ve paid £328m to wind farms not to generate – mostly to onshore Scottish wind farms, though England’s offshore farms have also started to get into the act. Last year, the total was £82m. This year, it’s already reached £50m.
The result is that there is a perverse incentive to locate wind farms in Scotland, even though they aren’t welcome and the grid can’t take their output. In fact, some wind farms that are already being “constrained off” on a regular basis are considering major extensions to their capacity.
Take Fallago Rig in the Borders. This 48-turbine wind farm, with a capacity of 144 MW, was built in the teeth of fierce local resistance in 2013. Since then, it has received £21,713,858 in payments to stop generating, at an average price of £82/MWh – roughly double the lost income. That lost generation, about 264,954 MWh, is equivalent to 16 per cent of its output during that period.
In spite of this, its owners EdF, the economic wizards behind Hinkley Point C, are proposing to add a further 12 turbines, each over 126.5m in height. Is this about saving the planet? Or because the farm’s owners know they are on to a very good thing and are determined to make out like bandits?
Yet remarkably, this isn’t the end of the counter-economic insanity. When a Scottish wind farm is stopped from generating because of a bottleneck in the system, it throws the whole British market out of balance: supply no longer matches demand. A generator that was contracted-in to the market has been told to stop. That means that the market on the other side of the bottleneck is now short. National Grid, which is responsible for fixing these problems, has to buy last-minute supplies to make up for it. And that is very expensive indeed.
It’s quite difficult to determine which payments to these emergency generators – who are said to be “constrained on” to the system – are caused by Scotland’s capacity and export problems, and which by power station failures or errors in demand forecasts (among other factors). But either way, it’s big money.
And in a supreme irony, it is more than likely that the same large companies getting constraint payments on one side of the bottleneck (because the Scottish grid can’t cope) also get paid to start up their gas turbines in England to make up for the shortfall. Laugh? It’s enough to make a grown bill-payer cry.
The remedies are obvious. First, existing wind farms should not be allowed to demand compensation in excess of income lost. Second, we should carefully weigh up the costs and benefits of building new grid and reinforcing existing lines. It may well be much cheaper to shut wind farms down and compensate their owners, at the correct rate of course, rather than build another subsea interconnector on the east coast – or reinforce the landlines over the border to the main centres of load.
Third, and most importantly, the Government in Westminster should put its foot down, in the interests of us all, and stop Holyrood consenting new wind farms and extensions in Scotland. Or at least ensure that if MSPs want to play fast and loose with consumer bills, those should be Scottish bills. That might focus minds.

We used to ask if we could borrow Australia's Tony Abbott.  Today we're asking can we borrow Georgia Meloni.
This was picked up on the first part of Irina Slav's piece:
“The end is the beginning is the end”
Irina Slav
Note: I borrowed the title from a Smashing Pumpkins song for a Batman movie. It is fitting both in terms of title and of content.
Browsing energy news headlines these days is not for the faint of heart. Every day serves another broken record (pun unintended and only noticed during proofreading) in the price of diesel, soaring gas prices, burning tankers, along with pipelines, and rate hikes. Imminent total collapse is all the rage. But there is, as always, the occasional glimmer of hope, along with a generous serving of transition ridiculousness.
The glimmer of hope this week comes from Italy. Actually, it came last week but I’m only writing about it today. Anyway, Italy’s Prime Minister said last week the country will be boosting its oil and gas production. What she didn’t say was that Brussels can go to hell and take its transition plans with it, because Signora Meloni is polite. But the implication of her message was pretty much the above. I suggest you hold on to your seats. You will now see sense being spoken by a European politician.
“We want to move ⁠ahead with increasing domestic oil and gas production, because it makes little sense to buy ​this energy from abroad when we can also produce it here in Italy,” Georgia Meloni said last Thursday, detailing plans to reduce bureaucratic obstacles for energy companies willing to risk it.
To say that it is not every day one hears a sensible statement by a European politician is to say nothing. And yet here it is, Italy’s response to $107 Brent and 83-euro natural gas. The push has come to shove for Italy. It’s also come to shove for everyone else in the EU but they’re slower on the uptake. Also vain. Also, they’d rather die than admit they were wrong. The derangement is so strong in some heads, their respective mouths are saying “Clean energy is the surest path” and boasting that green hydrogen has become competitive.'

records.bodyText:
Energiekontor's contractors have been riding roughshod in Sutherland.  They removed around 1000 tons of earth in excavation of a hillside - along with trees and vegetation - at a junction on the A9, so that turbine deliveries could negotiate the road on their way to the Lairg 2 wind farm.
The contractors didn't think they needed permission!  A retrospective application is with The Highland Council.
We agree with one of the objectors mentioned in this Northern Times article, Shona Paterson:
We are concerned that if this xxx company gets away with this, then the others will be allowed to do whatever they want purely to maximum their own profits. There are already major concerns that SSEN and Murphys on their behalf are doing considerable damage in "preparatory works" for the Spittal to Beauly overhead line, pylons and substations, that are much opposed by the communities affected, not yet approved and going through a long public inquiry process at present.
Please make sure that Energykontor pays heavily for ignoring our planning procedures and for its very scant regard for the people of Rogart and those in the wider Sutherland area so negatively affected.
https://www.northern-times.co.uk/.../land-grab-at-the.../...
'Contractors working for the developer of a wind farm in Sutherland removed an estimated 1000 tons of earth from the side of a hill without planning permission, it has been confirmed.
The ground, along with vegetation and trees was excavated at the junction of the A9 and the A839 at The Mound, south of Golspie, to create space for wind farm construction traffic carrying abnormal loads, particularly turbine blades, to manoeuvre.
The contractor involved, who was working for Energiekontor, developers of the Lairg II windfarm, did not “think planning was required”, according to the background papers submitted to Highland Council.
Energiekontor has submitted a retrospective planning application for the works, which is now under consideration.
Meanwhile, Councillor John Murray, who represents the East Sutherland and Edderton Ward, has suggested that a dedicated slip road or deceleration lane could be constructed at the cleared site.
The renewable energy firm is developing the 10-turbine, 49.9 MW Lairg II wind farm on open moorland around 4km south east of Lairg and directly south of the existing Lairg Wind Farm
Five of the turbines have a tip height of up to 200 metres, two have a tip height of up to 190 metres and three have a tip height of up to 150 metres.
Deliveries began under police supervision on Monday, July 20, with the turbine blades being transported first. Work to make the route passable was undertaken in preparation for the start of deliveries.
Highland Council has so far received three representations from members of the public regarding the retrospective planning application.
Shona Paterson, a resident of Rosehall, said that she was horrified that a large foreign-owned wind farm company had completely ignored planning regulations and carried out major access works without first seeking consent. She said that if the application was granted it would create a worrying precedent and other developers could follow suit.
Barbara Watt of The Mound said that she and her husband, Roger, were concerned about the plans for the site. They were against any slip road as they felt it could lead to an accident. The couple are keen for the grass to be restored and wildflowers to be planted.
Paul Cuilfail of The Mound, said that developers should not be allowed to “ride roughshod over the planning process without consequence; otherwise there was no point in having planning legislation. He added that he was “vociferously” opposed to the idea of a slip road and in favour of a wild flower meadow.
The application for retrospective planning consent was discussed at a meeting of Rogart Community Council in Pittentrail Hall on Monday, September 7.
Community council chairman Frank Roach said an objection to the planning application had been submitted on behalf of the community council.
The community council considers the application to be deficient and is calling for a fuller and more accurate account of the unauthorised works and their environmental, transport and community impacts.
The objection states that plans fail to show the amount of hillside that has been removed and the extent of the temporary road surface.
The objection also highlights errors in the plans showing how large vehicles would negotiate the route, including the claim that road widening was required despite no widening taking place, and states that the plans are also said to identify the wrong road and an incorrect windfarm.
Concerns have also been raised about the absence of an Environmental Statement and Transport Assessment.
The community council says more information is needed on tree felling and habitat loss, including the volume of timber removed and whether Scottish Forestry was consulted.
Questions have also been raised about the amount of excavated material removed from the site, where it was taken and whether the relevant requirements were met.
The objection also questions how construction traffic and parking were managed, particularly while the Mound car park was closed. It states that a proper transport assessment should have considered the impact of HGVs on the surrounding roads.
The objection also highlights the lack of community involvement and a landownership plan, and states earlier engagement could have provided an opportunity for a lasting local benefit from the works, while a landownership plan would have clarified Scottish Ministers’ interests.
Highland Council has consulted Transport Scotland regarding the retrospective application, and the agency said it would not object.
At the community council meeting, a member present said that the work had made the junction “a lot safer”..
He said that, previously, tractor drivers turning from the A839 onto the A9 would have had to pull out over the white line before they could see oncoming traffic.

It is time for the Scottish Government to  PAUSE and call for a pan Scotland Planning Inquiry Commission.
Today, Community Council Conventions representing many areas across Rural Scotland have written an OPEN LETTER to Gillian Martin MSP, Cabinet Secretary for Climate Action and Rural Affairs. 
 
The Scottish Government previously asked the Conventions to provide evidence on cumulative impacts, communities facing multiple energy developments and regional differences in concern.
That raises a very obvious question: if this strategic evidence is now needed, why has it not been properly examined by the Scottish Government BEFORE consenting major energy infrastructure application after application?
This is precisely why the Conventions across Scotland are calling for a pan-Scotland Planning Inquiry Commission. 
The Government is now asking communities to identify the very strategic and cumulative issues that a Planning Inquiry Commission should examine independently and transparently across Scotland.
The message is clear: the impacted communities have identified the problem. Now the Scottish Government should PAUSE and do the strategic homework needed to address it.
This letter is signed by Community Council Convention leads representing Highland, the South of Scotland, North East Scotland, Shetland and Perth & Kinross. 
Thank you,
Helen Crawford

The Scottish Farmer has a good piece on the forthcoming Agricultural Session of the Kintore-Tealing PLI.
John Campbell, project manager for NOTKUP, said the announcement represented a significant development.
“SSEN argued only last week that these issues were not within the reporters’ remit and that no hearing was required.
“Just three days later, the hearing date was announced.
“The fact that the reporters have now called a hearing and set out this agenda clearly shows they think differently.”
We will, of course, be watching the session.
https://www.thescottishfarmer.co.uk/.../26541128.../...
'The agricultural operations hearing, scheduled for September 23 in Brechin, is expected to run into a second day.
The hearing follows a decision by reporters to seek additional environmental information from SSEN Transmission after concerns were raised by campaign group NOTKUP and land agents Galbraith during the public inquiry.
The agenda published by the Directorate for Planning and Environmental Appeals (DPEA) sets out a wide-ranging examination of the potential consequences of the proposed overhead line for agricultural businesses.
Among the issues to be considered are whether human health risks have been properly assessed, whether electric shock risks have been demonstrated to be ‘as low as reasonably practicable’, and whether reliance on ‘safe work procedures’ is justified.
The reporters will also consider the practical implications of the line for machinery clearances, day-to-day farming operations and agricultural productivity.
NFU Scotland welcomes scrutiny
Andrew Connon, president of NFU Scotland, said the hearing would provide an opportunity for farmers to make their experiences and concerns part of the decision-making process.
“This hearing provides an important opportunity to consider the potential implications of the proposal for farming businesses and agricultural activity. The views and experiences of those working on the land must be properly understood and taken into account as part of the process.
“While we recognise the importance of strengthening Scotland’s energy infrastructure, this needs to be considered alongside the need to support productive agriculture and the long-term interests of rural businesses.
“Major infrastructure projects can have significant implications for those working the land, and it is important that these are fully understood and appropriately considered as part of the planning process.”
The renewed focus on agricultural operations comes after campaigners said SSEN had recently argued that the issues fell outside the reporters’ remit and that no further hearing was required.
John Campbell, project manager for NOTKUP, said the announcement represented a significant development.
“SSEN argued only last week that these issues were not within the reporters’ remit and that no hearing was required.
“Just three days later, the hearing date was announced.
“The fact that the reporters have now called a hearing and set out this agenda clearly shows they think differently.”
The hearing will examine the distinction between transport and operational modes for farm machinery, including whether passing or normal clearance requirements should apply.
The reporters will also consider what could happen to agricultural activities if farmers have to alter their working practices to accommodate the overhead line.
Another issue is whether impacts on agricultural operations and productivity could fall between SSEN’s classifications of ‘significant’ and ‘not significant’ effects.
The reporters will consider whether additional mitigation could be required.
Nearly 200 pages of evidence
Ian Thornton-Kemsley, consultant at Galbraith, said the volume of evidence submitted on agricultural issues underlined the complexity of the dispute.
“This is a very significant step. Farmers and landowners have been saying for some time that the practical realities of working land under and around a 400kV overhead line need much closer examination.
“The written submissions on agricultural matters from NOTKUP and Galbraith alone ran to close to 200 pages. Given that volume of evidence and the complexity of the issues involved, we believe a second day may well be needed.”
Campbell said campaigners could now prepare specifically for the issues identified in the hearing agenda.
“We are very pleased to finally have the agenda. It means we can now put the right team together for what is clearly a very important hearing.
“The reporters have set out a detailed programme covering health, safety, machinery clearances and impacts on farming operations. That underlines the seriousness of the issues that have been raised.”
The Kintore-Tealing overhead line application was made under section 37 of the Electricity Act 1989.
The proposed 400kV connection has become a major point of contention, with the latest hearing putting the practical consequences for farmers and landowners firmly back at the centre of the inquiry process.
Hearing agenda – Effects on agricultural operations
To be held at Brechin City Hall on Wednesday, 23 September 2026 at 09:30
1. Introductions
The reporters will outline how the session will be conducted, highlighting that it will be an informal discussion led by them. Participants will be asked to introduce themselves.
2. The scope of the reporters’ assessment
The discussion will consider the extent of the reporters’ – and Scottish Ministers’ – remit in assessing risks to human health, and how that might be reconciled with or influenced by the significance criteria adopted in the applicant’s Additional Information of June 2026.
3. Assessing whether there would be likely significant effects on human health
The intention is to:
• discuss whether it has been demonstrated (and/or whether it needs to be demonstrated) that the risk to human health (electric shock risk) would not exceed the ‘as low as reasonably practicable’ test;
• consider the basis for reliance on ‘tertiary mitigation’ in concluding that there would be no significant effects on human health; and
• discuss what it means for risk to human health to be ‘adequately managed' through safe work procedures.
4. Transport mode vs operational mode of agricultural machinery, and the case
for passing clearance vs normal clearance
Parties will be asked to explain and justify their respective positions on the mode and height of machinery and the clearances required to minimise risk of conflict with the proposed overhead lines.
The implications of these conclusions for the assessment of significant effects will then be considered in the context of regulations and guidance relating to required clearances.
5. Assessing whether there would be likely significant effects on agricultural operations and/or productivity
A discussion on the implications of agricultural activity / productivity of the land from implementing procedures required to safely manage any clearance constraints will be led.
The potential scenarios which fall between the descriptions of significant and not significant effects on agricultural land use in the applicant’s Additional Information will be considered.
6. Other considerations
The reporters will seek views and/or clarification on other relevant issues raised in evidence, including (but not necessarily limited to) the position of the Health and Safety Executive; and the implications for their assessment of existing overhead lines on some affected land holdings.
7. Mitigation
The scope for further mitigation to be provided, should it be considered necessary by the reporters and/or Scottish Ministers, will be considered. The means by which that might also be secured will be discussed.
8. Next steps and close of hearing.
Deadlines for closing submissions will be confirmed.'

Audit Scotland has found that the proportion of ScotWind developers' committed supply-chain expenditure expected to be spent in Scotland has fallen from 38% to 30%. It also found that the substance of developers' supply-chain statements was not used in the final ranking of successful bids, because officials considered the information insufficiently robust at the time. The Auditor General is now recommending stronger evaluation and contractual enforcement in future leasing rounds.
One interesting piece from the report is this:
Using ScotWind money in this manner contributes to the wider
financial management challenge facing the Scottish Government
as it looks to address fiscal sustainability and reform pressures.
Placing reliance upon offshore wind funding means that the budget year
starts in a non-recurring balanced position. This can have a significant
organisational impact, potentially weakening budgetary control. As the
Scottish Government continues to progress its public service reform
agenda, the impact of the current approach of using ScotWind money
and other non-recurring sources of funding to address underlying cost
pressures should be considered more fully.
In October, Audit Scotland will be publishing an audit of renewable energy.
This is an extract taken from its audit scope:
The overall aim of this performance audit is to assess how strong the arrangements for the £500 million public investment to support the growth of the offshore wind supply chain are, to secure value for money. The audit aims to answer the following questions: 
• Has the Scottish Government set out a clear rationale and sound approach for the investment? 
• Are the arrangements for making investment decisions well-placed to deliver the programme aims? 
• Is the programme on track to achieve its aims?

Dieter Helm has a piece out today about the Government's proposal to cut regulation.  He refers to over-regulation as 'the dangerous dog theorem'.
Although the article covers other utilities, it has a fair bit about the energy regulators and we've selected some of those paragraphs.
In energy, regulation has spun out of control as the outcomes get worse rather than better. DESNZ owns the sole share in the National Energy System Operator (NESO). NESO combines running the system operations, advising on policy and net zero, and taking on functions like capacity modelling, which were once the job of the Department. Not that this stops the Department doing the same stuff as NESO. NESO is a public corporation to get around the constraints on civil service salaries. Therefore it needs a licence as a monopoly and OFGEM has the job of regulating NESO as a result. OFGEM has to second-guess NESO and do lots of the same stuff too because it also has a duty to further the net zero objective. Instead of abolishing OFGEM when NESO was set up and transferring the network regulation to a cross-utility body (as recommended in the “Cost of Energy Review”), new regulators need regulating. Perhaps we might add an OFDOG, a watchdog and regulator of all the regulators?
Some of this is straight out of Yes Minister. It is amusing, like Yes Minister, but it is also extremely costly and damaging to delivering the outcomes. And so it has turned out. There are now thousands of people regulating the electricity and gas industries where once there was a small office in the Department of Energy covering the Central Electricity Generating Board, the Area Electricity Boards, British Gas, the National Coal Board, and looking after North Sea licensing. Now there is a major industry in place – one area of the economy where there definitely is growth.
And:
As government has discovered the necessity for system planning and system regulation, it has begun the process of establishing new system regulators misleadingly called system operators. Energy is the prime example, though catchment planning and regulation are coming in water.
Adding a new planning and regulatory body should mean that the existing regulators can be pruned back – and hard. In the energy case, the bizarre outcome has been to add NESO to the context of both DESNZ and OFGEM and then to make OFGEM the regulator of NESO. Two becomes three, but the arithmetic increase in bodies has led to a geometric overload of regulation.
End the regulation of NESO by OFGEM and, as above, break up and close OFGEM.
And:
Abolishing system planning and system regulation does not make the problems go away. In many respects it makes matters much worse. Take electricity: much of the generation is in the wrong places because the project developers have no incentive to locate in the right places from the system perspective. The grid and the renewables have not been co-planned and their roll-out integrated. The result is that Britain has an increasingly dysfunctional system. Wind generators, for example, are constrained off (paid for generating electricity that no one wants and cannot get to market), and Britain’s electricity is amongst the most expensive in the developed world. This should be recognised as a disaster for industry and households.
The high cost of energy is a major “blocker” to economic growth. This is partly the result of very badly designed regulation.
And:
In energy, DESNZ shadows NESO and oversees OFGEM’s activities. HMT shadows DESNZ. OFGEM regulates NESO, which is owned by the Secretary of State.
In the old, nationalised days, a very much smaller Department for Energy did the modelling and shaped the energy mix, granted licences and did the necessary supporting policy analysis. Now DESNZ does all this, overlapping with NESO and OFGEM. And it gives guidance to both.
And:
Since privatisation, there has been a large increase in propaganda and lobbying both by government departments and by the regulators. They now spend lots of money on “corporate relations” departments and PR consultants. DESNZ pays significant sums to “influencers”; NESO is accused of having corporate relations people in the control room in a semi-emergency tightness of capacity event and a risk that the lights may go out. This is getting out of control.
An immediate analysis of the total corporate relations and PR consultancy spend by regulatory bodies and by the sponsoring government departments should be conducted. The default should be to bring this to zero unless there is an overwhelming national emergency or other urgent need to communicate with customers and the public.
This is a muddle, with large duplication and a consultants’ paradise. Each second-guesses the other.
It is actually worse. On top of all this are the Climate Change Committee (CCC) and the National Infrastructure and Service Transformation Authority (NISTA), both doing analysis too.
DESNZ has a big staff. It could easily absorb back several of the core policy functions and at the same time reduce its headcount.
https://dieterhelm.co.uk/.../how-to-reduce-regulation-by-25/

Those four words were ringing in our ears when we were reading the publication of the report from the Energy Security & Net Zero Committee on 'Zero sum game: How the UK can reframe the energy transition'.
What the Committee's report says:
The Committee's report looks at how public support for the energy transition might be maintained or rebuilt. Its central argument is that Government communication has become too focused on the term Net Zero and on the emissions target, rather than explaining the wider claimed benefits of the transition - including energy security, health, jobs, warmer homes and potentially lower bills. It recommends reducing the use of 'Net Zero' in Government communications and even dropping it from the Department's name.
A substantial part of the report concerns trust and information. The Committee argues that Government is not necessarily a trusted messenger and that scientists, local organisations and civil society could have a greater role. It is also concerned about what it calls 'credibility laundering' of misinformation online and recommends that Government consider giving Ofcom further powers and resources to regulate misleading information about the energy transition, including the possibility of speedy interim decisions on complaints. It also recommends exploring ways of giving information from 'trusted sources' greater prominence on social media platforms and search engines.
The report also acknowledges some of the cost and fairness problems associated with the transition. It recommends that no household in or at risk of fuel poverty should be left worse off by the costs of decarbonisation, and that Government should publish an annual assessment of the distributional impact of energy-policy costs.
But there is another side to the report:
The Committee held a public-engagement event involving 21 people selected from 250 respondents to an earlier invitation. Interestingly, the Committee says that providing information to participants did not bring them towards consensus; it appeared to polarise opinions further, with little agreement over sources of information, facts or which organisations could be trusted.
And the Annex contains written comments from participants themselves, including some quite substantial criticisms of the event and the way its conclusions were summarised.
Some participants argued that their views - particularly sceptical or critical views about the speed, cost and consequences of the Net Zero transition - had not been properly represented. One said the summary did not accurately reflect dissenting views and that the event appeared, in their interpretation, to have an aim of converting sceptics to support Government policy.
Other participants made the opposite criticism: that the discussion had given disproportionate weight to minority or allegedly misinformed views, and that the format and facilitation did not adequately reflect the balance of views at their table.
There are also comments about local democracy, infrastructure, costs, biodiversity, the methodology of the exercise and whether participants were given a genuinely open discussion. One participant specifically argued that the presentations had not fairly presented the cost question because the costs of not transitioning had not been set alongside the costs of transition.
And then there is Sir Christopher Chope's intervention when the report was formally agreed on 8 September. He proposed that the Committee should not proceed with the report because, in his view, it engaged in Government propaganda and made dangerous suggestions concerning restrictions on freedom of expression. His amendment was defeated 1–5, after which the report was agreed 5–1, with Chope again the sole dissenting vote.
So, we say again - it's a matter of trust!
There are some submissions worth going into in a bit of detail, which we will cover separately over the next couple of days.

records.title: Wind Energy's Absurd
records.bodyText:
There is something about the current electricity transmission planning process that doesn't sit comfortably.
The Strategic Spatial Energy Plan (SSEP) is intended to establish what the future energy system should look like and, importantly, where generation and storage should broadly be located.
The Centralised Strategic Network Plan (CSNP) then takes that strategic picture and works out what transmission network is needed to connect it.
But the SSEP has now been delayed until 2027, with the CSNP following in 2028.
Meanwhile, the Pathway to 2030 transmission programme is already well underway, with major new overhead lines and substations being progressed through the planning system.
Ofgem acknowledges the potential problem. In its letter agreeing to the revised CSNP timetable, it says:
“There is a risk that a later publication of the CSNP could delay transmission build. However, without the SSEP, the CSNP doesn’t have the key input it needs to start.”
The answer, apparently, is to rely on transitional planning arrangements to keep the existing programme moving while we wait for the strategic plans.
But this raises a rather obvious question:
If the SSEP is supposed to determine the future spatial distribution of generation and storage, how much confidence can we have that transmission infrastructure being consented and built today represents the network that the eventual SSEP and CSNP will determine is actually required?
And perhaps the even more important question:
If the eventual SSEP points in a different direction, what happens to projects already committed under Pathway to 2030?
We're not suggesting that projects can simply be cancelled or that the eventual SSEP will necessarily change anything. We don't think the documentation allows us to say either way at this stage.
But when the strategic spatial plan comes after the infrastructure programme intended to serve the future energy system, it is reasonable to ask whether we have put the cart before the horse.

We said, when we posted the summary of the Energy Security & Net Zero Committee report on 'Zero sum game: How the UK can reframe the energy transition', that we would look at some of the written submissions in more detail.
This is the first, from Brian Wade.  The image is what he refers to in the text; we've highlighted the section. 
I am responding as an individual but also representing Save Our Mearns, a community action group with over 30,000 members and one of 5 similar groups fighting SSEN plans to build a line of monster pylons up to 72m high from Kintore in Aberdeenshire to Tealing in Angus. We are not anti-net zero, we are against the way the UK government are trying to respond to global warming a 21st century with 19th century solutions, pylons.
We are well aware of the contrast between our neighbours on the European continent and the self-destructive policies of the UK government. The very nature of these questions indicate just out of touch DESNZ are with the feelings of the population and how they are set on solutions which only benefit private, profit focused companies such as National Grid Transmission and SSEN.
Question 1.
Has the Government properly explained the potential benefits of the energy transition to the average citizen?
It is not a case of whether the Government has properly explained the potential benefits of an energy transition but whether they have any logical and defensible arguments for their idea of an energy transition. Nations like Germany, Belgium, the Netherlands and Denmark have the same issues as the UK with a need to transmit large amounts of renewables sourced energy from dispersed and remote locations to the areas where there is demand. These nations have embraced solutions such as underground HVDC, integrated offshore grids, energy islands and upgrading existing infrastructure before building new. These solutions are demonstratively of much lower environmental, health and community impact and are also, in the long term cheaper to the consumer than the pylon-based proposals insisted on by the UK Government.
UK energy policy is heavily based on the publication National Policy Statement for Electricity Networks Infrastructure (EN-5) [1]
This document contains the statement “Given that underground lines are not without a range of adverse impacts of their own, and they are significantly more expensive, it is considered better to adopt the policies set out inEN-1 and EN-5”
When obliged under a Freedom of Information request to produce the source material and justification for this statement, DESNZ could only point to a report, known as The Parsons Brinkerhoff report[2], written in 2011 and published in January 2012. This report was itself was based on historical data. In its day the report was a creditable representation of the situation but now belongs in a museum. In no way does it represent contemporary data. Maybe this is the difference between the UK and Europe? Modern cost/benefit studies and reports reflecting current costs and values present a very different picture to that used by DESNZ, for example: https://www.nationalgrid.com/document/151426/download  Appendix F or https://www.neso.energy/document/304496/download
Given the fact that the current technology and methodology solutions represent higher long-term costs to consumers as well as totally unnecessary and devastating environmental and socioeconomic impacts, it is hard to see where the benefits are to the UK population.
Question 2.
Is there a clear understanding of the costs of the energy transition to householders and businesses?
The answer to this question is definitely “No!!” and the reason is that DESNZ have no idea of the costs themselves. DESNZ have totally failed to produce a cost/benefits analysis of their plans using contemporary data and predictions. The ASTI framework basically gives transmission owners an open cheque, Ofgem have completely failed to lock in costs and ESO and Ofgem have failed to follow Treasury Green Book requirements including the need for costed alternatives or environmental impact assessments. Ofgem removed the requirement for open competition and ESO simply let transmission owners submit their own projects. The SSEN TKUP project was supposed to be an upgrade of an existing line, but after being granted ASTI status morphed into a whole new line with substations bigger than the Sellafield Nuclear facility without either of these features being included in Pathway to 2030. The transmission owners decide what they want the consumer to pay for and ESO, Ofgem and DESNZ just rubber stamp consent. There have been lots of unsubstantiated claims made in public by the Secretary of State, for example: net zero will increase energy security and reduce bills by £300/year. Relying on intermittent renewables will only increase UK reliance on French nuclear and Norwegian hydroelectric power, neither of which can be guaranteed. Spending many billions of pounds building infrastructure to transmit wind generated power from Caithness to Surrey is only going to increase consumer costs. A recent modelling exercise by Professor Gordon Hughes said” What the analysis reported here makes clear is that implementing the CP30 strategy will push up total generating costs by a lot, almost certainly by 50% and quite probably by more than 70%. The claim that the CP30 strategy will reduce electricity bills by as much as 20% is simply absurd”.[3]
The general public are very wary of government trying to force them to adapt expensive technology such as electric vehicles and air sourced heat pumps. Common sense suggests the question “if these things are so good why am I being forced into using them?”
Question 3.
Is there a need for public campaigns to counter the anti net zero narrative?
It is not an anti-net zero narrative that DESNZ should be deliberating, it should be public demands that there is honesty and integrity when it comes to what the Government idea of net-zero is. It is very difficult for someone, who is suffering severe mental health issues, caused by finding that the dream home that they spent years paying for is now essentially valueless because someone wants to build a totally unnecessary and damaging pylon line next to it, to feel sympathetic towards the Government drive to reach an arbitrary target date of 2030 which has no scientific or engineering origin, just political rhetoric.
The UK government have been very dishonest with the UK public and are then surprised why there is massive opposition to their plans. The government have insulted the public by describing  genuine concerns and fears of members of the population who want a democratic right to object to badly conceived and damaging  projects as those of NIMBYs and Blockers. The most recent insult has been a derisory offer of £250/year to those who have pylons built next to their properties. That is just ridiculous if a property has been devalued by £200-300thousand. DESNZ and the Prime Minister’s Office have declared war on rural communities, insulted them and then talk about an anti-net zero narrative. The very question just demonstrates how out of touch the clique of DESNZ, Ofgem and NESO are. There is so much silo thinking reinforced by groupthink. A publication, produced by what was then NG-ESO[4], showed their consultation with so called stakeholders.  (Tℎe image)
This single illustration epitomises what is wrong with the UK Energy industry governance and why they see public resentment as an anti-net zero narrative. They are not listening to the general public, just big energy and those with a financial interest in covering the country in pylons and turbines.
Question 4.
How should the Government be more positively engaging the public with this goal? 
The government could more positively engage with the public simply by listening to them rather than carrying out a 1930s style alienation and hostile condemnation of a section of the population who are simply asking for a just transition. It is very obvious that there is far more influence  on UK policy and the direction of travel by big business, who are focused on profit rather than what is good for the UK. They are promoting the “anti progress” rhetoric, which is being taken up by politicians for their own personal means. Their version of progress is what creates revenue for them.
The UK is supposedly a democratic country, but the human rights of the population have been eroded, removing the freedom and ability of concerned residents to influence what happens in their neighbourhood. There is now a headlong rush to make bad decisions more quickly. There is now no accountability, central government routinely grant planning consent to projects simply to make a political statement with no consideration of the horrendous consequences. That is not engagement, it is dictatorship.
On 5th November, 2024, Fintan Slye, the executive director of NESO, made the importance of engaging community support clear;
“I am acutely conscious that building infrastructure, pylons, does impose on people and their locality. “it is really important…that we bring people and communities with us on this journey”, and that the transition to net zero only works “if we can bring society with us”.
The NESO publication  Clean Power 2030 (page 61)  says “Community consent and maintaining public support is vital to the delivery of net zero in Great Britain. Those asked to host energy infrastructure should continue to be effectively engaged throughout the development process, even as it accelerates, and should feel tangible benefit from the critical role their areas play in building a clean, secure and low-cost electricity system”.
There is scant evidence of such engagement with the UK Government now seeking to further reduce the ability of communities to influence decisions on infrastructure projects by removing automatic public local inquiries in Scotland if a local authority object to a S36 or S37 application. Public input is being removed, not encouraged.
The UK Government have declared war on those they describe as Nimbys and blockers and the Scottish Government refuse to meet campaign groups while at the same time they are being wined and dined by SSEN, a clear breech of the ministerial code. There has been, and continues to be, a gradual erosion of rights to speak out against poorly conceived and damaging policies.

A piece in the Spectator about the select committee's report.  
'First, the good news. The Commons select committee on energy security and net zero has called on the government to drop net zero. Now the bad news: they only mean the term ‘net zero’ not the actual policy of trying to eliminate net carbon emissions by 2050.
They complain that the term has become a ‘lightning rod for opposition to climate action’, and that it has become a ‘distraction’, even though it describes perfectly what the government is – ruinously – trying to achieve. They want the policy to continue, but under a different name – though possibly not ‘net stupid’, which is Reform UK’s preferred term. Presumably it would be known by some propagandistic euphemism or other. How about a Sovietesque ‘glorious transition’?
Sorry, but changing the name isn’t going to negate the utter foolishness of legally committing ourselves to eliminating net carbon emissions by some random date
Sorry, but changing the name isn’t going to negate the utter foolishness of legally committing ourselves to eliminating net carbon emissions by some random date, 2050 or otherwise. Rebranding is what happens when a product is failing, and often fails even heroically once the rebrand is complete because it becomes open to ridicule. No one was remotely fooled that the Morris Ital was anything other than a Morris Marina (Google it if you are under 50), and they won’t be fooled by calling net zero something else.
The reason support for net zero is collapsing is that people are slowly coming around to realising the implications of something which at first sounded abstract and too far in the future to worry about. Now, however, voters can see that there is a link between our high electricity prices and the mess being caused by Ed Miliband’s target of decarbonising the national grid by 2030 (one of the staging posts on the way to the 2050 target).
They understand that building endless wind and solar farms without the storage to cope with the intermittency means we have to build two parallel, and extremely expensive, energy systems.
Voters understand, too, that net zero will mean the end of flying for foreign holidays. Maybe when MPs nodded through the net zero target in 2019 it was possible to think that conventional planes would be replaced with hydrogen ones or use biofuels. But it has become pretty clear since then that new technologies cannot be magicked into existence to meet some government target. People are starting to understand, too, that net zero is forcing us to offshore our carbon emissions, along with jobs and wealth, to China and elsewhere, to no benefit to the environment. 
The energy security and net zero committee has another, sinister proposal. It wants Ofcom to crack down on what it calls ‘misinformation’, which we know from previous experience means anyone who makes any argument against net zero. The only example of ‘misinformation’ cited in the MPs’ report was a claim by a broadcaster that the Climate Change Committee had said that by 2050 a quarter of our energy would still be coming from fossil fuels. Actually, that was a former government interpretation of the Committee on Climate Change’s data. That hardly seems a huge piece of misinformation compared, for example, with Ed Miliband’s porky that his renewable energy policies were going to save us £300 a year on our energy bills. But of course the mainly Labour MPs on the select committee aren’t the slightest bit interested in correcting such stuff, only denouncing material which they find inconvenient to the cause of the climate lobby.
Trying to rename net zero is an attempt to regain control of a narrative which is collapsing: that eliminating net zero will bring us cheaper energy, more jobs, and just about everything else you could possibly want. It is a sign of desperation which will fool no one.'
