Shane Oxer on what came out of the Energy Security & Net Zero Committee report.
Our take was - 'it's a matter of trust'.  The trust is eroded on a daily basis.
ORWELL’S 1984 — 40 YEARS LATER
This isn’t about claiming Britain has become Orwell’s Oceania. It is about asking where the line should be drawn between government explaining a policy and government managing the information environment in which that policy is judged.
A new House of Commons Energy Security and Net Zero Committee report recommends reducing the use of the term “net zero”, making greater use of “trusted messengers”, increasing the prominence of authoritative information online, and examining further measures to tackle what is considered misleading information about the energy transition. 
Orwell warned about the power of language, approved narratives and control over information.
Forty-two years after 1984, those warnings are worth reading again.
My latest article looks closely at what Parliament has actually recommended , and asks a simple democratic question:
Who gets to decide what truth is?
 Read it here:
http://hopetosaveourcountryside.com/.../orwells-1984-40.../

records.title: Wind Energy's Absurd
records.bodyText:
One more, for today - Andrew Montford's written submission for NZW:
Introduction
The committee seeks to understand the increased opposition to Net Zero, and asks for input on possible ways to counter it.
The questions posed presuppose that decarbonisation is a rational response to climate change, and that opposition to the policy arises out of a lack of understanding on the part of the public – either of the costs or the benefits or both. Once an evidence-based view of the costs and benefits of Net Zero is set out, it is clear that the opposition to the policy is entirely rational, and that the committee’s concern should be with how officialdom has so perverted the policymaking process and the public discourse on climate change.
Understanding of the costs Net Zero
Understanding of the costs of the energy transition – both among politicians and the general public – is poor. This is because official pronouncements on the subject have risen little above the level of outright disinformation.
From 2017, Whitehall claimed that the costs of renewables – the biggest single cost of Net Zero – had collapsed and, ever since, the public has been bombarded – by politicians, the media and activists – with a false narrative of ‘cheap renewables’. It is remarkable that this position has been maintained in the face of the ongoing need for subsidies to keep wind and solar installations afloat (now running at around £12 billion per year, and predicted to increase to £15 billion by the end of this Parliament), and in the face of irrefutable evidence from financial accounts that the costs of windfarms remain very high.
While aware of this evidence, DESNZ has refused to correct the record. This is unfortunately, because its figures are cited almost universally – by NESO, the National Infrastructure Commission, the Climate Change Committee, by the Royal Society and in the media. Thus the discourse on decarbonisation has been perverted by false information. The public has been left with the impression that renewables are cheap, and indeed cheaper than fossil fuels.
The Climate Change Committee’s 2019 Net Zero report claimed that decarbonisation of the economy as a whole could be delivered at modest cost. It suggested a figure of around £50 billion for 2050, but was vague about the intervening years. The CCC’s figures are long-since discredited. While it attempted to withhold the underlying calculations, but when ordered to release them by the Information Tribunal, it was found, for example, that:
It assumed a collapse in renewables costs.
It only calculated the costs in the single year 2050, thus missing out the higher costs in earlier years.
The electricity system modelling was entirely inadequate, failing to take into account the full range of weather-related variation in renewable electricity supply and entirely failing to consider the effects of interannual weather variation on demand. Indeed, the committee’s modelling of the supply of wind power was based on weather data that appeared to be an invention – the number of windless days modelled was impossibly low (thus making the amount of expensive electricity storage required unrealistically low too).
Remarkably, it assumed that the cost of EVs was already lower than ICE equivalents.
National Grid ESO produced a better costing of Net Zero in 2020, however, it too was flawed:
It failed to model weather-dependent supply and demand properly.
Its costings were not based on real-world data.
Net Zero Watch has produced an independent estimate of the costs and benefits of Net Zero. It is the only estimate that models temperature-dependent supply and demand on the electricity grid, and uses real-world data as its starting point for unit costs. With current technology, the cost of decarbonising the main parts of the economy would be nearly £10 trillion in discounted terms. Even with the kind of cost-reductions assumed by the CCC for 2050, it would still cost more than £6 trillion. Hard-to-decarbonise sectors, such as aviation and shipping, would raise both figures, presumably significantly.
Understanding of the benefits of Net Zero
The potential benefits of the energy transition are the prevented harms of global warming. These harms are highly speculative, resulting from the outputs of computer simulations of the climate (global climate models – GCMs) fed into separate computer models of the economy (integrated assessment models – IAMs). Neither kind of model can be said to enjoy a reputation for verisimilitude; indeed one widely held view is that GCMs have no predictive value at all. However, if we accept the results as given, the typical estimate of the net harms of global warming is in the range £30–100 per tonne of CO2. According to the IPCC, unabated climate change leading to a 3.66°C warming will cause a loss of GDP of 2.6%, compared to a 0.3% loss at 1.5°C. These are relatively small numbers – the UK lost 4.2% of GDP in 2009 as a result of the global financial crisis.
That the impacts of climate change are manageable is confirmed by the Committee on Climate Change, which suggests that with 2°C of warming, the annual cost to the country would be £13 billion in 2021 prices, rising to £20 billion at 4°C.
Part of the reason for the costs being manageable is that the main harms of global warming – flooding, sea-level rise and heat-related mortality – are impacts of which we have long experience, and which can be dealt with at low cost. For example, the CCC suggests we would have to spend less than £10 billion (in discounted terms) to deal with sea-level rise to the end of the century.
That climate change is a manageable problem has never been explained to the general public. Politicians, scientists, bureaucrats and activists have promoted a narrative that we are in a so-called ‘climate catastrophe’. It is notable that the scientific assessment of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) only uses the expressions ‘climate crisis’ or ‘climate emergency’ in a section on media coverage.
The climate catastrophe narrative has left the public with the impression that weather patterns have deteriorated dramatically. This is in stark contrast to the IPCC’s most recent scientific review, which reports it has been unable to detect significant changes in most weather- and climate-related phenomena, including river floods, pluvial floods, aridity, hydrological drought, agricultural and ecological drought, wind speeds, wind storms, tropical cyclones, sand and dust storms, snow, glaciers and ice sheets, snowfall, ice storms, coastal floods, coastal erosion, marine heatwaves and ocean acidity.
Thus the real-world data show we are not in a climate emergency. There are only some highly problematic computer simulations that suggest we might be at some point in the future. The almost complete failure of epidemiological models during the Covid years should give the committee pause for thought as to how useful computer simulations are to policymakers. As a further example, a report for Net Zero Watch noted that in NASA’s climate model sea water fails to freeze at -20°C and the proportion of the sky that is cloudy at times goes negative.[11] These failings in the models would be comical were they not so serious for public wellbeing.
The false narrative of climate catastrophe has left the public with the impression that the benefits of Net Zero are large and certain. That they are hypothetical, and therefore may be illusory, and that even if they are realised will be small (and shared with other countries) is information that has been systematically excluded from public discourse.
Improving public understanding
As noted above, the committee has started out in error, assuming that Net Zero is rational and that doubts about the wisdom of the policy are a function of public ignorance. This could not be further from the truth. In all the scenarios considered in the Net Zero Watch costing, the public is made trillions of pounds worse off by pursuing Net Zero, even once the impacts of climate change are taken into account. In other words, the costs of Net Zero vastly exceed the benefits. The policy is therefore irrational.
It is therefore those who still support the policy that should be of concern to the committee. They are probably still a majority of the public. This is because, for over 20 years, there has been a rigidly maintained ideological uniformity among the main political parties on climate and energy policy. Similarly, debate on climate change and Net Zero has also been suppressed in most of the media, with IPSO and Ofcom weaponised against sceptical voices, so that even media outlets that are inclined to ask questions have to bowdlerise themselves so as to avoid trouble from the authorities. This is shameful.
In essence, society’s ability to identify and rectify policy mistakes has been severely attenuated.
That being the case, there is no case for ‘public campaigns to counter the anti net zero narrative’. There is a case for politicians to encourage the public debate that has been missing for the last 15 years or more, and indeed to consider the possibility that everything they have done for the last 20 years has been a mistake.

records.bodyText:
Andrew Bowie, the shadow energy minister, accused the government of sacrificing growing British companies and jobs in its pursuit of net zero. 
“The government can do one of two things: they can either reindustrialise this country and prioritise British jobs and manufacturing, or they can sprint towards an unachievable pie-in-the-sky target of green power by 2030,” he said.
He accused Labour of relying on technology “imported, supplied and developed overseas”.
Andrew Bowie, quoted in a Times article on what was said during a constituency dinner held by Bill Esterton,  Chair of the Government's Energy Security & Net Zero committee.
Apparently, storage was discussed, and Ofgem was found wanting.  Ofgem hasn't finalised its list yet, following the consultation closing in August, on the first application window of the long duration electricity storage (LDES) cap and floor regime.
https://www.thetimes.com/business/energy/article/uk-batteries-lithium-energy-electricity-storage-kp2d3z38l?utm_source=Sailthru&utm_medium=email&utm_campaign=Business%20Sun%2020%20Sep%202026&utm_term=audience_BUSINESS
'Tucked away a stone’s throw from the pretty seaside town of St Annes and a 35-minute drive from Liverpool, Formby golf club provided a picturesque setting for Bill Esterson’s constituency dinner on Thursday night. 
The longstanding Labour MP for Sefton Central, and chair of the House of Commons energy security and net zero committee, had gathered 250 local business leaders together to set out what Andy Burnham’s reindustrialisation agenda might mean for their corner of the northwest. 
But as guests tucked into a three-course meal of pear and stilton, beef fillet, and cheesecake, conversation turned to a more immediate concern: the decision of energy regulator Ofgem to provisionally back battery storage projects largely underpinned by Chinese lithium-ion technology, rather than some of the newer technologies being developed by British manufacturers. 
Esterson is said to be sympathetic to the plight of businesses such as Invinity Energy Systems, a British manufacturer backed by a £25 million investment from the taxpayer-owned National Wealth Fund. The company was lined up to supply vanadium flow batteries to 21 projects applying to Ofgem’s long-duration energy storage scheme, but only one of the projects selected uses its tech.
Chief executive Jonathan Marren said the decision was likely to result in the scrapping of a planned Scottish expansion that could have created up to 1,000 jobs. 
Ofgem’s Long Duration Electricity Storage (LDES) scheme is designed to make it easier to finance large-scale storage projects. Under this system, projects are guaranteed a minimum level of income, with consumers making up some of the shortfall if revenues fall below that floor. If revenues rise above an agreed ceiling, or “cap”, some of the excess is returned to consumers.
At Thursday’s dinner, the ire of some attendees was directed at Ofgem, with one diner describing its decision-making as “illogical”. There was also frustration over what some see as a lack of “joined-up” thinking between government departments, public bodies and regulators. Invinity, for example, despite the investment by the National Wealth Fund, has so far secured little support through Ofgem’s scheme — a disconnect that Marren has struggled to explain to frustrated shareholders. 
And there are growing questions about Burnham’s drive to reindustrialise the UK when decisions that affect manufacturers in the clean energy sector don’t seem to tally with this vision. 
There is potentially billions of pounds at stake. The National Energy System Operator (NESO) has estimated that between 3GW and 5.3GW of long-duration electricity storage could be needed by 2030. Industry estimates put the capital requirement at about £2 billion to £2.5 billion per gigawatt, implying investment of roughly £8 billion to £15 billion this decade. 
The need for storage is being driven in part by the growing amount of electricity generated from wind and solar. When renewable generators produce more power than the grid needs, they are paid to reduce their output while other generators elsewhere are paid to increase theirs. These so-called “constraint” costs reached £1.9 billion last year, according to the National Audit Office, and could rise to £7.8 billion a year by 2030.
Storage can reduce some of those costs by absorbing electricity when there is a surplus and releasing it when demand is higher or generation is lower.
Richard Green, professor of sustainable energy business at Imperial College London, said the current cost of managing constraints was equivalent to about 2p per unit of electricity, although the savings from additional storage would depend on where it was located and how the grid develops.
“More storage, or more transmission, cuts that number, but imposes its own cost,” he said.
Batteries also have a role in keeping the electricity system stable as the number of conventional power stations falls, and can respond rapidly to changes in frequency. “They will be helpful [in] smoothing things out during the day, and providing a very fast reaction if something happens,” Green said.
But the question of what type of battery Britain builds is becoming increasingly important. Lithium-ion is the dominant technology and is manufactured on a huge scale, particularly in China. About 85 per cent of global battery-cell manufacturing capacity was in China in 2024.
That scale has helped to drive down prices, making established lithium-ion technology cheaper and quicker to deploy than newer technologies being developed by British companies. 
The white gold rush: how lithium became our most precious metal
The debate is not simply about whether Britain needs more batteries, but which technologies it needs, and whether the government should take account of the wider economic benefits of developing them in Britain when deciding how to build the system. 
Andrew Bowie, the shadow energy minister, accused the government of sacrificing growing British companies and jobs in its pursuit of net zero. 
“The government can do one of two things: they can either reindustrialise this country and prioritise British jobs and manufacturing, or they can sprint towards an unachievable pie-in-the-sky target of green power by 2030,” he said.
He accused Labour of relying on technology “imported, supplied and developed overseas”.
Not everyone is so critical of Ofgem’s Long Duration Electricity Storage scheme, however. The London-based Statera Energy had three projects given the provisional green light in the scheme: a pumped storage hydro project in Scotland, based at Loch Ness; and two battery projects that use lithium-ion technology.
Tom Vernon, chief executive of Statera, said: “LDES provides a cost-effective solution that avoids the need for more of these very expensive overhead lines and network reinforcement.”
Statera sources batteries from South Korea and China, which Vernon said offered “a significant cost advantage”.
“Our suppliers have all been very reliable and deliver a high-quality product, which is safe,” he said. However, he added: “At all stages we are doing as much as we can to onshore supply chains.”
Thursday’s dinner was also a chance for industry leaders to swap theories about what might happen next. One diner said the dominant hypotheses were that Ofgem would either add some projects that support UK manufacturing to the ones already selected, or it would consider making a secondary round of support available in 2027.
A spokesperson for Ofgem said: “Long duration electricity storage is essential to a cleaner, more secure and flexible electricity system.
“Our provisional decisions are based on a rigorous, evidence-led assessment using published criteria to identify the projects that deliver the greatest overall benefits for consumers and the energy system, including potential benefits they could bring to the British economy.
“We are carefully considering feedback to our consultation before publishing our final decisions.”
A spokesperson for the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero, which is thought to be keen to prioritise projects that can deliver quickly, said: “The clean energy transition is a reindustrialising force for communities, creating 400,000 jobs and boosting British supply chains, while cutting our reliance on global fossil fuel markets.” '

The Times has a piece on BICS under the headline 'Help for business energy bills won’t go as far after Iran strikes'.
We thought we'd refresh our memories on who pays for BICS.
BICS will remove certain electricity-policy costs from the bills of qualifying energy-intensive manufacturers - potentially saving them up to £600 million a year.
But those costs do not simply disappear.
Normally, if some electricity users stop paying levies, the cost would be redistributed among the remaining electricity consumers. The Government says it does not intend that to happen with BICS.
Instead, the cost is to be covered through a combination of:
Savings elsewhere in the energy system, including changing Renewables Obligation and Feed-in Tariff indexation from RPI to CPI and removing Carbon Price Support from electricity bills.
Exchequer funding (general government funding/taxation), which will be paid to the Low Carbon Contracts Company (LCCC).
The Exchequer money will reduce the amount LCCC needs to collect through the CfD Supplier Obligation. In simple terms:
Treasury money → LCCC → lower CfD levy on suppliers → less cost passed through electricity bills.
So the £600m is not simply £600m being taken off electricity bills and nor is it £600m coming entirely from taxation.
It is a transfer of the burden of electricity-policy costs away from qualifying manufacturers, with the Government using a mixture of energy-system savings and Exchequer funding to prevent the cost being shifted onto other electricity consumers.
The important figure we don't yet know is how much of the £600m will ultimately come from the Exchequer. The Government has said the detailed funding requirement will be set out alongside the BICS Impact Assessment and at the Autumn 2026 Budget.
That makes the Budget on 28 October particularly interesting: the key number to look for is the actual Exchequer contribution to BICS, rather than simply the headline £600m annual cost of the scheme.
We will be listening carefully to the Budget in October, and studying the accompanying detail which comes out with it.  
https://www.thetimes.com/business/energy/article/business-energy-bills-help-scheme-iran-kmvn7gcm5?utm_source=Sailthru&utm_medium=email&utm_campaign=Business%20Sun%2020%20Sep%202026&utm_term=audience_BUSINESS
'A landmark scheme to cut £600 million from electricity bills for 10,000 businesses will be far less generous than intended due to rising energy prices, the government has been warned.
The British Industrial Competitiveness Scheme (Bics) aims to cut electricity bills by up to 25 per cent by giving relief from green levies for businesses which meet criteria for the amount of the energy they use and the types of products they manufacture. The government expects the scheme to cost £600 million a year until it ends in 2035.
Brokers said the government would be deluged with applications when the portal for applications opens on October 1, with businesses able to apply until November 30 ahead of the scheme’s launch in April.
But, business groups are warning that the scheme will be less valuable to companies than when it was announced as part of the government’s industrial strategy in 2025, because wholesale energy prices have rocketed since the outbreak of the Iran war.
Paul Wilson, policy director at the Federation of Small Businesses, said: “As a proportion of bills, Bics will be less than would be anticipated prior to the Middle East crisis. We’ve seen wholesale prices basically double since the end of February [when the war began]”.
Patrick Matthewson, senior policy manager at lobby group MakeUK, said that while the scheme was “well intended” it did not go far enough. “It was proposed as part of the industrial strategy and in a different set of circumstances: we didn’t have the Iran war, we didn’t have this massive increase in energy costs coming”.
October is a key month with many business’s electricity contracts coming up for renewal. Liam Conway, managing director of broker Greenfields Energy, said that prices had moved dramatically in recent months. He gave the example of a client whose current electricity contract cost £136,000 a month and was due for renewal. The customer faced a rise to £188,615 at prices quoted in June, but that quote has now risen to £211,349.
Pursuit of net zero has failed to cut British energy bills
Conway has been contacted by 300 companies preparing applications for Bics and said that even if the scheme was less generous than intended it was “still a phenomenal benefit”.
Allan Isherwood, business development director at energy and sustainability adviser Eyebright Utilities, said he had seen strong interest from businesses looking for information about Bics. “It could provide valuable support for qualifying businesses at a time when energy costs remain a significant concern,” he said.
A government spokesperson said: “The scheme will reduce electricity bills by up to 25 per cent for over 10,000 manufacturing businesses, and we will review the scheme in 2030 to assess how well it is operating and improving competitiveness for businesses.” '

A comprehensive piece in the Telegraph under the heading 'Britain’s rush to net zero fuelled China’s energy dominance'
https://www.telegraph.co.uk/.../britains-rush-to-net.../...
'Walkers ambling along the Saxon Shore Way can’t miss the Cleve Hill solar farm.
Standing on the north Kent coast, near Faversham, its hundreds of thousands of panels stretch as far as the eye can see, covering the equivalent of 500 football pitches.
The 370-megawatt scheme is the biggest of its kind in Britain, generating enough power for some 100,000 homes on sunny days.
It is one of a number of mega-projects springing up as part of the push towards net zero, with Quinbrook, the developer, saying it supports “growth, jobs and cheaper power for UK households”.
However, another trend that Cleve Hill typifies is less remarked upon by its owners: the spread of Chinese technology through Britain’s power system.
According to planning documents and photographs, the project’s 550,000 panels were produced in China, by Trina Solar, along with its battery systems and solar inverters (made by CATL and Huawei, respectively).
This is not unusual. China has a vice-like grip on global supply chains, producing almost 90pc of panels and controlling even bigger shares of mid-level manufacturing.
But according to critics, the scheme underlines how Britain’s rush towards clean power risks giving Beijing critical leverage over the UK energy system, because China provides masses of cheap solar panels, minerals, batteries and electric vehicles needed to power it.
There is no suggestion of wrongdoing by the companies involved at Cleve Hill. But some experts are concerned that Chinese suppliers – beholden to Beijing at home – could build “back doors” into software running on energy projects, or hide components that are excluded from equipment schematics.
Perhaps just as worryingly, others fear it will leave Britain exposed to diplomatic and trade policy coercion, as UK jobs and infrastructure increasingly depend on Chinese goodwill.
Labour ministers say their clean power plan – to produce almost all the UK’s electricity with green energy by 2030 – will break Britain’s addiction to gas produced by “petrostates and dictators”, and insulate us from price shocks that have followed recent crises in Ukraine and Iran.
They have claimed it is possible to be vigilant about the risks posed by China, while using its cheap goods to deliver cheaper power.
The question within Whitehall and other European capitals is: can we safely harness Chinese green technology – or are we naively trading our fossil-fuel dependency for a different vice altogether?
“The excessive amount of electricity you can create from the sun and the wind will be transformative for our economies, our lifestyles, everything,” says Caspar Hobhouse, an analyst at the European Union Institute for Security Studies.
“But if you’re buying it from China, you have to be aware you are surrendering a lot of your grid and capabilities to someone who then has control over how this works.
“You have to understand that there are two sides to this coin.”
Britain and China took fundamentally different approaches to net zero from the start.
This country pledged emissions cuts under the 1997 Kyoto Protocol, then passed the Climate Change Act 2008, introducing legally binding carbon budgets.
In 2019, the UK became the first country to enshrine a 2050 net zero target in law, compelling every arm of the state to work towards that goal.
Britain also developed policies and subsidies to encourage demand for renewable electricity. The Renewable Obligation, launched in 2002, handed generous top-up payments to wind and solar farms for the electricity they generated, funded by levies on consumer bills.
A feed-in tariff came after in 2010, paying households and businesses for rooftop solar power. Contracts for difference, launched four years later, then offered renewable schemes guaranteed power prices.
Yet what was conspicuously absent, despite Britain’s position at the vanguard of the transition, was any accompanying plan to boost manufacturing of green technologies.
It has been largely foreign companies, such as Denmark’s Vestas and Germany’s Siemens Gamesa, that have built the 12,000 wind turbines erected in the past two decades.
A 2023 government report found that the UK’s share of capital spending on projects “rarely” exceeded 25pc. UK Steel separately found that “almost none” of the steel used in British wind farms was domestically produced.
By some measures, the green energy rollout has still been a success – our carbon emissions have fallen by around 50pc since 1990 and a study for the Confederation of British Industry last year found net zero supports more than one million jobs.
But this has coincided with a halving of manufacturing’s share of national output, so it has arguably come with significant costs as well.
Beijing’s Communist government, by contrast, has taken a command-and-control approach to the green transition, with a heavy focus on production and abundant, cheap energy.
China was outside the World Trade Organisation and classed as a developing country when Kyoto was agreed.
And while the UK has pledged to cut emissions by 81pc on 1990 levels by 2035, China has only promised a 7pc-10pc reduction from an undefined peak by then (and net zero by 2060).
This is because, experts say, China’s primary reason for adopting clean energy is not to cut carbon emissions but to insulate itself from geopolitical pressure.
In 2003, Hu Jintao, China’s then president, warned of the “Malacca dilemma”: the dependence on a shipping corridor that Beijing could not control.
About two thirds of China’s trade passes through the South-East Asian strait, including oil and gas from the Gulf, while US naval vessels ply the same waters.
Beijing has responded by seeking to reduce its reliance on imported energy. From this strategic concern, China’s green energy revolution was born, says Sam Geall, an expert on Chinese energy at Chatham House, a think tank.
“Most of what China’s done can be explained in terms of its own national self-interest, rather than in terms of what has happened at the UN,” he says.
China viewed renewable energy as a means of reducing its reliance on chokepoints, such as Hormuz and Malacca, and volatile prices set by cartels and conflict. By adopting electrified technologies, such as electric vehicles (EVs), it could become less dependent on supplies of foreign fuels.
“It was always quite geostrategic, and always had quite a hard edge,” Geall says.
After widespread power shortages in the early 2000s, Beijing also sought both greater efficiency and more generating capacity.
A 2005 renewable energy law gave provincial governments incentives to go green, unlocking investment in utility-scale wind power.
“For the first time, it was at utility scale. And it was about energy security,” says Philip Andrews-Speed, of the Oxford Institute for Energy Studies.
Then in 2006, China became the world’s largest greenhouse gas emitter and pressure grew to join the West’s bandwagon.
Beijing still resisted challenging climate goals, arguing that a developing economy should not shoulder too much of the burden. But in 2011, renewable energy and transport electrification became major parts of the Communist Party’s five-year plan, unleashing even more state support.
So far, so planned. But from this point, Beijing was also fortunate.
Europe was also embracing the green revolution. Beijing saw an export opportunity, and backed its own manufacturers. And the Europeans regarded Chinese raw materials and finished products as a much cheaper way to meet their targets.
“There are a number of critical minerals where there is refining and processing and industries across the world,” Geall says. “But many countries then just said, ‘Actually, we’ll just let China handle that.’”
China’s growing dominance of these supply chains was “a happy coincidence, and benign neglect on the part of other countries that allowed it to happen”.
Jane Nakano, of the Centre for Strategic and International Studies, agrees. “I don’t think it was necessarily any nefarious strategy. There was an opportunity that the Chinese enterprises could seize on, capitalise on.”
But after Donald Trump became US president in 2016, Beijing increasingly saw control of supply chains as imperative.
Its “Made in China” strategy focused on winning the race for technological supremacy, accelerating the development of wind, solar, battery storage and electric vehicles.
China has since become the world’s largest builder of renewable energy. While Britain hopes to have up to 126 gigawatts (GW) of wind and solar capacity by 2030, China is building more than 400 GW a year, according to the International Energy Agency.
Wind and solar now generate almost a quarter of its electricity. This demand has created large domestic industries, with Chinese companies accounting for about 78pc of wind turbines built worldwide.
Yet China also continues to consume vast quantities of coal, unlike Britain, which has closed its coal plants and taxes gas generation.
Chinese coal consumption hit 4,953 million tonnes in 2024, and the “dirty” fuel still provides 54pc of China’s electricity, although its share is shrinking.
Meanwhile, the electrification of transport is gathering pace. EVs now make up two-thirds of new car sales in China and one-quarter of new truck sales.
On the world stage, China is also converting green energy into diplomatic clout.
As Western aid and climate finance budgets shrink, it has started to present itself as an ally to poorer, developing countries, offering them cheap finance and technology while accusing the West of hypocrisy, Oxford’s Geall says.
This is good business, too. Chinese net zero tech and EV exports to South East Asia have surged as countries, such as Vietnam, Indonesia and Malaysia, seek to reduce their dependence on Gulf oil and gas.
China’s clean energy industry generated $2.1tn (£1.6tn) in economic output in 2025, according to the Helsinki-based Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air, equivalent to 11.4pc of its GDP and driving one-third of its economic growth.
But its dominance now poses major problems for European governments, as the spread of Chinese technology starts to erode the market shares of Western firms.
The demise of Germany’s solar industry offers the starkest case of how China can obliterate the competition.
Europe’s biggest economy commanded 21pc of global solar panel manufacturing in 2007, supporting 111,000 jobs.
But after China poured tens of billions of state-backed financing into solar, panel prices plunged and the centre of gravity shifted.
Saxony-Anhalt-based Q-Cells, once the world’s largest solar cell producer, collapsed in 2012. Other German companies soon followed.
Today, China controls 93pc of polysilicon manufacturing, 97pc of wafers, 92pc of cells and 86pc of panels, according to the Washington-based Center for Strategic and International Studies. It also controls 80pc to 90pc of the market for solar production tools.
The lesson here is that once an industrial ecosystem has been lost to China it is extremely difficult to rebuild, argues Sander Tordoir, the chief economist at the Centre for European Reform.
And Europe can no longer assume it can simply import low-value components while retaining the high-value production items for itself, he adds, pointing to the way that China has gone on to control both solar panel manufacturing and production of the machines used to make them.
“European governments have to think very carefully about ecosystem effects,” he adds.
China has been able to build “massive industrial capabilities in the lower rungs of clean tech”, he says, before moving into the “higher rungs of the value chain”.
This has also been the case in EVs, he adds, where China started off producing low-value car parts and batteries – and now dominates the sector.
In Germany again, cut-throat competition from Chinese rivals, such as BYD, is forcing the once-invincible Volkswagen to cut tens of thousands of jobs and close factories to become more competitive.
This time around, the EU has been more defensive and put tariffs on Chinese EVs to mitigate the flood of imports.
Across green industries, Tordoir says, time is running out to protect domestic industries. He is in favour of policies such as the “Made in Europe” framework, which will funnel subsidies towards European carmakers, while requiring 70pc or more of components to be sourced on the Continent.
Even stricter rules have been imposed in America, where the use of Chinese “connected vehicle” components – which could be used to transmit data with the internet – are to be banned.
Hobhouse, at the European Union Institute for Security Studies, also agrees that Britain and its allies need to ensure alternatives to Chinese suppliers survive, particularly in sectors such as wind where Europe still maintains some strength.
That is becoming more difficult as China’s companies attempt to muscle in on the Continent’s markets with turbines that are up to 45pc cheaper.
Research by the Oxford Institute of Energy Studies has found that Chinese turbine makers have reduced their costs from $1,200 per kilowatt in 2019 to less than $420 today, compared with more than $1,000 per kilowatt in Europe.
Companies such as Mingyang have also expressed a desire to supply turbines to key markets, including the UK, where there were plans to build a floating wind farm off the coast of Scotland using Chinese technology.
Its £1.5bn plan was ultimately blocked by government ministers, on the grounds of security concerns, although there is no suggestion of wrongdoing by Mingyang.
The company is lobbying for a reversal. Meanwhile, Chinese companies continue to supply solar farm kit, batteries and grid equipment to Britain and its allies.
Roughly 70pc of the UK’s operational grid-scale batteries in 2024 were Chinese-made, according to research by Modo Energy. The biggest suppliers by far were CATL and BYD.
Hobhouse, however, argues that relying so heavily on China carries unquantified risks, pointing to reports last year that secret so-called kill switches were found inside Chinese-made solar power inverters in the US. These cellular radios were capable of remotely turning the devices off.
“The ability and the capability is very much there,” adds Hobhouse. “So then it’s a question of whether you’re willing to stomach the risk.”
The European Commission has previously said that 70pc of inverters installed in Europe come from China, with two companies – Huawei and Sungrow – together controlling more than half the market.
Luke de Pulford, the head of the Inter-Parliamentary Alliance on China, says that Xi Jinping, the Chinese president, has explicitly stated a desire to control supply chains and use them for leverage.
“I do not know why we have walked headlong into this trap,” he says.
Yet pushing back against Chinese net zero equipment may also provoke protests from energy companies, who have argued that reducing competition will push up energy prices.
Hobhouse argues that this “security premium” is worth stomaching.
“You can’t just allow things to hinge on [price],” he says. “It’s not huge values, if you look at the inverter costs, it’s probably about 5pc more, which is relatively small.”
“With wind turbines, it’s a little bit different, but not massively more,” Hobhouse says, adding that the cost of not being secure, or being beholden to China, is far higher, he says.
Dan Marks, at the Royal United Services Institute, says the UK Government should also lay out a more coherent China strategy, instead of making ad hoc decisions about firms such as Mingyang or the Sizewell C nuclear power station, where China General Nuclear was ousted as an investor.
“It keeps happening,” he says. “But if they looked at it more seriously up front and were more hard-nosed about it, there’d be less delays.”
For example, according to Marks, the National Wealth Fund indicated that it was open to joint investment with Japan, South Korea and China in battery production.
“But again, will that really stand? Or will they just waste loads of time trying to get Chinese investment, and ultimately annoy their Chinese counterparts more?”
Still, Chinese firms themselves don’t appear happy to take a back seat.
In the UK, BYD is investing in a national network of EV charging stations and fellow Chinese giant CATL has partnered with Octopus Energy, Britain’s biggest energy supplier, to build battery-swapping stops for lorries up and down the country.
Octopus, which previously sought to partner with Mingyang in the UK, has argued that any concerns posed by Chinese technology can be mitigated through tight cyber security and corporate governance practices. It says that neither CATL nor Mingyang would have access to British data.
“We shouldn’t be naive about the security risks,” says Greg Jackson, the company’s founder.
“But we shouldn’t be naive about China’s lead in energy technologies, either – not through state subsidy but outstanding research and development.”
He points out that some of Britain’s most sensitive conversations and data are already carried on iPhones made by Apple in China and yet “we’ve found ways to secure them”.
“Surely we can do the same with less-sophisticated hardware like wind turbines and batteries,” he adds.
“We now need to grit our teeth and do the same with China in energy – with all the appropriate safeguards – to catch up rather than be left behind.”
So far Britain has hesitated to take a tough line on China’s dominance of the materials and kit needed to deliver net zero – or, indeed, on almost any Chinese imports.
Unlike the rest of Europe, it has placed no additional tariffs on imported Chinese cars, which are now some of the most popular on sale in the UK.
In the first eight months of 2026 alone, vehicle brands, such as BYD, Jaecoo and Geely, tripled their market share to 11.7pc of new car sales – up from 3.8pc during the same period in 2025.
European firms continue to complain this is down to the artificially low prices offered by Chinese brands, who are in search of export markets amid vicious price wars back home.
But Labour ministers say that pushing back would be counterproductive, as Beijing would retaliate against British companies, such as Aston Martin, Jaguar Land Rover and Bentley.
“If you put trade protections up, you’ve got to understand that they’ll probably be reciprocated and you’ll lose out,” Jonathan Reynolds, the Business Secretary, told The Telegraph last week.
But Britain also runs a risk if it takes its economic weapons off the table.
In an echo of the row about Huawei telecoms equipment a decade ago, some have warned that becoming too dependent on Chinese technology could prompt a painful – and expensive – reckoning should Washington decide to impose tariffs or other export controls.
Donald Trump, the US president, like his predecessor Joe Biden, has pressured allies to put national security and economic sovereignty priorities first.
This has included urging countries to block some Chinese investments in energy, telecommunications or infrastructure.
Washington, like Brussels, is wary of other markets becoming a conduit for cheap Chinese goods to enter their own.
“There’s a bigger risk for Britain in doing nothing on China. If Washington and Brussels conclude that Britain has become the back door for Chinese overcapacity, the squeeze comes from them instead,” says Alicia Kearns, the shadow foreign minister.
Kemi Badenoch, the Conservative leader, has called for Chinese technology to be banned from the energy system.
Yet this highlights another inherent tension between these security concerns and Britain’s current approach, which began under the Tories. UK government documents admit that without China, it will be all-but-impossible to meet official net zero goals.
Back in Kent, Cleve Hill is a prime example of this trade-off in action.
With so much Chinese technology already embedded in our energy system, Labour can only hope it won’t spectacularly backfire.'

As green energy continues to rampage across Scotland - its North, South, West and East - there is an intensifying pincer movement, determined that community voices will be properly heard and acted upon.
Coming at it from one angle are those Community Councils, speaking on behalf of their communities, who have banded together, as this article today in The Herald states - 'Rural revolt: 200 councils demand inquiry over Scots green revolution'.
We've posted details since the very first Highland Convention, led by Councillor Helen Crawford, right through to the most recent - the letter of 14th to Gillian Martin, signed by the five Community Council leads and Councillor Crawford.
The new concerns have been sparked by a July 21 letter to Highland community council convention leader Cameron Kemp, from the Scottish Government’s energy and climate change directorate asking the group to identify areas where communities had flagged a “high risk of negative impacts from further infrastructure development”. It also wanted feedback from communities already experiencing “multiple energy infrastructure proposals or developments” and how the “cumulative impacts” of those developments might be affecting them.  (Herald)
It said it wanted to ensure communities were “fully represented” in a final Strategic Spatial Energy Plan being drawn up to provide a "blueprint of Great Britain’s future energy system". (Herald)
Mr Kemp said: “This is a significant moment. The Scottish Government is now asking communities to identify cumulative impacts, spatial pressures and regional differences across Scotland. "But if that strategic evidence now needs to be gathered, the obvious question is: why has it not been properly examined before major infrastructure continued to be consented application by application?
"The Government is now asking communities to identify the very strategic and cumulative issues that a pan-Scotland planning inquiry commission should examine independently and transparently across Scotland.” (Herald)
We are mystified.  We had two posts during the week; one where we said that John Swinney had the wind up because the rumour was that only two of the six potential pathways covered Scotland's offshore wind farms and grid connections, and the other on the SSEP and the CSNP, the latter taking what the SSEP says and working out the transmission requirements from it.
Given that the six pathways will be presented by NESO to Miatta Fahnbulleh at some point between now and the year end, and will be put out to delayed consultation at some point in 2027, what opportunities will there be - and in what time frame - for Community Councils to have a proper and meaningful dialogue with the Scottish Government?  
It's very obvious that bodies previously set up to have dialogue with the Scottish Government and its planning bodies have very little real impact, if any, to speak of.  Despite our logical query above, we would hope, of course, that the Scottish Government is not proposing to treat the Convention members in the same manner.
But it is one major reason why planning must hold sway.  We asked the planning consultant Ian Kelly to give us a short summary of his thinking on the current and urgent priorities for action - the other, professional, arm of the pincer movement.
 1. A Moratorium
With the potential gross over provision of supply from the excess of installed and consented capacity going well beyond any predicted future demand, now would be a reasonable time to pause and think and to allow the late running National and Regional Energy Strategic Plans to catch up with events. However, the Scottish Government has consistently refused to implement any moratorium, maybe it is just the implications of that word that they do not like. But there is another way to effectively secure a moratorium, or maybe better to call it a pause for up to two years. If the Councillors on local planning authority committees could be persuaded to refuse or to object to every renewables application that comes before them then, on the evidence of what is already happening, the DPEA could not cope with the workload and very significant delays would result. The outcome would be the very much desired pause in a way that would not involve the Scottish Government. 
2. Scotland’s Regional Energy Strategic Plan
NESO are currently “recruiting’ for the Strategic Advisory Board and memberships of working groups in relation to preparing the Plan. SSE and Scottish Power are already making big plays on the importance of their investments and pressing for involvement. Therefore, it is essential that activists really encourage and push senior planning committee Councillors to look to be onboard with working groups and, very essentially on the Strategic Board too, both as individuals and through COSLA, or else the preparation of the Plan and its implementation will be dominated by industry interests. That must be avoided. We lack proper joined up thinking just now and it is essential that Councillors, as decision takers, look to ensure that there is a joined up Plan that represents everyone, especially communities, and a Plan that is then a material consideration in decisions.
3. Local Government Elections
Finally, and a key point. The Scottish Government elections are now history and we know the outcome. But we are only just over 7 months away from the date when local Councillors can be held to account as to whether or not they supported or harmed their constituent communities. This should be a key “keep this in mind” point when Councillors are being pressed by individuals or local groups for action in support of actions to pause or stop renewables projects.
Ian Kelly has applied to be a member of NESO's RESP Working Group.  His experience and knowledge would be invaluable, in our view, but we are conscious that experience and knowledge are not necessarily prerequisites of either the Scottish Government or the UK Government bodies; we will wait and see the outcome.

'A group representing 200 rural community councils have united to demand an independent inquiry into the impact of huge multi-billion green energy and electricity infrastructure projects across Scotland.
The move from The Rural Scotland Convention of Community Councils follows concerns that the Scottish Government is only now getting round to assessing the wider impact.
The group, which stretches across five areas of the country, with community councils groups in Highland, the South of Scotland, North East Scotland, Shetland and Perth & Kinross are demanding a pause on major energy developments in the meantime while raising new concerns with the Scottish Government.
It comes as the National Energy System Operator (NESO), the publicly owned organisation responsible for planning and operating Great Britain's energy system, has warned that Scotland’s electricity network does not have enough capacity to carry all the renewable power being generated to England where much of it is needed, with a key cross border link operating as a major bottleneck.
The main electricity connection between Scotland and England can currently carry 6.7GW of power. But NESO says around another 10GW of capacity is needed across the Scotland-England border to meet current demand.
The problem is already having an effect. When the network cannot carry all the electricity being generated in Scotland, wind farms can be ordered to reduce their output.
But the plans for expansion are meeting resistance.
The community councils' demands have been sparked by the Scottish Government in a July letter seen by The Herald to Cameron Kemp, lead community councillor for the Highland Convention asking to identify areas already facing energy developments to assess their combined impact.
This has prompted angry campaigners to ask why ministers are only now gathering evidence on problems they say should have been examined before major infrastructure was consented.
Calls for an inquiry are contained in a new letter to rural affairs secretary Gillian Martin and signed by the leads of five regional community council conventions.
The nucleus of the campaign had its roots in the Highland Council area where a movement of community councils demanded a summit with energy ministers in the summer of last year over a "barrage" of major renewable energy proposals. There are currently over 180 live applications ranging from wind and hydro projects to energy storage and transmission grid plans.
There are concerns at being "overwhelmed" by multiple, complex major applications, from well-funded overseas developers and domestic developers.
It has been described as a 'David and Goliath' experience with concerns raised that local democracy has been "overridden".
Helen Crawford, chairman of the Rural Scotland Convention of Community Councils, said: "This is not about stopping renewable energy. It is about whether Scotland is planning its energy transition properly.
"At some point, you have to step back and look at the whole picture. Communities across much of rural Scotland are now united in saying that time has come.
"This letter comes from a very simple concern: communities across rural Scotland are saying there is no overarching plan or proper assessment of cumulative impact to ensure that the right kit is put in the right place for the right reasons.
"We say that the Scottish Government needs to do its homework first. It now appears to be asking communities to provide the very evidence we have been saying is needed to understand the cumulative and regional impact of these developments.
"That makes the case for a pan-Scotland planning inquiry commission even stronger. Before more decisions are made piecemeal, the Government needs to properly understand the scale and cumulative impact of what is being proposed, so that the right infrastructure is put in the right place, rather than simply consenting projects one application at a time.
The demand comes as Scotland undergoes a massive expansion of the electricity network to carry power from new renewable developments to where it is needed.
SSEN Transmission’s Pathway to 2030 programme is worth about £29 billion and involves new overhead power lines, substations and other infrastructure across the north of Scotland. SSEN says the investment is required to increase the capacity of the transmission network as renewable electricity generation grows.
The scale of the programme has already produced a mixture of planning approvals, council refusals, appeals and public inquiries.
The new concerns have been sparked by a July 21 letter to Highland community council convention leader Cameron Kemp, from the Scottish Government’s energy and climate change directorate asking the group to identify areas where communities had flagged a “high risk of negative impacts from further infrastructure development”. It also wanted feedback from communities already experiencing “multiple energy infrastructure proposals or developments” and how the “cumulative impacts” of those developments might be affecting them.
It said it wanted to ensure communities were “fully represented” in a final Strategic Spatial Energy Plan being drawn up to provide a "blueprint of Great Britain’s future energy system".
Mr Kemp said: “This is a significant moment. The Scottish Government is now asking communities to identify cumulative impacts, spatial pressures and regional differences across Scotland. "But if that strategic evidence now needs to be gathered, the obvious question is: why has it not been properly examined before major infrastructure continued to be consented application by application?
"The Government is now asking communities to identify the very strategic and cumulative issues that a pan-Scotland planning inquiry commission should examine independently and transparently across Scotland.”
The community councils coalition has already begun gathering evidence in response to the Scottish Government’s request.
But it warns that the work is being carried out by elected community councillors who are unpaid volunteers.
They say that properly gathering and analysing evidence about the combined pressure created by infrastructure would require work beyond what could reasonably be expected of volunteers. And they have asked the Scottish Government to provide resources so that it can undertake the work properly.
Ms Crawford added: "We have identified the problem, we have set out a constructive solution, and we are asking the Scottish Government to use the powers it already has to address it.”
She added: “Community Councils across Highland, the South of Scotland, the North East, Shetland and Perth & Kinross have come together behind these asks. That is significant. "We are not asking someone else to solve this problem. We are asking the Scottish Government to use its own devolved powers to make sure that the strategic planning and evidence base are in place..."
SSEN said in June that around three-quarters of the planning applications required for its £29 billion programme had been approved, with several projects moving from development into delivery.
Among the most controversial plans is a new 400kV overhead electricity line running for more than 100 miles from Beauly through Blackhillock and New Deer to Peterhead.
The project is designed to carry more renewable electricity generated in the north of Scotland through the transmission network and on to areas of demand elsewhere in Britain.
The scheme will involve steel lattice towers, commonly known as pylons, along with new substations and converter stations. SSEN Transmission says the new line is needed to support the growth of onshore and offshore renewable energy and increase the capacity of the electricity network.
The company submitted its planning application to the Scottish Government in September 2025. A public consultation on the proposals closed in December, with objections submitted by Highland and Moray councils. The pylons are expected to average around 57 metres (187ft) in height, according to SSEN's project information.
The application has now been referred to the Scottish Government's directorate for planning and environmental appeals for a public local inquiry. Once that process is complete, it will be considered by Scottish ministers, who will make the final decision on whether the project gets consent.
There is currently no decision on the scheme and no confirmed date for one.
A Scottish Government spokesman said: "Where new development proposals come forward, our Fourth National Planning Framework (NPF4) ensures the impacts of proposals on communities and nature, including cumulative impacts, are important considerations in the decision-making process.  "All applications are subject to site specific assessments on a case by case basis." '

Yesterday, Allison Pearson had an article in The Telegraph - 'Net zero is a national suicide pact' with a sub-heading 'I implore Andy Burnham: please find just 30 minutes to watch this devastating analysis of Britain’s energy policy by the former head of MI6'.
That's Sir Richard Dearlove whose lecture we posted last week.
Burnham has been bumping his gums on net zero.  Allison Pearson says:
Andy Burnham said this week that the country must fully commit itself to reaching net zero by 2050. “I am determined that we meet the commitment on which Labour was elected… I want Britain to believe in itself again.”
His ignorance is staggering. The Prime Minister was talking dangerous tosh, timed to woo Green voters in the forthcoming Holborn and St Pancras by-election.
The PM might be new; the zealotry isn't.  And neither is the disregard for security.

'Greenhouse gas effect, global warming, climate change, global heating (a new one on me), climate emergency, net zero. The terms for the forthcoming apocalypse change every few years. Who now remembers the briefly famous “hole in the ozone layer” caused when an entire generation of teenage girls tried to copy Farrah Fawcett’s iconic 1970s feathered hair and used several trillion cans of hairspray to unsuccessfully (in my case anyway) keep the flicked-back sides in place? Did the hole heal when girls moved on to imitating Jennifer Aniston’s “The Rachel” cut, which could be achieved without assistance from aerosols?
Admittedly, Farrah’s Fringe is not a scientifically proven explanation for the phenomenon, but, if you ask me, it’s every bit as plausible as some of the theories accounting for changes in what we used to call “the weather”. Anyway, after almost 20 years of hysterical banging on about the need to reach “net zero” by 2050 lest 70 million Britons start to resemble the crusty bits in a fish-fryer, a cross-party House of Commons committee this week recommended the Government stop using the phrase because it had become “toxic among the public”.
Well, hallelujah! Was this a rare and welcome outbreak of sanity among the climate cultists who were finally acknowledging that decarbonisation and running a successful G7 economy are not, given the present state of technology, compatible? Don’t get your hopes up, please. The committee of MPs suggested finding a new phrase for the same old nonsense. Because “net zero” no longer had a positive image with the public and consensus over the transition to clean energy had broken down amid “misinformation from sceptics”.
Gosh, cults are remarkably impervious to reason, aren’t they? If “net zero” has become toxic, it’s because, despite an overwhelming media consensus designed to stifle debate, the public has managed to pick up pieces of information from those pesky sceptics. People can see for themselves the effect of net zero in their vertiginous energy bills. They can see that the cost of electricity (among the highest in the world) is destroying manufacturing (Denby Pottery, established 1809, is only the latest casualty).
They also realise that reducing 0.8 per cent of the world’s CO2 – the UK’s puny contribution – is going to have no effect on the climate, not when our competitors are busy building coal-fired power stations and increasing their emissions like billy-o. As for paying Norway £20bn a year for oil and gas when we could drill our own in neighbouring North Sea fields, has any nation ever conspired so successfully in its own downfall?
Consumers, it turns out, don’t care to be patronised by scientifically illiterate MPs, mouthing the approved dogma, when people like me have been pointing out that green taxes are slapped on bills to subsidise Ed Miliband’s renewables cronies. As for what the Commons’ committee calls “tangible wins” such as new jobs – there are, indeed, thousands of green jobs. Unfortunately, most of them are in the People’s Republic of China (PRC) where, unsurprisingly, the UK’s 2050 net zero target is hugely popular. “Never interrupt your enemy when he is in the middle of making a mistake.”
Sir Richard Dearlove quoted that acrid line in his devastating lecture for the Global Warming Policy Foundation (of which I am a board member) in London on Wednesday night. In “Energy Security: Blowing in the Wind”, the former head of MI6, who is one of our best geopolitical brains, outlined in excruciating detail the epic folly of British climate policy, which has failed to give sufficient weight to the strategic vulnerabilities created by dependence on foreign manufacturing, imported components and a national grid that is increasingly at the mercy of whether the sun shines or the wind blows (but not too hard!).
The implications for national security are dire. Deindustrialisation, Dearlove pointed out, has not only led to the closure of vast tracts of our manufacturing capability. In the event of an emergency, we have lost much of the ability to rebuild our own energy infrastructure. (“Uncertain access to equipment and spares – for example, generators and transformers – is a graver and more chronic danger than a temporary shortage of gas.”) Should we experience the blackouts many experts predict for this winter, it won’t be the brief, homework-by-candlelight affair some of us remember from childhood. During the three-day week in 1974, thanks to the large interruptible load, a shortage could be absorbed by factories rather than households, but that ability has been lost in the reckless rush to decarbonisation.
After a major blackout in the Iberian peninsula last year, it took approximately 23 hours for Spain’s electricity grid to be fully declared back to normal. There seems little hope that a Britain diminished by the destruction of its power stations (and the loss of its ability to make virgin steel at Port Talbot) in the cause of net zero would be able to rescue a similar situation that speedily. “We have very little industry left to protect and we cannot rebuild non-existent industries which lie in foreign jurisdictions,” was the former spy chief’s bleak assessment.
The well-informed audience was clearly shocked as Dearlove painted a humiliating picture of the UK having to join a queue for materials and components (“large-scale transformers ordered today now take two years to arrive”), often from “the very country which the director general of MI5 has identified as the most serious threat to Britain’s national security”.
The degree to which the United Kingdom has become China’s bitch should horrify us all. Dearlove would not use such vulgar language, of course, although his angry disbelief was felt in fact after damning fact; at one point, he did answer a question with a pithy: “We’re screwed.” Asked whether China could turn off the lights in the lecture theatre where we sat, he said they probably could, and he suggested PRC spies had infiltrated climate-change groups, just as Russian spies penetrated CND during the Cold War.
I urge you to watch Dearlove’s powerful lecture for yourself. All I can say is he left those of us in his audience badly shaken. Richard Tice, deputy leader of Reform UK (he coined “net stupid zero”), is normally an upbeat fellow, but he confessed: “I am really anxious. It’s unreal how stupid our leaders have been for decades.”
Should there be significant power cuts this winter, Tice said Reform “will demand a general election and criminal prosecutions for negligence and malfeasance in public office”.
Both Reform and the Conservatives have sensibly said they will scrap Theresa May’s 2050 target made legally binding by the Climate Change Act 2008. Maybe then arguably the greatest act of national self-harm in the history of these islands can begin to be repaired. Except Andy Burnham said this week that the country must fully commit itself to reaching net zero by 2050. “I am determined that we meet the commitment on which Labour was elected… I want Britain to believe in itself again.”
His ignorance is staggering. The Prime Minister was talking dangerous tosh, timed to woo Green voters in the forthcoming Holborn and St Pancras by-election. For the same party-before-country reason, Andy has also postponed a decision to approve the development of the Jackdaw gas field in the North Sea.
“I urge our leading politicians to take very careful note,” Sir Richard Dearlove said. “We are not the victims of a conspiracy to make us vulnerable; we have quite casually done this to ourselves. We have, as a nation, negligently wandered close to a cliff edge and the adversaries I have described stand ready to help us over it; and the fragility of the present international order enhances the risk.”
Are you listening to the man who has forgotten more about national security than you will ever know, Prime Minister? You really should. The phrase “net zero” has not been discredited by “misinformation”, but by reality. Net zero will not happen by 2050, but the doomed pursuit of that target will cause untold economic damage, give comfort to our enemies and discomfort our own people. Don’t change the phrase, change the crazy policy. The cliff edge is frighteningly close.'

LOCAL GOVERNMENT REFORM – AND WHAT COULD IT MEAN FOR RENEWABLE ENERGY PLANNING?
The Scottish Government has published a proposal for fundamental reform of local government. It is very much at the discussion stage, but there are some parts which could have significant implications for planning and major infrastructure projects.
The proposal is for Scotland's existing local authorities to be replaced by '6–10 regional authorities', alongside '120–160 community authorities'.
The proposed division of responsibilities is particularly interesting.
The regional authorities would have responsibility for matters including 'strategic planning, regional economic development, housing and infrastructure', working alongside a proposed 'national planning hub'.
Community authorities would have responsibility for more local matters, including 'householder planning applications, community planning and licensing'.
That raises an obvious question for large renewable energy and electricity infrastructure projects.
Where would applications for major wind farms, BESS, substations and transmission infrastructure actually sit within this new structure? Would they become primarily matters for the new regional authorities? What would happen to the present role of individual planning authorities, DPEA and Scottish Ministers?
The document does not answer those questions yet.
Indeed, the Scottish Government makes clear that these are proposals intended to stimulate discussion, not its final position. It wants to reach a shared direction on reform before the end of this year - so it says - with more detailed proposals to follow.
There is therefore no basis yet for saying that renewable energy planning is about to be removed from councils.
But it is something worth watching very closely.
The proposal would represent a substantial shift towards regional strategic decision-making, while simultaneously promising greater decision-making at community level.
For those of us concerned about how major energy developments are assessed, scrutinised and determined, the important question will be how that balance is eventually drawn and who exercises the strategic planning power.
We will be watching.
https://www.gov.scot/publi.../public-sector-reform-proposal/

records.bodyText:
The Institute for Fiscal Studies adds weight to the growing questions over the cost of the 2030 clean-power target.
It has warned that the Government's drive to almost completely decarbonise the electricity system by 2030 risks pushing electricity costs higher than necessary.
The IFS is not arguing against the UK's 2050 net-zero target. Its concern is the speed and sequencing of the transition.
Grid upgrade and balancing costs are entering what the IFS calls a 'crunch' period. Together they cost around £7 billion a year in 2024–25 and are expected to rise by around £12 billion a year by 2030–31.
A major part of the problem is that renewable generation - particularly wind in the north - is being added faster than the transmission network can carry the electricity south, hence the swingeing constraint payments and the costs of conventional generation to balance the grid.
The IFS says that pushing electricity to decarbonise faster than other sectors may not be the cheapest way of achieving the UK's overall emissions objectives. A slower route to a low-carbon electricity grid could still be compatible with net zero by 2050, while reducing some of the immediate cost pressures.
Coming immediately after the National Audit Office's warning about the cost of the 2030 target, this is another significant intervention in the debate over whether Britain is trying to build its generation and grid infrastructure too much, too quickly - and at consumers' expense.
Moreover, rapidly expanding renewables when the grid is already struggling to integrate existing capacity does risk exacerbating near-term cost increases, especially when there are already concerns about the timely delivery of existing grid upgrades (National Audit Office, 2026). (IFS report)
https://ifs.org.uk/publications/electricity-prices

We were struck by one word in particular in an excellent piece from Hebridean Horizon, but we've added 'intentional' to it.  The article is entitled 'The Scale of Community Effort and The Human Cost' and is focused on the fight to save the waters surrounding the islands off the West coast of Scotland from SP's Machair Wind proposal.
The group has done so well in their campaign.  And what they say is recognisable to every campaign group and Community Councils too - lay people having to become as expert as they can be in a multiplicity of fields; wading through thousands of pages of technical material, many of whom are holding down jobs and/or juggling domestic and family needs, too.
It's not a level playing field.  This is one extract from the Hebridean Horizon piece:
By the time the detailed MachairWind consultation opened, we were already on the back foot. The developer has been able to work on MachairWind over years, with professional teams, consultants and communications resources behind it – communities do not enter the process with equivalent resources.  And the imbalance begins even earlier.
W1 – the proposed site of MachairWind – was identified by the Scottish Government through its strategic marine planning process before communities were faced with the detailed MachairWind proposal. Scottish Government’s own guidance says island communities should be meaningfully engaged from the outset when decisions may affect them, yet this simply did not happen – the strategic consultation amounted to two emails, neither of which conveyed the significance of W1 for Iona and the neighbouring islands.
We are going back to 2008 and the submission from Jane and Julian Davis to the House of Lords Economic Affairs Committee:
We are quite sure that the Government has no concept of the immense amount of time, money and emotional energy expended by villagers, in the vicinity of each inappropriate application. People are trying not only to protect the visual amenity of the area in which they live, but also not to lose the very thing which they have spent their lives working and saving for, notably an environment that promotes the health and well-being of families, as well as the peace, tranquillity and amenity of their homes and gardens. (And fast forward to 2026 - of their seascapes and marine businesses, too).
And on public local inquiries:
They (developers) employ barristers and their legal teams, in addition to an array of planning consultants, often for extended periods. Local authorities and campaign groups struggle to represent local concerns and protect community well-being, even though financial resources are stretched and strained to accommodate this process. Such unequal financial burdens may already be affecting the ability of many councils to address such responsibilities. Many will be unable to fund proper defence of decisions through the Appeal Courts.
We've been looking at the extraordinary volume of material being placed on to the DPEA by SSEN - everything except the kitchen sink.  And that is only some documents which makes it to the website - not everything submitted to Objective Connect (the file sharing facility used by all parties submitting to the inquiries) gets on to the website, it seems. 
The Community Council Convention, asked by the Scottish Government's Directorate for Energy & Climate Change  (belatedly - indecently belatedly in our view) to address the three areas as per our image, has demanded the resource to do so.
Councillor Helen Crawford stated in a post at the beginning of the month:
We are seeing Community Councils across Highland having to raise funds simply to ensure that they can PARTICIPATE in the planning process as communities face proposals backed by organisations with vastly greater resources.
We often hear how this is a “David and Goliath” situation.
Community Councils are the first tier of our democratic structure. They are closest to the communities they represent, yet when faced with the scale and complexity of the infrastructure now being proposed, they find themselves having to put out a begging bowl to fund the professional advice and expertise needed to make their communities’ case.
Back to Hebridean Horizon for the final words:
We will keep doing what this process asks of us for as long as we have to.
But we shouldn’t have to.
https://www.hebrideanhorizon.co.uk/.../community-effort.../
