Bang on cue, following our earlier post about the imbalance experienced by communities, comes this e mail from the planning consultant Ian Kelly to the DPEA, copies to SSE and The Highland Council, following the DPEA issuing a Procedure Notice following the PIM on the Spittal to Beauly OHL - in images.
Good morning,
I write on behalf of the objector group that I represent.
This overall proposal of the OHL and Hubs is the largest ever, most expensive ever (using electricity bill payers’ monies), and most environmentally damaging renewable energy project in the Highlands. It has resulted in very strong statutory consultee objections and considerable public objections. It deserves to be the subject of the most careful and holistic consideration, including taking full account of the views of the public. Instead it is being made the subject of a rushed PLI conducted in line with a clear political agenda that is being masqueraded as guidance. The Procedure Notice issued late yesterday simply confirms that the process is fundamentally inadequate. My clients are of the very firm view that such a process should not be happening.
In that context, my client group of community interests who will be directly affected by this proposal have already invested considerable amounts of their own time and, and unlike SSEN, they are now self financing consultancy advice through crowd funding efforts.
Reviewing all of the correspondence, including the latest Procedure Notice, my clients do not have the necessary confidence that the Reporters, acting independently, will either rigorously control and limit the lodging of Inquiry documents (three weeks after the process started there are already 828 documents on the file) or adjust the deadlines to allow the time for reasoned and considered responses on behalf of the affected community interests. They are also concerned that rushed responses based on just a skim read of extensive documentation could actually prejudice their case by failing to notice and respond to something important.
It is considered by my clients that this situation needs to be recognised and acted on by them so as to take control of matters from their perspective.
They have absolutely no intention of withdrawing from the case but a decision has had to be taken to ensure the most effective presentation of their evidence.
Therefore, for the above reasons, it is intended that the group that I represent will now strictly focus their further involvement on the following aspects:
- the written exchanges on need within WS Batch 3 (both deadlines of 5/10 and 16/10, as currently there is no quantified need case presented by SSEN)
- the Community Hearing Sessions (where the written statements might be slightly longer given this revised approach)
- the accompanied site visits (we would wish to be involved in arranging these and in suggesting locations)
- the consideration of conditions (we would ask to be copied in on correspondence)
- an overarching closing submission
As I will remain an opted-in party on their behalf then I will continue to receive and monitor the Objective Connect document lodging notifications.
It is a matter of regret that the basis on which this Inquiry has been set up, a basis for which there is no legal requirement of any sort, has led to this. But the group of directly affected objectors simply needs to take actions to ensure that they are in control and focussed.
Can you please confirm that this revised approach has been noted.
Regards,
Ian
We've mentioned the volume of material in our first 'Intentional Imbalance' post, and that's reinforced in Ian Kelly's e mail.
What we want to concentrate on is the volume of further written submissions and the tight deadlines, for both responses and comments on the responses. It's ludicrously tight and, in our view, wholly supports the stance taken by Ian Kelly and his clients.
That the focus should, perforce, be on the need case is, in our opinion, supported by the comments made in the Procedure Notice, viz.
The reporters have noted all of the evidence submitted to them in respect of the need for the project and potential alternatives to it. That evidence will inform their report to Ministers. They have noted, however, two recent decisions by Ministers consenting the Alyth to Tealing (Ref ECU00005167) and the Tealing to Westfield (Ref ECU00005168) 400kV Upgrade (Reconductoring) projects which are associated with the wider Accelerated Strategic Transmission Investment programme. These decision letters set out Minister’s findings on, amongst other matters, the need for those projects.
This is the section, in both decision letters, to which the Reporters are referring:
Given the scale and pace of the required investment across the electricity transmission system in Great Britain, Ofgem proposed a package of measures in August 2022 aiming to facilitate accelerated delivery by the Transmission Owners, implementing a new Accelerated Strategic Transmission Investment (“ASTI”) regulatory framework to fund the large strategic onshore transmission projects required to deliver the UK Government’s 2030 ambitions. In December 2022, the Company submitted to Ofgem its plan to deliver the required strategic investment in the transmission network for the north of Scotland where it set out its commitment to accelerate the construction of nine projects. These nine projects were included in Ofgem’s decision (published December 2022) on accelerating onshore electricity transmission investment, which confirmed that all nine projects are required. The proposed Development is one of these nine projects. It is also part of a smaller group of projects collectively known as ‘East Coast 400 kV Phase 2’
Those two decisions relate to two projects which are hugely different from the proposed Spittal to Beauly OHL.
They are both reconductoring and re-using the majority of the existing tower infrastructure. None of the involved planning authorities objected, there being no significant environmental impact.
To us, all of this represents confirmation of the indecent haste with which the Public Local Inquiry is being conducted, the further requirements needing to be addressed at hearing sessions or inquiry sessions, not just left to a window of less than one month in total.

records.bodyText:
A connection is being made here between data centres and wind farms; however, it seems mainly to be geared around community benefit.
Does anyone know if Hannah Mary Goodlad has spoken, in reference to data centres, about anything other than comm ben - electricity usage/water usage/noise impacts to neighbours?
**  
'So often what’s going on with hyperscale data centres and communities feels like offshore wind all over again. During this past week I’ve dropped in on three different community campaigns, one objecting to a wind farm, another a new electricity substation, and a third - visited for our The Future of AI and Data Centres series- a proposed hyperscale data centre site in the wilds of the Lammermuirs.
There was a persistent sense of déjà vu. The same topics raised in rural locations, rich in nature. Noise, vibration, the grid, visual impact, effect on wildlife, fears over house prices, scepticism over promised jobs.
The hyperscale data centre rush is coming on fast - which makes it all the more welcome that the Scottish Government is putting a pause on planning decisions till Christmas, when new guidance is set to be produced.
I was pleased to hear in an interview with the Scottish Minister for Public Finance, Hannah Mary Goodlad, this week that community wealth and benefit are to be looked at.
What’s clear is that any data centre policy needs to look at what the deal is for communities – in terms of jobs, community benefit, business rates and other positives. We don’t want to look back in ten years’ time and think that what happened with AI and data centres was the same as wind all over again, or even worse in terms of what it gives back.
As yet there is no guidance on community benefits for data centre developments. Last week, in an interview, Jaap Roell, managing director of Sunlaws Development Company, which is behind a proposed data centre near Longformacus on the Duke of Roxburghe’s land, observed that “weirdly, the government currently doesn't have any guidance for how data centres should or should not provide public benefit in the way that there is for wind farms.”
Some developers have made commitments. Sunlaws says it will create a community fund similar to the Fallago Rig Environment Fund.
Apatura, which is developing several gigawatts of proposed data centres has voluntarily proposed adopting the same £6,000-per-MW-per-year approach as is recommended for onshore wind. With wind such contributions are voluntary, rather than mandatory. Then there are the jobs.
Earlier this week, The Herald writer Brian Donnelly revealed the results of forecasting by Glic, which predicted that beyond the four-year construction stage, around 910 permanent roles in North Lanarkshire would be supported, with 567 working at the centre itself.
Developers and government have made headline claims amounting to nearly 25,000 jobs from six proposed Scottish data-centre developments, although the figures include temporary construction and wider indirect employment and are not a measure of permanent jobs inside the centres, and are often disputed or regarded as unreliable.
It’s also worth acknowledging, as Goodlad points out in my intervew, that onshore wind has a “larger job footprint than the predicted AI footprint”.
In other words, we are talking about less jobs for AI data centres than were delivered for onshore wind.
Meanwhile, who stands to make the big money? And how big? Apatura and developers such as ILI Group are creating consented sites to sell on to hyperscalers. ILI's Mark Wilson describes potential buyers as “the biggest names”, potentially including the global tech giants whose annual profits run into tens of billions.
These are companies which annually report tens of billions in profit. Microsoft’s 2025 annual report recorded $128.5 billion operating profit. Meta made $60.5bn net profit in 2025. Google’s parent company, Alphabet, for instance, just reported the biggest quarterly profit in its history.
Developers also promise significant business rates, although Rufus data-centre campaigner Lisa Beacham questions how much will filter back to communities.
Let’s for a moment go back to our comparison with wind farms. What’s striking is the difference in scale of investment. A substantial Scottish onshore wind farm may represent investment in the hundreds of millions of pounds. The largest proposed AI data centres represent investment in the billions.
For instance, SSE's 208MW Strathy South wind farm represents around £400m of capital investment. Apatura estimates its proposed 550MW Ravenscraig data centre would involve £3.9bn, almost ten times as much.
Developers tell us that the projects would also generate significant business rates, providing an additional contribution towards public services. But campaigners like Lisa Beacham, who has been campaigning against the ILI Group Rufus data centre, question how much will filter back to communities.
We have to do better this time than we did with wind. With wind, Scotland could have pursued greater community ownership, mandatory rather than voluntary benefits, and an index-linked payment - and we live with a feeling of having already missed the moment.
We now have another land-and-energy-intensive industry promising enormous inward investment. With onshore wind, the debate about who should capture the value came largely after much of the industry had already been developed. There aren't the same obvious opportunities for community ownership with hyperscale data centres as there were with wind.
But, as Goodlad told me, these are the relatively early days in which big ideas can be thrashed out. It was good to hear her say: “What I'm wanting to see is how far can you push things in terms of, if a community is going to host this, what is the benefit for them, long term, and how do we use that to attract to real wealth within that community.”
Of course many campaigners aren't so much interested in the benefit as simply stopping the development.
Right now, communities feel like hyperscale data centres are being done to them, an unstoppable force coming to their neighbourhoods that is likely only to bring pain, leaving them feeling peripheral. Can we put them at the heart?'
HERALDSCOTLAND.COM Data centres look like wind all over again. When will communities get gain, not pain?

AMENDED to include a cracking response from The Highland Council solicitor Rhoda Banfro, and also the DPEA's response, below these two.
**
Guess who?  SSEN are calling the shots.  Just have a look at this exchange.
The Highland Council quite reasonably ask for a small extension of time:
22 September
Subject: [EXTERNAL] Beauly to Peterhead Closing Submissions
Dear DPEA Beauly to Peterhead Team,
I write to request a brief extension to the deadline for the Council’s closing submissions, currently due on 24 September 2026, until 28 September 2026.
The request arises principally because legal counsel has only returned from holiday this week and requires sufficient time to review and settle the Council’s closing submissions. In addition, submissions in relation to the Spittal to Beauly proceedings are due on Friday, 25 September, which places a further significant demand on counsel’s time this week.
In those circumstances, the Council would be grateful if the Reporter could agree to the short extension sought to 28 September. We hope that this modest extension can be accommodated without causing any material disruption to the inquiry timetable.
I would be grateful if you could confirm whether the extension is acceptable.
Kind regards
Rhoda
Rhoda Banfro | Solicitor | Regulatory Services | The Highland Council 
And this is the shocking response from SSEN, most especially that last sentence.
23 September
Dear Sir/Madam,
We are no longer surprised at THC refusing to meet a deadline.  The repeated refusal to respect deadlines is disrespectful to the process, the other participants and Reporters.  In particular, the timing of this request is in itself disrespectful. 
 It was made clear that any change to the original timetable would cause significant professional and personal difficulties on the Applicant’s side.  That included family holidays which had been planned by reference to the original timetable being re-arranged by core members.  So, the Applicant does not accept that explanation is one which justifies a change.  This further delay will cause further material difficulties. 
 If, however, this latest refusal to meet a deadline is going to be indulged, at the very least a consequential change should be made to the Applicant’s deadline so that the period they have to consider and respond to THC submissions is not reduced.
For the avoidance of doubt, the Applicant expects Reporters to adhere to the 3 December date for submitting their Report.
Yours faithfully,
SSEN Beauly to Peterhead 400kV Section 37 team
Rhoda Banfro to the DPEA
Dear DPEA Beauly to Peterhead Team,
 We refer to the email below.
 The Council does not accept the characterisation of its request as a “refusal to meet a deadline”, nor does it consider the repeated suggestion that its conduct is “disrespectful” to be either reasonable or necessary. The tone adopted in the correspondence is regrettable and, in our view, falls below the standard of professional courtesy that ought reasonably to be expected in correspondence between Scottish qualified solicitors participating in this process.
 The Council has sought a limited extension for legitimate reasons and has done so through the appropriate procedural route. The fact that an extension has been requested should not, without more, be characterised as a refusal to comply with a deadline. Whether that request should be granted, and whether any consequential adjustment to the timetable is appropriate, are ultimately matters for the Reporters.
 It is also important that the practical context in which the Council is operating is properly recognised. The Council has a very small legal team dealing with planning inquiry work across the whole of the Highland area. At present, only two solicitors are dealing with all such inquiries, supported in this matter by a small number of planning officers who themselves have wider responsibilities across the authority. The Council is also supported by legal counsel who is instructed in a number of other planning inquiries, many of which also involve the Applicant. Those limited legal and planning resources must therefore be deployed across a number of concurrent and competing inquiry, statutory and litigation commitments.
 The Council does not have the same level of dedicated resource available to it as may be available to an applicant and its wider professional team in relation to a particular development. This is not advanced as an excuse for non-compliance with procedural requirements, but it is plainly relevant context when a reasonable and limited request for additional time is made, particularly where the Council, its officers and instructed counsel are simultaneously engaged in a number of other substantial planning inquiries.
 Requests for extensions are, in any event, not unusual in matters of this nature. The Applicant has itself sought extensions in relation to other matters with which the Council is dealing. By way of example, in the Fanellan Appeal, an extension of approximately one and a half weeks was sought by the Applicant and was not objected to by the Council. The Council approached that request reasonably and pragmatically, recognising that legitimate circumstances can arise which require procedural timetables to be adjusted.
 There is therefore a clear inconsistency in the Applicant now characterising the Council’s own request for a limited extension as a “refusal to meet a deadline” and as conduct that is “disrespectful” to the process, the participants and the Reporters. It is difficult to reconcile that position with the Applicant having itself sought additional time in another matter, where the Council did not seek to criticise or impugn the Applicant but instead dealt with the request proportionately and professionally. The Council would have expected the same degree of professional courtesy and pragmatism to be extended in the present circumstances.
 The Council notes the Applicant’s position regarding a consequential adjustment to its own deadline. That is likewise a matter for the Reporters to determine in the interests of procedural fairness. For the avoidance of doubt, should the Reporter’s consider the Council’s request as acceptable, the Council would not object to such an adjustment.
 Finally, the Council notes the Applicant’s statement that it “expects” the Reporters to adhere to the 3 December date for submission of their Report. The management of the procedure, including the timetable for the Reporters’ work, is of course a matter for the Reporters themselves.
 The Council respectfully suggests that future correspondence should focus on the substantive procedural issues requiring determination and be expressed in appropriately professional terms.
 Kind regards
 Rhoda
 DPEA response:
Good Afternoon
The reporters recognise the competing pressures of the councils and are content with a short extension to the closing submissions deadlines to 28 September 2026
(for parties except the applicant) and to 12 October 2026 for the applicant. They also note the applicant’s concerns in relation to the overall inquiry timescales,which they believe will not be significantly impacted by this change.
Kind Regards
DPEA BEAULY TO PETERHEAD 400KV TEAM

ADDITION:  Reporters have confirmed that the date for closing submissions will be 12 October, with SSEN's responses by 26 October.
**
Yesterday, thanks to a recording volume we could hear, we caught up with the PLI session on Agriculture. The summary is long, and for that we apologise, but the session was long and we want to get as much down on record as we can.
The Reporters are David Liddell and Christopher Warren; the latter led in this session.
Taking part were:  
SSEN - Alasdair Burnett,KC with SSEN personnel and land use and planning consultants including  Sarah McMonagle from the land use consultancy LUC and  Norman MacIver from Knockmuir Farms Consultancy.
NOTKUP - John Campbell , KC with other personnel from the team - Merle Boyd and Mark Skimmington (Strathmore Estates); Eileen West; Brian Wade; Dr Iain Stirling; William and Alice Foster; Alan Joiner; Ralph Pace
Galbraith - Ian Thornton-Kemsley and affected parties - David Carnegie; Daniel Fleming.
NFU Scotland - Rhianna Montgomery; Lorna Scott
Trevor and Jean Reid
John Wilson
Christopher Warren opened by saying that in SSEN's responses to comments made, they had stated that much of the content is beyond the remit of Reporters and of Scottish Ministers to decide if the proposal is compliant with other statutory duties under Health & Safety legislation.  He said that they could see that most other parties did say that it was relevant.  While Reporters had to take care that matters are relevant, land use and environmental effects are relevant and risks to human health are recognised in EIA regulations. So his first question was, did parties agree with what he had set out.  
Alasdair Burnett referred to SSEN's comments of August but agreed with what Christopher Warren had said.
John Campbell explained why his opinion was that safe working practices were very much within the Reporters' jurisdiction.
Ian Thornton-Kemsley said that Reporters must take into account that the onus is on the landowner and that there is a gap between the role of the Health & Safety Executive and the role of who is the enforcing authority on an electricity provider.
When asked by Christopher Warren if there were any other views on what the scope should be, John Campbell said that it is actually an Electricity Act inquiry under which they were all there, not under the planning system.  CW agreed as did Alasdair Burnett.
So the section on effects on human health was next.
Christopher Warren said that the Additional Information provided by SSEN identifies a significant risk to human heath - electric shock risk which exceeds ALARP (As Low As Reasonably Practicable).So, there are two parts - the ALARP test and whether risk can be adequately managed.
Discussion ensued,  between Christopher Warren and Alasdair Burnett, with Christopher Warren saying that he was struggling with the separation of ALARP and adequate management.
Brian Wade, whose department was health and safety and quality management, said that the whole process started with design.  He had sent a FOI 6/8 weeks ago, to SSEN.  There is a requirement to form a health and safety file, but he had been told that SSEN didn't have it and were not at the stage where it's required.  Brian said that contradicts regulations which say that it starts with design.  His point was that SSEN is expecting the rest of the world to adapt what they do to match SSEN's shortcomings.  He reiterated that they should have been looking at health and safety from day 1.
At this point, Brian got a round of applause, but Christopher Warren gently pointed out that everyone had a difficult job to do, though he was aware that there is a strong difference of opinion and strength of view.
John Wilson said that farmers are very much aware of their responsibility re health and safety but that does not allow SSEN to remove themselves from their legal and regulatory duties and introduce a multiple fatality risk.  He said that the crux of the matter is who is the introducer of risk, and that if the project was not coming over farms, there would be no need for tertiary mitigation.
Ralph Pace said that SSEN say that the risk is insignificant, but the risk is serious. He said that the regulations are perfectly sensible and a guideline for every developer, not just in energy.  Before you even start design, you find out what goes on in agriculture; what size of machinery, and do all the due diligence before the design state.  But SSN has said they did not take that into account.  Mr Pace said you would have thought that would be the first step, and that safety of farmers would have been paramount, but it was now working backwards.  He said that the size of agricultural equipment could not be shrunk and that they see a significant risk introduced to the majority of farmed land.  It is not just electric shock - it's electrocution risk.
Alasdair Burnett said that it's a question of what risk actually is and compliance with regulations.  Christopher Warren asked SSEN if it is incumbent upon an applicant to minimise risk by design - primary mitigation instead of tertiary.  There followed an exchange, mainly between Christopher Warren and Alasdair Burnett, punctuated by comment from SSEN's Calum Grant, on ALARP, and minimisation of risk.
John Wilson came in to refer to regulations that SSEN are supposed to abide by.  He pointed out that some regulation is from the 1950s when machinery height was much lower.  He said that SSEN have introduced risk and they seem to be trying to partake in passing on risk to normal foreseeable farming practices.
Dr Iain Stirling - former scientist, and a doctor, spoke of his experience with industrial injuries and spoke of risk to human health.  He referred to population and human health having been scoped out, directly against the advice of the Director of Public Health Scotland who said in 2025 that it is the power operator's responsibility to do a population and human health assessment, and that he, the Director, had also said, 'Scottish Government colleagues advised me of this.'
Dr Stirling went on to talk about the fact that they must distinguish between electric shock, electric injury, electrocution and microshock.  He said that there is a long case law history, referring to one assessment which concluded that primary mitigation is the answer to the question of electric safety and electrocution.
After a bit of to-ing and fro-ing with Sarah McMonagle, Dr Stirling said that the mitigation hierarchy says - avoid, prevent, reduce, offset.  The first thing is to avoid and that avoidance here is the risk of electric shock and potential risk of fatality.  If they are looking at binary - significant and non-significant, what's left out are severity, exposure, scale, frequency, duration, permanence, and the population affected.
Brian Wade then came in with a cracker of an analogy.  The Road Traffic Act says that you can drive at 70 mph on a dual carriageway - that's the equivalent of a 7.3m clearance.  But if you drove in freezing fog at 70 and crash, you would be done for dangerous driving.  'ALARP - simple', he said.
Ian Thornton-Kemsley said that he represents receptors upon whom this may be imposed.  SSEN had suggested that CDM Regulations were (he said) 'how shall I put it - none of your business'.  He said it was very much part of Reporters' business as CDM regulations apply from the concept.  HSE guidance makes it clear that it begins pre-construction and applies from conception to completion.  He referred to what Dr Stirling had said previously, and said that SSEN are required to compare the sacrifice of money, time and operational complexity against safety and that SSE have failed to meaningfully address cost benefit or socioeconomic matters despite Reporters' directions of 14 May.
Christopher Warren then said he wanted to go back to the question of ALARP and whether it is separated out from mitigation.  He said that in the Additional Information, it says 'electric shock risk meets the ALARP test or can be adequately managed through safe work procedures'.
The use of the word 'or' seems to separate the two out.  He said, if it's a single test, how can it be either/or.  He needed to be clear.
Sarah McMonagle first said that it's treated as a single test and that safe work can manage risk to health, so farming can continue safely under the OHL.  But Christopher Warren came back to the word 'or' and said was that a drafting error or was he misunderstanding?  
She said she needed to check with a colleague.  The answer came back that it was a typo and the word should have been 'and'!!
Alasdair Burnett came in with what we can honestly only describe as 'word salad' which actually seemed to reinforce Christopher Warren's questions, but eventually the Reporter said that he didn't want to go round in circles, but he asked why there was different terminology in the Additional Information for the mitigation hierarchy, from that used in the EIA.
Sarah McMonagle said it was felt that the description was not detailed enough in the EIA to cover tertiary mitigation.
Christopher Warren clarified.  EIA = embedded mitigation; AI = primary.  EIA = additional; AI = secondary.  EIA = applied; AI = tertiary
The Reporter continued to drill down into the precise reason for the change and much of the discussion revolved around the hierarchy of mitigation and what constitutes risk
Ian Thornton-Kemsley said that the Health & Safety At Work Act requires SSEN to consider the safety and wellbeing of anyone who may be affected by the OHL, such as those farming the land under the structure.
Calum Grant then spoke about clearances/sag/hot curve clearance/machinery heights - and said that all these incidents would need to happen at the same time for there to be risk, so there was quite a low chance.  
In response to one of the SSEN personnel saying that there was an inherent assumption that people were working safely, John Wilson said that they don't get ENA documents.  They don't know the danger zone for flashover, and that there are thousands of close contacts every day.
Christopher Warren said that from Ian Thornton-Kemsley's FOI response from the Health & Safety Executive, it shows 28 fatalities; 68 injuries and 7196 near misses between 2010 and 2025, not just in agriculture, and that this shows that conflict exists, and that it's likely that there has been a failure in protocol and that it doesn't mean that safe working can mitigate risk.
Calum Grant jumped in to say that it didn't give a distinction of voltage and the incidents would primarily have been wood pole lines.  They had had only one strike since records began.
Christopher Warren said that these incidents do occur, so he is less interested in the height of the conductors - the OHLs are resulting in fatalities, injuries and near misses so is the reliance on health & safety regulations sufficiently robust?  And that SSEN had said that risk is managed by working practices, so it's got to be consistent.
Ian Thornton-Kemsley said could he ask SSEN what length of its existing infrastructure is across prime agricultural land.  Alasdair Burnett said that it wasn't unique and what was I T-K saying.  Ian Thornton-Kemsley said that the reason he is asking is that this is a line uniquely across prime agricultural land and what he's driving at is can Reporters be satisfied that SSEN has sufficiently studied the issues in this new line as opposed to using stats from the Beauly-Denny line for instance which is primarily - except for the Beauly and southern end - across heather moorland where harvesters and combines will not be used.
John Campbell said that Calum Grant had given a clear explanation of circumstances where the line height might change (sag), but how is an operator, say, on a combine, supposed to know whether he's driving under a hot curve line, or height of that line.  He said let's assume the operator knows what the safety parameter is for his machine on that day.  Should he be carrying an inclinometer to measure the height.  JC said that it must be remembered that conditions of combine harvesting vary greatly.  These are not people who work an 8 hour shift and that they work ridiculous hours at harvest , and they get tired; they also work in the dark.
Calum Grant, responding to what Ian Thornton-Kemsley had said, said that the existing K-T line goes primarily through prime agricultural land as this new one will and appears to be adequately farmed, and it's got lower clearances because it's a 275kv line.
In response to JC, he said it was designed to a worst case scenario and that landowners will be issued with clearances including worst case scenario clearances, and that anyone can reach out to SSE and they will come and measure! 
Jean Reid asked if SSEN could give a guarantee that the OHL will not fall down.  She quoted two instances of lines falling, one killing a Shetland pony and the other causing a huge fire.  Calum Grant said that these were distribution lines and that he did not consider it a likely occurrence on a transmission line.
Brian Wade referred to Calum Grant having talked about a unique set of circumstances (sag) and said it's why we use the precautionary principle - why we have worst case scenarios in all assessments and why there is hierarchy of mitigation.  He said that's the pyramid.  You don't eliminate risk altogether, so you go down to the next level.  People fly planes into mountains.  They have lots of instruction beforehand.  You can't move the mountain.
Christopher Warren asked if it's appropriate to take human error into account.  The SSEN response was that it takes it into account and their clearances are significantly higher.  Christopher Warren asked if SSEN are saying that all conductors will be high enough to avoid conflict, or is it overlaid with health & safety regulation?
Calum Grant replied that with the exception of exceptional circumstances, yes.  He said if one takes the lowest clearance of 9.07m (the next being 9.3m) the largest machinery proposed by 'objectors' is 7.2m so there is still clearance.
Ian Thornton-Kemsley said that that statement brings in a new argument.  Not many farmers will pay £85 to obtain ENA documents.  
John Wilson made the point that when crossing, for example, telephone lines, SSE will underground 3 poles, so he asked why the discrepancy when it would be considered unsafe to have overground for their distribution engineers.
The answer from Calum Grant was that there is less risk during construction and maintenance is more straightforward; it's not about safety.
John Wilson said that he had been told categorically by distribution personnel that it was for the safety of their engineers, and asked why agriculture is not being treated in the same way.
After lunch, the session moved on to machinery heights, and the documents available to farmers - for instance Look Out; Look Up.
Ian Thornton-Kemsley made the point that he was not aware of an arcing issue before this inquiry.  The ENA document does, but they have never had a copy of it.  He said that in 50 years, he had never had any advice from SSE about the existing line.
Mark Skimmington said that he develops farm safety, and heights are a major issue.  They have countless near misses every year with power lines and going round the pylons.  He made the point that sprayer booms are 36m.  Another farmer has a potato harvester about 7.5m high, and he said that in his opinion, this line needs to be at 12m.
John Wilson said that in the last 10 years they've had three actual contacts, and this summer, there was an outage because the combine harvester could not fit underneath the line.
Christopher Warren said he wanted to test some assumptions.  He said that machinery types were given in the Additional Information and asked why those had been selected.
Norman MacIver answered.  He said that he was also a farmer, and that machinery, for example potato harvesters will have the elevation as low as possible so as not to bruise the potatoes.  There followed quite a debate between Mr MacIver and others, particularly John Wilson, about when operators would need to have high elevation.  David Carnegie made the point that pickers are higher than the machine and so safety has not been properly considered.  Alan Joiner said that root trailers would be significantly higher, and that night working must be taken into account.  He said that often operators would forget where they were, and also that combines go under OHLs more than potato harvesters.
The point was also made that farm machinery, given the changes in the last 20 years, is likely to get even bigger.
Ian Thornton-Kemsley made the point that farmers do not necessarily use the same machinery year to year.  One year they may use contractors and that foreseeable use has to look at the technology.  Not every farmer can afford a bulker and not everyone wants one as they can damage potatoes.  (Explanation here.  Norman McIver had said that potato picking machines could unload away from the OHL.  Harvesters that have a bunker to hold the potatoes can continue to harvest without the need for another tractor and trailer to drive alongside to collect the potatoes.)  I T-K said it may help if Reporters were to visit farms to see how operations work.
Ralph Pace said that they had spoken about lowering machine heights, but had not looked at the highest possible size.  The conductors would be too low, the reason being because steps were not taken at the beginning - to make an assessment and then build the design.  He said they would not be putting the camel through the eye of the needle, and that they are playing with fire as they are talking about the need to change farming practices.
Christopher Warren said that where they are in agreement, it's for the operators to determine when a machine shouldn't go over a certain height, thereby creating potential for conflict.  He asked which clearances should be applied.  
Discussion then took place between working clearances and passing clearances.  John Wilson made the point that manufacturers will give height as cab height but that height can change - for example, if different tyres are fitted. In discussion on bubble up augers on combines, Ian Thornton-Kemsley said that bubble up augers are either up or they are down, and that Reporters should speak to true farmers (in a fairly obvious swipe at Norman MacIver who replied in answer that he is).
Next on the agenda was the percentages of spans.  Ian Thornton-Kemsley said that the significance of clearances is underplayed and that the clearances impacting on every span over agricultural land should be looked at and referred to a farmer operating under pressure - weather and night time pressures - assuming that the line can even be seen.  Christopher Warren acknowledged his comment.
William Foster said that SSEN had not taken salmon fishing and electrical risk into account.  Rods are 4.9m long and there is a flashover risk.  He would have to ask his fishing clients to sign a disclaimer against electrocution.  He said that fishing under the line would effectively be sterilised.  Christopher Warren said that in fairness they had not asked SSEN for comment on fishing.
Ralph Pace said at the moment they have agricultural fields with no risk, but in the best case scenario, somewhere over 75% would have an introduced risk and would have to contend with virtually every field having a hazard.
Rhianna Montgomery spoke of the pressures on farming.
Brian Wade asked why there was no span by span risk assessment.  Christopher Warren said that they had asked where there was a risk.  Calum Grant said that they have it in Additional Information, but Christopher Warren said it was but it didn't extend to farm by farm/machinery evaluation, etc.  Calum Grant said that there were practical limitations.
Christopher Warren said that he could see both sides.  He finds it difficult to judge conductor heights and can see operational difficulties.  That SSEN makes the point that farming takes place all over the UK and he asked - setting aside danger - what are the practical effects on farming per se?  If smaller machines were used, would it take longer?
John Wilson said it was simple.  Land would be sterilised; compensation doesn't happen. He said that horizontal dimensions were difficult, too as they have to be 15m away from outside conductors.  So irrigation is restricted too.
Ian Thornton-Kemsley said that Norman MacIver had made great play of working under distribution lines.  He said he, I T-K, was unaware of guidance.  Distribution networks had never once said this is the height and this is what you should be doing.  He made the point that if he had a digger, near a pipeline, National Gas would be at his door.  It doesn't happen with networks and yet there is the same sort of risk.  He said that reference to legacy lines is of very little relevance to new lines.
The session touched on irrigation and the impact of the OHL on that.
John Campbell said that in the additional information, it is clear that there is to be no irrigation at less than 30m but they say some can be used near, so he asked what types and at what distances.  He said it seemed imprecise for an EIA.
Stuart Smart said that it was 30m to the gun nozzle, not to the extent of the jet.  JC asked if the operator had to get it right.  Christopher Warren asked if a jet was near the conductor, was there a shock risk and why would the risk reduce, but Stuart Smart said they couldn't go into that detail.  John Campbell persisted, asking what if the rain gun sprays n to the conductors.  The answer was that as long as it's 30m away.  So JC asked would it explode or what?  Stuart Smart said he didn't know and he was himself not qualified but was saying that the tech advisers say.
Brian Wade said it was another example of operator decisions.  His background is in oil and gas and that a lot of lessons were learned in 1988 (Piper Alpha); people relied on other people's judgment and this is the fundamental problem.
Christopher Warren moved to 'other considerations'. He referred again to the figures and said that the near miss data seems indicative that conflicts can occur and he was not sure that existing lines demonstrate health risk.  John Campbell said that on the 79% of farms which have existing OHLs, has there been any survey on each of the 122 holdings, farm by farm.
Calum Grant said that discussions are being held/likely machinery, but JC said he couldn't find it in the EIA or the AI and asked has there been interrogation, farm by farm.  Has anyone been to John Wilson's farm?
Christopher Warren said that there had not been one and asked if that were correct.  Calum grant replied yes.
Christopher Warren then asked is the risk different on legacy lines.  Wooden poles, for instance, are less likely to get missed or forgotten.  But very long spans at 9m high and not at eye level.  Does that represent a different risk?
Calum grant replied that the conductors would be larger and thicker wires.
Christopher Warren said that there are limitations - of weather and night time operations. He said that the Health & Safety Executive had not objected, and that absence is a factor which they and Ministers may take into account. But, reading the HSE consultation response of 2025, it is limited to land use, with no consideration to health except at work.  Employers are to do risk assessments.  He asked does that give us comfort or they haven't thought about it.
Alasdair Burnett said what weight it's given is a matter for Reporters, but it's a relevant matter and is not raising any concerns.
Christopher Warren asked if SSEN took comfort.  It's limited to major industrial hazards and he doesn't think that it provides reassurance and its a no comment.
Alasdair Burnett responded that it's a matter for Reporters.  (We've tried hard to encapsulate the rest of what he said, in a logical fashion, but we will simply, once again, say 'word salad'.)
Ian Thornton-Kemsley said he wanted to draw attention to SSEN saying that HSE are responsible.  He said that HSE go on to say that they have no locus re ESQCR (Electricity Safety, Quality and Continuity Regulations)  And that Reporters should be less sure that comfort should be taken.
John Campbell said that this is the practice of HSE; they are reactive, not proactive and he is surprised that SSEN are saying that comfort can be taken.  He would invite Reporters to take no comfort at all.
Brian Wade said that on the HSE website it explains their 'playing field'.  It clarifies that it will not involve itself in planning/PLIs.
Christopher Warren said that if they or Ministers decide that the line does represent danger, are their any remedies through this process - to use vertical LoDs?
Calum Grant said in theory the likelihood is low.  The challenge of increasing height would have a knock on effect - increased bases; greater land sterilisation; longer to build; larger foundations; added risks during construction; more traffic on roads; licence obligation/cost to consumers.
Alasdair Burnett came in to talk about reasonableness and necessity (to solve a problem that's not line-wide) and said it was not an easy fix.
Christopher Warren said that it is not a proposal; he is trying to think of all possibles.
Stuart Smart said that height wouldn't take away the responsibility of operators and it could be more dangerous but Christopher Warren said that if the conductors were high enough, it would be a safer position.
John Campbell came in to say that they were there under the umbrella of EIA regulations and that one requirement is the consideration of alternatives.  They have not been presented with alternatives.  Have alternatives been exhausted?
Some discussion followed on LoDs and other alternatives.  Ian Thornton-Kemsley stated that an increase in height is clearly available as SSEN staff including the Head of Land Acquisition had said that heights could be increased.  But SSEN chose not to, and expect landowners to mitigate.
Eileen West made the point that LoDs are available for construction.
Christopher Warren said that, if the line is consented, SSEN are free to use LoDs as they see fit.
Brian Wade said that health is scoped back in, but other issues should have been, too.  One biggest risk is the effect on mental health of people affected; those people who were at the PLI sessions telling their individual stories are representative of thousands of people who are affected.  He said that they are now asking people who have mental health issues to make decisions in the field about whether their combine can go under a line.  The two things are mutually incompatible and he firmly believes that it's something that Reporters can't make a recommendation to the Ministers without investigating several other topics.  He said he realised that was their decision but personally he believes that mental health issues should not be whitewashed out.
Christopher Warren said what was scoped back in was the health risk associated with agricultural use and potential clearance issues.  The question of mental health effects is a relevant consideration to the Reporters, but it's not a matter which they've taken the decision to scope back in and require additional information on, but they have the evidence on it.  He said it might not be sufficient from Brian Wade's perspective but they are satisfied they have enough information and what we've heard during the inquiry to be able to advise Ministers on the point, but they're relevant considerations even though not part of the EIA itself.
Alasdair Burnett said they would reflect, but there was one minor point - that they have to clarify what information is given to farmers once the line is built.  (Yes he did say that).
Calum Grant said that clearance profiles would be given.  Beyond construction, they can measure heights.
When Christopher Warren went on to 'next steps' John Campbell said that it was his intention to make an application for expenses against SSEN.  Ian Thornton-Kemsley did the same.
Christopher Warren passed the session to David Liddell to close.  David Liddell said that they now had enough evidence and so they are not proposing further procedures.  He asked for closing submissions - if people wished to do so - to be submitted by 9 October, with SSEN's response by 23 October.  John Campbell put in a plea for 19 October and this was supported by John Wilson and Ian Thornton-Kemsley (who has wayleave meetings the weeks before).  Alasdair Burnett asked for additional time too, in that event, and he also said that because of school holidays in October, the time frame could be problematic.
David Liddell said they would write out the dates.  He thanked everyone for their input at that session and in the whole inquiry.  John Campbell thanked the Reporters for a very civil inquiry.

records.title: Wind Energy's Absurd
records.bodyText:
We went back on a couple of issues picked up from the Kintore-Tealing OHL agriculture session, one of which was when Brian Wade spoke about the fact that mental health should be scoped in.  His comment chimed with something we had clocked from The Highland Council a couple of days earlier.
A reminder of what Brian said:
Brian Wade said that health is scoped back in, but other issues should have been, too.  One biggest risk is the effect on mental health of people affected; those people who were at the PLI sessions telling their individual stories are representative of thousands of people who are affected.  He said that they are now asking people who have mental health issues to make decisions in the field about whether their combine can go under a line.  The two things are mutually incompatible and he firmly believes that it's something that Reporters can't make a recommendation to the Ministers without investigating several other topics.  He said he realised that was their decision but personally he believes that mental health issues should not be whitewashed out.
The Reporter Christopher Warren replied that it is a relevant consideration to Reporters, but, although it wouldn't be scoped in, they have the evidence on it.
We believe, in general, that mental health is a missing part of the jigsaw in the impact of all of the industrial hardware which is being foist into Scotland (we are not ignoring the rest of the UK here, though).
Although mental health is increasingly being put at the top of many trees, it factors nowhere into renewable planning considerations.
Quite apart from the obvious mental health effects from built infrastructure, allied to physical effects, experienced by many folk, the 'green'rush brings enormous mental stress to so many others - fears and anxieties that peace and tranquillity will disappear; sense of place...gone; house prices through the floor; the feeling of helplessness in the face of a juggernaut of unabated infrastructure.
We mentioned The Highland Council.  This was in the planners' recommendation for the forthcoming determination by THC, as a statutory consultee, on the Allt an Tuir Energy Park at Rosehall:
Non-Material Considerations 
A significant number of objections submitted against the application make specific appeals to Human Rights and mention of mental health effects, such that it is considered appropriate to address these issues in more detail here for the benefit of Members.   
In terms of Human Rights, Members are reminded that planning legislation and policy in Scotland must take account of provisions within the Scotland Act 1998, the Human Rights Act 1998, and the European Convention on Human Rights (ECHR), along with other legislations including for equality etc.  
Scottish planning legislation states that the purpose of planning is “to manage the use and development of land in the long-term public interest”. It is section 36 of the Electricity Act 1989 that sets out the statutory process of determining applications for generating stations with capacity above 50MW. The process is designed to facilitate sound decisions that are fair and legal.  
To that end, the legislation sets out the rights of applicants and third parties alike within the process of determining applications, which includes the right to notification, consultation, and engagement. Officers are satisfied that these statutory rights have been applied in the processing of this application in so far as the process is managed on behalf of Scottish Ministers by the ECU, including this consultation made to the Council as the Local Planning Authority. Members are advised that the large number of representations that have appealed to Human Rights have, unfortunately, not specified which Human Rights the development, whether at application stage or once operational, would be in breach of, nor have they explained how the development would breach them.
 Further information and advice on the rights of applicants and third parties within the Scottish planning system is available on the Planning Aid Scotland website at the following link: https://www.pas.org.uk/wp-content/uploads/2023/04/7.-Rights-andChallenges-in-the-Scottish-Planning-System-04-2023.pdf.   
Mental health as a material planning consideration is specifically mentioned in NPF4 Policies 14 Design, quality and place, and 21 for Play, recreation and sport, while consideration of the issue is implied under Policy 23 Health and Safety, which seeks to improve outcomes for health and wellbeing in addition to protecting people and places from environmental and physical harm.    
The former policies advocate for improved opportunities for play, socialising, relaxation, and physical activity in line with the designing for healthy outcomes quality of the 6 qualities of Successful Places. These healthy outcomes are listed as 1) lifelong wellbeing, 1) healthy and active lifestyles, 3) accessibility and inclusion, 4) social connectivity, and, 5) environmentally positive places (see NPF4 Annex D).    
The purpose of planning for these outcomes is to improve the collective physical and mental health of our communities. The current proposal for a renewable energy generating station would not be detrimental to any of these healthy outcomes and, indeed, is also supported under the designing for sustainable outcomes quality of Successful Places. On that basis, individual claims against mental health impacts as a result of a development (whether at application stage through to its eventual construction) are private matters for the individuals concerned rather than strategic land use matters of public interest, which again, is the proper remit of the planning system. 
Q.E.D.

records.title: Wind Energy's Absurd
records.bodyText:
We've already posted up what Miliband was bumping his green gums about in New York, and we've had the debunking from Paul Homewood about Miliband's apocalyptic mutterings.
But it didn't end there.  What Miliband said has grown arms and legs, as seen in this piece by Jaime Jessop.  We haven't included the conversations which the author refers to, or the examples.  The whole piece should be read.  We are putting it here for our archives, primarily.
https://jaimejessop.substack.com/.../no-milibrain...
'This is what Mad Red Ed said at the New York Climate Week recently, having flown there (and back, unfortunately) and in the process used the equivalent of half my annual CO2 emissions in just one overseas business class climate jolly:
I was here last year as the Energy Secretary. I’m now the Foreign Secretary of the United Kingdom, but I come here as passionate about the cause of New York Climate Week, the cause that we are all fighting for.
And I want to make a simple argument to you today, which is that climate and nature loss represents an urgent national security issue and demands action equal to the scale of the challenge, and that it demands a shift in our thinking and a shift in who in government takes an interest and cares about these issues and puts them front and centre.
And I think you all know the picture, and it is gloomy, I warn you, but I’m just going to say some of it to you today because we need to be truth-telling about this.
Over 150 million hectares burned globally in the first four months of 2026 alone.
Record extreme heat causing widespread loss of life.
Nepal’s devastating floods happening due to glacial collapse and the coming El Nino, as Prime Minister Albanese said, is already forecast to be the strongest in living memory.
And the nature loss crisis is just as acute, with ecosystems being degraded in every region of the world.
That is the conclusion of the UK’s recent nature security assessment, which you can all read.
This is why. These facts. What is happening in our world. Is why climate breakdown, in my view, must be an issue for foreign ministers and prime ministers, as well as energy and climate ministers. The security community, not just the activist community, the generals, not just the green campaigners.
He’s lying about the alleged impacts of the climate crisis, as Paul Homewood points out.
But he’s also deliberately misleading us about the Joint Intelligence Committee ‘climate and nature crisis’ “nature” (national) security report, which we can’t read, because it was due to be published in October 2025, but wasn’t, and hasn’t been since, apart from a few redacted pages. By conflating El Nino, the hot summer in Europe and the US and (most outrageously) the rock shelf collapse which caused the glacial collapse and flash flooding in Nepal with a ‘climate and nature crisis’ which is identified as a national security threat by the JIC, he is playing fast and loose with the truth and deliberately deceiving his audience. But the climate activist media go one better. 
Clearly, she implies that the coming El Nino was assessed as a national security and defence threat by the JIC report. That’s not explicitly what Milibrain said. But why bother about such a minor detail? He probably meant for brainless hacks like Fiona to grasp the wrong end of the stick and run with it in print anyway. I challenged Fiona on this on X and she accused me of not bothering to read stuff, then went silent when confronted with her own words, which I'd bothered to read, namely:
The UK has warned countries around the world that the climate and nature crises and the coming El Niño threaten their national security and defence, presenting foreign ministries with the findings of a report suppressed under Keir Starmer.
The JIC report, as I pointed out, could not possibly have mentioned anything about the upcoming El Nino posing a defence and security threat because it was completed and ready to be published in October 2025, six months before El Nino started to develop in the central Pacific. But Fiona lied to her readers that it did and FuseEnergy were even more explicit in their lies:
The JIC report addresses global biodiversity loss and ecosystem collapse, painting a stark picture of future risks. It highlights that global ecosystem degradation and collapse threaten UK national security.
The report specifically highlights the immediate threat posed by the coming El Niño phenomenon. Miliband’s warning about the “most intense in living memory” El Niño cycle underscores its potential to exacerbate existing vulnerabilities. Such intense climate shocks are predicted to strain food and water security, displace communities, and put immense pressure on global markets.
That’s a lie. The JIC report cannot have said anything about the threat posed by the coming El Nino, because when it was written, it wasn’t coming, simples!

'The boss of a Chinese renewables firm, backed by the SNP to build a controversial factory in Scotland, was named in a bribery scandal, The Ferret has found.
Ming Yang Smart Energy announced plans last October for a £1.5bn wind turbine factory at Ardersier in the Highlands, promising up to 1,500 jobs at the former oil and gas yard.
The project was effectively blocked by Westminster on national security grounds in March. First minister John Swinney branded that decision “anti-Scottish” and last month called on new prime minister Andy Burnham to reverse it.
But now his government’s years-long support of Ming Yang is under renewed scrutiny after we unearthed a court judgement from a 2015 corruption trial in China. 
It shows Ming Yang’s chairman, Zhang Chuanwei, admitted paying $20,000 (£14,800) to the head of a government department in the southern province of Guangdong between 2011 and 2013.
The money is described in the judgement as a “bribe” to thank the Chinese state official for his support. The department he led had previously awarded Ming Yang 25.3m yuan (around £2.8m) in research funding.
The official was jailed for life for accepting the payments and other bribes used to pay his son’s gambling debts. 
Ming Yang has told us that Zhang, who gave evidence as a witness, was not convicted, charged, or penalised in connection with the allegations.
However, Luke De Pulford, executive director of the Inter-Parliamentary Alliance on China, claimed the case raised “alarming questions” about the security risk posed by Ming Yang and could be used as “leverage” by the ruling Chinese Communist Party (CCP) over Zhang.
He said that the Scottish Government’s continuing support of the company “without identifying or confronting basic court records” was a “staggering failure of due diligence”.
Ming Yang, which is privately owned, says it is not controlled by the Chinese state and poses no threat to the UK.
The Scottish Government insisted its due diligence was “proportionate to the nature and stage of investment proposals and any public support under consideration”. 
Authorities tightened the rules around this Scottish business scheme after years of exploitation for financial crime. Moscow entities – and a man accused of facilitating child sex abuse – are still selling it to clients seeking “financial privacy”.
Despite the fact we highlighted the bribery case to the Scottish Government earlier this month, on Friday, the SNP stuck to its position that blocking the factory was Labour being “entirely political”.
The party's Westminster energy spokesperson, Graham Leadbitter, said the fact Ming Yang had been blocked from investing in Scotland – but that Chinese companies continued to hold stakes in the UK’s energy network, including in battery storage – “confirms what we all suspected – the decision to block 1,500 Highland jobs appears to be entirely political”.
He continued: “If this UK Labour government is so concerned about national security, then why is it allowing Chinese firms to invest in battery storage, nuclear plants, airports, and super-embassies south of the border - is it because it’s in the Highlands and not Hertfordshire?”
Swinney has reportedly received a briefing from UK ministers over the national security threat that allowing Ming Yang to set up in Scotland could pose to the country. 
But despite this, the first minister has continued to advocate for its investment in Scotland.
The first minister hosted Zhang at his official residence, Bute House, in July 2025. The pair bonded over their mutual love of running at that meeting – their second in less than a year – with Swinney describing Zhang’s business career as “impressive”.
Concerns raised about the use of Chinese turbines include that they could be used to spy on UK waters or allow Beijing to remotely disrupt power supplies.
There are also fears the UK could become dependent on Chinese energy technology, leaving it vulnerable to price hikes or if relations deteriorate. 
The US reportedly warned UK officials about allowing Ming Yang into the country last year, around the same time it cautioned Keir Starmer against giving the go-ahead for Beijing’s so-called “super-embassy” in London.
Britain’s security services have also reportedly been feeding into a review of China’s role in the UK energy system in recent years. 
Some industry figures argue Britain will struggle to meet green energy targets without Chinese equipment, and say its components are already used in offshore turbines.
Ming Yang, one of the world’s biggest turbine makers, has denied the Chinese government could use a so-called “kill switch” to remotely shut them down. 
It says all data from UK projects would be controlled in Britain with “strict access protocols, independent oversight, and certified cybersecurity systems in place”.
The Scottish Government has been criticised for failing to turn the country’s wind power boom into more manufacturing jobs. This made the potential investment at Ardersier, near Inverness – where 4,500 workers were once employed to build platforms for the North Sea oil industry – particularly attractive.
De Pulford argued that despite this, Scotland should “not be handing over critical energy infrastructure to companies tied to state-sanctioned corruption and security risks.”
He said the incident raised “alarming questions about vulnerability, coercion, and national security risk”. 
“In China’s political system, unresolved legal liabilities like this don’t just disappear, they become state leverage,” De Pulford claimed.
Power struggle: The billionaire, the Chinese oil giant and Grangemouth’s forgotten workers
Grangemouth should have been Scotland’s big opportunity to realise its ambition for a just transition – moving workers into cleaner, greener jobs. But embittered power struggles got in the way, The Ferret finds.
Johanna Krebs, an analyst at the Mercator Institute for China Studies, said Beijing did not require leverage of this sort to influence private companies abroad because it already had sweeping powers to do so.
Krebs said European leaders were being faced with a dilemma about Chinese involvement in European renewable energy projects, which required them to balance efforts to tackle the climate crisis with real concerns about national and economic security.
“This includes the threat that Chinese companies could disrupt European grids and that the entry of Chinese companies into the European renewable market could undermine domestic manufacturers and cause even more dependence on Chinese exports,” she said.
Andrew Bowie, the Conservative shadow secretary for energy security, said Swinney appeared “so desperate to do business with Beijing” that he was “willing to brush aside every warning about the risks to Scotland’s security”.
He added: “Swinney must stop dismissing legitimate security concerns surrounding Ming Yang and come clean on how much background checks they carried out on this firm and its leadership.”
The Scottish Government’s commercial “due diligence guidance” states that it is “crucial to understand the ownership” of potential investors as well as “key figures within the operation”.
It adds that: “This information is required to ensure proper due diligence can be undertaken as to the owners and associated personnel of a business to ensure reputational risk to SG [Scottish Government] is considered.”
A spokesperson for the Scottish Government said: “Any decision to enter into a partnership with, or to provide public financial support, with any organisation would be subject to appropriate and robust due diligence.”
It said these checks could include issues related to bribery, corruption and other serious misconduct.
A UK Government spokesperson said it had a “strategic” approach to relations with China “whilst never compromising on security and resilience”. There were no plans to change the Government's position on Ming Yang, they said.
A spokesperson for Ming Yang said: “Neither the company nor its relevant personnel have ever been convicted, charged or received any penalties issued from any competent authorities, including for bribery for the cases mentioned.
“As a listed company on both the Shanghai Stock Exchange Main Board and the London Stock Exchange, Ming Yang Smart Energy strictly complies with the laws and regulations of all the countries in which it operates, and firmly opposes all forms of commercial bribery and corruption.
“During the IPO application processes the company was subject to rigorous due diligence reviews by regulatory authorities of the Shanghai Stock Exchange, in 2019, and the London Stock Exchange, in 2022, regarding its internal controls, integrity, compliance, and anti-bribery systems.” '
THEFERRET.SCOT Boss of SNP-backed wind firm named in bribery scandal

records.bodyText:
This is a prime example of where planning in Scotland is going wrong, resulting in the potential for decisions to be made as a result of decision-makers not having the complete picture.  
And this is because of the goldrush of renewable infrastructure which the Scottish Government has allowed, and is still allowing.  
We go back to the calls from Community Council Conventions to have a moratorium.
Everyone is swamped.  Communities; Campaign Groups; Community Councillors; Councils; the ECU; DPEA; Reporters.  All struggling.
We have some sympathy with Council Planners who are required to produce reports in advance of a meeting where decisions will be made; they have no recourse other than to check on the ECU website and if the ECU hasn't got representations up, the planners are scuppered. 
We see the DPEA and Reporters being driven by Scottish Government timeframes - and, in the case of the OHLs in particular, by SSEN.
Lyndsey Ward has said, on CB4PC:  I thought their new system was supposed to be more efficient and faster.
She's right; they did.  It was one of the alleged reasons for them preventing objections by the time honoured e mail route.  
The omission has been uncovered in time, fortunately, so that NPAC Councillors can be presented with the true picture of community concerns, particularly as far as the EIA is concerned.

Viewed financially, the harder question is not whether the programme costs billions. It is how many billions belong to the complete system.
