records.title: Wind Energy's Absurd
records.bodyText:
AMENDED to include an Energy Voice piece focussing on what Kathryn Porter has said regarding Jackdaw.  This is at the end.
**
Kathryn Porter has a new report out - it's long and detailed.  We've summarised it as best as we are able, from our lay perspective.
The central argument is that gas remains fundamental to UK energy security for much longer than current policy appears to assume - for heating, industry and electricity generation.
The UK is simultaneously allowing domestic gas production and infrastructure to decline while becoming more dependent on imported electricity.
Where electricity comes in:
Gas does not simply 'set electricity bills'. Gas and carbon pricing determine the wholesale electricity price, but she calculates that this represents about 38% of the electricity bill; excluding carbon, gas accounts for about 35%. Network costs are already about 27%.
She argues that the big emerging cost problem is the electricity network, rather than gas. The enormous grid expansion required for the renewables build-out is increasingly being recovered through electricity bills.
Intermittent wind and solar also increase balancing costs, while inadequate transmission capacity means increasing constraint payments. 
She highlights the National Audit Office's criticism of Connect & Manage: renewable generation has been allowed to connect faster than the grid can accommodate it, with the resulting grid-upgrade costs falling on electricity consumers.
The network-cost trajectory is particularly striking: NESO expects transmission charges to rise from £8.9bn in 2026/27 to £13.6bn in 2030/31. Kathryn adds her voice to other experts who regard this as a lower-bound estimate because investment costs are already rising.
The really important electricity/gas link is that Britain is becoming increasingly dependent on electricity imports through interconnectors. She argues that this is a security risk because an interconnector does not create electricity - it merely transfers electricity that another country may itself need.
The problem is correlated weather: a cold, still period can mean low wind in Britain and neighbouring countries simultaneously. So precisely when Britain needs imported electricity most, neighbouring countries may have less surplus available.
That matters directly for gas: if imported electricity is unavailable, British gas-fired generation has to fill the gap.
Norway is particularly important. She estimates that losing the 1.4 GW North Sea Link could require around 67 GWh/day of additional gas burn, roughly 2 TWh over a winter month - about 5% of GB winter gas demand. And how often she has warned about the Norway interconnector.
France presents another risk because of its ageing nuclear fleet. A significant reduction in French nuclear availability would reduce electricity available to Britain and could also affect Belgian and Dutch exports. Again, the consequence for Britain is greater reliance on gas generation.
She also points to NESO's increasing use of interconnector restrictions, arguing that this makes the assumption that imports will always be available still less secure.
She says that NESO's hierarchy in Clean Power 2030 does not actually eliminate gas from the electricity system - demand response; short duration storage; interconnector imports; unabated gas (in that order).
Although gas is formally the last resort, if the preceding options are much less certain than the plan assumes , gas becomes the most important source of flexibility.
And, meanwhile, roughly 23–24 million UK homes remain gas-heated, so gas demand cannot disappear anything like as quickly as some policy assumptions imply.
Kathryn herself summarises her report, on Watt-Logic, from where the report can be downloaded.  One paragraph which we highlight, as it's the crux of the matter.
Gas security is impossible to separate from energy security. It’s not a subordinate or transitional concern to be addressed once the “more pressing” work of decarbonisation is complete. And energy security cannot be separated from national security. A country which is unable to reliably power and heat itself, maintain essential services or sustain its industrial base is inherently vulnerable. Every major energy-policy decision should be subjected to a national-security test.
https://watt-logic.com/.../gas-security-the-foundation.../
Kathryn Porter, founder of independent energy consultancy Watt-Logic, has issued a new report tackling why there’s a “myth” around arguments that North Sea gas – particularly from the Jackdaw oil and field – is a globally traded commodity so cannot reduce household energy bills.
The report comes as pressure mounts on UK prime minister Andy Burnham to make a decision on the North Sea field, the second largest hydrocarbon field in the UK continental shelf which is awaiting a government decision on whether or not it goes ahead.
Porter argued that commodities pricing and the UK’s marginal pricing model was little understood by policy makers and that claims UK North Sea production was in “terminal decline and no longer worth bothering with” was “both dishonest and stupid”.
She said: “Once this marginal pricing mechanism is understood, the case for maximising domestic production becomes obvious.
“North Sea gas is not only cheaper than imported LNG, it is also cleaner, so preferring it is a no-brainer for anyone not completely brain-washed by Just Stop Oil zealots.
“UKCS gas is also more secure than imported gas – it is directly connected to the National Transmission System (“NTS”), and, unlike an LNG cargo, it cannot just sail away when a buyer elsewhere in the world offers more money.”
She added: “The Jackdaw field is large enough to fully displace price-setting LNG for between two and four months of the year, which would have a meaningful impact on summer gas prices.”

records.title: Wind Energy's Absurd
records.bodyText:
In December, The Highland Council voted to agree with planners' recommendation and raise an objection to the proposed Shinness wind farm in Sutherland - 15 x 200m turbines. So a public local inquiry was set in train.  The Preliminary Inquiry Meeting was held in July.  At that PIM, it was stated that the applicant, in communication with the Council, had suggested the venue for hearings - which were set for 2,3,4 November - be Lairg Community Hall.
So far, so good.  Shinness to Lairg is 7 miles.  A reasonable distance to get to on rural roads on very possibly dismal November days - on dark, very possibly dismal days when folk would be returning from the hearings.
But, no - not simple.  The inquiry will now be held in Brora, which is over 30 miles away.  This e mail thread explains what happened.  So, we ask ourselves, why was it not possible simply for the applicant/agent to unbook the hotel accommodation at Lairg and change to the venue at Rosehall, which is 16 miles away - and why did the DPEA not insist on it?
It started with an e mail from the DPEA to the agents, David Bell Planning and to THC on 24 September.  (NB.  Tony is Tony Bridge, the local campaigners' lead.  Adrian Phillips is the case officer with the DPEA.  We have not put any salutations or closings in the majority of the e mails.  Ian Kelly is acting for three estates.)
Mr Kelly and Mr Bridge have been in contact and advised they are not happy with the choice in venue. They have requested that the meeting be held in Rosehall Village Hall as an alternative. The reporters are considering the request. They have asked I advise you both that you may not want to book accommodation until the matter is resolved.
I will keep in contact regarding this once I have more information.
Deidre Thom's response (Senior Associate at David Bell: also on 24th.
Further to you (sic) note below, I am writing on behalf of the Applicant to express serious concern regarding the suggestion that the venue for the forthcoming Inquiry may be changed in response to Mr Kelly and Mr Bridges requests. This development is both unexpected and problematic.
The venue selection process has already been extensively delayed and in reliance on the confirmation of the venue this week from the DPEA we have booked accommodation for six people for the duration of the PLI. Further, cancelling the hotel for the inquiry may mean they will have lost bookings. 
In short, the reconsideration of the venue for Rosehall Village Hall is unacceptable to the Applicant. We waited until we received the formal confirmation from DPEA before making confirmed reservations and to change this now is unacceptable and introduces unnecessary delay and uncertainty for all participants.
We urge the Reporters to proceed with the originally identified venue. Anything less could set an unhelpful precedent.
I would appreciate confirmation that the event arrangements will continue as planned.
DPEA responded to parties, also on 24th:
The reporters have considered the parties’ comments regarding the venue for the forthcoming inquiry. Given that the DPEA confirmed the booking of the Royal Marine Hotel, Brora to parties, and that parties have already proceeded to make arrangements on this basis, they have decided to proceed with this Brora option.
Ian Kelly, planning consultant, to DPEA, also on 24th.
With the greatest of respect that is completely the wrong analysis.
There was a more local venue, one that was mentioned by Tony, but which you failed to check, and which is available.
Brora is a totally remote location for this Inquiry, the fact that you made a mistake in booking it without any PRIOR discussion with the objector parties is not a valid reason for continuing with a mistake.
I, for one, had not made any arrangements for a PLI in Brora, nor had the local objectors I would assume.
Please eat some humble pie, admit that mistakes were made, and change the venue to the more local and available Rosehall village hall.
On 25th, Ian Kelly wrote again:
I note that there is no correspondence about the venue on the case file and so I had not seen the original emails in the trail, but I do see that you had indicated to the applicants that they might not want to book accommodation until the matter of the venue was resolved. 
Therefore, it was at their own risk that they made a booking.
Adding the exact times of the relevant communications to the email below fully confirms my reasoning that the venue could easily have been changed:
- your email advising of the Brora venue (the first that I had even heard about this possibility) was received on the 22nd at 1745
- the availability of Rosehall village hall and the provisional booking was notified to you on the 23rd at 08.58
So, basically the venue check and confirmation of availability was completed overnight. On that basis you could have advised parties of the change of venue to the more local location very first thing in the morning of the 23rd i.e. on the morning immediately after your evening email.
Deidre Thom responded to Ian Kelly and the DPEA, also on 25th:
I am emailing to clarify a point below, for the avoidance of doubt, and as noted in my email, we waited to book accommodation until receipt of the formal DPEA letter, which as noted was received in the evening of the 22 September with accommodation being confirmed thereafter by the Applicant on the 23rdSeptember.
It was not until yesterday, 24th September, that we were made aware of any concerns with the venue and advised holding off booking accommodation.
We trust the venue is as confirmed.
Ian Kelly to Deidre Thom, on 25th:
Good morning and thanks for that. 
Can you please confirm that the email at 1745 on the 22nd was the very first time that you knew anything at all about the Brora venue (certainly I knew nothing about issues with venues up until that point).
Also, were you aware that some two weeks ago Tony had supplied Adrian with a list of local venues that included Rosehall village hall.
Ian Kelly to Deidre Thom  on 25th:
Apologies for pressing on this matter but I am considering seeking client instructions on whether or not to submit a formal complaint to the DPEA about the Public Inquiry venue selection process.
However, to enable me to evaluate matters, and as I was not copied into any correspondence, I need to have a better handle on exactly what happened between the correspondence Adrian - Tony - Adrian on or around the 8th September, which identified three local alternative venues of which Rosehall village hall was one, and the email notice on the evening of 22nd September that the Inquiry was to be at Brora.
Reviewing what I say below in the light of that, my question is really in two parts:
- did Adrian contact you in any way after the 8th September to discuss Inquiry venues, and
- when did you first become aware that Brora was being considered as a venue
I look forward to hearing from you so that I can seek client instruction over the weekend.
Ian Kelly, again on 25th:
I simply note that you have not replied to my two simple questions below. 
In seeking instructions on the matter of a possible formal complaint to the DPEA I will now need to simply form my own assessments as to what has happened here. But it is perfectly clear that there is no plausible scenario of Adrian moving from being advised of three local venues on the 8th September (with Rosehall village hall always having been available) to then booking The Marine in Brora late on the 22nd September, without having communicated with anyone at all in between those dates.
Deidre Thom responded, on 25th:
Apologies, I have been tied up in other matters today. Notwithstanding, I consider this to be a matter for the DPEA.
Ian Kelly, on 25th, in response:
Thanks Deirdre,
But with respect, confirming if you had heard from Adrian after the 8th September, and confirming when you first knew of the proposal to use Brora, are matters for you to answer and not for the DPEA to answer.
In those circumstances your non answer is very disappointing and not what I would have expected, but it does basically confirm my assumptions.
Deidre Thom's response:
It is for the DPEA to arrange the venue for the Inquiry.
We were advised on Tuesday 22 September, that the DPEA were making arrangements for the Brora venue, following a request from me for confirmation of a venue. The DPEA advised this would be formally confirmed, which it was later that evening. 
I had correspondence from Mr Philips on the 8th of September to confirm that the DPEA were looking at a number of local venues, namely Dornoch Community Centre, Bonar Bridge Community Hall and “The Barn” ran by Kyle of Sutherland Development Trust but nothing was confirmed. Rose Hall Village Hall was not mentioned nor was the Brora venue.
Tony Bridge wrote to the DPEA, with copies to IK, Deidre Thom and THC, on 25th:
I am extremely disappointed at the decision of the Reporters to keep the location of the hearing at Brora and dissatisfied with the reasons given. My understanding is that a PLI should take place as local as possible to the proposed development site. The clue, after all, is in the name. Whilst I accept that Lairg Community Hall is not available, the second most local venue is available and has been kindly booked by Mr Kelly.
Brora is not local to West Shinness. It is an hour away on a normal journey on our poor roads, particularly after dark (as it will be on the return), and half the distance again of Rosehall. There are no public transport links. This means additional time commitment and, given the current price of fuel, especially in the local area, considerable extra cost. It is likely this will deter some local people from attending. As importantly, there are no real community links between the two places. Brora is very much regarded as a separate community, unlike Rosehall which is very much related to Lairg, or even Golspie which has close community links.
It seems to me that this decision has been made for the convenience only of those attending from the south. After all, there is no difference in time or cost in travelling to either Rosehall or Brora from Edinburgh. No consideration has been paid to the needs and wishes of the local community for whom the PLI is allegedly convened. My concern is that this decision will only serve to feed the growing sense of injustice in this area that local democracy is being increasingly ignored and the whole energy consent process, which has huge power over the lives, livelihoods and wellbeing of locals, is biased against considering the needs and wishes of the local community. There is currently a never-ending stream of ill-considered applications that threaten to change the local landscape, economy and way of life for so many people who, sadly, increasingly feel little more than inconvenient collateral damage in the face of profiteering by multinational companies, and increasingly let down by a process of government that is at best opaque and inaccessible, at worst biased or simply a tick-box exercise.
I strongly ask that the decision on location be reconsidered.
We understand that no acknowledgement was received from the DPEA.
Ian Kelly to the DPEA with copies to THC, Tony Bridge and Deidre Thom, on 27th.
I now wish this matter of the Inquiry venue to be treated as a formal complaint and I ask that the whole correspondence file on the venue is passed to the appropriate person in the DPEA for, hopefully, an early assessment and response.
The substance of the complaint is as below:
- there are only four parties to this Inquiry and so it is very easy to communicate with everyone at the same time
- when it was discovered that the Lairg hall was not available it appears that only Mr Bridge was contacted about possible venues
- the reply gave three possibilities but no contact details
- there was no email to me asking if I knew of contact details (which I did) 
- the applicants were then emailed, around the same time as the local objectors, to say that three venues were being looked at, none of which had been mentioned by Mr Bridge
- there was no communication with myself at all about venues at that stage or in the subsequent two weeks
- then on the evening of the 22nd an unexpected email was received saying that the venue would be Brora, a totally different locality
- no explanation was given as to how this had come about when a more local and previously used venue, the Rosehall village hall, had always been available
- the objections to the use of Brora were rejected on the simplistic basis that an email about the venue had already been sent out
- the subsequent detailed submission from the local objectors has basically been ignored 
- there has been no explanation as to why all parties were not contacted at the various stages to assist with finding a venue
- this process has been stressful for the local objectors who have been left facing at least a one hour drive each way to attend the Hearing
- that is not a fair or reasonable outcome for the local objectors
- the above “story” goes completely against the the normal DPEA approach of actively seeking a local venue
The remedies that are requested are as below:
- an acknowledgement that mistakes have been made 
- the venue changed to Rosehall village hall, which has always been available, and for which venue all parties would need to do some driving, a perfectly equitable and fair outcome
I would be grateful if this matter, which is unlike anything else I have ever come across in some 25 years of renewables PLI work, could be addressed quickly.
Ian Kelly has confirmed to his clients  'having received the Brora venue email at about 5.30pm on the 22nd I had the Rosehall village hall booked and that booking notified to the DPEA before 9am the next morning.'
The e mail exchanges are still, at the time of this post - 28th @ 12.30, still not on the DPEA website.
What an utter shambles and, to us, it seems as if once again the DPEA is perceived as kowtowing to developers and their associated personnel, but it's a good job that someone, at least, is trying to look after the lawful interests of local communities.

We just watched the ten minutes of Miatta Fahnbulleh's inaugural speech at the Labour Party Conference.
She presented well, without all the swivel-eyed pomp and hand-waving of Miliband.
But she gave the industry sod all.  She did whip up the conference about climate change and the fact that, in her view, the effects are here, as proven by this summer  'Climate change is here - there can be no doubt about it and yet, today, there are politicians who can't see what we can all see, who are prepared to play politics with our communities, our children's futures'.  
And she went on to slag off Kemi Badenoch and Richard Tice, and then to say all that Labour had done and how they had to drive bills down because energy is not a luxury, it's an essential and is unaffordable for millions.  
The public need to be in control, she said, and went on to praise Great British Energy and the local power plan - and the great homes upgrade.  
Energy Voice, in a short round-up of the speech, imply that any industry wallahs who were there today, hoping for an indication of something meaty for them, were short-changed, and we're inclined to agree as a day pass to the balcony was in excess of a thousand quid.  
She is more attractive than Miliband - we'll give her that - and possibly did not have as much of his overt zealotry about her as we might have expected.  (That does sound a tad sexist, but never mind; it's what we thought.)
https://www.energyvoice.com/.../fahbulleh-rosebank-jackdaw/
'Industry figures at the Labour Party Conference hoping for some movement and direction from across the energy sector were left wanting as Miatta Fahnbulleh focused on the cost of living throughout her address.
All eyes were on Fahnbulleh as she took to the stage for her inaugural party conference speech as Energy Secretary.
Questions around Rosebank and Jackdaw approvals were circling the show floor, alongside whether the hydrogen strategy would be referenced or the carbon capture space would get an indication of what could come in 2027.
Naturally, groundbreaking policy announcements rarely come from such speeches, but the hefty entry fee for industry to attend the conference hardly paid for itself over this ten-minute monologue.
Rather than speaking of upstream policy – which Miliband became accustomed to –  Fahnbulleh centred her speech on the cost of living crisis.
Fahnbulleh told conference delegates, “Energy is an everyday essential, yet something so basic has become a core issue in the cost of living crisis”.
She also sniped at Tory leader Kemi Badenoch and Reform’s Richard Tice for their decision to scrap net zero and repeal the Climate Change Act. She said both parties would fail in their “duty to protect our community” if they were in power.
Fahbulleh leaned on the creation of GB Energy under a Labour government and the rollout of nuclear developments such as Wylfa through GB Energy Nuclear.
She also announced plans to devolve the warm homes plan, giving regional mayors more say on the £15 billion public investment programme launched in January 2026 to upgrade up to 5 million homes by 2030.
Energy minister Michael Shanks had already done the media rounds in the build-up to the annual Labour conference, rebutting claims that the government is delaying a decision on Rosebank and Jackdaw for political reasons – namely the upcoming by-election in former prime minister Kier Starmer’s Holborn and St Pancras seat.
As leader of the Green Party, Zack Polanski is standing in the seat; there is speculation the government could delay a decision in a bid to thwart his attempt at putting energy policy at the heart of the fight for the London seat.
However, Shanks said the government will make a decision on controversial UK oil and gas fields, Jackdaw and Rosebank, “as soon as we can”.
Published last week, a consultation on the controversial Jackdaw field showed majority support. 
Outside of the traditional oil and gas sector, there was no reference to the delayed hydrogen strategy either – as the industry clings on to the 2022 hope that is yet to materialise.
The same could be said for carbon capture and storage, which also failed to get any love from the energy secretary.
Fahnbulleh’s speech was on brand for Burnham’s direction, since toppling Kier Starmer – putting the cost of living at the forefront of every government department.'

records.title: Wind Energy's Absurd
records.bodyText:
Earlier, we watched Andy Burnham's speech at the Labour Conference to see if we could glean anything more than had been reported in the media - we didn't.
However, looking for something else which we may post about shortly, we came across a piece on the DESNZ website giving more detail about The Great British Grid proposal.  
We've decided to concentrate on one section only for now - reforms to expand self build connections.
The Government says it will reform the system so that 'businesses and developers can build their own grid connections', rather than having to wait for a network company to construct them.
So what does that actually mean?
At present, a large project - such as a data centre, industrial development, battery or generation project - can be waiting not only for a place in the connections queue, but also for the network company to design, procure and construct the physical infrastructure needed to connect it.
Under the proposed reforms, a developer could potentially 'construct some of that high-voltage connection itself', to standards and requirements set by the network operator.
In simple terms:
Current system:
Developer → network company → design/procure/build connection → connect project
Proposed system:
Developer → arrange/build connection → network operator approves/controls connection → connect project
The idea is that this could remove one of the bottlenecks and allow projects to be connected more quickly. The Government points to experience in Ireland, where similar arrangements have reduced connection times by up to 11 months.
But there is an important caveat.
Self-build does not mean that a developer can simply build whatever electricity infrastructure it wants and plug into the grid.
The network still has to be capable of accommodating the new demand or generation, and the connection has to meet technical and safety requirements.
Ofgem is already developing this reform under its 'Connect Accelerate' programme. Significantly, it is looking at both:
'self-build and transfer' - the developer builds the infrastructure and subsequently transfers it to the network operator; and
'self-build and ownership' - the developer may retain ownership of the infrastructure.
Ofgem is due to consult on these arrangements.
There is therefore a much bigger question underneath today's announcement:
Who actually builds - and potentially who owns - parts of Britain's future high-voltage electricity network?
This is also why the development of the Regional Energy Strategic Plans (RESP) and other strategic network planning is important.
Strategic planning determines what the electricity system is going to need and where. Connections reform determines which projects should connect and when. Self-build potentially changes who constructs the infrastructure needed to make those connections happen.
These reforms are being developed in parallel rather than waiting for the full RESP, which is not expected until 2028.
So today's announcement isn't simply about creating another public body called the Great British Grid.
It is part of a much wider restructuring of how Britain's electricity network is planned, financed, built and connected.
And with the enormous expansion of electricity infrastructure now being proposed across the country, that is something worth watching closely.
https://www.gov.uk/.../great-british-grid-to-speed-up...

records.bodyText:
Councillor Karl Rosie was in the Chair.
Early on, Councillor Richard Gale wanted to refer to the volume of work needed to properly scrutinise the applications before them.  He said that the number of meetings should be increased, or the timeframe for dealing with applications.  Rhoda Banfro, the legal clerk, said that she would discuss with the relevant people.
Councillor Jan McEwan wanted to know if the last two items could be heard first so that they didn't slip at the end, but the Chair said that, although he appreciated her point, the order would be kept.
We recognised instantly that the first item should have been the Acheilidh wind farm but was, in fact, the Abhainn Dubh wind farm and were shouting at the screens; amazingly, however it wasn't picked up until  Councillor Gale highlighted the issue at the beginning of the second item, and this then caused problems for the committee - see at the end of this section.
As with Acheilidh, this had been returned to NPAC as additional information had been provided in respect of Raeshaw.
Councillor Gale said that so much was being assumed and without all the information that the committee needed.
Councillor Angela MacLean said it was a chicken and egg, or a Catch 22 situation and asked how confident should the committee be that they would have control over the grid connection route.  The applicant has said it would underground some, but SSEN says that there are options to overground.  
Councillor McEwan asked if they could defer.
The planner and Peter Wheelan tried to explain the multi stage condition process, but appreciated that it was difficult.
Councillor Sarah Atkin asked if this was going to happen a lot, post-Raeshaw, and the answer, from Rhoda Banfro, was yes.  Prior to Raeshaw, it was piecemeal and now they are having to pick up on Raeshaw.
The planner suggested that this could be dealt with by delegation.  Rhoda Banfro agreed, but said that should be a wider discussion.
Moving to debate, Councillor Rosie said he was content to move to recommendation.
Councillor Gale said that their decision would be based on what ifs and he couldn't do that, therefore he would be raising an amendment to object.  Councillor Isabelle Campbell said she would second Councillor Rosie, and Councillor MacEwan said she would second Councillor Gale.
Although Councillor Atkin said that she read this as nothing happens unless it all happens, and that they are stabbing in the dark and it's hanging in the air, she was minded to say that planners' recommendation was sensible.
Rhoda Banfro said that  multi-stage can function and until those conditions were satisfied, the wind farm would not go ahead.  It would come back to THC - either for under- or overgrounding.
Councillor MacLean said that it was very emotive for communities as they had to live with the committee's decisions.  She said that Councillors are inundated with e mails from communities on any infrastructure; that the committee walks away but communities live with it; that edicts from Westminster and the Scottish Government on national priorities doesn't help; that it's salami slicing and has impact on communities; that their role is to make recommendations based on evidence, but that what's stated in the report in two sections ** does bring comfort; that the system is the problem; she supports raising no objection but understands colleagues.
So it went to the vote - Motion to raise no objection;  Cllr Rosie; seconded by Cllr Campbell, and Amendment to raise objection; Cllr Gale; seconded by Cllr McEwan.  Voting was 4-3 in favour of the motion.
**It looked to us as if the two paragraphs Cllr MacLean referred to were actually in the Acheilidh planners' recommendation and that was absolutely right because....
After Cllr Gale highlighted that there had been an error, and that Acheilidh and Abhainn Dubh had been transposed, there was a break to discuss the situation.
Rhoda Banfro explained - and this was approximately at 11.10 - that there had been an oversight on behalf of officers and, as members thought they were discussing Acheilidh, the whole process needed to be started again.  She said they should have picked this up.
Councillor Atkin asked if both of them should be deferred on the basis of 'stress, time, good God'.  
Rhoda Banfro said that they had to go through both, but she recognised that it was a lot of effort and if members are exhausted at the end of the day they can choose to defer what's left, to be determined on another day.
Councillor Atkin made the point that these are important to communities.
Rhoda Banfro suggested starting again and  at 5 pm they could see if they wanted to defer some applications.
Councillor Struan Mackie asked if members could vote to change the order as some members would not be able to be there.  Rhoda Banfro confirmed that they could, so Cllr Mackie proposed that Abhainn Dubh and Acheilidh be taken at the end.  Cllr MacEwan seconded this.
But Cllr Gale said that some members would not be able to stay until the end.  Rhoda Banfro said that there are members of the public outside who may be there for the items on Allt an Tuir and the housing (SSEN).
Councillor Rosie said to Councillor Mackie that they would consider items 8.1-8.5 and then Abhainn Dubh and Acheilidh would be determined at the end.  Cllr Mackie agreed.
We remain at a total loss to understand how nobody picked this up until Councillor Gale did when it came to the second item.  We have decided to leave the above, even though the determination had to be done all over again.
Allt an Tuir Renewable Park- REG/ESB.  7 x 200m; 1 x 180m; 1 x 167m turbines; BESS; solar array, etc.
The planner opened by saying that the ECU has altered and so recent representations are not included in the planners' report.  There are 73 representations on the website; he made mention that the Creich Community Council objection is on the website.  (As an aside, we suspect that these points may have been made in light of the criticisms of the planners' report and the mismatch between what's published on the ECU website by the time planners write their reports).
He said that environmental grid effects are not known and traffic and traffic impacts are also not known, and so planners have prepared conditions.
Councillors John Edmondson and Richard Gale had several queries relating to the National Scenic Area; to the Wild Land which would be lost.  Normally, we'd go into a bit more detail as to who said what, but the error at the beginning, and the volume of applications to be determined, makes this impractical.  The planner's angle was that it's not a huge scheme and not of such magnitude that the landscape couldn't accommodate it.
Councillor Laura Dundas asked at what point is cumulative effect unacceptable.  She was concerned about noise for receptors.  In his response, the planner said that visual effects were considered to be localised.  Councillor Dundas asked how long construction was expected to go on for.  The answer was 23 months.  The planner said that the construction would be quite far from receptors, but there would be traffic movement.
Councillor Tamala Collier asked several questions - what part of the Wild Land would be lost; what mitigation had been considered; concern about roads and abnormal loads through Invercassley and how they would be communicated to residents.
The planner said that it was for NatureScot to advise Ministers on Wild Land; that traffic needs to be assessed; that a Community Liaison Group would be established and plans would be based around community events, etc, although this can't be conditioned.
Councillor  McEwan asked about noise impact on 70 residents.  She also asked if blasting would take place.  She was concerned about the number of HGVs on delicate roads and asked if the turbines would be on peatland.
The planner said that they could not hold construction up because of noise but they would require it to be managed through conditions, especially as there would be more noise in forming the track near to Rosehall.  Environmental Health control noise.  He confirmed that there would probably be blasting of borrow pits, and said that there will be disturbance of peatland, with the expectation that peat will be managed through SEPA.
Councillor McEwan asked if there is compensation for third parties whose land was involved, and she asked about shadow flicker and aviation lighting.  She had got a bit confused on the shadow flicker front and so the planner put her right - that aviation lighting did not cause it and that there had been a shadow flicker assessment; that conditions would be put on aviation lighting for sensoring to be used as soon as it is approved for use in the UK.
Councillor Chris Baird spoke about his concerns on flooding at certain times of year, and also about noise as the developer admitted that noise could exceed ETSU levels at some Rosehall residences.  He corrected a statement that on the road to Invershin there are 70 properties; he said there are 90.  On noise - and a little further questioning from Cllr Baird the planner said that everything including noise would be conditioned.
In the debate, Councillor Edmondson referred to significant adverse effect within the NSA and asked if effects had been avoided or mitigated.  He said that if he took a large bite from an apple, it's still recognised as an apple, but diminished. He also spoke about ancient woodland, and ended up saying that he did not see how a conclusion could be safely reached and he would raise a motion to object.  Councillor Gale said that this represented a significant effect on the landscape, and an encirclement of Rosehall; that they were paying lip service to Raeshaw; there was not enough information in front of them and he would be happy to second.
Councillor Michael Baird said that it was salami slicing and he was happy to back his two fellow Councillors.
Councillor Liz Kraft asked, because they are not the decision-makers, was there a risk that they might lose the multi-stage conditions.
Rhoda Banfro said that multi-stage conditions will still feature, to protect the Council's position.  She had asked for a check as to whether a holding response had been sent from the Council, and Peter Wheelan confirmed that it had, in October last year, and so as that pre-dated the new regime, it would trigger an automatic public local inquiry.
Councillor McEwan said that she was concerned about cumulative impact - if everything went through, there would be 801 turbines in the area.  She agreed with raising an objection.
Rhoda Banfro asked Councillor Edmondson to read his proposed grounds for raising an objection, for the benefit of the public, which he did, very ably and concisely, raising the points which had been discussed.
Councillor Rosie said that he was content to move an amendment to agree planner recommendations, and Councillor Kraft seconded.
Apart from Councillors Rosie and Kraft, the voting was unanimous - 11-2 - to raise an objection.  So this will go to public local inquiry.
Because Councillor Rosie had to leave at 3.30, and Councillor Kraft couldn't chair the Acheilidh determination, it was decided to bring that one forward.  This is Energiekontor.  12 x 200-230m turbines, BESS and was sent back to THC re Raeshaw.
The planner apologised again for the mix up earlier.
He highlighted the Catch 22.  There is no grid connection planned in detail until the wind farm is agreed.  However, as we highlighted in our post with the Agenda, planners have put this caveat:
Subject to a multistage condition being applied to any consent. As set out in the report, the condition would ensure that works to construct the wind farm are not commenced until such a time as the grid connection is approved following assessments of any significant effects.
Councillor Gale said that there were a lot of unknowns.  Peter Wheelan emphasised that if an application is made for a grid connection, that will come back for determination.  And if a connection is not granted, the wind farm will not get built.
Councillor Rosie said that he thought the wind farm was acceptable in principle, with the multi-stage conditions.  So he moved to agree.  Councillor Isabelle Campbell seconded.  Councillor Gale said there are too many unknowns and he needed more clarity and no salami slicing, and was moving an amendment to raise an objection.  He was seconded by Councillor McEwan.  
The vote was 4-3 not to raise an objection and it was agreed that conditions would be delegated.
The next application was the Lochend wind farm extension - Constantine Wind Energy for 5 x 149.9m turbines and BESS.  
Councillor Rosie asked Councillor Kraft to take the Chair.
Councillor Atkin expressed concern about noise to residents, saying that there was no price to pay on people's health; she referred to low frequency noise, and asked for clarification that turbines would be 500m from some properties and that 17 had financial agreements.  Peter Wheelan explained that under ETSU-97 and the new guidance, a higher noise level, by 10db, was allowed if there are financial agreements, or financial interests.
Councillor McEwan asked whether Orkney Council had been consulted; how far the site is from the Castle of Mey, and what economic benefit there is to Caithness.
Rhoda Banfro pointed out that economic benefit is not a material consideration.  Councillor McEwan asked why it was in the EIA.  Rhoda said it was considered by a different part of the Council, to give a rounded overview.
The planner said that Orkney Council had not been consulted as it was considered that distance was not significant; that the proposal is 5km from the Castle of Mey.
Councillor McEwan asked about it having been stated that working could take place outside normal working hours.  Peter Wheelan said that they may need to seek dispensation - weather if erecting a turbine, for example, or for concrete pours and it would be very occasional.
Councillor Rosie said that he considered that the proposal complies with policy and was content to move the recommendation; Councillor Kraft seconded.
Councillor Atkin came back on the subject of noise and said it was trying to make it easier to put turbines nearer to residences; she said she found that shocking.  It was a 'just transition', she said.  And that they needed more planning training.  She said that it was still lives which could be impacted and why were they making it more difficult to put things right.
Councillor McEwan raised the question of cumulative effect.  That Dunnet Head was a well known viewpoint and she was also concerned about bird mortality.  She said that the overload of wind farms was getting out of hand.
Councillor Mackie said this was being presented as an extension, but is not what people think of as an extension (ie a house extension) when it dwarfs the original.  He, too, referred to Dunnet Head and the Castle and gardens of Mey; the fact that the latter is associated with the late Queen Mother and that the King visits every year.  He also referred to the NC500 and said that it is not in keeping.  And proposed an amendment to reject.
Councillor Gale said that they had been lulled into thinking that one more won't make a difference, and that he was happy to support the amendment.
Councillor Edmondson said that he was concerned that as turbines were getting bigger, they were getting noisier, and distance from properties should be increasing.
Peter Wheelan referenced the Hollandmey wind farm which was granted by Scottish Ministers and was for a larger wind farm, with turbines of the same height.  He expressed concern at the validity of an argument to reject, given that.
Rhoda Banfro said that Councillor Rosie had left the chamber so his motion to grant would fall, but Councillor Kraft proposed one and it was seconded by Councillor Christine Gillies.  Councillor McEwan withdrew her amendment in favour of one from Councillor Mackie who read his amendment.
Rhoda Banfro echoed what Peter Wheelan had said about the Hollandmey wind farm; that that wind farm was rejected on similar grounds.  She was concerned that the same argument ran risk and therefore of expenses risk.
The vote was narrow - 6-5 in favour of the motion.  So the extension was granted and it was agreed that conditions would be by delegated powers.
Then  Greenswitch BESS,  Thurso came next.  The recommendation was to raise no objection.  THC had submitted an objection and it was proposed to withdraw that.
There were a few questions, one of which was quite amusing.  Councillor Mackie asked if there was a standard for acoustic fencing.  He said that it just looked like an ordinary fence.  The planner said that he was not aware of a standard.  Peter Wheelan said that acoustic fences were typically timber without gaps.  Councillor Mackie said 'so an acoustic fence is a fence; nothing inherently special.'  Peter Wheelan said 'a robust fence'.  
Now we know nothing about acoustics, but we had imagined that an acoustic fence did have some special property.  Silly us!!
There was no debate and Councillor Kraft moved to agree the recommendation.  Delegated powers were also agreed.
Next, Councillor Kraft said that there had been a request from planning that they bring the Abhainn Dubh application forward from its new place at the end.  Rhoda Banfro said she knew it had been a long day (she wasn't kidding) and planners were concerned that, if left to the end, it might not get decided and, with a deadline looming, the ECU may just issue consent.  It was agreed to bring that forward and get through the remainder of the agenda.
There were a couple of questions over and above this morning's questions and debates on the application, but it was agreed to accept the recommendation not to raise an objection and to grant delegated powers.
Last - for us at least - was the application from Ian Elliott Ltd. to build 49 housing units at the Muir of Ord, 40 of which would be to accommodate SSEN workers, with 20 due to be transferred back to the Council, at a discounted rate (not buckshee) at the end of a four year period - 12 x 2-bed; 8 x 3-bed).
Councillor Gale asked if they were primarily for workers would they need to apply for HMO listing, and he asked who would maintain the gardens while they were occupied by SSEN.
The planner said that they were Class 9 houses as most were 2-bed.  The garden maintenance would be down to the landlord.
Councillor Collier asked what would happen if construction were delayed.  The planner said that there are ongoing discussions between SSEN and the Legal Department.
Councillor MacLean referred to a lot of concerns in the community and that Muir of Ord had been chosen for housing because of housing need.  And that if legacy housing, then the community should get first option - to local people on the waiting list.
Councillor Edmondson wanted to know what was the position if SSEN didn't take the houses; are SSEN giving additionality; he would want to know the status of conditions and was trying to understand the mechanism of a change in allocation.  The planner's response was that they would be discounted and that they would be legacy houses.  The Planning Manager said that if a developer wanted to change they would need a S42 to do so.
Councillor MacLean spoke about school capacity; she said that parent councils are concerned that it would be a question of shove a portacabin up.  The planner said that the information came from Education Planning and she was not able to comment on the school roll.
In debate, only Councillor MacLean spoke to say that the community have worked hard on their amenity, taking on board active travel - walking/cycling and that this should be an opportunity for local people.  She was not against the proposal as they need more properties and so she accepted the recommendation.  There were no dissenting voices and it was agreed  to grant, and that delegated powers would be used going forward, including seeing if housing need can be included in conditions.
And with that - we breathed a huge sigh of relief.

records.title: Wind Energy's Absurd
records.bodyText:
The Herald has a piece on Audit Scotland's report, out today, on The Scottish Government’s £500 million Offshore Wind Investment Programme (OWIP), established in 2023 to develop Scotland's offshore wind supply chain and attract private investment.  The paper's version is slightly sanitised.
There has been progress, but the report makes clear that delivery is slower than expected and there are significant risks to achieving the programme's intended outcomes.
Some of the key findings:
 £141 million of the £500m available had been contractually committed by July 2026, across 17 projects. A further eight projects had been approved but were not yet contractually committed.
 The programme has attracted £413 million of private investment, apparently putting it on track for its target of £3 private investment for every £1 of public funding.
 However, there is a very important qualification to that figure: £327 million of the £413 million is associated with the Sumitomo subsea cable factory at the Port of Nigg.
 Without the Sumitomo project, the remaining 16 committed projects have attracted only 70.5p of private investment for every £1 of OWIP funding.
 There is also a significant difference between the type of public investment being made and the programme's original 'Commercial First' approach. Of the £141m committed, £109m is grant funding, with only £32m provided through loans or equity. Grants cannot be recovered and recycled in the same way as commercial investment.
 Audit Scotland also says there are gaps in the evidence needed to demonstrate that public investment is being directed where it will have the greatest impact, and that the extent to which investment is genuinely additional - in other words, would not have happened anyway - is not yet clear.
 The programme suffered a commercially sensitive data breach in December 2024. This resulted in restrictions on information sharing between the delivery partners and meant that the Delivery Board stopped making collective investment decisions for more than a year. A new information-sharing agreement was finally agreed in July this year.
 Progress has also been affected by reduced investor confidence and wider regulatory and policy issues. The Scottish Government has not yet updated the programme's business case to reflect the changed market conditions, although work on this is underway.
 And perhaps significantly, there is currently no clear plan for what happens after March 2029, when the five-year programme is due to end. Audit Scotland says this creates uncertainty and risks to longer-term planning.
Audit Scotland is careful not to conclude that the programme has failed. Indeed, it acknowledges that important investments have been made, including the Sumitomo cable factory and port infrastructure.
But it says that at this stage it is not possible to conclude whether the investments will ultimately deliver value for money. Its assessment is therefore focused on the risks to achieving that value for money.
The report's own conclusion on progress is stark:
'Significant investments have been made but progress is not on track and there are risks to achieving outcomes.'
The fact that so much of that private investment is concentrated in one project, that the majority of public funding is being provided as grants, that additionality has yet to be established, and that the programme has no clear post-2029 plan are all worth watching.
Audit Scotland has made a series of recommendations to strengthen the programme's governance, project prioritisation, value-for-money assessment and longer-term planning.
It will be interesting to see what happens next.
https://www.heraldscotland.com/.../26594258.500m.../
https://audit.scot/.../renewable-energy-the-scottish...

The planning consultant Ian Kelly has heard back from the DPEA with reference to his complaint about the DPEA's handling of an appropriate venue for the Shinness wind farm hearing.
E mail from Ryan Gunn's office  to Ian Kelly, 30th September:
Afternoon Mr Kelly,
Please find attached communication regarding your complaint.
Kind regards
The attachment was a generic e mail, stating that the response to the complaint should be handled within 20 days.
Ian Kelly's response, also dated 30th:
Good evening Ryan,
Thank you for this, received three days after the complaint was lodged.
However, your timeline of 20 days will take us to the week before the Inquiry is due to take place and, at that point, there might be practical difficulties in reverting to the normal DPEA practice of finding a local venue for S36 PLI cases.
If I can be blunt, faced with a very obvious set of emails, exactly how long does it take an organisation to accept the basic facts that it:
- failed to consult all of the four parties when the original agreed venue was no longer available 
- failed to follow up with the four parties when the local objector representative suggested other local venues for which he did not have contact details 
- failed to consult any of the four parties before booking the remote venue of Brora for the PLI
- failed to respond with any proper reasoning to the objections to the Brora venue 
Throughout this period the alternative local venue of Rosehall village hall was always available and I had contact details, but knew nothing until the evening of the 22nd September and indeed when notified of the Brora venue I was able to provisionally reserve the Rosehall venue overnight.
This is not some sitting at my desk at home computer says no game. The totally inappropriate choice of venue will result in local people having to travel for over an hour each way at considerable costs to attend the Inquiry whilst the applicant’s team relaxes at their hotel.
There is absolutely no reason why you cannot address this matter this week.
And a subsequent one from Ian Kelly to Ryan Gunn:
So, I get an out of office email response - Ryan is not back in the office until Monday.
It is like a Little Britain send up farce, but just rather more serious.
But, in absolute fairness to the DPEA and to the other dedicated and incredibly helpful case officers, I need to state that this is the only wind farm PLI where we have any procedural concerns whatsoever over a venue and over keeping all (four) parties informed and consulted. 
Ian Kelly is fuming on behalf of the community he is representing, and rightly so.  As he says, the parties staying in Brora will be able to have a leisurely breakfast and stroll down to the inquiry room, while the community members - those impacted - will have to drive miles to the venue, and in all probability drive back home in the dark - and in possibly inclement weather conditions.

records.title: Wind Energy's Absurd
records.bodyText:
It's much quieter today than it has been for a while, and so we've been catching up on news from the rest of the UK and around the world.
One thing which caught our eye was a post from Bonnie Brady in the States, who had posted a link to Wind Europe who produced a report in April entitled 'Wind Energy Dis- and Misinformation'.  
No, not what you might think - holding their hands up to weasel half-truths and obfuscation. The report lumps campaigners of all sorts in with various politicians - in the UK Claire Coutinho and Richard Tice, cop it, along with Putin, Macron and others from various countries.  This is one of the mentions Tice got:
Richard Tice, Deputy Leader of Reform UK, called wind energy “very expensive” and “a con job’’ on X, despite wind and solar being Europe’s cheapest sources of energy, even when factoring-in system costs.  
We see that in our energy bills in the UK, don't we?
Macron is mentioned because he had said that the Iberian blackout was caused by renewables.  This is what Wind Europe says about that:
authorities clarified that renewables were not the cause
There we have it.  Did- and misinformation right there.  We know that Kathryn Porter is not the only energy expert to have clarified that the cause was absolutely renewables, but we have what she said to hand, from a speech she gave in Edinburgh in March:
There has been a lot of misinformation about the incident, with many renewables advocates insisting it wasn’t caused by renewables. I can tell you categorically that it was.  And she went on to explain precisely why it was.
We are reminded of 2013 when Vestas linked up with Greenpeace and, in their 'Act on Facts' campaign, said that they were starting with Australian anti-wind groups (Stop These Things and The Callous Wind were at the top of that country's targets) and would then come for us in Sweden, Ireland and the UK.  
They even paid universities to try to find us all.
We said 'Bring it on' and we also said that they had wasted money - we would have told them buckshee.
Nobody heard another dickie bird about them coming for us.
Nothing changes.
One thing we had to smirk at in the latest report from Wind Europe is under Recommendations, with this as one of the sub-headings:
Ensure social media platforms contain dis- and misinformation.
https://windeurope.org/.../wind-energy-dis-and.../...

Chris Stark, Miliband's answer to Tom Cruise - Head of Mission Control - is moving on after only two years in the job - which was to spearhead a vaccine delivery-style effort to hit the 2030 target.  It was said at the time that he would work with Ofgem and the National Grid to help resolve grid connection delays; that's gone well.
But, Michael Shanks in a eulogy on Linkedin (no we don't mean that Stark has moved that far - a eulogy for the living) has sung Stark's praises, and it has brought a little flurry of activity.  This is what Shanks said:
As Chris Stark CBE moves on from his role with the best title in the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero - Head of Mission Control (much better than Energy Minister) I wanted to say a huge personal thanks for all his experience, ambition, enthusiasm and effort. 
It seems inconceivable looking back that we should have made as much progress as we have on what were seemingly intractable problems in the deployment of clean power. And yet the Clean Power Unit led by Chris over the past two and a half years has broken new ground in how government delivers complex things and works together across Whitehall. 
The ambition we set out coming into government was always at the outside edges of what was possible, but that was the whole point. Get momentum behind something and sort problems as you go. We were incredibly close to hitting 100% clean power on our system just a few weeks ago - which just shows what’s possible when we focus on something. 
On a personal level I also want to say for all the ups and downs Chris has also made it good fun as this photo testifies… (who knows what the topic was here!) That was a photo of Shanks/Stark and others laughing round a table.  (Don't tempt us to tell him what the topic may have been!)
All the best for whatever challenge you take on next.

records.title: Wind Energy's Absurd
records.bodyText:
Dieter Helm, writing for the Times:
It’s not long ago that Ed Miliband was telling us the net zero 2030 target for electricity was going to give us £300 off our energy bills, because renewables are so much cheaper than fossil fuels. Even better, net zero would all be home-grown and give us energy security. And even better still, this would set a shining example, one that Miliband can now as foreign secretary offer to the world at the UN and the forthcoming Cop31 in Turkey in November. Cheap, home-grown and secure. Britain leading the world.
Except it’s not cheap, it’s not home-grown, and it’s not very secure. Britain is now the global leader in energy costs, with among the most expensive energy in the developed world. No amount of tinkering with bills will change these costs. A temporary VAT cut, some public money into a new Great British Grid and switching some subsidies from customers to taxpayers does not alter the costs. Nor do industrial energy subsidies. Rearranging the deckchairs will not make these high costs go away. They are locked in through to the end of the 2030s.
Miliband will find it a struggle at Cop31 to sell the British model he is responsible for designing. No world leader is looking to Britain to work out how to make energy cost so much, and no world leader wants the deindustrialisation that goes with this. No major energy-intensive business wants to locate in the northeast of Scotland to get close to very expensive intermittent offshore wind. They want internationally competitive power. In the jargon, they want electricity that meets the five nines: 99.999 per cent reliability. Sadly, wind and solar do not.
But aren’t these costs explained by the high and volatile gas prices from which renewables are designed to protect us? Isn’t it all the fault of the US and Iran, and Russia and Ukraine? Shouldn’t we just get out of oil and gas as soon as possible? Isn’t it just an energy utopia postponed?
It is true that gas prices have gone up a lot as the Russians invaded Ukraine, then back down a lot, then back up when the US attacked Iran, then down again, and then back up again as the Strait of Hormuz remained impeded. But it is also true that gas prices have gone up everywhere in Europe, and in China, India, Japan, Taiwan and South Korea. Yet Britain still has the highest costs. Of course, oil and gas prices might go down again. They probably will. Protecting Britain from low and stable oil and gas prices might even turn out to be Miliband’s legacy.
It’s not just other world leaders who are appalled. An increasing number in Britain are too. The wider net zero consensus has been shattered. Even Burnham has retreated back to the net zero 2050 target, comforted that it is a quarter of a century away. Miatta Fahnbulleh, Miliband’s successor as energy secretary, has drifted off the net zero 2030 target towards the 2035 target the Conservatives had previously adopted. The PM wants to get back to the average European prices (currently very high, just not as high as Britain’s) — in 2036.
With the illusion that renewables would usher in a new era of British competitiveness and a great advantage for all the new AI and data centre-based industries now sacrificed on the altar of high prices, the high prices are encouraging deindustrialisation and deterring new industries. The casualty list keeps growing, from refineries to fertilisers, steel, pottery, fibreglass and into farming and the service sectors. That’s why a US ban on diesel exports is such a serious threat. We don’t make enough any more. Voters are turning away, having been promised lower prices and been confronted with high ones.
All the while, climate change is getting worse. All this British pain is not making any noticeable difference. There is no let-up in the increase in concentration of carbon in the atmosphere. Having risen by around 2 parts per million (ppm) per annum since 1990, it is now rising at about 3ppm. More oil, gas and coal are being burnt year by year as a growing world economy still relies on fossil fuels for around 85 per cent of its energy. This is 85 per cent of a world economy almost three times bigger than it was in 1990 and for Britain nearly twice as big — though Britain’s territorial emissions are down due to the exit from “home-grown” coal, now replaced in part by the coal embedded in imports from countries like China.
The bad news for the climate is that a further great surge in energy demand is on its way. The new tech industries are all incredibly energy-intensive, with data centres just one part of the projected doubling of energy demand by 2050. OpenAI paused a multibillion data centre project in the northeast of England earlier this year, citing high energy costs. If the world economy continues to grow at 3 per cent per annum, and energy demand grows at about the same rate, there will be two world economies in 2050 compared to now and twice the energy demand.
The consequent enormous scale of the climate challenge requires not only that we decarbonise the existing economy, but also a whole new one as well and one that shows every sign of rising energy intensity. The very idea that a combination of energy efficiency, wind and solar could meet most of this demand is dangerously utopian. Energy efficiency increases energy demand because it makes energy cheaper and wind, even solar, cannot meet the scale of this demand. What this tells us is that there is no transition yet from fossil fuels to renewables. It isn’t oil, gas and coal or renewables. It’s likely to be both and lots of nuclear too. More of everything, including nuclear, will comprise our energy supply.
Climate realism is grounded in these challenging facts, not hope or ideology. Renewables have high system costs. In Britain’s case, twice the capacity, twice the grid and all the batteries and storage are already additional costs for the same output.
Renewables are not “clean energy”. Nickel mines in Indonesia on cleared rainforest, cobalt mines in the Democratic Republic of Congo and copper mines in Chile and Mongolia tell a very dirty story. Lithium extraction is energy and carbon-intensive, as is all mining. Mineral refining and the manufacture of solar panels and batteries (both dominated by China) are coal-intensive. A new great age of mining is well under way. The result is that the neat and simplistic distinction between “clean” and “dirty” energy is just naive.
These facts point to the enormity of the task ahead. It is all but inevitable that global warming is going to exceed 2C of preindustrial levels. We are currently heading for far worse. This isn’t pessimism: it’s realism. It is the path we are on. Our climate future lies in the hands of China, the US and the fast-growing developing countries, notably India, Indonesia, Nigeria and Brazil. It does not lie in the relatively declining Europe or Britain.
China’s energy policies are driven by its national military and industrial ambitions, and its ability to withstand pressure from the US. It is overwhelmingly a coal-based economy, by far the world’s greatest polluter at more than 30 per cent of carbon emissions, significantly greater than those of the US and Europe combined. It burns well over half of all the world’s coal. Even if its emissions peak, continuing at the current level will be a global climate disaster. It has coal (a falling share in an ever-bigger economy), nuclear and hydro, with some renewables. To this it is adding a very large nuclear programme. What it doesn’t have is oil and gas. Its coal has been its cushion in the Iran war.
The US has oil, gas, coal, nuclear and quite a lot of renewables. It is the global energy superpower — the largest oil producer in the world, the largest exporter of liquefied natural gas and with “good rocks” that could enable it to develop its critical minerals eventually. Europe is in retreat as its share of the world economy withers (partly due to its high energy costs). Britain doesn’t really count at all.
None of the above is really serious about coming to some great legally binding global agreement to tackle climate change. Multilateral world government and institutions are all in retreat. The UN is clinging on with its fingernails to maintain some global credibility. The UN-driven Cops provide a platform for grandstanding politicians, or at least they used to. At Cop30 it was only some of the middle powers that used the stage. The US and China (and Russia, and India) did not push the agenda forward, while the host — Brazil — decided it was a good time to announce its aim to be the fourth-largest oil producer in the world (after the US, Saudi Arabia and Russia).
It is left to the smaller countries to demand reparations and subsidies before an increasingly uninterested global audience, while China may see an opportunity at Cop31 to promote the exports of its solar panels and EVs, and gain a greater geopolitical grip on the critical mineral supply chains.
If we have the wrong net zero targets, if renewables are not as clean or cheap as advocates assume, and if global energy demand is growing strongly, do we just give up and adapt or is there a way out of this climate nightmare?
There are answers, but you probably won’t like them. I’ll come to some of these but first it is obvious that adaptation is necessary and that there is going to be a lot of climate change anyway. That is another bit of climate realism.
Lots of people live in very hot climates and some in very cold climates. They already have to spend a lot of time indoors. What they need is heating and cooling. Both are energy intensive. A rapidly warming Arctic might need less heating in winter, but in the Middle East and the Tropics a lot more air conditioning will be essential. Even in Britain, the long evolution from open coal fireplaces to oil and gas central heating and now with added air conditioning is well under way.
More energy demand means more climate change. More fresh water requires more energy too. There is likely to be a great surge in desalination. Rising sea levels will require greater flood defences and some relocation. As with excess heat and lack of fresh water, these are problems that come with considerable costs. But they are not insuperable.
Climate change is not the end of the world. There are many other threats between now and 2050, including rogue AI and wars. In the great scheme of things climate change comes with great costs and, for some, benefits too. Russia sees economic opportunities, not least of extra oil and gas and Arctic sea lanes. It’s an opportunity China is also keen to exploit. No wonder Trump wants Greenland.
Climate realism has at its core the recognition that addressing climate change is difficult precisely because it is going to be expensive. The fantasies about cheap renewable energy, with the leading world economies trying to emulate Britain by relying primarily on wind and solar with a bit of nuclear and a residual smidgen of gas are just that — fantasies. There are no cheap answers. There is no free lunch. And short of radically reindustrialising, for countries such as Britain, wind and solar are not securely based on home-grown mining, refining and manufacture. Almost all are foreign, mostly Chinese.
Facing the fact of higher energy costs is the corollary of recognising that we are living beyond our environmental means. We could choose to live within our climate means. There is a lot we can do personally. Stopping flying, especially for holidays, is one obvious example. Some of us do but most of us don’t want to rein in our carbon consumption and we don’t want to pay for our pollution. That is why we can all say we really care about climate change, as long as it has little or no costs to doing anything about it. That’s why when the cost of energy goes up, we shy away from the measures necessary to reduce carbon emissions. We don’t want to pay a carbon tax. We want energy subsidies, not energy taxes.
In response to the Iran war, more than 90 countries are already resorting to energy subsidies. Burnham and his chancellor John Healey are also looking in this direction for the budget. Affordability trumps climate change, and as long as it does the emissions will keep going up. We resist the obvious solutions to climate change and hence we get more climate change.
The extra twist is that not only should we pay for the carbon pollution we cause, but all the big emitters need to do so at the same time. China, the US, India, Indonesia, Brazil, Canada and Nigeria need to do so simultaneously. Carbon border taxes should be common; carbon should be at the heart of all and every trade negotiation. They aren’t and it isn’t.
Do you think Cop31 and another 31 Cops will do this? You might but I don’t. Do you think Britain should accept the highest energy costs in the developed world, allow our existing industrial base to contract further and miss out on, as Sir Keir Starmer declared, the ambition “to be an AI superpower”?
Or do you think Britain should pay for its pollution and spend on climate measures that make a difference to global warming. Britain has great science, great engineering and it has great places to try out some of the newer technologies. We have great opportunities to share our technological contributions with others and hence help reduce the emissions where it will most count. Climate change is global, and we should focus on where we can make the most difference. So far, Britain’s main contribution has been to demonstrate to the world how not to do it.
“Time for climate realism: Net Zero 2030 is only making us poorer” – Wind and solar alone can’t power the future, says Dieter Helm in the Times. There are better options that could actually help curb climate change.
#savethisland #rethinkrenewables #UKEnergy #ClimateRealism

What we missed, subsequent to this post - and we are grateful to the WEA friend who sent us the detail today - Ofgem are now cracking down on the oversubscribing of BESS too.
'Ofgem now says it is minded to approve an Oversubscribed Technologies Commitment Fee (OTCF), which would require projects to demonstrate a minimum level of financial commitment – starting at GBP 3,000 per MW and rising to a maximum of GBP 25,000 per MW if the queue remains oversubscribed.'
The proposal went out to consultation on 17 September, with a short response time, closing on 1 October.
https://www.pv-magazine.com/.../uk-regulator-plans.../...
https://www.ofgem.gov.uk/.../CMP470-Minded-to...
OFGEM MOVES TO TACKLE THE DATA CENTRE CONNECTIONS FREE-FOR-ALL
Ofgem has today launched a consultation on proposals to tackle the extraordinary growth of data centres seeking connections to Britain's electricity network.
The scale is remarkable.
Between November 2024 and June 2025, contracted demand in the connections queue increased from 41 GW to 125 GW. Ofgem estimates that around 73 GW of this is data centres, comprising approximately 315 projects.
To put that into perspective, peak electricity demand across the whole of Great Britain in 2025 was just 45 GW.
Ofgem does not believe all of these proposed data centres are likely to be built. It says the present connections system makes it relatively inexpensive to obtain and retain a position in the queue, encouraging speculative and non-viable projects which can lock up scarce grid capacity, distort network investment decisions and delay projects which genuinely intend to proceed.
And land is an important part of the story.
Ofgem says the value of land can increase significantly once planning permission and a grid connection have been secured. That creates a strong commercial incentive to obtain suitable land and grid capacity even where the party making the application does not ultimately intend to build or operate the data centre itself.
It identifies several types of developer now operating in the sector, including energy and infrastructure developers and "powered land developers". The latter acquire or secure land, planning permission and grid connections and then package the development as an investment proposition for another developer or investor to take forward.
Ofgem also says developers may maintain portfolios of proposed sites to hedge against projects failing or being delayed. A developer which does not intend to build all those projects may need to sell only one or a small number of them to realise the increased value created by securing land, planning and power.
There is another interesting crossover with the battery storage boom: Ofgem found that between May 2024 and August 2025 at least 9 GW of projects in the transmission queue changed their connection request from battery technology to data centre.
Ofgem is now proposing two main measures to weed out speculative projects.
Data centres above 40 MW would have to provide a substantial financial commitment, secured from acceptance of the connection offer until energisation. The proposed amount is between £237,500 and £712,500 for every MW of requested capacity. For a 100 MW data centre, that means securing approximately £23.8 million to £71.3 million. The money would be returned if the project proceeds, but could be forfeited if it terminates or fails to comply with the requirements.
Developers would also have to pass new queue management milestones, providing evidence that their project is genuinely progressing. That includes demonstrating a credible compute customer or end-user, procurement of long-lead electrical equipment, financial capability and technical readiness. Projects which fail the tests could lose their place in the queue.
Ofgem is not proposing to limit the number or total capacity of data centres. Its immediate aim is to distinguish projects which are genuinely capable of being built from those which are speculative.
But once the speculative projects have been stripped out, a much bigger question remains:
How much genuine data-centre demand is Britain actually prepared to accommodate — and what new generation and network infrastructure will be required to supply it?
The consultation, Curate – Demand Connections Reform, closes on 16 September 2026.
