Judge Humphreys needs to be hauled over the coals for his latest remarks - still on the second case we referred to in 2024.
In 2025, the judge dismissed most of the grounds, but left the issue of the kingfisher and freshwater pearl mussel, and it's these concerns which has been the subject of the latest judgment.
Despite finding that the objectors were right on substantive environmental law relating to the bird and the mussel, he agreed that they were harmless errors and refused to quash the decision to grant the wind farm.
The crucial thing which he said, going back to the slap he received from Ms Justice Costello, was:
'the applicants end like the dogged Japanese soldier still fighting World War II in the Philippine jungle, decades after everyone else has admitted defeat.'
https://www.irishtimes.com/.../judge-compares-wind-farm.../
In 2022, An Bord Pleanála granted permission for the Carrownagowan wind farm at  in County Clare for 19 169m turbines.  The developers were Future Energy Ireland, comprising a 50/50 partnership between Coillte and ESB.  FEI then set up a dedicated company for the purpose - FuturEnergy Carrownagowan DAC.
The Carrownagowan Concern Group brought judicial review proceedings which were heard by Mr Justice Humphreys in the High Court in 2023.
He dismissed four core grounds, but used language which clearly did not impress the Court of Appeal, in particular the president  Ms Justice Caroline Costello who has now upheld the High Court decisions.
What Mr Justice Humphreys said was:
'“One does not simply walk into Mordor – or into the High Court. Before litigating, one has to set the case up properly.”  And:
'“Examples of gaslighting the decision-maker don’t get much better than this.”
She said:  '“Judgments must be written in clear, understandable language but that does not mean it is appropriate to resort to slang or colloquialisms (other than in quotes); it is inappropriate and militates against the precision and clarity required in judgments of the High Court'.
We reckon, while some people are not familiar with Lord of the Rings, most people will today understand what gaslighting means.  After all, it's something that the renewable industry and their hangers-on do on a daily basis - make us question our own perception of reality!
Mr Justice Humphreys clearly has a penchant for colourful language and imagery.
We were looking at another case he heard, again it was Future Energy Ireland and a wind farm in County Kilkenny.  The group Save the South Leinster Way and a resident were a day late in seeking a judicial review.  
The judge said:  '“The message to applicants is – try to avoid depleting the energy of the court with this sort of application and instead put in place some kind of margin for error, rather than living for the thrill of a do-or-die scramble to get the last seat on the last helicopter off the embassy roof in Saigon.”
Had the decision been able to go to appeal and had Ms Justice Costello heard it, she would doubtless have smacked the good judge on that, too.

Walshaw Moor - a lovely unspoiled place, photographed by Shane Oxer and highlighted in a piece entitled 'Take A Walk.  Then Make Them Show The Evidence'.
Britain needs reliable electricity at a price households and businesses can afford. It also needs productive farmland, healthy habitats and places people can enjoy. A serious national assessment should show how the proposed energy system will meet those needs, and compare practical alternatives.
That means explaining what must be built, how much land will change, what the whole system will cost and who will pay. It means looking at neighbouring developments together, including their connections and supporting works. People should be able to follow the complete picture without having to assemble it themselves from separate applications.
And we know this very, very well from all the salami slicing which goes on in Scotland.  And that, although the question of need has been asked for repeatedly by CB4PC and lately, by the planning consultant Ian Kelly, it has not been answered.
Shane highlights his petition.  It needs many more signatories, so please, if you have not, put your name to it.  The country needs a full impact and cost assessment.  
https://petition.parliament.uk/petitions/780321
Looking at the view of Walshaw Moor, we were reminded of a very sad piece we spotted on the fb page Block East Pye Solar - South Norfolk from Angela Pyke:
My heart is broken when I envisage what might be forced on our lives.  It is hard to overstate how much grief and anger I feel.
South Norfolk is a beautiful county which has already taken its fair share of infrastructure and in deed we have the Norwich to Tilbury pylon route, proposed.  The Tasway Energy Park 3,600 acres, sleeping.  A 5,000 acre solar park in Gissing, proposed.  There are many more as well as ones already under construction in Attleborough and Palgrave.  
Norfolk is the latest Gold Rush for foreign investment.
The villages proposed in the East Pye solar are beautiful historic and architectural delights which have grown up over the centuries.  The villages are situated in picturesque countryside and are very close to each other and can be walked to and from the network of footpaths criscrossing South Norfolk.  They being made by villagers long gone who had no transport and took the most direct route across fields to the next village.  It is a unique feature of this landscape and myself and my husband walk various footpaths everyday for excercise and the pure enjoyment of the landscape and wildlife.  This is why we live in South Norfolk. 
To take this away, the peace, the dark skies, the wildlife which abounds would be like a death sentence, akin to living in a prison.
Please hear our feelings from the bottom of our hearts and refuse this monstrosity.
I haven't even touched on food security and the financial affect this would have on peoples homes and rural businesses which contribute hugely to the economy.
I lay awake at night worrying.
All over the UK, people are anxious and distressed.

This morning, we were sent, by Kathrin Haltiner, a piece from the John o' Groat Journal, and her letter to the paper; both are in images.
The article tells how SSEN are using dynamic line rating (DLR) on the network between Beauly and Dounreay.
DLR  uses real-time weather and wind data to determine actual transmission line capacity moment by moment, thus allowing grid operators to safely optimize power flow through existing infrastructure when conditions permit, the key weather factors monitored being
Wind speed – Cooling effect increases line capacity
Ambient temperature – Higher temperatures reduce capacity
Solar radiation – Heating from sunlight affects conductor temperature
And therein lies the irony - Wind farms produce more electricity when it's windy, and the wind simultaneously cools the transmission lines, potentially allowing those lines to carry more of that electricity.
Kathrin's letter rightly points out that it doesn't matter how much DLR is put on to existing lines in Scotland if the bottlenecks are further down the track and so how can it be said that constraint payments will be saved?
We took a look at what SSEN had said previously about reinforcing the existing 275kV lines - from 2022, 2023 and 2025.
In all of them, the financial details have been redacted - capex, opex, SSEN costs, constraint savings and allowances requested.  Commercial/confidentiality grounds notwithstanding, this is public money when it comes to allowances - and constraints.
What exactly has been withheld and why, particularly because this is an Ofgem-funded transmission investment and SSEN's case is explicitly framed around benefits and savings to consumers?
From the 2025 document - The cost of this solution will be recovered by savings made from alleviating future network constraints.
How?
An example of redactions is taken from the 'Need' section of the 2025 document:
A significant amount of renewable generation is contracted to connect north of Beauly substation, in the Caithness region of our network. At the time of our MSIP re-opener submission in January 2022 redacted MW of new renewable generation was contracted to connect in the area. There is now approximately redacted MW of new renewable generation contracted to connect in the area with a connection date prior to October 2030.

Tom Ramage says, in the Strathy newspaper's round up of news:
Feel free to disagree, but it strikes us as hugely ironic that as we fear the ravaging of our landscape by global warming and assorted climate changes we appear ever keener just to do the job ourselves. 
There is a kind of petulance in refusing to wait for nature when we have all the weaponry we need here and now.
Having gone to all the trouble of setting up 'the green belt', 'national scenic areas', 'sites of special scientific interest' and the like, we can't wait to get the diggers into them. Some sceptics believe that all these labels are stuck on our landscape as some sort of road signs for the developers.
But of course, we stand to be corrected and surely will be when those behind  the Highland Wind Farm - dubbed 'the son of Allt Duine' by some witty journalist (his name escapes us) - have their say at Wednesday's drop-in sessions.  (That witty journo was Tom Ramage - we also referred to it as Son of Allt Duine from the on.)
Here's one: "Scottish Wild Land Area, noted for outstanding natural beauty and the absence of industrial-scale structures."  That's another road sign for developers, say the sceptics. NESO has now cancelled the Electricity Margin Notice. Demand at 3pm was around 614 MW lower than NESO had forecast this morning, while the market is also delivering increased imports into GB during the evening peak.
**
FURTHER UPDATE:  NESO have just made the situation ten times worse by tweeting this bunkum:
NESO has issued an Electricity Margin Notice for this evening’s peak period. This is a routine and precautionary operational tool, there is no risk to customer electricity supplies and Great Britain’s electricity system remains secure.
There are various comments, among them this from Kathryn Porter:
Since when does the peak last from 3pm to 11pm?
UPDATE:  Shortfall now at 679MW.  Kathryn Porter has said the next update is at 3.30 by which time interconnector trading may be known.
**
This morning, NESO has issued two EMNs; this is the second one, showing that the system margin shortfall has risen from 1840 MW to 1880MW.
Kathryn Porter said, after the original EMN:
This is an unusually wide timeframe covering far more than just the evening peak
So what's going on?
Wind is set to be low dipping to 1700 MW at 6pm
Solar will peak at 6758 MW at 1pm, be at 5882 MW at 3pm and zero from 7pm
Interconnectors are nominated to export the max capacity of 8756 MW between 12:30pm and 2pm. Imports and then nominated to fall to 6285 MW at 3pm, 435 MW at 5pm and then flip to exports reaching 1979 MW between 6:30pm and 7pm. Exports are then set to fall, with the cables flipping to imports of 528 MW between 8:30pm and 9pm before heading back to export mode with exports reaching 1282 MW at 10:30pm which is the last available time right now
Demand is forecast at 33,203 MW at 3pm, peaking for the evening at 33,940 MW at 7:30pm and then falling to 25,843 MW by 11pm
The grid will be tightest between 5:30pm and 8pm where NESO will need imports to meet demand
As before I expect NESO will turn to intraday SO-SO trades on the interconnectors to resolve this. It has been consistently buying back up to the cap for quite a large part of the past day and since 5:30am this morning

Unusually, the expected shortfall has GONE UP!!

BOEM Aware of Lost Boat M/V Mistress in 2020
October 6, 2026
https://www.windtaskforce.org/.../boem-aware-of-lost-boat...
2019, the Bureau of Ocean Energy Management (BOEM) had a regulatory and planning agenda for offshore wind energy development. As a government institution under the U.S. Department of the Interior, BOEM executed several key initiatives to advance offshore wind planning.
BOEM operated under Executive Order 13783 (issued in 2017), which explicitly directed federal agencies to promote offshore wind.
The fishing industry and maritime interests argued for 2-nautical-mile spacing of offshore wind turbines for safety. Federal agencies and developers focused on financing, ignored safety concerns, and chose a standard 1-nautical-mile grid layout for major offshore lease areas.
On January 1, 2019, the fishing boat F/V Mistress sank in a storm near the Block Island wind turbines. A Coast Guard MH-60 helicopter spent 37 minutes searching for the boat. Radar clutter from the turbines interrupted the search. The Coast Guard determined the boat was lost.
A Green Oceans dive team recently conducted a "targeted" dive at Block Island wind turbine #1 and found what appears to be a boat. Green Oceans has asked to reopen the investigation.
So the question is, did BOEM forget to tell anyone about finding a boat, burying one sentence in a 263-page report, or an intentional omission to protect the one-nautical-mile setback decision made by federal agencies and offshore developers?
A 2020 BOEM document, "OCS Study BOEM 2020-044," shows a boat on page 184, just above Figure 79, at the base of Block Island wind turbine #1.
https://espis.boem.gov/final%20reports/BOEM_2020-044.pdf
Top Page 184: "On the final day of dive survey, partial boat debris (e.g., paneling from a small boat hull) was observed around Turbine 1, but no footage was obtained."

You may have seen the news....the Glen Earrach Pumped Storage Hydro (PSH) scheme is to face no objection from the Highland Council.
Following some debate at the Highland Council South Planning Applications Committee meeting today, councillors voted 6-6 when it came to deciding whether or not to raise an objection to the scheme.

The casting vote fell to committee chairman Councillor Paul Oldham (Nairn and Cawdor, SNP) who chose to raise no objection to the plans and it was given the green light to proceed. 
To help understand the opposing positions of our councillors (and the views expressed by others), we recommend you watch the meeting and following debate: https://highland.public-i.tv/core/portal/home

The scheme still requires the approval of the Energy Consents Unit. If approved, no works can currently commence until applications for the grid connection and the required Dochfour weir upgrades have also been approved.

Coast Guard & Sinking of F/V Mistress January 1, 2019 & MP 4 Video
The U.S. Coast Guard (USCG) is legally mandated to investigate the sinking of the F/V Mistress. Under 46 U.S.C. § 6301 and 46 CFR Part 4, the Coast Guard has a strict statutory requirement to investigate any reportable "marine casualty" occurring on the navigable waters of the United States
Because the January 1, 2019 sinking of the 52-foot commercial fishing vessel resulted in both the total loss of the boat and the loss of life, it automatically met the legal criteria for a Serious Marine Incident (SMI).
While the initial mandate was technically satisfied, a major shift occurred in September 2026. The nonprofit group Green Oceans located the wreckage 92 feet underwater—just 50 feet from Turbine 1 of the Block Island Wind Farm—and discovered what are believed to be human remains
While the law mandates that the Coast Guard conduct an investigation, it leaves the decision to reopen a closed case to agency discretion. Maritime advocates and the families of the victims are actively arguing that the discovery of new forensic evidence and potential human remains legally obligates the Coast Guard to reopen the file, recover the remains for DNA testing, and thoroughly re-examine how the nearby wind turbines impacted the initial search-and-rescue radar and flight operations

records.bodyText:
Electricity generation per person in the United Kingdom has fallen by a third from its early-2000s peak.
Globally, electricity generation per person has grown by more than 50% this century.
In the United Kingdom, things have moved in the opposite direction. Its generation per person peaked in 2003 and has fallen by more than a third since then.
You can see this in the chart, which shows generation per person since 1920. Today, levels are back to where they were in the late 1960s.
Some of that decline is a change in electricity imports, rather than demand: net imports have increased from 1% of electricity demand in 2010 to 9% in 2025. But it's still true that the UK consumes much less electricity than it used to.
The most common explanation is deindustrialization: as the economy shifted from manufacturing to services, electricity demand fell. That's part of the explanation, but far from all of it.
Sectoral data from the International Energy Agency confirms that electricity consumption in industry has fallen by one-quarter since 2005 (more if we calculate this per person). But residential and commercial electricity use has fallen by just as much.
Deindustrialization has reduced demand, but improvements in energy efficiency - such as the shift from incandescent to LED lightbulbs and the introduction of efficiency standards for appliances - have played an important role too.

Rosyth Dockyard Power Station (Commissioned 1912)
Power Station (Building No 333), Rosyth Dockyard, A Category B Listed Building in Rosyth, Fife
Summary Category B
Group Category Details 100000019
Date Added 19/12/2006
Local Authority Fife
Planning Authority Fife
Burgh Dunfermline
NGR NT 09970 82330
Coordinates 309970, 682330
Construction by Easton Gibb and Son Ltd of Westminster for Royal Navy, 1910-15. 3-storey and attic/single storey with false attic and 2-storey and attic/single storey and attic and 2-storey; also with concealed basement; overall L-plan power station; comprising 3-storey and attic/single storey and attic main block.  
Building interior consists of steel-framed roof-trusses to main block, which is largely open to roof. Brown glazed tiled dado to ground floor; white glazed bricks to arched basement. Formerly contained steam turbines (since removed). Retains original crane (inscribed 'Marshall Fleming & Co, Motherwell' and dated '1914').
The Rosyth Dockyard, Basin and the Pumping Station, the @power station was the earliest building to be completed on the site (it is shown nearing completion in a photograph dated 1912). One of the key buildings at the dockyard, it would have supplied power to the whole complex, including to any ships stationed there. It remains one of the dockyard's landmarks, despite having lost its original industrial chimney, which also served as a clocktower. It is amongst the earliest non-public electric power stations remaining in Scotland. Rosyth dockyard is the largest facility used by the Royal Navy outside southern England. It constitutes the only newlybuilt naval dockyard in the UK since the Napoleonic era.
The decision to construct a major naval base facing Germany was announced in 1903. Subsequently the Admiralty purchased 285 acres of foreshore and 1184 acres of inland around Rosyth. Operations did not begin however until March 1909, with Messrs Easton Gibb and Son Ltd of Westminster appointed as contractors. It was intended as a support and heavy repair base for warships of the Grand Fleet.
At the outbreak of the First World War very little of the work had been completed. Work was underway on the main basin and the tidal basin to the east had been constructed (although its entrance was obstructed by a clay dam); the generating station and pumping station had been built but were only in the process of being equipped. More manpower was sent to speed up the construction process and the dockyard was officially opened by George V in June 1915. The main basin however was not entirely completed and flooded to full depth until September. Between March 1916 and the Armistice, 78 capital ships (dreadnoughts, superdreadnoughts and battle cruisers), 82 light cruisers and 37 small craft were docked and refitted at Rosyth. The yard's value soon became apparent, when a number of damaged warships were towed in for repair following an engagement with the German High Seas Fleet off Jutland in June 1916.
The design and building of the electricity generating station became an early priority. As soon as the plant was commissioned, its power could be used both during the construction period and later for Naval operational use.
The provision of Naval repair facilities were to be of the highest standard. The workshops were to be comprehensive and able to undertake all types of ship repair and reconstruction following damage of warships in battle. The workshops would provide the best mechanical cutting and turning lathes available and these had to be supplied by reliable electric power. To service these excellent facilities there was the need to build a correspondingly excellent generating station. The contract specification for the generating plant was as follows:
Five separate engines will be provided, each rated 250 horse-power, each with its own dynamo giving an output rating of 175 Kw at 550 volts. When working at full power a total horse-power of 1,250 would ɓprovide 875 Kw of electricity.
With this multiple power plant it would be possible to maintain supply should any unit fail or be under maintenance.The combined output from this central generating plant was considered generous when first proposed. However, soon other generating stations in the United Kingdom would soon outstrip the total electric capacity of Rosyth.
The decision to use coke as the primary source of power resulted in the engine fuel being water gas. This does not give the highest calorific value of the alternatives, but it is easy to produce and relatively cheap. This is a gas made up of carbon monoxide and hydrogen, C+ H₂0 CO + H2
The five driving engines were to be powered using this fuel by a method known as the Suction Gas process. The gas was obtained by passing steam over incandescent coke. When ignited in the cylinders the exhaust gases were carbon dioxide and water. The reason for the name of suction gas arose from the engine cylinders directly sucking the gas from the adjoining coke firebox. The engine ran on the four stroke principle conceived in 1876, ironically by the German inventor Nicolaus August Otto. The actual units installed were listed as "National, twin cylinder, suction gas engines, running on the Otto principle". The ignition sparks were created by low tension magnetos. How these big engines were started is a mystery. The cranking mechanism would not have been manual and was probably driven by a small separate engine, using a belt lying round a clutched pulley.
During the construction of the generating station, a fire broke out on 11th June 1910. The cause was in the timber shuttering and a large fire resulted. It would be some weeks before replacement parts to the metal coke stoves were available.
The dockyard was run down after the Armistice and closed to naval use between 1928 and 1935. However during this period at least one dry dock was used for breaking up ships salvaged by Cox and Danks after scuttling in Scapa Flow. It came back into full operation during the Second World War. After the war it was kept operational to support forces deployed to counter the Northern and Baltic fleets of the Soviet Navy. In the late 1960's it was designated a major refitting base for the Polaris (strategic ballistic missile) nuclear submarine fleet.
This is an extract from a Dockyard history which may be of interest:
1955 -Rosyth Dockyard stopped generating its own electricity supply in the Generating Station. After that date, high voltage AC was imported from the National Grid and transformed down to suit the various levels of supply required around the Yard and aboard ship (ie 440V/415V 3 phase 50 & 60 Hz, 115V single phase 50 & 60 Hz and Direct Current). The frequency of the shore supply remained at National Grid level of 50 Hz and was changed to 60 Hz by synchronising machinery for supply to ships. Ships under refit did not use their own generators to produce electricity and this was supplied from the Dockyard and known as the shore supply..
Following the end of the Cold War, operational ships and the majority of uniformed personnel were withdrawn between 1993 and 1996. The dockyard was transferred to commercial management in 1987 and sold to Babcock in 1997 (with limited guarantee of naval contracts). It continues in use as a working dockyard on both naval and commercial contracts.

Kilbraur Wind Farm
A twenty-seven turbine wind farm within the valley of the Scottarie Burn, 7 miles (11 km) west northwest of Brora in E Sutherland, Kilbraur Wind Farm was built in two phases 2006-08 and 2009-11. 
The first phase comprised 19 German-built Nordex turbines which, together with their support towers, were delivered by sea to Invergordon and then moved to site by road. Each is 70m (230 feet) in height, with blades which are 90m (295 feet) in diameter, giving a total height to blade tip of 115m (377 feet). 
The first phase also necessitated the construction of 4½ miles (7.5 km) of access road, some sections of which were built on bed-rock while others float on top of deep peat formations. 
A second phase, costing £29 million, brought a further eight turbines mounted on 80m (262 feet) towers, but with the same blade dimensions, giving a total height to blade tip of 125m (410 feet). All of the installed turbines produce 2.5 MW of electricity, giving the site a total peak generation capacity of 67.5 MW.
The project was developed by RDC Scotland and West Coast Energy Ltd., with work undertaken by contractors Tulloch Civil Engineering Ltd. and R.J. McLeod Ltd. 
The wind farm is owned and operated by Kilbraur Wind Energy Ltd., which is a subsidiary of Falck Renewables (now Nadara). Kilbraur Wind Energy Co-operative was established in 2008 to allow local people to invest in the project and a community trust fund also distributes grants to support local projects.— at Kilbraur.

records.title: Wind Energy's Absurd
records.bodyText:
We've lost count of the number of times we've had a cash cow image relating to matters electricity, or the times we've realised that the industry has managed to pull another raft of dosh from consumer pockets.  Here's another which we came upon by chance, doing some investigation into a memory on Connect & Manage (which we may post later).  
So, fundamentally, storage - and the increasing goldrush for BESS - is exacerbating another situation - Repetitive Re-Trading.  It's complex, so bear with us - we've simplified as much as we can so that we could get our heads round it.
When there is surplus electricity, a battery can charge, or a pumped-storage hydro scheme can pump water uphill into its upper reservoir. Later, when electricity is needed, the battery can discharge or the water can be released through turbines to generate electricity.
But the market does not always reward storage for behaving in the way that best helps the electricity system.
Under the current arrangements, storage operators respond to the national wholesale electricity price. That price can encourage them to export electricity even when their local part of the transmission network is already congested.
This is the central difficulty identified by Ofgem: storage intended to help balance the system can, under certain market conditions, end up increasing the cost of managing constraints - and cause our trouser pockets to become even lighter.
What is 'repetitive re-trading'?
This is the heart of the paper. 
Imagine a battery that has electricity ready to sell.
Step 1 - The battery sells electricity
It agrees to sell electricity because the wholesale price makes doing so commercially attractive.
Step 2 - NESO tells it not to export
The local transmission network is constrained. NESO accepts a bid to stop the battery exporting at that time.
Step 3 - The battery reschedules its sale
Because it has not discharged the energy, it can arrange to sell it in a later period, or it may avoid a planned charging cycle.
Step 4 - The process repeats
If the constraint persists, NESO may again need to prevent the battery exporting. The battery can reschedule again, while NESO arranges replacement electricity elsewhere.
This repeated cycle is called repetitive re-trading (RRT). The same stored energy is repeatedly rescheduled for sale, rather than delivered when originally intended.
The crucial point is that the battery may retain the energy while NESO still has to arrange replacement generation elsewhere. If this process repeats, the additional balancing costs can accumulate
What is this costing consumers?
Ofgem reports NESO's estimate of the balancing costs attributable to repetitive re-trading by storage assets:
2024–25   -    £64 million                                  2025/2026  -   £99 million
Source: Ofgem's June 2026 paper, using NESO's 12-hour analysis window. 
These are estimated balancing costs attributed to the behaviour, not a direct tally of payments.
Pumped storage hydro accounts for the majority. Ofgem estimates it represented around 80% of the balancing costs associated with repetitive re-trading over the two-year period examined.
But battery-related costs are increasing. Ofgem reports that the estimated monthly cost associated with battery assets rose from £90,000 in April 2024 to £3.9 million in March 2026.  As BESS installations grow, the number is only likely to increase.  
The main cost is often replacement electricity. NESO must obtain electricity elsewhere to meet demand. That replacement is usually sourced from gas-fired generation, making the costs heavily influenced by gas prices.
There are caveats. NESO's method estimates which trading changes may be linked to earlier instructions to reduce output. Ofgem acknowledges that some activity may be incorrectly attributed and that the method misses some cases. The figures should therefore be described as estimates, not exact audited totals.
Ofgem says that repetitive re-trading is not prohibited outright by the existing market arrangements. It can occur even when a storage operator is complying with the rules.
There are, however, existing restrictions:
Generators must submit physical notifications that reflect their best estimate of intended output or consumption.
 False or misleading notifications may breach the Grid Code and market-manipulation rules.
The Transmission Constraint Licence Condition prohibits licensed generators from obtaining excessive benefits from bids during constraint periods.
Ofgem expects storage operators to take account of the additional commercial benefit they may obtain from rescheduling energy when setting their bid prices. But the licence condition does not, by itself, prevent the repeated rescheduling or eliminate the resulting replacement-generation costs.
What does Ofgem propose to do?
Ofgem is working with NESO and DESNZ on measures to make storage work more effectively for the system.
These include reviewing how NESO dispatches storage assets behind constraints, improving operational decisions and considering changes to market arrangements that could reduce unnecessary re-dispatching.
The intention is to ensure that storage helps resolve constraints rather than making them worse, reducing the associated balancing costs.
We were inspired to make this new cash cow image by this, in Energy Storage News:
It’s a situation that is causing issues because it is pushing up the bills for everyone else. While the bidding and energy release process was designed to balance and stabilise the grid, it has turned into what some call a ‘cash cow for private investors’ at the expense of other energy consumers—a point that is argued by the Prospect trade Union. 
Prospect had a piece in September entitled 'Government must end battery rip-off and take control to lower bills' and issued a report, following Burnham's arrival in 10 Downing Street, calling for public control.
The way that battery operators are currently ripping off the public is a clear example of a broken system that enriches investors and impoverishes the public.  Sue Ferns, Prospect Senior Deputy General Secretary
The issue we have is that, again, we are relying  almost completely on private investment to  build out storage capacity, and many of the private investors being attracted to the sector are those who understand storage as an 
attractive trading opportunity. Rather than supporting the stability and efficiency of the system-at-large—and helping pass on the low costs of renewable generation—they exploit the low marginal cost of charging and discharging, to buy low and sell high, making handsome profits as they exploit loopholes and system vulnerabilities. This creates an incentive for 
capital to flow into the sector and for storage capacity to be built out, but again, the logic of ‘clean equals cheap’ is undermined: clean assets are only being built out because their prospective owners are able to charge high prices, not because they want to help pass on low prices.
Lastly, it is vital to acknowledge that renewables cannot provide security of supply on their own, a fact which is significantly underappreciated in debates about renewable deployment. 
Renewable technologies are intermittent by their nature, and we need other technologies which can generate power on the occasions when renewables do not provide enough supply to meet demand.
...renewables and storage are being sold as technologies which can help reduce our reliance on fossil fuel based technologies, all while reducing costs and 
increasing our energy security, but we have ended up in a situation where we are paying private investors a pretty penny to build out renewables and storage capacity, while we have become increasingly reliant on expensive foreign 
imports to compensate for the shortfalls of the newly deployed technology.
As we saw on October 6th when the Electricity Margin Notices came, and so did the imports, at cost. 
While we part company on several points with Prospect, their report is well-written and there is much that we do agree with.  This is the link to the Prospect article, from where the report can be downloaded.
https://prospect.org.uk/.../government-must-end-battery...
This is the link to the Ofgem article from which their report can be downloaded:
https://www.ofgem.gov.uk/.../repetitive-re-trading...
In the meantime, Bessie the cow will continue laughing all the way to the bank, unless Ofgem, NESO and DESNZ get their fingers out and start protecting consumers.

The Daily Sceptic has an excellent piece by Richard Lyon entitled 'Britain is Heading Towards Blackouts'. He explains, very simply, how the grid operates and what are the risks to Britain's electricity.  
When reading it, we were reminded of Dr Euan Mearns' Doomsday posts from 2018.  Sadly, these are no longer available - the main reason why we now mostly include text of posts so we can go back to our archived material.  But we do have the start of Kathryn Porter on the subject, from August this year.
https://dailysceptic.org/.../britain-is-heading-towards.../
'This week the Scotsman published a piece of mine asking whether Britain’s power grid would pass the safety test every North Sea oil platform must pass before it can operate. This is the background to that article: how a grid works, how it fails and why an engineer from a safety-critical industry is uneasy about ours.
A machine the size of a country
A grid must make exactly as much electricity as it uses, every instant, because wires store almost nothing. Engineers watch two dials to see whether it is healthy.
The first is frequency: the beat of the alternating current, 50 times a second in Britain. It is the same everywhere on the connected grid. That shared beat is what defines a grid: not everything wired together, but everything running in step. Produce less than customers use and the whole grid slows; produce more and it speeds up.
The second is voltage, which works like pressure in a water pipe. It differs from place to place, and only equipment nearby can correct it.
Both dials must stay inside tight limits to protect the machinery. Power-station turbines are built to spin at one speed, and running at a different speed wears them out. Too much voltage breaks down the insulation in cables and equipment, and too little makes motors overheat. Outside the limits, machines disconnect to save themselves, usually just when the grid needs them most.
Three jobs that came free
For a century, the big spinning generators in coal, gas, nuclear and hydro stations have held both dials. Besides making energy, each does three other jobs, bundled into the price.
Its heavy spinning mass works as a flywheel: when another station trips, it resists the slowdown and buys seconds for backup to arrive. Engineers call this inertia.
When lightning or a fallen tree causes a short circuit, a spinning generator pours out a surge of current several times its normal rating, straight from physics. That surge is the alarm that tells the grid’s automatic switches which damaged line to cut out.
And its controls push local voltage up or down to keep it in its band.
Wind, solar, batteries and the cables to Europe connect instead through power electronics called inverters. Most in service today add no inertia. Their electronics cap their fault current close to normal output, because more would burn them out. And they help hold voltage only if designed and instructed to. Swap a gas station for a solar farm of the same rating and the alarm falls to a fraction, and the switches may struggle to tell which line to cut out before the fault spreads.
Grids are run to a rule engineers call N-1, said ‘N minus one’: the grid must be able to lose any single power station or line without anyone losing power. Britain appears to have broken it on June 23rd, in a heatwave. And even when the rule holds, trouble comes when several things fail together.
.Each machine that disconnects hands its load to whatever is left. If the survivors are near their limits, they trip too. The inquiry into North America’s 2003 blackout put it bluntly: a cascade “cannot be stopped by human intervention once started”.
The last defence is to cut off blocks of customers automatically, sacrificing some to save the rest. On August 9th 2019 in Britain, lightning struck a line, and an offshore wind farm and a gas station dropped out. About a million customers lost power, and all were back within 45 minutes. The grid held. That was a controlled cut, not a blackout.
Spain on April 28th 2025 was a blackout. It was a quiet, sunny day with low demand, and lightly loaded lines push voltage up. Too few conventional plants were running to pull it down, and some of those failed to. As voltage rose, generators tripped one after another, each trip pushing it higher. Cutting customers made it worse, because less load meant higher voltage still. About 27 seconds after the first big trip, Spain and Portugal were dark.
Net Zero closes the machines that did all three jobs and replaces them with machines that do few or none. Every function that came with a coal, gas or nuclear station must now be bought back, or done without.
Britain is doing both. NESO, which runs the grid, now pays for stability as a standalone function: mostly spinning machines that burn no fuel and sell no energy, there to provide weight and fault current. Two of its stability tenders cost £328 million and £323 million. That cost reaches your bill as a balancing charge, and part of the “Balancing costs” line on our Subsidy Clock. Meanwhile, the minimum spinning weight it keeps on the system has been cut by 15%, approved by the regulator, Ofgem, in May. The review behind that cut is charged with weighing the cost of a safety margin against the risk of losing it. This year, the margin lost.
The danger has also moved. A cold, still week in winter is a shortage you can see coming, and the answer is planned rota cuts: unpleasant, but controlled. The blackout risk now gathers on light, sunny days, when demand is low and few spinning plants are running. Those were Spain’s conditions. British demand fell to 12.8 gigawatts last year, against a winter peak of about 46.
A mild day sounds a safe one to lose power. It is not, because a blackout stops everything that runs on electricity at once: phones and the internet, home-based medical equipment, water pumping and sewage, petrol pumps, card payments and cash machines, and with them the shops. The Government’s worst-case plan has everyone reconnected only after five or six days. But that’s a guess: Britain has never had a total blackout, so it has never had to restart the whole grid for real.
And that last defence – rota cuts – is weakening. It works by cutting off whole neighbourhoods to reduce demand. But at midday on a sunny day, many of those homes are also making power from rooftop solar panels, so each cut removes supply as well as demand and does less good. With less spinning weight on the grid, frequency also falls faster, leaving less time for the cuts to work. NESO’s own research says the scheme was not designed for either problem, and that this “reduces the effectiveness”.
Defenders of the detransition say all this is solvable. Fuel-less spinning machines and newer inverters that imitate a flywheel can do much of the work, and NESO is already buying them.
But solvable is not solved, and it is not free. None of these costs appears in the wholesale price quoted to show that renewables are cheap. They are bought piecemeal, after the plant that once provided the functions rolled in has closed, while margins are trimmed to keep the bill down.
Nor has it been done before. No large grid anywhere has yet run mostly on wind, solar and batteries with so little spinning plant behind it. NESO’s Chief Executive calls its stability programme “world-first“, and means it as praise. Britain is running a colossal experiment on a system that cannot be allowed to fail.
None of this means the lights are about to go out. It means the grid’s safety is shifting from physics, which came free, to contracts, settings, judgement and experiments which do not. Spain went from trouble to darkness in 27 seconds. The judgement that mattered had been made months before.'
Kathryn Porter - August
'Imagine this. At 8.37pm tonight, as one section of the national grid is hit by a sharp imbalance between electricity supply and demand, the entire network starts to go down. One piece topples the next, like dominoes.
The country goes dark. The lights switch off in every home and business. Airports, hospitals and other essential utilities scramble to switch to back-up generators.
Trains and lifts judder to a halt. Mobile phone transmitter towers switch to battery and back-up power, but networks rapidly become congested and coverage progressively deteriorates.
Firefighters struggling to contain wildfires across the country face catastrophic disruption as computer systems and terrestrial communications fail or become overloaded.
Emergency service radio networks and satellite phones continue to function at first, but communications become increasingly difficult as back-up systems are stretched, batteries run down and generators exhaust their fuel.
With the blazes spreading, the services find it harder to establish which towns and villages are most in danger. Orderly evacuation becomes impossible, with confusion and panic spreading in the worst-affected areas.
By 10pm, with millions of homes in complete darkness, the risk of house fires begins to rise as people turn to candles, camping stoves, barbecues, portable generators and improvised methods of cooking and lighting.
Because fire crews are already stretched beyond capacity, some fires cannot be reached quickly and spread rapidly.
Road accidents increase as traffic lights, street lighting and electronic road signs fail. Police and safety crews are slower to respond because communications are degraded and roads obstructed, meaning some minor incidents develop into more serious collisions and create congestion.
With roads blocked and petrol stations unable to supply fuel because the pumps need electricity, thousands of drivers are stranded, spending the night in their cars or at the roadside, many without water, unable to tell loved ones what is happening.
By morning, the streets are crowded with people demanding to know what's going on. The absence of internet, wifi and reliable phone signals stokes the confusion. Sporadic rioting breaks out, forcing the government to consider deploying the Army.
And this is just the first 12 hours.'

The gent throwing money around like confetti is Fintan Slye, NESO's CEO.  Of course, this is our own image and not a real photograph.  However, the buck stops with him, and NESO has been throwing around taxpayers' money - £400k worth to PR firms following  whistleblowing earlier in the year.
This is what Kathryn Porter had to say on the subject:
'Why are energy bills so high?
Well this won't help.... 
@neso_energy spent £400,000 of OUR money on PR after the near blackout on 23 June when it was forced to cut exports to the Netherlands and allegedly breached multiple grid constraints while frequency sagged
According to @thetimes, *NESO, which is government-owned, has disclosed that it agreed to spend £250,000 plus VAT with Burson and £85,806 plus VAT with iNHouse Communications to provide “strategic counsel and guidance” and “media support” in the wake of the incident.
The agreements were signed after whistleblower allegations and scrutiny of Neso’s management of grid stability during the June heatwave."
So first NESO does a bad job of keeping the grid stable, being forced into emergency actions
Then whistleblowers claim the grid wasn't secure, constraints were breached and that the comms team was involved in operational decision-making, something which NESO admitted was true
Instead of addressing the concerns it decided to spend £££ on a nothing-to-see-here PR campaign
While issuing multiple previously unheard-of summer and autumn margin warnings, breaching interconnector trading limits, making big forecasting errors and having to undertake emergency actions again just this past evening
Clearly it was money well spent 
And this is The Times piece to which Kathryn refers:
https://www.thetimes.com/.../neso-agreed-to-spend-400k-of...
'Britain’s national grid operator signed contracts worth £400,000 for PR advice after a near-blackout incident.
The National Energy System Operator (Neso) is under investigation over claims it mishandled the incident during a heatwave in June when whistleblowers and experts claim Britain came close to blackouts.
Neso, which is government-owned, has disclosed that it agreed to spend £250,000 plus VAT with Burson and £85,806 plus VAT with iNHouse Communications to provide “strategic counsel and guidance” and “media support” in the wake of the incident.
The agreements were signed after whistleblower allegations and scrutiny of Neso’s management of grid stability during the June heatwave.
The Times revealed this year that an internal Neso report on the incident showed that the grid breached five separate safety limits, with control room whistleblowers saying that management was systematically failing to address concerns they were “flying blind” due to lack of data. 
After repeated questions from Claire Coutinho, then shadow energy secretary, Neso and Ofgem convened two separate investigations, one into the grid’s management and another, conducted by the law firm Eversheds Sutherland, into whistleblower allegations that Neso had been dodging freedom of information law by failing to keep adequate records of its actions.
Coutinho, who obtained details of the PR contracts via a freedom of information request, said: “Our arms-length bodies should not be blowing £400,000 of taxpayers’ money on their own PR.
“Along with the Neso’s ill-advised and highly political support for Ed Miliband’s energy plans, it is clear that Neso needs a significant overhaul to focus on making sure the electricity grid is secure and affordable.”
Neso said that it agreed to spend extra money with iNHouse Communications, which was already providing PR services, after the June incident due to an “unprecedented volume of inquiries”. It hired Burson Group after a competitive tender to provide support to its board and executive team.
Burson specialises in communications and reputation management. Fintan Slye, Neso’s chief executive, has come under criticism for prejudging the outcome of inquiries by claiming allegations made by whistleblowers to Coutinho were false.
Neso also initially denied that Craig Dyke, the director of operations, had said that whistleblowers were “letting the company down”, which was contradicted by a subsequent recording of his statement published by The Telegraph. Slye was paid nearly £1 million in salary and bonuses for the 2024-2025 financial year.
Neso had originally planned to conduct the investigations in the June incident itself and to provide regular updates to its executive team. But after further political pressure, Ofgem was forced to take a supervisory role, require a technical investigation and commission a separate inquiry into whistleblower allegations, and Neso agreed that Eversheds would report to an independent panel.
Ofgem has said in its terms of reference for the investigation there was “no disruption to customer supply” in June. The Neso initial report on the incident seen by The Times states, however, that Britain was abruptly forced to cease supplying electricity to the Netherlands in order to avoid instability on its own grid.
Analysis commissioned by Neso and seen by The Times revealed that the grid is becoming harder and more expensive to manage thanks to the growing volume of weather-dependent power sources such as wind and solar, as well as variable demand created by smart meters and electric cars, and the connection of small-scale solar panels that do not send any data to the grid operator.
To keep the grid stable, engineers must balance power supply and demand second by second. Unpredictability of suppliers and users makes this harder and requires the purchase of more spare capacity. The cost of balancing the grid is ultimately borne by electricity users.
Neso has also been criticised in the past for over-optimistic assessments about the feasibility of the government’s 2030 clean power target, which requires 95 per cent of electricity generation to be “carbon-free” in the next four years. Until 2024, the grid operator was privately owned by National Grid. The Tory government announced plans to nationalise it in 2022, a process completed months after Labour won power.
Neso said it “has a responsibility to provide accurate and timely information to government, industry, stakeholders, media and the wider public and, following unprecedented levels of enquiries, additional resource was secured to support Neso’s existing communications function and manage those demands”.'

We're reprising our image of five days ago which introduced the post and link that the Dogger Bank project was seeking a third exemption from the transmission licensing rules. 
The Times had a piece yesterday about delays to CfD take-up, starting with Dogger Bank, but going on to cover Seagreen (which Kathryn Porter and other energy experts have covered repeatedly).
SSE gets a special mention:
The ability to delay contract start dates was designed to accommodate commissioning problems such as those seen at Dogger Bank A. But SSE is among developers who have also controversially delayed contract start dates purely to cash in on higher market prices. 
We have so much in the archives about gaming of the system, delays to CfD start dates being just one.  And who suffers?  Consumers who are forced to pay market prices and not the contracted CfD ones.
From 2017 - a joint paper by Professor Gordon Hughes, Dr John Constable and Dr Capell Aris:
We introduced it thus:
Prof Gordon Hughes and Drs Capell Aris and John Constable, in a report for GWPF, pull out the teeth of the weasels and their other sock puppets - the gormless media - and the pollie parrots - one by one and without anaesthetic - because of the false hysteria and misinformation which has surrounded the offshore strike prices.
We've put a link to that report at the end.  It ended  with:
Contrary to media exaggerations, the low CfD prices are commercial speculation, not the dawn of a new age for offshore wind and renewables.
The Government did close the 'delay' loophole in 2023, but any project awarded a CfD before then can just carry on.  
In September, we had yet another post on gaming of the system.  David Turver was quoted:
The ability to delay the start of CfDs was originally intended to help developers manage the risk of construction delays.
But in some cases, the wind farms have been built already and they are simply choosing not to activate the contracts so they can get higher merchant power prices. 
And that same piece quoted an energy executive as saying that developers are 'making out like bandits' - an expression first used, we believe, by Matt Ridley and John Constable in 2017.
https://www.thetimes.com/business/companies-markets/article/dogger-wind-farm-north-sea-energy-dwcnsltqd?utm_source=Sailthru&utm_medium=email&utm_campaign=Daily%20Briefing%20-%20Monday%20October%2012th%202026&utm_term=audience_DAILY_BRIEFING
'The world’s largest offshore wind farm is struggling with serious construction problems that threaten to further delay promised cheap power for consumers.
The Dogger Bank project in the North Sea got the go-ahead in 2019 with a contract locking in a record-low price for the electricity it would generate for 15 years.
More than 80 miles off the coast of Yorkshire, it was originally scheduled to start delivering cheap power as early as 2023 but has repeatedly delayed its contract start dates after the failure of two turbine blades triggered “cascading” problems. 
It is still grappling with “unforeseen and significant technical issues with the installation, remediation and commissioning of wind turbines”, according to a government document.
Dogger Bank is due to comprise 277 turbines with a total capacity of 3.6 gigawatts, expected to generate enough clean energy to power the equivalent of six million homes. It is co-owned by SSE, the FTSE 100 energy group, Equinor, the Norwegian state oil and gas group, and the offshore wind company Vargronn of Norway. 
The wind farm is being built in three stages. Dogger Bank A has a contract priced at £55.01 per megawatt-hour (MWh) today, which would be cheaper than any operational UK offshore wind farm, and roughly a third of wholesale market prices, which have risen to £162.50/MWh. Dogger Bank B and C have contracts at £57.92/MWh.
When the project was approved the government said it would mean renewables generating “below market prices and without additional subsidy on bills” for the first time. 
However, it is not clear when this promised cheap power will now materialise.
Although Dogger Bank A generated electricity from its first turbine in 2023 it suffered a big setback the following year with two separate blade failures that forced it to slow construction work. It is still suffering “continuing knock-on impacts from the 2024 blade failure events and subsequent remediation programme”, including “ongoing technical defects and resource constraints”, according to the government document published last week.
Power that is being generated during the commissioning period continues to be sold at high prevailing market prices.
The first chunk of Dogger Bank A is required to activate its fixed-price contract by November 30 or risk contract cancellation, but it is not clear whether the project will meet required conditions to do so. It is unlikely to be in the government’s interest to cancel the contract, however, given the desire for cheap power to cut soaring energy bills. 
The entire Dogger Bank wind farm is scheduled to be supplying power at its guaranteed prices by the middle of next year, but developers could exercise the right to delay the contract start dates for some of the subsequent phases to as late as 2029 without risking cancellation.
The ability to delay contract start dates was designed to accommodate commissioning problems such as those seen at Dogger Bank A. But SSE is among developers who have also controversially delayed contract start dates purely to cash in on higher market prices. 
Its Seagreen wind farm, off the Angus coast in Scotland, which also has a contract priced at £57.92/MWh, was fully operational in October 2023 yet has repeatedly opted to delay its contract start date. Promised cheap power from that project is now not expected until at least the end of March and could yet be delayed further. 
A spokesperson for Dogger Bank Wind Farm said: “While some construction delays have previously been reported on Dogger Bank A, we’re maintaining commissioning momentum. We expect the project to be substantially all available for generation by the end of 2026, with final commissioning work continuing into 2027. As a project of unprecedented scale, Dogger Bank A will be a world-class asset once fully operational, providing much-needed secure and affordable energy for Britain.”
Hughes/Constable/Aris
https://www.thegwpf.org/.../09/OffshoreStrikePrice.pdf...

RAPID  - Rushing Approval, Prioritising Infrastructure Delivery (WEA's acronym)
RAPID  - The Routing and Planning through Interoperable Data (SSEN's acronym)
We already have SSEN attempting to rule the Northern half of the Scottish roost by leaning on Reporters to rush through the OHLs and associated infrastructure.
A reminder here of one example;  what Paul Reid, SSEN's KC said at the Beauly-Peterhead OHL Ornithology hearing:
The applicant would take any delay to that timetable very seriously and accordingly I should make clear that should the timetable be departed from, the applicant will request full written reasons for that, along with, and in addition to, the reasons which have already ben requested and which remain awaited for the agricultural decision.
What we said in one of the paragraphs of the summary of the close of the B-P OHL hearing, on Conditions:
Rosie Leven then ran through the timetable. When she'd finished, PR complained about the time frame. Rosie Leven so nicely put him in his place - and the matter into perspective - by saying that additional information meant that the timescale envisaged might not be met but they were very much trying to ensure that the overall timescale is met.
Then we've got the last part of SSEN's disgraceful e mail of 22 September to Rhoda Banfro, The Highland Council solicitor who had asked for four extra days for the Council's closing submission to be presented:
For the avoidance of doubt, the Applicant expects Reporters to adhere to the 3 December date for submitting their Report.
And, finally, we have all the e mails from the planning consultant Ian Kelly to the DPEA referring to the haste at which the infrastructure PLIs are being conducted.
This is part of just one:
The public perception in respect of these cases is already poor as a totally unseemly and unjustified haste is applied to the cases, largely to satisfy the time requirements of SSEN (there being no statutory requirements), and in the circumstances where the objectors, but seemingly nobody else, can see that there is absolutely no up to date justification of any sort for the expenditure of billions of pounds of bill payers' monies on infrastructure for which there is no need.
So, that's the background to why we say that SSEN are attempting to push the Reporters forward.
And now we have RAPID, announced by SSEN last week.  a joint initiative to accelerate grid development from around five years to two. The initiative has secured more than £450,000 from Ofgem's Strategic Innovation Fund to move into its next development phase.
SSEN Transmission is leading the initiative, and it brings together SPEN Transmission,  National Grid Electricity Transmission, NESO and Arup.
The next phase will run for six months and develop a common digital framework connecting engineering, planning, consenting and land information.
RAPID brings together transmission network operators, the system operator and industry partners to tackle a challenge we all share. By developing a more consistent approach to how data is structured, shared and used, we believe there is a real opportunity to significantly speed up the development of the infrastructure needed to unlock new clean energy projects. Brant Wilson, Senior Manager of Innovation at SSEN Transmission
Wait a wee minute!  If NESO is still developing its strategic picture of what is needed and where, as follows, how do we ensure that the drive to accelerate infrastructure delivery remains aligned with that evolving picture? 
SSEP - Strategic Spatial Energy Plan -  where generation and storage should be located across Great Britain.
Autumn 2027 for the final plan. Draft plan and environmental report consultation expected in early 2027. 
RESP - Regional Energy Strategic Plan - what energy system Scotland and each other region will need, taking a whole-system view. 
2028 for the first full plans. The transitional RESP (tRESP) was published on 30January 2026. The final RESP methodology is now due by the end of 2026, subject to approval. 
CSNP - Centralised Strategic Network Plan - what networks are needed to transport energy around Great Britain, including electricity, gas and hydrogen. 15 December 2028 for the first published plan. Ofgem has formally revised the timetable to align with the delayed SSEP
We say:
SSEN has much to say about development and delivery, but where, in this account, are the communities who will live with the infrastructure?
https://www.ssen-transmission.co.uk/.../industry-wide.../

This was one of the images accompanying one of our posts about the renewed threat to Barningham Moor in County Durham, this time by Fred Olsen - the Hope Moor wind farm.  
The lady referred to is the late MaryElizabeth Mann, as she was known to all her many anti-industrial wind campaigner friends across the UK (no solar, BESS or any of the other infrastructure threats in the days, nearly 30 years ago, when she took up her sword and fought - although had there been, we are sure that she'd have fought as valiantly now as then.)
The sword has been picked up by many, including Shane Oxer and Suzy Wilson who are known to our page.  Lord Botham (Sir Ian Botham) and Alan Hinkes, the accomplished mountaineer, have joined the voices trying to protect moorland and yesterday, a walk took place across the moor.
Shane has written about it - 'Hope Moor: The Day People Stood on the Land and Said No'.
'Mary Mann carried the old fight. Lord Botham has helped give the new fight a national voice. The people who gathered on the moor showed that the spirit of resistance is alive on the land itself.
For Barningham. For Hope Moor. For the views across the Pennines and beyond  For the North. For England’s living landscape.
Stand up. Speak out. Defend the moors.
Because the land remembers — and so must we.'
We believe that our late friend MaryElizabeth would have cheered the walkers on and been so proud of them. 
https://hopetosaveourcountryside.com/.../hope-moor.../...

The wind farms the MoD objected to include three onshore developments in northern England and near the Scottish border, along with a proposed offshore wind farm in the Irish Sea.
As [The Guardian](https://www.theguardian.com/.../mod-objection-four...) reported, the objections present a challenge for the UK’s [renewable energy](https://www.adsadvance.co.uk/bristol-airport-s-solar.../) expansion: ensuring new wind turbines do not compromise military surveillance, air traffic control or flight safety.
The MoD’s objections do not automatically prevent construction, but developers must prove that any [radar](https://www.adsadvance.co.uk/tag/radar/) interference can be satisfactorily addressed.  https://www.adsadvance.co.uk/mod-uk-wind-farms-military.../

Scotsman letters
John Swinney announced (your report, 8 October) that the UK government must “take the brakes off” to help realise Scotland’s “world leading ambitions”for floating offshore wind.
Before ministers accelerate any further, the public deserves an honest account of what this technology is likely to cost.
In correspondence in response to an enquiry, the National Energy System Operator (Neso) admits that the strike prices used in Clean Power 2030 were those for fixed offshore wind, even though floating offshore wind “would indeed have higher strike prices”. An example of this is the £216.49/MWH awarded by GB Energy to two floating wind projects. this is drastically different from Neso’s indication of £71-£83/MWH. There is also every likelihood of this increasing as these are index linked and benefit from inflation caused by energy pricing.
In other words, one of the most expensive parts of the offshore wind story was not properly reflected in the headline cost assumptions.
That is no minor detail. Floating wind is not being sold as a niche extra. In Scotland, it is being promoted as a strategic economic prize and a pillar of the net zero transition. Yet if the modelling used to support that vision relies on fixed-bottom offshore wind prices as a proxy, ie they didn’t like the look of the actual total cost so used only fixed offshore wind prices as a reasonable approximation instead, then the public has every right to ask whether offshore wind’s viability has been made to look rosier than it really is.
Mr Swinney wants policy barriers removed. Fine, but cost reality cannot be removed with them. If floating wind is significantly more expensive, that should be stated transparently, not blurred into more favourable offshore averages.
This matters all the more because DESNZ (the  department of energy security and net Zero) itself is now saying affordability is the government’s “No 1 priority” and floating wind must show a path to lower costs before winning more subsidy support. that is a tacit acknowledgement that it is not a cheap or settled proposition.
Neso is described as “independent” yet emerged from the National Grid and, at the time, Ed Miliband as Net Zero Secretary was the sole shareholder of Neso on behalf of the public. This is not some distant technocratic quibble. It goes to the heart of how ministers,agencies and industry frame costs.
If Scotland is to have a serious debate about energy, it must start with honest numbers. Ambition is not a substitute for arithmetic.
Eileen West Banchory, Aberdeenshire
Richard Lyon wonders if the lights might go out this winter (Perspective, 7 October). He says we are relying on imported electricity. He is correct and in the last 12 months the UK has had to rely on the Netherlands, Norway, Belgium, Denmark and France for 12.5 per cent of our electricity.while wind and solar produced 42.3percentitisunreliable, whereas “nasty” gas can be relied on and has produced 27percentdespitebeingthefirst to be shut down without the payment of constraint payments. Nuclear provided 12.2 per cent and cutting down and burning trees provided 7.5 per cent.
The wind and solar companies have harvested, or more accurately pillaged, constraint payments from electricity consumers which since 2001 total £240 billion, yes billion.
Richard Lyon concludes by saying:“the lights will probably stay on this winter but ‘Probably’ is not a safety margin.” How right he is.
Clark Cross
Linlithgow

Herald letters
Andy Burnham’s eagerness to drag Britain back into the EU – greeted with open arms by the Labour left and Scottish nationalists – is a reckless distraction from the real problem of meagre growth (“Could Andy Burnham’s Brexit words turn out to be a watershed moment?”, The Herald, October 7).
At the time of the 2016 referendum I voted to remain. I accepted the democratic result which was not in my favour. My concern then was not whether the world’s then fifth largest economy could adapt and thrive outside. It was that the EU, stripped of Britain’s steadying influence, would drift into economic stagnation and become less strategically secure.
Unfortunately that concern has been vindicated.
The EU, once economically on a par with the United States 15 years ago, is now significantly smaller. France endures near eight per cent unemployment and public debt substantially higher than ours.
Germany, once the industrial powerhouse, is in deep trouble, its car industry facing particular difficulties as Chinese manufacturers seize the electric vehicle market, helped by dominating the supply chain.
Uncontrolled immigration has overloaded housing, schools and public services, driving voters sharply rightward across the continent. Just look at the ongoing disturbances in France over overcrowded schools.
Re-joining would be no salvation. We should be careful what we wish for. Especially while our own net-zero dogma continues to wreck competitiveness, drive up energy costs and leave families freezing.
The United States shows what cheaper, abundant energy delivers: stronger growth, industrial revival and lower bills. We still buy the same goods; they are simply imported, so we export both the emissions and the good jobs.
The endless EU debate is a massive distraction. We could make an immediate impact by ditching net-zero and prioritising domestic energy in all its forms: coal, fracking, nuclear, and gas and oil from the North Sea.
Britain needs cheaper energy before it needs another European debate.
Ian Lakin, Milltimber, Aberdeen.

records.title: Scottish Electricity Generating Stations
records.bodyText:
Torr Achilty Hydro Power Station (Commissioned 1950s) Installed Capacity 15MW.
Torr Achilty power station is built into the dam behind which lies Loch Achonachie, formed by its construction. The dam is of mass gravity construction, over 245m wide, 23m high and has a capacity of almost 37,000m3, bypassed by a Borland fish lift. discharging into the Cromarty Firth. Loch Achonachie is also used to absorb any sudden changes in the flow level of the River Conon. The station is situated at the bottom of the scheme and because of the cascade system which works across the scheme as a whole it receives water which has previously been used by all of the other stations on the scheme. The dam does not have any particular storage function, instead it is used to even out the flow of the river downstream of the power scheme and includes flood gates to accommodate this. 
This station is a good example of an integrated dam and power station. The station was also built as the control centre for the Conon Scheme and has a number of ancillary buildings forming workshops and a main connection to the grid. In addition to the turbine hall the main building in the station complex also houses a generous reception hall and staircase leading to offices and control rooms.— in Muirton Mains, Highland.

records.title: Scottish Electricity Generating Stations
records.bodyText:
Grudie Bridge Hydro power station (Commissioned 1950) Installed Capacity 18.6 MW. Plant was the earliest to be developed on the Conon scheme with water provided via a tunnel from Fannich Dam. The turbine hall has two turbines with a transformer station to the rear providing the connection to the grid. 
The station was designed as the control for this section of the scheme and has offices and workshops to accommodate this. The turbine hall oversails the tailrace which discharges into Loch Luichart before being used again for generation at Luichart Hydro power station. There has been a degree of later alteration to the interior of the station for continued use and there is upgrading to turbines for compliance with ROC. Later alterations also include the installation of an oil coolant system. The design is broadly functional with squared red sandstone rubble and large rectangular windows characteristic of the modernist designs seen across the sector. The building also makes reference to its context with carved panels depicting a variety of mythical Celtic beasts. this is a relatively small example of a barrage which is still operating as designed to control flow of the river and divert water through Achanalt power station. There has been modification to the control gates as required to allow for continued use. 
Dam Location
Ross-shire, Scotland
Coordinates
57°38′30″N 5°00′10″W
Loch Fannich was dammed and its water level raised as part of the Conon Hydro-Electric Power Scheme, built by the North of Scotland Hydro-Electric Board between 1946 and 1961. An underground water tunnel leading from Loch Fannich to the Grudie Bridge Power Station required blasting out a final mass of rock beneath the loch, a procedure which was referred to popularly as "Operation Bathplug".
There is no public road to the loch, and the distance from the A832 makes access difficult.
In the 1950s, the rising waters of the dammed loch subsumed the Cabuie Lodge (near the village of Achanalt), once home to Sir Arthur Bignold, MP for Wick Burghs in the early 20th century.— at Grudie Bridge Power Station.

records.title: Scottish Electricity Generating Stations
records.bodyText:
Loch Errochty Dam constructed in 1955, North of Scotland Hydro-Electricity Board. Spectacular diamond-headed buttress structure, 354m long and 49m high, built across the River Errochty to form the man-made reservoir of Loch Errochty. Water is fed to the loch from the River Garry and its upper tributaries by 19km of tunnels; a further 9.6km tunnel supplies the Errochty Power Station.
The diamond-headed buttress dam was built at the east end of Loch Errochty as part of the enlarged [2nd] phase of the Tummel catchment area scheme; there is a tunnel from this dam to Loch Tummel via the Errochty power station. The contractors were A and M Carmichael Ltd.
The dam at the east end of the Errochty Reservoir and forms part of the Tummel Hydro-Electric Scheme. It falls entirely within the parish of Blair Atholl.
The location assigned to this record defines the centre of the structure. The available map evidence indicates that it extends from NN c. 71335 65402 to NS c. 71487 65752.
Errochty is a 75MW hydro power project. It is located on Errochty river/basin in Scotland, the UK. The project is currently active. It has been developed in single phase. Post completion of construction, the project got commissioned in 1955. The project is currently owned by SSE.
The hydro reservoir capacity is 32.48 million cubic meter. The gross head of the project is 186m. The project generated 103 GWh of electricity.
The English Electric was selected as the turbine supplier for the hydro power project. The company provided 3 units of francis turbines, each with 25MW nameplate capacity. GE Renewable Energy supplied electric generator(s) for the project.
This power station houses three turbines, and is the largest on the scheme, using water brought by buried pipeline and tunnel from Errochty Dam some 10 km to the northwest. The tailrace exits into Loch Tummel which goes on to provide water for both Clunie and Pitlochry stations further downstream.
The turbines are recessed to be on a level with the incoming penstocks which are buried into the hillside behind, which forms part of the rear wall to the powerhouse. The front elevation and access deck are built on large concrete pilottis and oversail the tailrace. 
The design of the station echoes that of the other stations of a similar date on the scheme, notably that at Guar Hydro plant. The station is a relatively early example of the change in emphasis in the design from the bold modernist forms of the pre 1943 schemes, notably at Galloway, to a design which melted into the landscape to a greater degree. The design of the station retains some of the bold features of the earlier modernist designs, such as the rectangular form, and large evenly spaced glazing pattern, but is constructed from coursed random rubble, clearly echoing the Scottish vernacular tradition. The modernist form of the building is more fully recognised to the interior, with a largely functional design making use of large concrete pilasters to support the travelling crane which is retained in situ. 
The station is prominently sited adjacent to the B8019 road and additional interest in gained from the front façade which is a dramatic composition with large glazed areas and the slender columns which allow the building to oversail the tail race. 
The Errochty hydro-electric power station is one of the stations in the Tummel hydro-electric power scheme.
Loch Errochty dam at the Eastern end of the loch.The dam is 354 metres long by 49 metres high. The dam was built in 1957 and the lake is man-made.The loch stands at 330 metres above sea level. Water flows from the loch to the Errochty power station at the Western end of Loch Tummel, through a ten kilometre long tunnel.
Errochty power station is at the top of the map in the middle on the channel connecting it to the River Tummel.
Errochty power station has three turbines and a maximum output of 75 MW.
The Errochty power station and Loch Errochty have a potential to be upgraded into a 16 GWh pumped storage scheme.
Loch Errochty’s main feeder streams are the Allt Sléibh and the Allt Ruighe nan Saorach which both rise in the high ground to the west of the head of the loch. Other small streams flow directly off the 892-metre-high (2,927 ft) mountain of Beinn a’ Chuallaich which stands just to the south. Supplementary water is diverted into the loch from the east by the Errochty catchwater, a system of tunnels and surface pipelines at a height of approximately 380 metres which redirects water from five small tributary streams of the River Garry, and the Garry itself. The catchwater then goes through a tunnel in the hill which separates the Garry and Errochty valleys to join the loch. This method of re-directing water allows it to be used more often to generate electricity. Some of the water within the Tummel scheme passes through five of the power stations and thus generates electricity five times.
It was completed in 1957 and constructed by AM Carmichael ltd. Errochty is a diamond headed buttress dam that is 354 metres long and 49 metres high.These buttresses provide extra strength to deal with possible tremors from the Highland Boundary Fault which runs to the south of Pitlochry.
Loch Errochty is entirely man made and was created by the damming of Errochty water, the river that runs through this glen.The loch is 330m above sea level and water enters by tunnels from the upper reaches of the rivers Garry and Bruar.
Errochty PS main intake gate house is located on the Lochs southern shore.
Compensation water is released from the Dam and flows down an above ground pipeline for approx. 1 mile to the small Trinafour Hydro Power Station and discharges into Errochty Water.Trinafour has one 0.5 MW turgo turbine, this was designed and installed by Gilkes Hydro. This impulse water turbine is for medium head applications so best suited for the gross head of 91m.The runner of the turgo is made up of a single row of buckets and is supplied with water from a single spear valve.The site is also installed with a deflector plate mechanism to ensure comp water could always be passed in a network disturbance.This PS was commissioned in 1959— at Loch Errochty.
