records.bodyText:
Dounreay was the UK’s centre of fast reactor research and development between 1955 and 1994 and is now described as Scotland’s largest nuclear clean-up and demolition project. In April 2005 the Nuclear Decommissioning Authority (NDA) took over the ownership of the Dounreay nuclear facility in Caithness on the north coast of Scotland from the United Kingdom Atomic Energy Authority (UKAEA).
From April 2023 Dounreay joined the Magnox Division of the NDA. Then in October 2023 Magnox Ltd changed its name to Nuclear Restoration Services (NRS). NRS is responsible for safely decommissioning the first generation nuclear and research sites across the UK. It joins together of the twelve Magnox sites (including Harwell and Winfrith) and Dounreay. It will also, eventually, decommission the seven advanced gas-cooled reactor sites (AGRs), currently managed by EDF, for decommissioning.
Interim End State
Until recently, the decommissioning programme was due to reach its interim end state – the point at which all redundant facilities have been cleared and the resultant radioactive waste is in storage – by 2033, but many thought this target was unrealistic. This date has now been extended to 2070. 
Officially Nuclear Restoration Services hasn’t said what the cost of extending decommissioning work at Dounreay from 2033 to 2070 is expected to be. The cost of the programme was previously said to be about £2.9 billion but costs are expected to jump to almost £8bn. 
The biggest problem is decommissioning the Fuel Cycle Area. The NDA explained at an inaugural Cross Party Group on the Nuclear Industry in the Scottish Parliament that the earlier cost estimate was based on the previous contractor’s plan to basically fill in the Fuel Cycle area with concrete and then chop it up. But we now know that was never going to work. As improved strategies for decommissioning the very complex Fuel Cycle Area are developed, work to dismantle the fast reactors and empty two historic waste disposal and storage facilities will continue.
At the start of Britain’s nuclear programme uranium resources were thought to be scarce. Fast reactors were thought to be the way forward. These reactors, generally fuelled by plutonium, can, at the same time as generating electricity, convert the useless portion of uranium into more plutonium. 
Officially the reason given for the end to Britain’s fast reactor programme was that these reactors proved to be more expensive than expected and by the 1980s uranium was no longer in scarce supply. So, in 1988, Britain decided it would not need fast reactors for the foreseeable future and the programme was cancelled signalling the end for Dounreay.
But Fast Reactors have been a disaster world-wide – economic realities, problems associated with reprocessing (separating plutonium from spent nuclear fuel), concerns over nuclear proliferation, serious technical problems and the risk of catastrophic accident have all come together to stop the development and construction of commercial scale fast breeder reactors. 
One major difficulty with fast reactors is that they use liquid metal as a coolant – usually liquid sodium, which explodes on contact with air. Currently, only one Fast Reactor of commercial scale in the world is operating–the Beloyarsk BN-600 FBR in Russia. India is only intermittently operating its Fast Breeder Test Reactor (FBTR) at Kalpakkam. The French closed down their Superphénix Fast Reactor in 1996 after it had achieved an average capacity factor of less than 7% over eleven years of operation. It had repeated shutdowns, the longest of which lasted four years. Japan’s fast reactor at Monju has been mostly shut since a leak of liquid sodium coolant in 1995. It was reopened in May 2010 but three months later, it was closed again after another accident. In the two decades since the reactor started tests in 1991, it has managed to generate electricity for only one full hour.
The Dounreay Fast Reactor (DFR) first achieved criticality in 1958, and operated until 1977. The Prototype Fast Reactor (PFR) opened in 1974 and closed in 1994. The site also housed a fast reactor reprocessing plant, as well as a research reactor reprocessing plant. Overseas research reactor spent fuel was imported for reprocessing up until 1974 when it stopped because foreign customers were unwilling to take their waste back. Then in 1992 Dounreay re-entered the research reactor spent fuel reprocessing business with spent research reactor fuel imported, mainly from Germany until it was announced in 1998 that Dounreay would not take on any new contracts. Dounreay was also site of a materials test reactor which operated between 1958 and 1969. The Vulcan submarine reactor test facility is also at Dounreay, and is likely to be closed and transferred to NWS for decommissioning.
In 1958 the Scottish Office authorised use of an underground shaft – built to remove spoil during construction of a sub-sea effluent discharge tunnel – as a disposal facility for intermediate level radioactive waste. More than 11,000 disposals took place between 1959 until 1977, when a chemical explosion occurred and the practice ceased. Decommissioning the 65-metre deep shaft is a major challenge. A second facility, the intermediate-level waste silo, also needs to be emptied and its contents made safe. A concrete-lined box built just beneath the surface, it was used to dispose of waste between 1971 and 1998. Contractors started to prepare the ground for a major new plant which will retrieve radioactive waste from the underground shaft and silo in March 2009. 
In 2021, Jacobs and its supporting partners were awarded a 6-year contract to provide a design management team to produce a fully integrated design for the shaft and silo project. This includes assisting with the management of several design and build work packages. While some of the contract will be delivered remotely, Jacobs will also sub-contract work to local companies.
Another major problem is the appearance of radioactive particles in the environment. These small fragments of irradiated nuclear fuel have been found on the seabed off Dounreay, on the Dounreay foreshore and on Sandside Beach west of Dounreay, which is open to the public. One particle was found in 2005 on Dunnet beach east of Dounreay. It will be around 200 years, before the activities of the larger particles, have decayed sufficiently that they can no longer be considered a potential hazard. 
Radioactive particles will keep polluting public beaches for decades to come, and the environment will never be completely cleaned up. It may not even be possible to aim to return the environment to a pristine condition. Despite assurances that the risk is low of a member of the public coming into contact with a particle which is a serious hazard to health.
Since 1983 almost 500 radioactive particles have been found on three local beaches near the Dounreay nuclear facility in Caithness and the Dounreay foreshore. More than 200 of these have been found on the publicly accessible Sandside beach.
Radioactive particles were also discovered on the seabed in 1997. As a result, a fishing ban was implemented to prevent the removal of fish, crustaceans and molluscs in an area of 2km (1.2 mile) radius centred on the disused Dounreay discharge point near where the highest density of particles has been detected. The particles lie in a “plume” on the seabed spread over an area equivalent in size to that of 600 Olympic swimming pools. The fragments are thought to be the source of nuclear material found on nearby beaches. Originating from the reprocessing of nuclear fuel, they were pumped into the sea up to 50 years ago.
Underwater clean-up started in August 2008, targeting a 60-hectare area of seabed where the most hazardous particles are found. By the end of 2012, more than 2200 particles had been removed from the seabed. Of these, 409 were deemed “significant” in terms of their potential health effects. By the end of 2012 all 60 hectares had been covered by the underwater detection and retrieval system. On 12th June 2013 the Caithness Courier reported that there would be no underwater particle retrievals during 2013.
The Scottish Environment Protection Agency (SEPA) has decided to give up on its aim of returning the seabed to a “pristine condition”. The Agency has admitted that the contamination will never be completely cleaned up. To do so, it said, could cause “more harm than good”. SEPA opted instead to encourage remediation “as far as is practically achievable” but to abandon any hope of removing all the radioactive pollution from the seabed.
Spent fuel from nuclear reactors, whether at Dounreay, Torness or Hunterston, is not officially defined as “waste” – because it contains “useful” plutonium and unused uranium.
The first of 90 rail shipments of nuclear material from Dounreay in Caithness to Sellafield in Cumbria was made overnight on 16th/17th December 2012. The BBC reported that the journey was understood to have been made under armed escort. The material to be transported falls into two categories.
The first category is around forty-four tonnes of “breeder material”, which was moved in about 40 trainloads over a four or five year period. This material formed the uranium-238 blanket in the Prototype Fast Reactor at Dounreay, so it is not thought to be very radioactive, but there is concern the plutonium formed by the neutron bombardment of the uranium could be a prime target for theft. The NDA estimated that although these transports would cost around £60m, it is a cheaper option than trying to deal with it at Dounreay. This “breeder material” was expected to be reprocessed in the old Magnox reprocessing plant at Sellafield to separate out the plutonium.
The second category is a mixed bag of material called “exotics”. This includes fuel containing unirradiated highly-enriched uranium; unirradiated plutonium and irradiated fuels. This was transported from Dounreay to Sellafield at a later date and will probably take another 50 or 60 journeys over six years and started between 2014/5.
Nuclear engineer, the late John Large, condemned these proposed transports. He said: “We’re talking about bomb-grade material that would be a target for terrorists. It is also fuel from an experimental reactor which will have got broken up and will have been in storage in an uncertain condition. It will be very difficult to inspect it before it is transported and the only safeguard is based on their assumption that they would not encounter an accident with a big enough impact to break open the flask.”
During the period 2014 to 2018 whilst both types of materials were being moved to Sellafield with as many as 15 transports per year.
At 2024, some breeder fuel elements remain within the Dounreay Fast Reactor (DFR) and are still to be removed. According to the NDA’s Business Plan (2024-27) the remaining fuel will be removed and brought to Sellafield over three years and placed in long-term storage, allowing timely decommissioning of the Dounreay site.
The long term plan is fully return the site to its previous condition prior to nuclear operation commencement with a target date of the year 2333.— at Dounreay Nuclear Power Station.

We've chosen this image to introduce this post, because it reminded us of what we said yesterday regarding John Campbell's courtesy in his delivery of NOTKUP's closing submission.  He has the same courteous manner in any hearings in which we've watched him over the years, but wallop he certainly did.
And, although comparisons are said to be odious, the same can't be said, in our opinion, for his fellow KC Paul Reid whose combative attitude we've noticed throughout the hearings on the Beauly to Peterhead OHL.  
Today, we've been going through SSEN's closing submission and it became apparent, very quickly, that the same combative persona came through in the written word as in the oral.
However, that's really beside the point, except that we have now heard so much - and seen so much - about SSEN's lack of consultation and lack of caring for those who will be heavily impacted by their proposals, that we believe it's a fine pairing.
The submission is slightly longer than John Campbell's was and we are going to do no more than highlight some of the sections of it, in as brief a form as possible.
Firstly, as with TKUP but arguably more so, the submission relies on what Ofgem has said by way of ASTI.  This was put into perspective by John Campbell:
'Ofgem’s function is to assess economic and technical need from a transmission system perspective. It is not to conduct the planning and environmental assessment that Parliament has assigned to the Scottish Ministers under s. 37. Neither Ofgem sanction nor politically driven ASTI approval can substitute for this inquiry or discharge the Applicant’s burden of demonstrating compliance with the mandatory content of Sch 9, the Development Plan (including NPF4) and other material considerations.'
An example from the B-P SSEN closing submission:
The Proposed Development is also included within the Accelerated Strategic Transmission Infrastructure (ASTI) framework, through which OFGEM has accepted the strategic need for the project and retains oversight of the efficient expenditure required for its delivery. In this respect, the Applicant is not in the same position as, for example, a commercial entity seeking to develop a renewable energy project for profit. 
A little later they educate the Reporters in what is and isn't a reserved matter.
As explained below, need has, the Applicant submits, been conclusively established by the ASTI framework decision. Looking behind that would “relate to” the reservation. Invariably, conditions will have only a consequential connection with the reservation and so no competence issue arises. A condition that had the effect of fundamentally compromising the Applicant’s ability to deliver the Proposed Development in accordance with the timescales set out in the ASTI framework, however, at least arguably relates to (i.e. has more than a loose or consequential connection) with the reservation in para.D1 of sch.5 SA 1998. Accordingly, such a condition would be of doubtful executive competence so far as the Scottish Ministers are concerned.
And
At this stage, the Applicant notices two points. First, rather than ‘salami-slicing’ the Proposed Development is the bringing together of two ASTI projects. Rather than sub-dividing recognised projects, the Application is a consolidation of two projects. Secondly, a detailed cumulative assessment has been done in the EIAR. Any other approach would cause precisely the disproportionate interference with the public interest in the delivery of the ASTI framework (there plainly being a strong public interest in the integrity and reinforcement of the transmission, distribution and supply network) that Sales LJ makes clear the environmental legislation is meant to avoid.
Although the submission goes on to state, in minute detail, most of that which occurred at all the hearings and to round on the people who had given evidence on behalf of the public bodies, particularly The Highland and Moray Councils , the submission disputing what had been said, the submission is light on some things.  Raeshaw, for example, using  EIA regulations to skirt around the subject, in our view.
We've read and heard evidence from so many people about the lack of proper consultation by SSEN and yet there is this:
For completeness, the Applicant notes that a number of complaints were made about the consultation processes which informed the Application. In short, the Applicant maintains that a proper and lawful consultation was undertaken which complied with the common law requirements of such consultations (cf. the “Sedley principles”: R v Brent London Borough Council, ex parte Gunning (1985) approved in R (Mosley) v Haringey London Borough Council [2014] . In any event, the lawfulness of those consultations is a matter which is not within the remit of Reporters (or the Scottish Ministers) and the time to challenge the lawfulness of those consultations has long since passed.
An indication of supreme arrogance, in our view.
On Landscape and Visual - 
It has not been disputed that the scale and nature of the Proposed Development is such that significant landscape and visual impacts are to be expected. Accordingly, the question that needs to be addressed is whether those significant landscape and visual impacts are localised and/or are appropriately mitigated. Put shortly, the Applicant’s position is that any significant landscape and visual effects are both localised and appropriately mitigated for the reasons set out in detail in the written evidence and in the summaries of the oral evidence below. Accordingly, the Proposed Development is in accordance with NPF4, Policy 11e)ii.
And
Whether impacts are localised or not - The assessments of the officers at Moray Council and Aberdeenshire Council who determined that the effects of the Proposed Development are localised are commended. THC’s approach, like that of Ms Anderson and Moray Council (contrary to the professional judgement of its officers), is at odds with the deliberate wording of NPF4 Policy 11e)ii. It would preclude the consent of any strategic OHL in fundamental conflict with NPF4’s overarching spatial strategy to deliver net-zero transmission infrastructure.
A little later, Aberdeenshire officers were commended.  (In Aberdeenshire Council's closing submission, they are maintaining the same line - approval but with conditions.)
On risk to capercaillie:
In short, NatureScot’s assessment is (a) unduly precautionary, (b) inconsistent with its own guidance and its responses to other projects, and (c) not supported by established science. It should not (indeed, cannot) properly be relied upon by the Reporters when formulating their recommendations to Ministers.
There was a slightly gentler tone when referring to closing submissions from non-statutory consultees - the submission referred to:  Dallas Estate; Kirkhill and Bunchrew CC; Fiona Allan, and Save the Deveron Valley.  We also must make mention here of Calum Kemp who had a special section, and see at the end.
The Applicant acknowledges the amount work and time that has been spent, particularly by the local communities, in responding to the Application and participating in the oral processes. Much of their evidence has been addressed in that of the planning authorities and in the further written submissions. Comment here, therefore, is restricted to matters not previously addressed.
Picking out two closing submissions referred to:
Kirkhill & Bunchrew CC - need for the Proposed Development has been conclusively established by the UK Government’s ASTI Framework decision. It is set out in detail in the EIAR and summarised above at paragraphs 13 - 21. In short, the issue that remains is how, not whether, to deliver the Proposed Development (and the other 24 ASTI projects). The Applicant’s position in respect of the decision in Raeshaw Farms Ltd v Scottish Ministers 2026  is set out in the further written submissions dated 14  & 28  May 2026 and 28 August 2026 . As noted above, nothing in Raeshaw questioned or sought to depart from the established authorities. The criticism was specific to that case such that the legal framework in which the evaluation falls to be carried out is unchanged. The Applicant’s positions in respect of the Fanellan substation and traffic and transportation are fully set out it the further written submissions dated 28 May and 11 June 2026.
Fiona Allan - The devolved competence of Scottish Ministers is set out above at Part C. The Applicant relies on its further written submissions and Part C above in respect of the implications of the Raeshaw decision. Similarly, the Applicant relies upon the EIAR and its further written submissions in respect of the effects of the Proposed Development upon ecology, private water supplies, gas pipelines  and public health.
 It is acknowledged that the Proposed Development will result in significant landscape and visual effects. As noted in NPF4 Policy 11e)ii these are to be expected for a project of the scale and nature of the Proposed Development. These effects are localised and/or appropriately mitigated in accordance with NPF4 Policy 11e)ii. As noted in Ms Rylott’s Inquiry Report  route alignment is the first and most effective form of mitigation. Planting and/or landscaping proposals and their subsequent maintenance and management would be secured by condition and management plans.
Calum Kemp's  evidence was more or less dismissed and so was his claim for expenses.
The submission also focused on conditions
..the Chief Planner has recognised that conditions should be framed proportionately, and they should not unduly delay the delivery of nationally important energy infrastructure . The Proposed Development is an example of such infrastructure par excellence. A practical application of that approach in respect of the Proposed Development would be providing for mitigation schemes to be agreed before energisation of the OHL (i.e before it comes into operation) rather than before development commences. That latter approach would be bound to delay delivery of the Proposed Development and would the Applicant submits be unreasonable (in the public law sense).
... as set out above at 14 the Proposed Development is presented within the context of the ASTI framework as established by OFGEM as part of its Pathway to 2030. OFGEM recognises that there are “significant potential consequences if the required onshore transmission upgrades are not delivered by 2030, including capacity not being able to be connected in a full and safe manner, increased constraint, and constraint costs that are ultimately passed on to consumers’ energy bills.” Three important points emerge from the ASTI framework decision and the fact the Proposed Development is included within the ASTI framework. Specifically in relation to timing, (a) the timescale for delivery represents a policy decision of the UK Government which relates to the transmission and distribution of electricity; (b) for the two projects that constitute the Proposed Development, the delivery date is 2030; and (c) the adoption of the ASTI framework was meant to bring with it a step-change to the delivery (which must include the consenting) of large onshore transmission projects.
Scottish Ministers issued the Priority Guidance in response to the ASTI framework. The Application falls within the first definition. Recognising the strategic importance of the Application, the Priority Guidance works towards, and expects the determination of priority applications within 52 weeks of their submission.
... with references to paragraphs 20 and 46 above, while the Scottish Ministers are the appropriate authority for the consideration and determination of the application, the generation, transmission, distribution and supply of electricity is a reserved matter.
As noted above, while conditions will invariably only have a consequential connection with the reservation (and thus no competence issue would arise), a condition that fundamentally compromised the Applicant’s ability to deliver the Proposed Development in accordance with the timescales set out in the ASTI framework at least arguably relates to (i.e. has more than a loose or consequential connection with) the reservation in para.D1 of sch.5 SA 1998. Accordingly, such a condition would be of doubtful executive competence so far as the Scottish Ministers are concerned.
The Applicant recognises the important role of conditions in securing mitigation, monitoring and environmental protection. However, a recurring feature of many of the objectors' proposed conditions is an assumption that matters said to give rise to concern are presently uncontrolled. That assumption is incorrect.
And the submission proceeds to list conditions that it has come up with, stating that objector conditions  and therefore many of the additional requirements sought are unnecessary, unreasonable and duplicative, and consequently fail the  Circular tests.
The focus was specifically on Micro-siting, Limits of Deviation and RVAA and where Councils had insisted that they should first be consulted; on LoDs and Woodland Compensatory Planting.  
SSEN have made their own suggestions if Ministers determine that conditions are necessary and present those arguments, on biodiversity enhancement; borrow pits; public road improvements; temporary compounds; temporary accommodation;  Distribution Network Works; multi-stage consent; construction traffic; construction working hours; Community Wealth Building; local employment; watercourse crossings and flood risk; noise.
We realise that we have selected a tiny number of paragraphs to highlight, but we do not consider that we have been in any way unfair to SSEN.

The risk is that hackers could gain access to such systems and use them to destabilise the grid, switching on or off large amounts of demand to create havoc.

records.bodyText:
From today's New Statesman. Must have been reading the posts in this group...
While many countries face higher energy costs due to the events in the Middle East and Russia, few have seen quite as big a spike as Britain has. Industrial power costs are comfortably higher than in most developed nations, with domestic costs not far behind. To some extent, this is a function of bad luck and geopolitics. Britain is particularly dependent on natural gas to provide the critical baseload power for its electricity, not to mention much of its domestic heating.
But higher energy costs are also the product of policy. Britain pushed faster and further towards net zero (the goal of diminishing carbon emissions to close to nothing in net terms) than most of its peers. The ambition, held by Labour and Conservative governments, was that the UK should be the global leader in decarbonisation – the flag-bearer for net zero. In one respect, the enterprise was a stunning success – Britain is one of the fastest-decarbonising major economies in the world.
The main catch in – and the cardinal sin of – the make-things-cheap economy is how it affects energy bills. For all that Boris Johnson and Ed Miliband insisted (and as far as I can tell, sincerely believed) that renewables would mean lower costs, the opposite has happened. Unlike solar power, the cost of which fell precipitously as the Chinese mastered the mass production of arrays, wind power has remained comparatively expensive. And so Britain’s ambitious offshore wind programme happened largely thanks to a complex web of subsidies and price guarantees. Those interventions will lock in higher power costs in this country for years.
There is a point – most likely a decade and a half in the future – at which the savings from net zero (less spent on gas and fuels) should outweigh the costs of building all the necessary infrastructure. But for the time being, the policy is expensive – nearly £30bn a year for the next five years, which is the equivalent of an extra 5p on the basic rate of income tax. One of the main reasons net zero is becoming so controversial (and will likely get more controversial) is that the majority of those costs end up on consumer bills.
The other problem is that much of this decarbonisation was achieved through deindustrialisation. In the face of higher energy costs and rising environmental taxes, many manufacturers relocated overseas. Indeed, more than half of Britain’s carbon footprint is now accounted for by imported goods. Paradoxically, the more steel mills and chemicals plants shut down, the better the UK’s environmental credentials, since net zero plans ignore the embedded carbon in our imports and focus solely on what is puffed out of domestic flues and chimneys.

Greater Providence
NationalPoliticsCrimeWeatherFoodArtsMore
Wreck Believed To Be Rhode Island Boat Found Feet From Wind Turbine, Reviving 2019 Mystery
By Maya Bushman
Published on October 14, 2026
Providence
https://hoodline.com/.../wreck-believed-to-be-rhode.../
More than seven years after the F/V Mistress vanished into frigid New Year's Day seas off Block Island, divers have located wreckage believed to be from the vessel in about 92 feet of water — roughly 50 feet from the base of Turbine No. 1 at the Block Island Wind Farm. Side-scan sonar and underwater photographs documented the site, reigniting scrutiny of a tragedy that claimed two local fishermen and left a lone survivor with a harrowing story of escape.
The 52-foot wooden trawler sank after radioing that it was taking on water in the early hours of January 1, 2019, according to 1420 WBSM. A NOAA incident report filed after the sinking found that the vessel began flooding off Block Island and capsized once its dewatering pumps could no longer keep pace with incoming seawater, as documented by The Scuba News. The boat carried a crew of three; only one man survived.
A Family Boat, A Family Loss
Captain Oscar Diaz and deckhand John Ansay Jr., who was also Diaz's nephew, were lost in the sinking, per the station's report. Tim Diaz was pulled from a life raft and rescued by the crew of the F/V Captain Bligh, according to the same account. The Mistress was owned by Hope Fisheries, Inc. and worked out of Point Judith, Rhode Island, according to Latti Associates LLC.
The scale of the original search underscored how dire conditions were that night. The Coast Guard deployed multiple cutters, an aircraft, and heavy-weather motor lifeboat crews from Station Menemsha, covering 2,152 square nautical miles over 72 hours before suspending active rescue efforts, according to MV Times. The Coast Guard's search continued beyond survivability models for people in winter seas wearing survival suits, per the same outlet.
Helicopter Search Cut Short Near Turbines
Coast Guard search-and-rescue logs from that night show an MH-60T Jayhawk helicopter aborted its search for the Mistress crew after roughly 37 minutes, citing severe weather, poor visibility, and proximity to the wind turbines, according to National Fisherman. The Coast Guard's investigation reached no conclusions about the sinking, and the Coast Guard later conducted training at the Block Island Wind Farm.
Fishing boats searched the area, and offers of help came in.
Divers Document Wreckage And Possible Remains
Scientific divers sponsored by Green Oceans inspected the seabed site in August 2026, documenting features consistent with a wreck believed to be the Mistress, including its propeller, shaft, fuel tanks, net drum, and deck hatch, along with apparent human remains, according to The Scuba News. Green Oceans marine professionals first located the site using side-scan sonar in July 2026, per National Fisherman's reporting. Green Oceans is a nonprofit that opposes offshore wind development off the Massachusetts and Rhode Island coasts, and believes there could be a link between the sinking and the wind farm's presence.
Michael Lombardi, president of Green Oceans, said the wreck's orientation merits investigating whether the crew made an emergency turn to starboard to avoid colliding with a turbine, per Fox News Digital. With the hull already full of water, he said, that kind of maneuver could have caused the vessel to roll and sink. The Coast Guard's original investigation reached no conclusions about the cause of the sinking, and Green Oceans has openly criticized how that inquiry was handled.
Push To Reopen The Investigation
Green Oceans has submitted side-scan sonar imagery and dive photos to the Coast Guard, the National Transportation Safety Board, and Rhode Island authorities, and has asked the Department of the Interior to coordinate an investigation, according to Newport Buzz. The group says the discovery raises broader questions about how rescuers can safely assist distressed vessels near offshore wind turbines in the rough conditions routinely encountered off the Northeast coast.
The Block Island Wind Farm, commissioned in December 2016 as the first commercial offshore wind project in the United States, consists of five 6-megawatt turbines standing 600 feet tall, about 3.8 miles off Block Island, according to background compiled by the Pacific Northwest National Laboratory. The facility has a capacity of 30 megawatts. Concerns have been raised about navigation and search-and-rescue near turbines.
For now, federal regulators at the Coast Guard and NTSB have not said whether they will reopen the case, and the identity of the human remains found at the wreck site has not been confirmed. Those questions remain open more than seven years after the Mistress went down, leaving Point Judith's fishing community, and the family of John Ansay Jr., still waiting for answers.

records.title: Environmentalists Against Wind Turbines
records.bodyText:
One thing that has frustrated me for years is the glaring inconsistency in how environmental regulation is applied in Australia.
During my forestry career in Tasmania, the protection of wedge-tailed eagles was taken extremely seriously. Forestry operations followed detailed environmental prescriptions designed to avoid disturbing breeding birds, including exclusion zones around active nests and seasonal operating restrictions. Compliance was built into every harvest plan and it wasn't optional.
Now compare that with what is emerging from some wind energy developments. Reports that 20 wedge-tailed eagles have been killed at the Rye Park Wind Farm in just 18 months have renewed calls for stronger wildlife protections and bird-strike mitigation technology.
I find that contrast difficult to ignore. Forestry was heavily regulated because it could disturb threatened species. Wind farms are being approved and operated in landscapes where there is a foreseeable risk of actually killing them.
I want to know why similar environmental values are regulated so differently depending on the industry involved. When forestry sought approval to operate, the burden of proof rested squarely on demonstrating that impacts on threatened species would be avoided or minimised. Failure to meet those requirements meant an operation couldn't proceed.
However, when protected birds are killed by wind turbines, the response often seems to be retrospective — monitor the deaths, trial new technologies, or adjust operations after the fact — rather than asking whether the project was appropriately located in the first place.
If the precautionary principle is genuinely important, it should apply equally to every form of development. Environmental protection should not depend on whether a project is labelled "renewable". The same threatened species deserves the same level of protection whether the risk comes from forestry, mining, urban development or wind energy.
Conservation loses credibility when one industry faces rigorous precautionary regulation while another is largely judged after the damage has already occurred.

records.title: Scotland Against Spin
records.bodyText:
Scotsman letters
There are lies, damned lies and statistics but now there are lies, damned lies and cheap electricity promises.
We have been promised cheap, reliable, green electricity and £300 off our bills for ages but nothing happens.
Figures from Octopus Energy’s “Wasted Wind” tracker shows figures that the wind industry and those of a green disposition would rather be hidden away from sight.
Last year consumers were hit with a bill for £1.47 billion, yes billion, to switch wind farms off and gas plants on. At the end of September this year the figure was £1.5bn. September alone harvested £404 million, with £30m on 30 September. Government analysis, cited in the Octopus Energy report, suggests that annual constraint payments could reach £10bn by 2030. No wonder there is fuel poverty.
One must ask who was the not-so-bright spark who agreed to pay wind turbine owners not to produce electricity. No wonder the cost of UK electricity is among the highest in the world and manufacturing companies cannot compete.
UK households and industry are paying for politicians’ net zero 2050 fixation. Meanwhile most of the rest of the world is harvesting and burning cheap fossil fuels, predominantly coal, to drive their economies.
Clark Cross Linlithgow, West Lothian 
Of the many recent letters praising Scotland’s renewable energy capabilities none have addressed the most essential factor – the efficiency of the total network system.
The simplest metric for this is constraint payments. For the last complete year 96 per cent of UK payments went to Scottish generators, so by some margin we have the least efficient part of the system, and this can only get worse if Torness is replaced by yet more intermittent generation.
A Mccormick Terregles, Dumfries

A SECOND council has changed how people can object to planning applications after it received an “overwhelming” amount of objections to a proposed AI data centre on the site of a 1000-year-old castle.
Fife Council has confirmed it will no longer accept planning applications by email after it received more than 14,000 representations to plans for a 600MW hyperscale data centre, near Auchtertool, that would see the Hallyards Castle destroyed to make way for the building.
The proposal includes a complex of data hall buildings, which could be as high as 35 metres, around 114 feet, which would be taller than The Kelpies in Falkirk, as well as electricity substations, security fencing, gatehouses and other infrastructure.
It is understood residents were told the change was also in response to the increasing use of AI by respondents.

records.title: Wind Energy's Absurd
records.bodyText:
Juliet Samuel had an excellent and comprehensive piece in the Times yesterday on the recent grid shenanigans; it's entitled 'Why are power grid bosses gaslighting us?'
She said:  As for today, whenever you’re reading this, who knows what fun lies in store for the control room?
Well, Juliet - we're a day late, but we can tell you what's happening this morning, thanks to David Turver who tweeted that frequency was going up and down like a yoyo - our words, not his. 
What he said was:  And even more frequency oscillations this morning. Frequency above normal operating limit at 6:05, below from 7:14 to 7:22 and then above again from 7:32 to 7:34.  Curiouser and curiouser
Kathryn Porter has just tweeted this:
It's getting embarrassing now... This morning  @neso_energy
has blown through the intraday interconnector trading limits again and like yesterday the frequency has been above and below the safe operational limits
Margins are perfectly fine so I can only think this is a combination of poor modelling and forecasting and the grid constraints affecting the SE
Yesterday saw record balancing costs of just under £50 million so this isn't just a curiosity, it's chaos that's driving bills higher (balancing costs are part of network costs)
https://www.thetimes.com/comment/columnists/article/why-are-power-grid-bosses-gaslighting-us-zk5q7ftfm?utm_source=Sailthru&utm_medium=email&utm_campaign=Times%20Politics%20-%20Thursday%20October%2015&utm_term=audience_POLITICS
'The first thing to know is that this is not normal. The people who run Britain’s electricity grid want you to think it is, but it isn’t. I believe the psychological term is gaslighting, but given the impending winter gas shortage, that’s optimistic.
The facts are these. In the past fortnight there have been four, maybe five, highly unusual events in the control room of Britain’s electricity grid: major forecasting errors, formal calls to the market for extra power and demands for “emergency assistance” from our neighbours in Europe.
Senior managers at the publicly owned National Energy System Operator (Neso) want you to believe these incidents are “routine”. Since the last “routine” incident in June, which is now the subject of both a technical and a legal investigation, Neso has signed PR contracts worth £400,000 to convince everyone they are doing splendidly. What they haven’t done is learn any lessons or produce any in-depth analysis of what the hell is going on.
Yet things keep happening. On September 28, Neso’s forecasts showed it was going to run out of power and it had to put out a call for extra, same-day (and expensive) generation. After about 15 hours, it cancelled the notice — its forecasts were wrong. On October 6, it issued another call. Luckily, even though the wind was low, demand was lower. Again, the forecasts were wrong.
On October 9, for no obvious reason, the grid suddenly ran so short of power that its frequency, or “heartbeat”, went out of the normal operating range for ten minutes, which is what happened in June. An internal “frequency event report” on the latest incident, which I’ve seen thanks to a concerned insider, shows that Neso had to push more power from north to south than the wires are meant to take.
It also had to offer a fortune to incentivise power production from generators in the south. When even that wasn’t enough, it issued a call for “emergency assistance” from France. A Neso engineer says we were one circuit trip away from a very serious situation. “All that was left was [to] scramble for emergency assistance from the EU, violate transmission constraints or disconnect demand.”
Incredibly, three days later, Neso was begging France again, issuing its biggest-ever call for power.
Despite plentiful wind on October 12, with cable maintenance slightly overrunning, power couldn’t get down to meet demand in the south. The next day, Tuesday, the grid’s frequency first spiked too high and then fell too low, for reasons as yet unknown. As for today, whenever you’re reading this, who knows what fun lies in store for the control room?
Given how often Neso is being caught off guard, I suppose you could argue this is indeed now “routine”. As Andrew Larkins, an energy consultant and former Ofgem adviser, politely puts it: “They’re at risk of normalising something that’s meant to be part of an emergency system … It shows how hard they’re having to work to keep the lights on.” Winter hasn’t even started yet.
Why is this happening? The technical answer is we don’t know because Neso isn’t opening up the incidents to scrutiny in the way that, say, an airliner is forced to facilitate an industry-wide post-mortem when an engine chokes. More successful modernising grids, such as Australia’s, take the opposite approach.
The broader answer is that governments, regulators and owners of the system have indulged a decade of wishful thinking and under-investment, pretending they know how to pull off a radical energy transition when they have devoted appallingly little forethought, planning and money to the question.
The electricity grid used to run off a hundred or so fossil fuel generators, which can be turned up and down on request and are mechanically stable because they spin big, heavy rotors. Demand also tended to follow a pattern. This made balancing power supply and demand fairly straightforward.
Now, large portions of our power (some days, all of it) come from a mix of undersea cables, renewables plants and batteries, all of which can abruptly and unpredictably turn off and on. Small units, such as rooftop solar, don’t even send data to the grid. Customers are using new, variable gadgets like smart meters and electric cars. Forecasting and responding to changes has become, to be technical, a total bloody nightmare. “We can’t see how much reserve we have,” says the engineer.
On top of this, you have a regulator and grid operator moving at the pace of a Siberian town clerk in a Chekhov play. The grid code, which specifies the grid’s technical requirements, is so out of date that when Neso discovered hundreds of wind farms had their meters fitted backwards, so they tell the grid they’re consuming when they’re actually generating, there was no one obvious to blame. But a single technical change to the code can take years of consultations and meetings.
The rules governing grid stability are similarly out of date. A programme to install more granular sensors to monitor frequency in dozens of locations is well overdue. While the US grids have for years had 2,500 such sensors, Britain’s ambition is to have 40 (a tenth of what Larkins says would be equivalent coverage), and even some of those aren’t sharing data in a useable form. A working group on protocols to stop cascades of generator trips, which took out the solar-reliant Iberian grid last year, is crawling along.
It isn’t all Neso’s fault. Private owners of grid infrastructure are in no hurry to make unprofitable improvements. But nor are they being hurried or penalised. Ofgem has repeatedly tolerated grid regulatory failings and delayed or refused investment proposals. As a result, Neso, which ultimately passes costs to users, must now pay a fortune to buy in power on the day it’s needed to avoid blackouts.
Meanwhile, plans to manage the new power system assume we can use advanced software to fine-tune supply and demand. For example, the commercial fridge industry says it can tweak power use up or down. Brilliant! Except that hackers got at supermarket fridges in France this week and cranked them up to 50 degrees. It spoilt a lot of food. If we’re not careful, a hack like that could spoil the grid.
Governments, regulators, operators and owners have all conspired in the delusion that everything is fine and we can keep going at breakneck speed to “clean power 2030”. But the strain is showing and the engineers won’t pretend any more. You can’t run an electricity grid on a news grid.'

Historic Environment Scotland. Hallyards Castle, Auchtertool
Thank you for your enquiry about Hallyards Castle, Auchtertool.
We have received some requests to consider this site for designation. We have assessed the significance of the site and recently published our report, which you can find here.
https://portal.historicenvironment.scot/apex/f?p=1505:300:::::VIEWTYPE,VIEWREF:decision,500004395
As you will see from the report, we found that the site met the scheduling criteria of National Importance. Our Designation Policy and Selection Guidance, however, sets out that we do not normally introduce new designations when there are development proposals at an advanced stage. In this case, we were satisfied that the current planning application amounts to advanced development proposals in the terms of our policy. Therefore, in line with our policy, we did not schedule the site of Hallyard Castle. You can read more about our reasoning in our report. The report has been published and may help inform the planning process.
Regards
Allan Rutherford
Dr Allan Rutherford | Deputy Head of Designations | Heritage Directorate

At last after 10 months, the Scottish Government has published the Onshore electricity generation - Electricity Act threshold: summary consultation responses.  This Consultation was in response to our Petition to the Scottish Parliament  which, among other things, requested that the current 50MW threshold be raised in order to allow more local decision making with Ministers focusing on the really major applications.  We also insisted that local rejection of a development must be a key material consideration in the decision making process.
We haven't scrutinised all of the responses yet but Q2 shows that the vast majority of respondents opted for raising the threshold to 150MW.  Development, Property and Land Management Sector and Agents were the only category who disagreed.  That was to be expected!
Great to see that so many of our members responded to the consultation.  
You can read the summary of responses here

Reply from East Lothian Council re Brownfield Site.......
In response to your email sent on the 28th of September, I would like to clarify that the requirements you mentioned i.e. for local authorities to prepare, maintain and publish registers of previously developed (brownfield) land is set out in The Town and Country Planning (Brownfield Land Register) Regulations 2017. This Regulation and also other policy requirements pertinent to the previously developed land included in NPPF apply to England and not to Scotland where a different planning regime is in place (the responsibility for planning matters was transferred to the Scottish parliament and Scottish Government under the Scotland Act 1998).
Regarding the site in question, I can confirm that this land is allocated in the East Lothian Local Development Plan (2018) under Proposal EGT1: Land at Former Cockenzie Power Station. This LDP Proposal states that “Land at Cockenzie may also present significant opportunities for renewable energy-related investment.”
The ELC Planning Service provides annual updates to The Scottish Vacant and Derelict Land Survey (SVDLS) which is available at https://www.gov.scot/.../the-scottish-vacant-and.../ This survey is undertaken every year to establish the extent and state of vacant and derelict land in Scotland. According to our last year’s survey (2025) the site at the former coal yard at Cockenzie was classified as derelict as it is on previously developed land which has a physical constraint caused by its previous use which hampers its redevelopment.
As mentioned earlier the site is allocated in the current LDP and over the last years public funding has been secured towards the works aiming to remove the site’s physical constraints and changing its derelict classification.

records.title: Scottish Electricity Generating Stations
records.bodyText:
ScottishPower has hailed a “global engineering first” after completing a record-breaking engineering operation on a major offshore wind farm.
The power giant’s renewables business has undertaken the work at the giant £4 billion East Anglia Two wind development. The project is being developed by ScottishPower Renewables, part of Iberdrola Group, in the southern North Sea.
The construction milestone saw the installation of the two cable ducts that will provide a protected pathway for the high-voltage export cables that will carry the green electricity from the 960 MW wind farm to shore.
At just under 1,800 metres long and 800mm in diameter, the giant ducts form the largest electricity transmission landfall of its kind in the UK, based on the combination of these two dimensions.
The completion of this colossal horizontal directional drilling (HDD), which is three times the length of an other East Anglia projects, is a huge achievement - quite literally - and a major milestone as we progress construction of third wind farm in the region.
Priority to deliver clean energy projects, and all the benefits they bring, in a responsible and sensitive way that is mindful of the environment and the people around us.
Landfall works are known to be one of the most technically challenging aspects of building an offshore wind farm, but thanks to precision planning and a great partnership with principal contactor OCU Group and duct manufacturer Pipelife, this programme has well and truly hit the mark - breaking UK and world records in the process.
HDD is a complex engineering process that goes deep beneath the ground to create an underground bore without the need to dig up beaches, dunes, cliffs or coastal habitats, minimising any disruption to the environment and sensitive landscapes. It is completed using rigs working onshore and offshore simultaneously.
The works are part of the East Anglia Two civil engineering programme being carried out by principal contractor OCU Group, with support from its subsidiary Peter McCormack & Sons. The contract is supporting more than 80 jobs during construction.
The first of the wind farm’s export cables is expected to be installed in summer 2027, with the wind farm working towards commercial operation in late 2028.
East Anglia Two located in the southern North Sea, will generate enough power the equivalent of almost one million homes.— at East Anglia 1 Offshore Wind Farm.

Notes from Community Council special Hyperscale Data Centre meeting.
I attended last nights meeting and left early as the meeting was not focused on the Hyperscale Data Centre.
The meeting was held by BenMorse the chair of the CC and the sub group of the community council specifically created to work on the Hyperscale data centre. Ther were no introductions only Ben Morse the chair speaking, no representatives from SDCL or ELC. The meeting was disapppointing and focused on what we already know about the power station site. It was a repeat of the last two meetings when they discussed the site. Anyone attending knows the history and whats on the site and is attending because they want to put a stop to the Hyperscale Data Centre after all thats what the meeting was advertised as.
I learnt that ELC, Councillors Gilbert and another along with representation from each development site, whether in person or via email met with the chairs of Prestonpans and Cockenzie and Port Seton Community Councils. These meetings have been set up to improve communication but no minutes were released only a mention of funding available from Inch Cape, the promise of jobs and that Seagreen have delayed building work.
This feedback was not helpful and not what I was led to believe these meetings were for.
Ben Morse chair of Cockenzie & Port Seton CC reminded the group that there were no plans yet for the data centre, which we are well aware of. He did not seem to appreciate that now is the time to email councillors as to the reasons why we dont want a Hyperscale data centre and that we have to try and stop the SDCL agreement being signed.
There was also no mention of the CC supporting the land asset transfer by the 360 project and no mention of the cc looking into the fact that the site was bought with public money and that deals were done behind closed doors.
There was also no mention that we need to be prepared for when the plans are released.
He stated a new ELC development plan was in the pipeline.
He also mentioned the gas leak but played it down. I then asked him if the community council had reported our health and Safety concerns to SEPA and the Health and Safety Executive re the accumulation of the fire, the gas leak, the contaminated dust, the asbestos, the working outwith hours, the monitoring of air quality etc. He said yes but no one had replied to their emails.
I explained ELCs complaints procedure to him and how we could following the correct procedures request a public enquiry.
I asked for the CC to be more active in supporting the community as we have no faith in ELCs health and Safety at the power station site see my previous letter to the cc which they have not replied to.
I feel that our concerns over H&S are what should have been discussed at the site meeting mentioned previously.
I then left as it was very clear that the meeting was going nowhere but over old ground.
Ive been informed the meeting finally got onto the data centre at 9pm. Im awaiting an update from anyone who was there.
If anyone is interested please join our community council they are short of members and definitely require more local people who are passionate about stopping the data centre.

Join us for a webinar at lunchtime Monday 19th October called 'who pays for Big Tech'
We will explore the findings of a recent report on the social, economic, and environmental costs of data centres in Ireland, with researchers from University College Dublin and Maynooth University.
Patrick Brodie and Patrick Bresnihan will cover their research on how claims about the economic benefits of data centres to Ireland are exaggerated, the costs of data centre development are socialised through existing industrial policy, and the current policy contradictory to long-term sustainability goals.
Link in bio
More about the speakers
Patrick Brodie is a Lecturer/Assistant Professor and Ad Astra Fellow in the School of Information and Communication Studies at University College Dublin. His research focuses on the environmental politics of digital infrastructures, and specifically the relations and entanglements of internet and other communications technologies with energy systems, global supply chains, and extractivism.
Patrick Bresnihan is an Associate Professor in the Department of Geography at Maynooth University. His work examines the contested politics of climate, land, and infrastructure in Ireland, and how these speak to broader questions of postcolonial development, dependency and the green transition.

records.title: RE-Think Wales
records.bodyText:
Planning Aid Wales (‘We support meaningful community engagement in planning in Wales’) are offering a series of online seminars on infrastructure planning. The first, Understanding Planning Infrastructure for Communities, provided an overview of the planning system, and how to engage in the new Significant Infrastructure Projects (SIP) process. For campaigners already broadly familiar with the planning system, there was nothing new, as such, but one or two things did fall into place for me.
The second 2 hour session, on 11 November, is on Responding to Infrastructure Planning Applications, and will explore “how communities can respond confidently to SIPs, with a particular focus on preparing evidence-based representations that can make a meaningful contribution to the examination process.” Cost is £20. https://planningaidwales.org.uk/.../planning-your-places-7/
Then on 11 November there’s a free Infrastructure Planning: Community Perspectives Roundtable. This will be “A facilitated, exploratory session to surface the questions and issues communities have about the new national infrastructure planning process in Wales…Bring your questions, share examples from your own area and hear from others facing similar opportunities and challenges. The discussion will explore how communities are engaging with the new process, what is working well, and where further support may be needed.” https://planningaidwales.org.uk/.../planning-your-places-9/
The final session, on 20 January 2027, is on Community Engagement in Infrastructure Planning Applications, and will explore “how communities can engage positively and effectively throughout the infrastructure planning process, from the earliest stages of project development through to decision-making.”
I know, positive engagement with Bute Energy/Green GEN and their ilk is an oxymoron.
The first session was run by the Planning Aid Wales Chief Executive, who proved open to challenge and willing to learn from participants’ experiences. On Monday he’s running a new session on Planning & Artificial Intelligence - Smarter Tools, Stronger Communities (cost £40). https://www.eventbrite.co.uk/.../planning-artificial...

Will the Havering data centre be built?
A significant impediment to its eventual development has become evident this week.
CoreWeave may not be a name you are familiar with but its problems may be a saving grace for residents near the proposed site.
CoreWeave is a big player in the data centre business with 51 sites, mostly in the US, currently in operation with many more in various stages of delivery.
The problem with CoreWeave and the AI phenomenon is its huge appetite for debt to keep pushing the expansion. As the chart below shows, the companies share price has dropped significantly but more importantly is the rise in the Credit Default Swap (CDS) premium. This is the cost of insurance bond holders have to pay if they want protection from an eventual default by the company.
This may blow over, it may be the canary in the coal mine. However, given the hike in government bond yields associated with seemingly out of control budget deficits, bond holders of government and corporate debt are in no mood to overlook spending which has little respect for revenues.
Time will tell but this development will make the cost of development in Havering less appealing.
If CoreWeave falters, I fully expect the lightning speed of data centre rollout to be curtailed.

CHAPELLCROSS: WHAT HAPPENED TO THE WIDER VISION, AND WHERE HAS THE PUBLIC MONEY GONE?
The earlier proposals for Chapelcross described a mixed-use employment, energy and innovation site.
The council’s May 2021 programme update included five themes:
• Green energy and net-zero industry.
• Sustainable agriculture, aquaculture and food.
• Clean mobility and logistics.
• Education, skills and training.
• Digital connectivity and data services.
The 2024 masterplan developed that wider approach through hydrogen, green industry, enterprise and energy campuses. It included flexible premises for smaller businesses, manufacturing and supply-chain activity.
Digital infrastructure was already part of the earlier vision. The question is how a development now dominated by hyperscale data centres delivers the wider economic and community benefits originally envisaged? And isn’t just a sudden jump onto the Data Centre bandwagon and a money grab!
Their ongoing use on this public funding now needs a clear explanation. Not the least because what’s now planned is substantially different from what received public funding.
Publicly available and published records show:
• A May 2021 report confirmed a £134,000 NDA payment to Dumfries and Galloway Council under a five-year £495,000 Chapelcross grant agreement.
• A SOSE freedom-of-information response recorded a grant of up to £150,000 over three years from 2022/23 to support the council’s Chapelcross business-case work.
• The council’s November 2024 report identified £15.3 million of proposed government funding through Borderlands, plus £5.5 million committed by the council, for roads and services to unlock the site.
• The Ferret reported this month that the Borderlands allocation was up to £17.3 million. Both Borderlands and the council told it that funding had not yet been awarded and remained conditional.
Now all these figures concern different dates, purposes and funding stages. And so they cannot simply be added together or described as money handed to CX Tech that’s now due to be handed back etc. 
But since the attendees at the first (and only?) public meeting reported that the CX representative stated “hat money would have to be paid back if the site is not developed” it might seem important that the council, Scottish and UK governments and the public get any relevant written explanations.
Questions that now seem important and need a clear legal answer include:
Which organisation received the money, how much, and when?
Which agreement or agreements now contain the repayment requirements?
What precisely triggers any repayment, and by what deadline?
Does any of this require this particular data centre scheme, does this change of plan now invalidate the original funding plan that was far more community oriented?
Could another suitable development meet the conditions of this hyperscale data centre does not?
Which elements of the earlier mixed-use vision remain, and where will they be delivered?
Does ANY of the original bison remain among thes enemies plans?
I remember seeing the original plans and how it was about regenerating a genuinely brownfield site to get some use for the local community and businesses. Not the current exploitative land and cash grab for the usual suspects. 
Please Google and look for the following documents yourself (perhaps the Green Party for example has the manpower and volunteers to dive deeply into this?):
“CX SSG Mark Fulton CX programme May21”
“Chapelcross Development Framework November 2024”
“Chapelcross council 5 November 2024 15.3 5.5”
“SOSE 127 FOI Chapelcross April 2024”
“Chapelcross Ferret October 2026 public funds”
I think we need to call on the council, all funding bodies and both governments to now examine and publish (any not available) the funding agreements, payments to date and repayment conditions for the site, CX and all stakeholders. 
The community and tax payers should be able to see exactly what has been funded and what obligations follow.

The problem we as a species face, is that AI is a fait accompli.
It has been unleashed way too quickly, before we were ready to comprehend it or prepare for its intrusion into every aspect of our [digital] lives. It arrived completely unregulated, released by tech billionaires who (to quote the character Ian Malcolm in Jurassic Park) were so preoccupied with whether or not they could, they didn't stop to think if they should.
It is here now and it is not going away. And exponentially snowballing demand for it means more and more datacentres to power it will be needed. So simply saying "don't use it" is utterly pointless. Like saying mobile phones and their network infrastructure will go away because you don't use one. The masts will still go up, regardless, as too many other people do. It is already everywhere. You're probably using it already without even realising it. Meta (that Facebook, Instagram, Threads etc is built on), now uses AI tools function. So does Amazon, Ebay, PayPal, your bank, the NHS, passport control, even your online supermarket shopping. It's being snapped up everywhere as a method of generating efficiencies.
We currently denounce and lambaste AI in the same way that luddites did against power looms in the 19th century. Power looms did not go away. Neither will AI. That horse has long since bolted.
However that does not mean that development of datacentres should just be allowed unopposed or unregulated. AI itself might be too far gone to restrain, but the datacentres that house it, still have to conform to planning regulations, environmental law etc. Our MPs, MSPs, councillors, community councils, and local planning officers all must be held accountable to public scrutiny, to ensure all environment safeguards and controls are fully adhered to.

SEAS and WALL (Walberswick Against LionLink) have both submitted detailed responses to Ofgem's consultation on the Sea Link Project Assessment, which closed on 29th September.
Although our starting points differ, the two submissions proved highly complementary, combining detailed regulatory scrutiny with a wider strategic and cumulative assessment of the project.
SEAS: the consumer and value-for-money case
SEAS questions whether Ofgem can justify committing consumers to £2.89bn £3.2bn for Sea Link when questions remain over Sea Link’s need, cost, technical operation and value for money.
It challenges the £1.1bn–£1.4bn constraint-benefit figures, arguing that network changes, including the relocation of Nautilus, need to be reflected. It also highlights Ofgem’s acknowledgement that the project does not fully resolve the harmonics issue.
SEAS points to the much cheaper alternative evidenced during the DCO examination and questions the funding arrangements, including early construction funding, contingency and cost reopeners, 
WALL: the wider strategic and cumulative picture.
WALL draws on its experience of Sea Link and LionLink and their impacts on Suffolk, but takes a wider view, questioning Sea Link’s cost, deliverability and incremental benefits, as well as cumulative impacts alongside Sizewell C, EA1, EA2 and other NSIPs.
WALL also highlights the wider question of whether the Great Grid Upgrade is being planned and delivered efficiently, drawing on the National Audit Office’s concerns about oversight, monitoring and regulatory scrutiny.
Two perspectives, a common concern
SEAS brings detailed economic and regulatory scrutiny; WALL brings the wider strategic and cumulative perspective. Both ask whether billions of pounds of consumers’ money are being committed on the basis of current evidence, realistic alternatives, technical certainty and proper whole-system assessment.
With the National Audit Office (NAO) itself questioning how the Great Grid Upgrade is being scrutinised, these questions deserve proper answers.
We now await Ofgem's response. 
#SeaLink #SEAS #WalberswickAgainstLionLink #SuffolkCoast #ConsumerValueForMoney

The UK completed its first full calendar year without coal-fired electricity in 2025. The milestone followed the closure of Ratcliffe-on- Soar, the UK's last coal-fired power station, on September 30, 2024.
Ratcliffe-on-Soar had operated for 57 years before shutting down, ending Britain's use of coal for electricity generation. The closure also made the UK the first G7 nation to completely phase out coal-fired power.
Britain's coal-fired electricity era began in the 19th century, with coal becoming central to the country's industrial development and power system. The 2025 milestone marks a major change in the UK's electricity mix, with coal no longer providing electricity throughout the entire year.

A'Chruach Wind Farm is located in Kilmichael Forest which is around four kilometres west of Minard in Argyll. 
The site's 21 turbines are spectacularly set in the rugged Highland terrain, towering over the managed pine forest and looking north towards Loch Glashan. 
Construction work began in November 2014 and was completed in March 2016. As well as building the turbines, the project required the completion of over 13.5km of access tracks, built with locally sourced rock. The concrete for the turbine bases was also produced on site to limit environmental impact. The wind farm began full production in March 2016.
The windfarm is located within the Kilmichael Forest on a ridge which extends southwest from the summit of A' Chruach in Mid-Argyll (Argyll and Bute). The site comprises 21 Senvion turbines of two different types; twelve of the MM92 model with an output of 2 MW, a hub height of 78m (256 feet) and a blade diameter of 92m (302 feet). In addition there are a further nine MM100 machines, each rated at 2.03 MW, a hub height of 80m (262 feet) and a blade diameter of 100m (328 feet). 
The total output is 42.6 MW. Construction began in November 2014 and the first turbines were commissioned in March 2016. Developed by Infinis Energy at a cost of £11.5 million, on land owned by Forestry and Land Scotland, the site is now operated by Nadara Energy. The principal contractor was Glasgow- based R.J. McLeod who were responsible for new access roads, upgrading of existing tracks and bridges, a new 20m-span bridge, turbine foundations, control buildings and electrical works.
For the next 25 years, the Windfarm will  provide around £150,000 from their annual income from this wind farm to support community projects in the local area.
Total capacity: 43 MW
Energy produced: 116,804 MWH/YEAR
CO2 reductions: 52,328 T/YEAR— at A'chruach Wind Farm.

Dunmaglass Windfarm is a major onshore wind facility located in the Monadhliath Mountains of the Scottish Highlands, roughly 25 km (16 miles) south of Inverness.
Located on a natural plateau at an average of 700m above sea level, Dunmaglass is SSE's highest wind farm to be constructed.
SSE acquired the project from RES in May 2013 and initial enabling works began in the summer of 2013 which included the upgrading of 11km of tracks and the construction of two timber deck bridges. The Windfarm consists of 33 GE Energy 2.85-100 wind turbines with a total installed capacity of 94.05 MW.
Project timeline: Approved in 2010, acquired by SSE in May 2013, energised in 2016, and fully commissioned in 2017. 
Built with 70-meter towers to meet local planning height limits of 120 meters to the turbine tip.
Highland contractor RJ McLeod was awarded the £16m main civil works contract in summer 2014. Dunmaglass became fully operational in 2017.
In February 2019, SSE sold 49.9% of Dunmaglass to Greencoat UK Wind PLC as part of a deal in which Greencoat acquired a 49.9% stake in both Dunmaglass and the nearby Stronelairg wind farm.
The height at which Dunmaglass is located presented its challenges during construction and the winter months brought high winds and plenty of snow. The site was fully completed and handed to the operations team in 2017.
In February 2019, SSE signed agreements for the sale of 49.9% of Dunmaglass wind farm to Greencoat UK Wind Plc (“UKW”). This sale was part of a £635m deal in which Greencoat acquired a 49.9% stake in both Stronelairg and Dunmaglass wind farms. The stakes equate to 160.6MW of capacity, with an average valuation for the two wind farms of around £4m per MW.  
Dunmaglass Community Investment Fund
make around £245,000 per year available for community and charitable projects. Between 2015 and 2040 we expect to invest £6.2million in local projects.

What happens when wind farm subsidies come to an end?  
David Turver's piece today covers Ørsted and the Gunfleet Sands wind farm/s.
We have plenty of references, in our more recent archives to Ørsted and its selling off of assets.  Nothing on Gunfleet as this was in the days when Ørsted was still Dong - and we weren't even a twinkle in anyone's eye.
Ørsted has bought back a 49.9% stake in its Gunfleet Sands offshore wind farm for just £15 million, having sold that stake to a Japanese investor in 2011 for £200 million. 
But the story goes well beyond the sale price because subsidies have been crucial. 
In 2025, nearly 70% of the wind farm's £71.4 million revenue came from Renewables Obligation Certificates (ROCs), rather than electricity sales.
The subsidies end in July 2029. David Turver estimates that, without them, the wind farm's income from electricity sales would be insufficient to cover its rising operating costs.
Decommissioning could be expensive. The wind farm's dismantling costs are currently estimated at around £60 million, but David argues that the actual bill could be considerably higher.
The wind farm may have to close early if it becomes uneconomic to operate after the subsidies end, potentially bringing forward decommissioning from 2034 to 2029–30.
Investors haven't done particularly well either. The minority investors received approximately £193.6 million in dividends over the period covered by David's calculations and are now receiving £15 million for their stake. His analysis suggests a very poor overall return once the timing of those payments is taken into account.
https://davidturver.substack.com/.../orsted-gunfleet...
