This is an interesting piece in The Telegraph - Microsoft has pulled out of the NScale Essex data centre.  Microsoft was its only customer.  
From September last year:
Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer said the UK was on its way to becoming a world leader in AI.
"Meaning more jobs and investment, more money in people's pockets, and transformed public services"  BBC
But, in the same article:
AI expert Dr Haider Raza said "awful" electricity costs could also stunt growth.
"We have to make data centres more efficient. This point is very, very important."
We have applications for data centres springing up all over the UK, many from developers who appear to have no experience of data centre build.  Step forward Intelligent Land Investments, about whom we've posted many times before - although it's maybe a bit unfair to single out that one developer, as there are many more.  
Has ILI actually delivered a data centre, or is its experience principally in proposing and promoting developments? On the evidence reviewed so far, we haven't found a completed ILI data centre.  This is the developer who moved swiftly from housing, to small wind farms, to storage and now to data centres; the firm proposing the 'Stoics' - their grandiose umbrella name for three hyperscale data centres named after the three Stoic philosophers - Cato (that one's in Fife), Aurelius (North Lanarkshire), and Rufus (East Ayrshire) - to allegedly form a Green Digital Corridor linking the West, East and Central Scotland.  (We do grudgingly admire their concept, but does that translate into workable data centres?)
https://www.telegraph.co.uk/.../microsoft-axes-ai.../...
'Microsoft has pulled out of an Essex data centre deal in a blow to British company Nscale’s plans for a multibillion-dollar listing.
The US tech giant, one of Nscale’s two largest customers, recently informed the company that it was pulling the plug on its agreement, which was announced last year.
It is a significant setback for Nscale, given Microsoft was to become the anchor tenant at the company’s first British data centre in Loughton, Essex.
Microsoft’s decision threatens to undermine Nscale’s attempts to push ahead with a Wall Street flotation worth up to $35bn (£26bn), despite a brutal sell-off in AI computing stocks.
Rival data centre developers have seen their share prices plunge over the last week on concerns that they will struggle to repay their debts as interest rates and inflation continue to rise.
The outcome of Nscale’s attempted stock market listing will be viewed as a crucial litmus test of investors’ continued appetite for debt-hungry AI businesses. Its success or otherwise will also have implications for Britain’s broader aspirations for the technology.
Nscale, which is backed by tech giants including Nvidia, has positioned itself as Britain’s “sovereign” data centre provider.
Ministers have talked up its Essex data centre project as emblematic of the UK’s AI ambitions, and have lobbied local councillors to push it through.
Microsoft’s backing for the project formed part of £22bn in UK investments promised by the tech company last year during Donald Trump’s state visit. Sir Keir Starmer said it was a step towards Britain “becoming a world leader in AI”.
The data centre site, which contains thousands of high-end Nvidia AI chips, was originally intended to come online next year.
However, it has faced repeated delays, with grid bosses telling Nscale that they do not expect a power supply until the 2030s.
Microsoft’s cancellation leaves the site in apparent limbo. The company was its only announced customer, having agreed to rent 23,000 Nvidia AI chips at the facility. Financing for the data centre boom hinges on securing long-term commitments from AI giants to buy up capacity.
More than 40pc of Nscale’s $103bn in contracted revenue comes from Microsoft, although the UK deal is believed to be a small part of that. Anthropic is another major customer.
Nscale, which boasts heavyweights including former Facebook executives Sheryl Sandberg and Sir Nick Clegg on its board, has been privately valued at $15bn.
It is seeking to raise billions of dollars in a float that could value it at more than twice that, making it one of Britain’s most valuable AI companies.
However, its plans have clashed with a major sell-off in AI infrastructure businesses amid questions about the data centre building boom.
Tech analyst Gartner said last week that $3.5tn could be written off by 2030 if the AI boom fails to deliver on its promises.
Separately, Nscale has also faced delays at a flagship data centre in Norway, reportedly leading to heavy penalties.
Australian rival Firmus cancelled plans for a $20bn IPO earlier this month, citing market conditions. Other “neocloud” companies such as CoreWeave and Nebius have seen their shares and bonds slump.
Neoclouds are heavily dependent on raising new investment and debt to keep building, and soaring market interest rates have increased concerns about the sustainability of their business models.
An Nscale spokesman said: “We remain committed to both the Loughton project and the UK and we are exploring alternative power sources for the site, in addition to other expansion sites in the UK.
“Our relationship with Microsoft remains strong and long-term, and this unfortunate London-wide grid issue has no impact on our other contracts.”
Microsoft did not comment.
Nscale was founded by Australian entrepreneur Josh Payne, a former coal miner, just two years ago, and has faced scrutiny for signing large contracts despite a lack of a track record in building data centres.
However, Jensen Huang, Nvidia’s chief executive, praised Nscale on Wednesday at an event in London, saying: “You could be the most valuable UK startup they have created in the last 10 years.”
High electricity prices and long waits for grid connections have been seen as a major barrier to building AI infrastructure in Britain.
In April, ChatGPT-maker OpenAI suspended plans for a “Stargate” AI facility with Nscale on Tyneside, citing Britain’s high electricity prices.'

records.title: Environmentalists Against Wind Turbines
records.bodyText:
TIME TO REOPEN THE FLAWED F/V MISTRESS ACCIDENT INVESTIGATION
OCTOBER 18, 2026
https://www.windtaskforce.org/.../time-to-reopen-the...
The Mayday call for the F/V Mistress was made around 1:30 AM on January 1, 2019. The Coast Guard handwritten notes show the Beacon ID ADCD 02005944C01 at 6:44 AM, and then the search ended between 7:02 and 8:39 AM. The MH-60 helicopter spent 37 minutes looking for the ship.
The wind speeds in the area were 35 knots, with 10-foot waves. The MH-60 regularly conducts search-and-rescue operations in sustained winds of 60 knots. The Coast Guard’s all-weather helicopter was unable to assist because of radar clutter and the turbines being too close together.
Green Oceans in August 2026 located the vessel in a "targeted" dive, 92 feet underwater and only 50 feet from the base of Block Island turbine No. 1 .
The GPS coordinates and distress call data, straight out of the Coast Guard's original handwritten accident file, coincide with the turbine. There may be information that past divers working around the turbine had seen the wreck in past years.
Based on the hull orientation, investigators noted that while the boat was taking on water during the storm, it appears to have made an abrupt starboard avoidance maneuver to dodge the turbine. This sharp turn in rough seas likely caused the 52-foot trawler to roll over and sink immediately.
Green Oceans has asked several federal agencies to reopen Coast Guard Search and Rescue case # 1158048 (associated with MISLE Activity 6618087).
Dr. John DiCecco issued a naval study in January 2019, which focused on boat identification #672568. Dr. DiCecco is a prominent Research Engineer at the Naval Undersea Warfare Center (NUWC) Division Newport in Rhode Island. His work from January 2019, titled “F/V Mistress Navy Analysis,” was a post-accident investigation that utilized Navy sonar assets to analyze underwater imagery and determine the location of the sunken fishing vessel, F/V Mistress, near Block Island.
The investigation relied on a sonar search performed using Navy assets to locate the vessel. It analyzed the January 1, 2019, F/V Mistress accident and resolved "discrepancies" between U.S. Coast Guard coordinate reporting and the actual wreckage location relative to local offshore wind turbines.
After the 2019 sinking, BOEM funded a benthic and epifaunal environmental monitoring program at the Block Island Wind Farm, carried out by field researchers from the University of Rhode Island and HDR Engineering. On page 184 of their subsequently published OCS Study (BOEM 2020-044), right above Figure 79, researchers explicitly noted "partial boat debris" on the seafloor during the final day of a biological dive survey later in 2019 near turbine #1
Attached is a file referencing a sonar search performed using Navy assets. It’s unclear how or why the Navy has been so specifically involved.
Importantly, the GPS coordinates used to direct this search are transposed from the USCG reporting.
Time to reopen the investigation

records.bodyText:
Scotsman letters
A McCormick claims that in the last year “96 per cent of [constraint] payments went to Scottish generators” (Letters, 15 October). ScottishPower is owned by Spain’s Iberdola but I do agree with the sentiment. Payments of £1.5 billion in 2025 and £1.7bn so far this year for turning off excess wind power seems ludicrous.
That’s what happens when governments fail to implement infrastructure to transmit power from Scotland to England first. Building more windfarms without the grid infrastructure will make constraint payments go up even further. Most constraint payments actually went to gas generators, according to Octopus Energy, when more expensive and mostly imported gas was needed as wind generated power got stuck in the grid bottleneck. This is why our bills are so high.
The solution, Octopus claims, is not just to build the infrastructure quicker, but prioritise making energy cheaper where supply is strong through regional pricing. This would bring down bills in Scotland by 5-10 per cent. According to Octopus CEO Greg Jackson it would give Scots the lowest electricity prices in Europe. The government rejected regional pricing as it would have increased bills in southern England, where most parliamentary constituencies are located.
It seems Scots have all the downsides of windfarms and pylons but no upside on bills. Not only do Scots subsidise southern English bill-payers they also get the highest standing charges due to transmission costs. Why should the coldest part of the UK pay the most for its power?
Neil Anderson, Edinburgh

records.bodyText:
Herald letters
ON land and sea, no other First Minister has done more damage to Scotland’s economy and environment than Nicola Sturgeon. Your report of her failure to secure adequate financial benefits from offshore wind-farm development (“Billions worth of investment money at risk over ‘weak’ penalties for Scot Wind firms”, The Herald on Sunday, October 11), is matched on land by her disastrous manipulation of planning policy for wind-farm development.
One week before she resigned, the Scottish Government bent over backwards to open the door for industrial-scale renewable energy developments in Scotland’s 42 Wild Land Areas.
These were established by her predecessor, Alex Salmond, to protect Scotland’s finest areas of unspoilt scenery from inappropriate wind farm development.
This initiative put Scotland at the forefront of efforts to protect some of Europe’s most cherished wild places. Sturgeon squandered that legacy in favour of the corporate cowboys now exploiting the planning loophole she created.
The stupidity of Sturgeon’s actions was exposed on September 1 when Professor Sir Dieter Helm of Oxford University gave evidence to the
Scottish Parliament’s economy, tourism and energy committee.
As an economist and one of the UK’S foremost experts on energy policy his message was very blunt: we should immediately stop building large-scale wind farms on land, not only because it is economic madness, but also because of the impact on Scotland’s natural beauty.
He explained that the fundamental problem is the cost of transmitting the electricity generated by these wind farms to places in England where it is needed, involving a massive upgrade of the electricity grid, with its associated pylons and substations. These grid costs are met by taxpayers and are contributing to the high energy bills currently affecting every citizen in the UK.
Such grid upgrades on land would be unnecessary if the UK Government adopted a different energy policy and we in Scotland focused more on smallscale wind turbine development. On land, we need turbines no more than 50 metres to the vertical blade tip, designed primarily to meet local community needs.
The monster turbines of the future should be off-shore, connected by subsea cables to the centres of need further south. Meanwhile, we need our politicians to study the evidence given to the Scottish Parliament by Dieter Helm and then reflect on Sturgeon’s folly. For the SNP, a change in direction on energy policy is urgent – earlier this year, it lost the constituency vote over vast tracts of the Highlands and Islands.
Come the next election, if more communities are faced with industrialscale energy developments on their doorsteps and in the hills, at huge cost to taxpayers, the SNP’S electoral situation could be dire.
Dave Morris, Inverness-shire . 
THE wind and solar industry monotonously tells us that the electricity produced by wind and solar is green and cheaper than “nasty” gas electricity, and is reliable. Pull the other one.
UK solar farms and homeowners benefit from numerous subsidies and grants. The ECO4 scheme, warm homes local grant, Smart Export Guarantees, 0% VAT on solar panels and even local council support.
That is costly to consumers but not as costly as the subsidies given to mostly foreign wind farm-owners. These subsidies include Renewables Obligations, Contracts for Difference, Feed-in Tariffs, and constraint payments. Since 2002, these subsidies have added £240 billion to our electricity bills.
No wonder the cost of UK electricity is among the highest in Europe. No wonder our manufacturing industries are unable to compete. No wonder 260,000 jobs have been lost in the UK oil and gas industry since 2015.
No wonder there is fuel poverty. No wonder that there will be thousands of more deaths this winter. High electricity bills are forcing people to either heat or eat.
All new wind and solar farms should not be subsidised.
Clark Cross, West Lothian.

records.title: Scottish Electricity Generating Stations
records.bodyText:
Methil Power Station
As part of an agreement with the National Coal Board (NCB), the South of Scotland Electricity Board (SSEB) took control of Kelty Power Station and agreed to build power plants capable of burning coal slurry. This slurry was a waste product from coal washeries located across the central belt of Scotland. As a result new power stations were constructed at Barony and Methil in 1960s.
Methil Power Station was situated in the town of Methil at Innerleven on the south bank of the River Leven on the Firth of Forth,
The plant was designed by Ross-Smith and Jamieson Architects and was built on an area of reclaimed land which was leased from Forth Ports plc.
The plant was a coal-slurry fired power station which utilised local Fife coalfield waste from coal washeries and had a total capacity 57 MWe output. It was a ‘sister’ station to the generating station of Barony in Ayrshire and was commissioned in 1965. It was finally closed in 1999 and demolition began in early 2010.
The site included the following elements:
Rail network - bringing in coal slurry to the east side of the main building.
Coal handling and crane gantry areas - the trains reversed into the gantry area where there were coal grabs. The coal would be emptied into concrete open ‘bund’ which was used as the coal slurry store. This would then be transferred by crane to the Milling Area bay into individual hoppers above each hammer mill.
Milling Area – where coal slurry was pulverised in hammer mill pulverisers (into a finer uniform powder) and dried by the hot air from the boiler furnace.
Boiler House – where the coal dust was blown into the boilers by fans. There was one boiler for each turbine. The coal dust would then be burnt, and water was heated to produce steam to drive the turbo alternator. Make water was stored in blue tanks on site and taken from the mains supply before treatment for use in the process.
Turbine Hall: the electricity was produced by the turbo alternators and supplied via transformers (stepped up to 33,000 volts) and then onto a substation connected to the National Grid.
Turbine Hall 2 x 30MWe English Electric Turbo Alternators and condensers and associated auxiliary equipment. Various administrative buildings and workshops and the best canteen in the SSEB
Electrical annexe - housed the transformers and switchgear.
Chimney – Methil had one brick (single flue) chimney, clad in concrete. This removed fuel gases from the process to atmosphere.
Precipitators – They removed dust from the flue gases and consisted of large, cladded, steel boxes with HV electrodes to charge the dust particles to collector plants. ID fans which draw the flue gases from the boiler and discharged@ to the chimney. Most precipitates were gathered in hoppers and removed from the site with the ash from the boilers.
Water Treatment – for treating mains water used to top up the process cycle.
Cooling Water Intake & Outfall. Seawater extracted from the Forth to feed condensers and discharged waste heat back to the Forth. The condenser cools steam leaving the turbine, back into water to allow reuse in the process cycle. Unfortunately the CW inlet was located close to the regional sewage discharge outlet...
The power station consisted of two 30MW English Electric Turbo Alternator generation units for a peak output of 57 MWe the station. It was commissioned in 1965 for the then South of Scotland Electricity Board. Built on the site of a golf course, it was designed to utilise low-grade coal slurry supplied from the washeries of the nearby Fife coalfield. This coal was delivered by road and rail wagons shunted into and out of elevated sidings. Like almost all other coal-fired power stations in Scotland, Methil did not use cooling towers, instead using sea water as coolant.
As the Scottish coalfields were exhausted or abandoned in the mid-1980s, waste accumulated in coal tips (bings), and this waste was used as a fuel in the Methil and Barony power stations. However, as the tips were cleared, operations at the two stations ceased due to lack of coal-slurry fuel and the uneconomical operation of smaller power stations.
The station ceased generating in 2000 and was put into standby as a strategic reserve. The power station was finally demolished in 2011 as part of a regeneration of this area.
The site was transferred back to Forth Ports plc after the site had been cleared.
— in Methil, Fife.

records.bodyText:
ORSTED HIRED COAST GUARD EXECUTIVE 6 MONTHS AFTER F/V MISTRESS ACCIDENT
August 2019
https://www.nationalfisherman.com/.../orsted-hires-coast...
The former Coast Guard waterways management chief for New England has joined offshore wind energy company Ørsted, as the emerging U.S. industry comes to grips with pushback from commercial fishermen and other interests.
Ed LeBlanc, a former Coast Guard officer and most recently chief of the Waterways Management Division for Coast Guard Sector Southeastern New England, will be manager of marine affairs for Ørsted U.S. Offshore Wind, the Denmark-based energy company’s American division.
In his last position of 16 years with the Coast Guard First District, LeBlanc was in the forefront of planning to how the newly arriving offshore wind industry could coexist with commercial fishing and maritime transportation traffic in the Northeast. An element of that will be safe vessel transit lanes through planned wind turbine arrays off Martha’s Vineyard, Mass.
Ed LeBlanc, the former chief of waterways management at the Coast Guard Southeast New England sector, is Ørsted's new manager of marine affairs.
LinkedIn photo.
https://www.linkedin.com/in/edward-leblanc-59492122/...
One conceptual layout proposed in late 2018 by the Responsible Offshore Development Alliance, a coalition of fishing groups, would set aside lanes with setbacks so fishing vessels can safely transit between ports like New Bedford, Mass., to Georges Bank and other fishing grounds.
The spacing and orientation of the turbine arrays is under intense debate, with commercial fishing groups in New England and New York warning the designs could make mobile gear fishing impossible.
The decision appears to be a sudden slowdown in what has been strong federal support for developing offshore wind. Democratic and Republican lawmakers from Massachusetts and Louisiana – both states that stand to gain jobs from building and operating the new offshore industry – wrote to Bernhardt and Secretary of Commerce Wilbur Ross Aug. 16 urging “your departments to work together to find a solution that will address concerns raised by stakeholders, protect the environment, and allow the Vineyard Wind project to remain viable.”
Signed by Sens. Ed Markey and Elizabeth Warren of Massachusetts and Bill Cassidy and John Kennedy of Louisiana, the letter makes the case that offshore wind power will benefit Massachusetts residents with reliable energy – and Gulf of Mexico states, where the prospect of building turbine foundations and offshore wind service vessels is a bright hope for the maritime industry. Reps. Joseph Kennedy III, Richard Neal, and William Keating of Massachusetts and Steve Scalise of Louisiana also signed on to the message.
The members of Congress wrote that “Louisiana and Gulf Coast companies that have decades of experience working in the Gulf of Mexico are eager to make needed investments to support this project and future offshore wind energy projects.”
For Ørsted, adding LeBlanc, with his 40 years' experience with the Coast Guard, to its team is part of a push to build relationships with the larger maritime community.
“We are thrilled to add such an accomplished veteran of the USCG to our team. Ed’s breadth of experience will be a significant addition to the Marine Affairs department,” said John O’Keeffe, head of marine affairs U.S. for Ørsted, in announcing LeBlanc’s move.
LeBlanc has "invaluable institutional knowledge of how the offshore wind industry interacts with the marine community,” according to the Ørsted statement. “His experience working with industry since its nascency in the U.S. mirrors Ørsted’s own experience with the industry’s beginnings in Europe.”
The company says it “will bolster its marine community outreach efforts as its projects move closer to the construction phase. Ørsted’s commitment to working with the marine community, including the fishing industry, demonstrates how it has successfully built offshore wind farms across Europe to deliver clean energy and economic development to local communities.”
Ørsted is holding three of those community outreach sessions in New Jersey next week to talk about its proposed Ocean Wind project off Atlantic City. The first will be held Aug. 26 at 6 p.m. in the Stockton University Atlantic City Academic Center, located at 3711 Atlantic Avenue, Atlantic City.
In addition to the company’s outreach campaign, LeBlanc will help coordinate the company’s safety operations with the Coast Guard, and aim to establish industry-wide standards. That is a critical area for the service’s vessel and aviation operators, who must train to safely transit and conduct search and rescue operations amid turbine arrays.
The Coast Guard recently conducted its first-ever such exercise working with Ørsted and General Electric at the Block Island Wind Farm off Rhode Island.
That five-turbine, 30 MW array is the first U.S. commercial offshore wind pilot project – and a fraction of the size proposed for energy developments on offshore federal leases.
Kirk Moore
Senior Associate Editor

On a wander through the back roads of the Planning Inspectorate, one of our supporters came across an interesting email.
The background to this is that a huge solar farm on the Cambridgeshire/Suffolk border, the Sunnica Energy Farm, which is a Nationally Significant Infrastructure Project (NSIP), was granted a Development Consent Order (DCO) by Ed Miliband in July 2024. The project covers three sites spanning 2,500 acres/ 1012 ha and would affect the villages of West Row and Mildenhall, Worlington and an area off the A14 near Newmarket. So far no construction has taken place.
On 8 April 2024, Claire Coutinho, at the time the Secretary of State for Energy Security and Net Zero, received an email with the subject 'Large DCO Appicayions ˜ Sunnica etc' (sic).
Coutinho's correspondent was writing 'to vehemently object' to the Sunnica proposal.
They wrote: 'Siting compounds and solar sites between and close to a number of closely related historic villages cause significant and detrimental industrialisation of a wholly rural area.'
Furthermore, they maintain that 'the development would, due to its location and scale, result in significant long-term harm to the character of the landscape including the setting of settlements.'
They go on to say that 'due to its location and scale, (the site) would fail to protect, conserve or enhance space between settlements and their wider landscape setting, key views into and out of settlements and the unspoiled nature and tranquillity of the area.'
The email was forwarded to the Department for Business, Energy and Industrial Strategy and was flagged as *Not a constituent*
Who could this person possibly be?
Why, none other than 'Christopher D G Wilson, Executive Chairman Worldwide Renewable Energy Global Ltd' (and founder of Calderdale Wind Farm Ltd).
I don't know precisely why Wilson got caught up in the campaign against Sunnica, but I suspect that, like his friend Richard Bannister, he is a racing man and may well be acquainted with the racing community around the Sunnica sites.
Let us hope that his concerns for the fate of the landscape around Sunnica also apply to our wholly rural moor, with its historic villages such as Haworth and its key views...
Just in case you were wondering what our campaign was doing at the time Wilson was firing off emails about his deep concerns for the environment, here's a lovely blog, published on 4 April 2024 and written by our supporter, the writer and cartographer Chris Goddard: https://markavery.info/.../guest-blog-walshaw-turbine-34.../

records.title: Our Power
records.bodyText:
There’s been a lot of splashy coverage about Galileo Empower’s plan to use "AI technology" to cover energy bills for nearby residents around the Dorenell Wind Farm extension near Dufftown and the Cabrach.
It sounds like a win on the surface. Who wouldn't want £0 at the bottom of their energy bill?
But let’s look past the slick PR campaign.
A £1.8 million annual fund and automated bill credits are corporate handouts, designed to secure planning consent while external developers and global financial funds siphon off tens of millions of pounds in long-term profits generated right here on Moray’s hills.
Here is why rural communities across Scotland deserve better:
Discretionary Handouts vs. Equity: Industry data shows that 100% community-owned wind farms return up to 52 times more revenue to local areas than corporate community benefit schemes.
Zero Real Control: An AI-managed discount scheme keeps local residents completely dependent on the corporation's terms. If energy price caps shift, tax laws change, or the asset is sold, those "handouts" can disappear.
True Local Investment: When a community owns its energy assets, the profits don't go to foreign shareholders, they stay 100% local to build affordable council housing, fund school retention, upgrade rural transport, and guarantee low-cost power permanently.
Moray’s land, wind, and landscape are priceless local assets. We shouldn't be settling for crumbs dropped off the bottom of a corporate balance sheet.
It’s time to shift the conversation in Scotland from "How much discount will you give us?" to "Why shouldn't the community own the energy?" 
 What do you think? Would you prefer a monthly bill credit from a multinational firm, or full community equity and ownership of local wind farms? Let’s hear your thoughts below.

records.title: Our Power
records.bodyText:
Another very busy day at conference, with plenty of opportunities to get around the exhibition stands, meet organisations and discuss issues affecting people across the constituency.
I was pleased to meet with RNIB Scotland and hear more about the issues affecting blind and partially sighted people, and the work they are doing to improve accessibility and support.
I also stopped by the MCS Foundation stand, where they had put together a Cowdenbeath-specific quiz as part of their snakes and ladders game on heat pumps and energy efficiency. It was a good way of highlighting just how far we still have to go in improving energy efficiency, moving towards cleaner heating and helping to bring down energy costs for households across the constituency.
I met with Our Power to discuss community ownership of energy assets and the potential benefits that could bring locally, and also visited the Movember stand to learn more about their work supporting men’s mental health and wellbeing, alongside their long-standing work raising awareness of prostate cancer and other men’s health issues. They even managed to get me into the barber’s chair for a quick tidy-up before the rest of conference!
A really useful conversation with StepChange focused on the support available to people experiencing debt and the importance of people getting help as early as possible. I’ll be making sure information about their services is available through my constituency office so that people know where they can turn for free and practical support.
I also learned more about the Bank of Scotland Foundation and the important core funding it provides to charities and community organisations across Scotland.
Alongside the exhibition, I joined a number of fringe events and had the opportunity to sit down with Forth Ports for further discussions about the Rosyth ferry and their decision to withdraw from the service. I also spoke with Scottish Swimming about community access to facilities in Inverkeithing and what the future may hold there.
It was an extremely busy day, but a very productive one, with plenty of useful conversations and a number of follow-ups now to take forward after conference.

F/V MISTRESS EVIDENCE: IT'S AT BLOCK ISLAND WIND TURBINE # 1

On January 1, 2019, the F/V Mistress took on water and sank near the Block Island wind turbines. The Coast Guard dispatched an all-weather MH-60 Jayhawk helicopter. Coast Guard handwritten logs show that, after 37 minutes, radar interference from the turbines aborted the search. They declared the trawler lost.
August 2026, Green Oceans located the vessel F/V Mistress in a "targeted" dive, 92 feet underwater and 50 feet from the base of Block Island turbine No. 1.
Green Oceans has asked several federal agencies to reopen Coast Guard Search and Rescue case # 1158048 (associated with MISLE Activity 6618087).
The evidence demonstrating that the vessel was tracking the straightest possible northward path home includes:
1. The F/V Mistress was inbound on a direct path to Point Judith, Rhode Island, which sits directly north of Block Island
2. When investigators plotted the GPS coordinates from the U.S. Coast Guard's original January 1, 2019 accident report and Mayday calls, the trajectory lined up perfectly with Block Island Wind Turbine 1.
3. The F/V Mistress crew's final radio transmission noted they were "right below the Block Island Wind Farm." VMS tracking data should confirm the location. (Commercial Vessel Monitoring System)
4. The orientation of the hull 50 feet from turbine # 1 shows they were on a northward course, and the trawler may have had to steer quickly, causing the boat to capsize.

records.title: Wind Energy's Absurd
records.bodyText:
Extraordinary!  
Following the Evershed and Ofgem reports on the state of NESO, the CEO of NESO, Fintan Slye, has been caught on a recording, stating that he knew about the issues - and did....nothing.  
This is known from a Times piece, below.  This is Kathryn Porter's take on it:
·
According to @thetimes @neso_energy CEO Fintan Slye who earned just under £1 million last year admitted he knew about the control room concerns but failed to act on them saying Neso may have incorrectly prioritised other things at a time when there was a “huge amount of change happening in the organisation”
How does the Times know this?
Because somebody inside NESO recorded the meeting and gave it to the press
Clearly NESO staff have lost confidence in their execs and have no issues embarrassing them in public
Although it's fair to ask why Fintan didn't make his mea culpa public himself. Perhaps he simply didn't want to admit either to getting it wrong or to allowing the focus on CP2030 and keeping the government happy to get in the way of keeping the grid secure 
There's a clear public interest in knowing this so I hope Fintan and NESO don't respond to this by trying to hunt the people who made and released this recording
The more productive approach would be to repair trust with staff, listen to and act on their concerns over grid security, and ensure cultural change so future concerns can be raised and acted on internally without staff feeling they have no options other than to leave or go to MPs and the media
https://www.thetimes.com/.../power-grid-boss-admits-he...
'The boss of the National Energy System Operator has admitted that he was aware of serious cultural issues at the government-owned body and failed to address them. 
Fintan Slye, who has been paid more than £770,000 a year to lead the organisation responsible for managing Britain’s power system, told staff he was “disappointed” in himself and “should have fixed” the problems before an independent report raised them. 
National Energy System Operator (Neso) is under scrutiny after whistleblowers raised concerns about its ability to keep the lights on and how it handled tight power supplies during the heatwave in June. 
An independent report published on Monday by Eversheds Sutherland, a law firm, could not substantiate specific whistleblower allegations that Neso deliberately altered operational records and took steps to avoid public scrutiny, or that corporate affairs personnel interfered in operational decisions in June.
However, Eversheds did find wider “control, cultural and governance issues”, which the energy regulator, Ofgem, described as “important and concerning” and which the government has told Neso to address “without delay”.
Eversheds highlighted four main underlying issues: “high levels of operational stress, a significant disconnect between the [control room] and executive leadership, a culture of reputational sensitivity affecting the perception of operational independence, and a gap between formal [whistleblowing] commitments and the lived experience of staff”.
In calls with Neso staff, recordings of which have been obtained by The Times, Slye admitted: “There’s nothing in any of those four themes that was a huge surprise, or that I could put my hand on my heart and say that I haven’t heard that from someone in the organisation.” Slye said the Eversheds report had made “difficult reading”.
“I’m disappointed in myself, in that we haven’t acted sooner to address [the issues], or more comprehensively to address them, such that they ended up having to be raised in a form and in a format like this,” he said. 
Asked by a staff member why the issues hadn’t been addressed, he suggested Neso may have incorrectly prioritised other things at a time when there was a “huge amount of change happening in the organisation”, but said he had no “easy answer” for why it had failed to act. “The answer is: I should have fixed them. I should have leant in to try, and got them fixed.”
He added: “All I can do is hold up my hands and say we will fix them now.”
Slye also admitted: “Sometimes I can be defensive, and I have to absolutely make sure that my reaction to this is not that.” 
A Neso spokesman said: “Slye’s comments referred to the broader organisational and cultural themes identified by the independent Eversheds Sutherland investigation, not the specific allegations, which the investigation did not substantiate. He was clear with colleagues that Neso should have acted sooner and more comprehensively on those wider themes, we accept that and are taking action to address them.” 
Slye received total pay, bonuses and other remuneration of £773,650 as chief executive of Neso in 2024-25, the last year for which accounts are available. He was separately paid a further £156,870 by National Grid that year under a performance scheme linked to the creation of the nationalised Neso. 
Michael Shanks, the energy minister, has said that the independent review “raises areas for cultural improvement in Neso where we expect significant action without delay”. 
Asked about Slye’s admission that he was already aware of the issues and failed to tackle them, a government source indicated that it retained full confidence in Slye.'

records.bodyText:
Well, today, the answer to the question is the letter which Andrew Bowie, the Shadow Energy Sec. of State, has sent back by way of reply to one from Michael Shanks, Energy Minister on the Eversheds report, etc. 
We did of course say that maybe Shanks has seen the light, with our tongues firmly in our cheeks, and we will forgive Bowie the two words we think he shouldn't have said to the media.
We did miss seeing, until she told us, that Kathryn Porter had put a  link in her blog to Shanks' letter.  So just now, we hotfooted onto X to have a look.
What a thoroughly abysmal letter from Shanks - and, living up to his surname, a killer of a response back from Bowie.

records.title: Wind Energy's Absurd
records.bodyText:
That's the expression which sprang to mind when reading this piece from the Stornoway Gazette - and thanks to the WEA friend who sent it to us.
We are, of course, keeping everything crossed that the  Spiorad na Mara, being outrageously close to Lewis, is sunk without trace.
https://www.stornowaygazette.co.uk/.../offshore-wind-is...
'Uncertainty about prospects for “floating wind” projects around the Scottish coast could have major implications for developments earmarked for waters to the west and north of Lewis. ​
“Scotland on Sunday” reported this week that “crisis talks” have been held to prioritise just four floating wind projects in the ScotWind round due to increasing costs and failure to develop a domestic supply chain.
Implications for the Western Isles could come in several forms:
- Increased pressure on the Scottish Government to ensure development of Spiorad na Mara, regardless of planning objections, as it is an outlier in the ScotWind programme as a “fixed bottom” site close to shore
- The Talisk site awarded to the Norwegian company Magnora, 35 kilometres north west of the Butt of Lewis, is not being quoted as a priority project giving rise to doubts about its development. The same goes for Northland’s Havbredey site.
- The 1.8 GW interconnector, currently going ahead, would be nowhere near capacity without these projects, which could create additional opportunities for community-led developments with plenty capacity to spare.
Kajsa Jernet, lead offshore wind analyst for Bloomberg, told a conference in Aberdeen: “The industry has been caught up in a negative spiral where the supply chain doesn’t have the order certainty it needs to invest which brings higher costs, leading to project delays and decreasing project viability.
“The first year of gigawatt-scale installations is still more than a decade away. We expect floating wind to remain niche in comparison to bottom-fixed offshore wind all the way out through to 2041”.
A senior industry source told “Scotland on Sunday” that the initial ScotWind announcement had created huge optimism “but we’re coming off that sugar rush now. ScotWind was a complete moonshot – there’s going to be more attrition. We will likely see more leases relinquished”.
They added: “We need to put forward a more credible offering, rather than kidding ourselves that we’re going to be deploying gigawatts and gigawatts of floating wind by 2030 or 2035. Actually, what this is now about is picking winners”.
Clare Lavelle, the industry chair of the Scottish Offshore Wind Energy Council, said: “I need to be absolutely honest in saying it’s an incredibly challenging environment in which to be progressing floating projects at the moment.
“We are nearly five years on from the award of the ScotWind projects. This was a programme we thought was going to be fully constructed by 2030. I don’t think we thought we would be in the position we are today.”
When the Magnora licence was granted, the company said its ambition was to achieve full consent in 2026, reach the final investment decision in 2028 and start production in 2030. However, these timescales do not now see remotely achievable.
While Northland continue to press ahead with their Spiorad na Mara plans, they have been refused planning consent for onshore developments by Comhairle nan Eilean Siar, though the final decision will rest with the Scottish Government.'

We've just been watching, on  Communities B4 Power Companies , a clip of Miatta Fahnbulleh speaking at the Energy Security & Net Zero Committee on 14 October.  She said (and when time allows, as we have a bit of a backlog,  we will delve into the rest of the transcript of that meeting):
The second thing is that I talk to my international counterparts and they are looking to the UK with envy. We are a leader in this world, but we are a leader in a massively growing economy. China is leading the race on clean power. It is a huge global economy. The thing I say to people who may be sceptical about climate change—I look at the science and the science is pretty clear—is: “Fine if you are sceptical, even if you don’t believe in it, but why would you not want to be part of that global economy that is growing?” Ultimately, I think the way that I and the Government should engage with people, and it is within their gift to be sceptical, is to say, “Look, we need to do this transition in a way that isn’t a burden, where we are unlocking billions of investment.”
You talked about deindustrialisation. My view is that our route to reindustrialisation, which the Prime Minister talks about all the time, is through our sector. There is a massive pipeline on talking to global investors, trillions that they want to invest in the net zero economy, and we can be part of that. Why on earth would we not want to be part of that?
If anything, she comes across as more zealous than Miliband - as we've said before, she doesn't roll her eyes quite as much as he does; her voice is obviously softer, and she doesn't wave her arms about as Miliband did.  How could anyone reckon that, on matters energy at least, that the UK is viewed with envy?  
Anyway, the piece jogged our memory that we had intended yesterday to find, on i player, the episode shown on Sunday of the Simon Reeve's Wilderness series, where he went to Mongolia.
Quite apart from the fact that it was a fascinating insight into Mongolia and its culture and its people, there was one part which would make one's jaw drop - in the middle of the Gobi desert - a humungous open cast mine.  These images are screenshots from the  video.  The third one is the snake of lorries waiting to be loaded with coal.  Some are there for three days, waiting in the queue.
Simon Reeve said that 80m tonnes plus go to China annually - that's in excess, he said, of 1 million lorry loads.

records.bodyText:
The Times has a piece on the NESO and Ofgem reports.
The responses are interesting.
Michael Shanks, the energy minister, said: “The independent review raises areas for cultural improvement in Neso where we expect significant action without delay.”
This is particularly interesting.  Has Shanks seen the light?  Because this was one of of our posts, only in July:
[‘It’s getting worse day by day. We’re now flying blind with the plane on fire. It’s not a matter of “if” there’s going to be a major blackout, it’s an engineering certainty.’
‘If we overload parts of the system, that means things will catch fire or explode. We’d have cables crashing to the floor, perhaps over motorways, then arcing over, spraying flames, before they hit the floor.’
They warned that colleagues are now ‘re-running the models’ to try to alter the calculations and claim there was no problem on June 23.'
Told to the Mail by a NESO whistleblower.  It's shocking that the grid engineers are now asking the public for help.
Kathryn Porter, David Turver and others are laying into Michael Shanks for saying this:
Britain has a highly resilient energy system. It's right that we continue to make sure that always remains the case. 
It is categorically untrue to claim that blackouts are an "engineering certainty". 
This is simply sensationalist nonsense.
Kathryn has said this:
You are not an engineer. Perhaps you should talk to the people who are, who actually run the grid every day and let them show you what they mean.
Because if you ignore this and people die, you will not be forgiven.]
We are not partisan and will have a go at any party's comments if we have reason.
Andrew Bowie, the Shadow Energy Secretary, has also commented.  There are, in our view, two words which he should not have used - 'all along'.  It was incautious, given that the everyday interpretation of the phrase would be 'from the beginning' as opposed to 'from the beginning of our tenure as the opposition'.  Apart from that, he was correct in his criticism. 
And NESO:
Paul Golby, the chairman of Neso, said: “The investigation’s findings are clear that there was no evidence to substantiate any of the allegations around inappropriate influence over decision-making or inappropriate record-keeping processes.
“The board will oversee the development of plans to address the issues raised in the report and ensure these are implemented as a matter of urgency.”
Well that will be interesting to watch - and it may well be that when Ofgem has finalised its report in January, there will be more for you to oversee, Dr Golby.
We retrieved from the archives a snippet from when NESO was about to be spawned, under the Sunak government:
In his role as chair, Dr Golby will help establish NESO as a trusted, expert body at the centre of the energy system. 
We make no comment to that.
https://www.thetimes.com/uk/environment/article/neso-engineers-review-national-grid-blackout-risks-6lqpq03sp?utm_source=Sailthru&utm_medium=email&utm_campaign=Daily%20briefing%20Tues%2020%20Oct%202026&utm_term=audience_DAILY_BRIEFING
'Engineers running Britain’s power system have “high levels of stress and concern” about their ability to keep the lights on because of the shift to renewables, an independent report has found.
Staff at the National Energy System Operator (Neso) believe its senior leadership do not understand how the control room works and feel their concerns go “largely unheard” because of the need to keep the government and others happy.
The report by Eversheds Sutherland, a law firm, could not substantiate specific whistleblower allegations about Neso’s handling of the power system during June’s heatwave, but did identify significant “cultural, governance and control issues” at the government-owned body.
These included a “culture of reputational sensitivity affecting operational decision-making”.
Control room staff said Neso should not have claimed the system was “not at risk” on June 23, given that “the system was consistently in breach of operational limits for a number of hours, with operators working around the clock to regain balance”. 
Michael Shanks, the energy minister, said: “The independent review raises areas for cultural improvement in Neso where we expect significant action without delay.”
A separate review overseen by Ofgem, the regulator, into whether electricity supplies were secure in June is being extended into next year. 
The investigations were prompted after whistleblowers contacted Claire Coutinho, then the shadow energy secretary, to raise concerns about events on June 23, when the frequency on the power network — a crucial marker of stability — fell below normal operational limits for a sustained period. Whistleblowers claim this brought the country close to blackouts.
The Eversheds review looked specifically at whistleblower allegations to Coutinho that Neso deliberately altered operational records and used document types that left no record of decision-making to avoid scrutiny, and that corporate affairs personnel interfered in operational decisions for reputational reasons.
Although it could not substantiate these claims, it did corroborate concerns raised by whistleblowers to The Times about the “unprecedented situation” the control room faced on June 23, including that five “safety boundaries” were breached amid efforts to keep the lights on.
Witnesses told Eversheds they felt public statements that the system was not “at risk” on June 23 were “misrepresenting the situation”.
One witness claimed that Neso should have issued more emergency warnings that day but did not do so because of the “optics”. The report claimed emergency warnings in general were seen as “uncomfortable to issue” because they would create “bad press and lots of inquiries”.
The Eversheds report, based on interviews with 28 senior staff from the control room and eight beyond the control room, also raised wider issues about Neso’s culture and governance.
It found “high levels of stress and concern within the [control room] regarding the current state of the energy industry and the longer-term ability to maintain system balance, given the challenges of the net zero transition and increased reliance on renewables, which are less flexible than conventional generation, as well as current energy market structures”. 
Unlike traditional power stations, many smaller generators and batteries do not engage directly with Neso, leaving engineers to estimate how much electricity they are supplying and unable to instruct them directly.
The report also found a “significant disconnect between the [control room] and the executive leadership team, with multiple witnesses expressing the view that those in senior leadership and executive positions do not fully appreciate or understand either the way in which the control room works, or the reality of the pressures faced by those on the front line who are responsible for ‘keeping the lights on’”.
Andrew Bowie, the shadow energy secretary, said: “Far from clearing the heads of Neso or this Labour government, this report raises more questions than it answers about the culture, management and operational independence of the organisation tasked with keeping the lights on in this country. 
“It also confirms what we Conservatives have been saying all along — that the net zero transition and the increased reliance on renewables is making the job of ensuring the grid continues to operate much more difficult due to the lack of flexibility and inertia in the system.”
One witness described an “implicit understanding and expectation from the leadership to hear what they want to hear”, saying they felt pressure to convey a positive message and reassure bosses that “everything’s fine”. One witness said that those raising concerns “get beaten down”.
Another described a culture of favouring good news that they believed started at the top of the organisation. Investigators found that concerns about Neso’s reputation were communicated to engineers directly, through senior managers or through staff perceptions.
The report concluded that this environment could affect how promptly and confidently engineers issued warnings about tight electricity supplies. It also cited witnesses identifying “a culture change in recent years, with Neso leadership deferring to government”.
The report said staff needed “targeted training to reinforce that operational decisions must be made solely on the basis of operational and engineering judgment”.
Paul Golby, the chairman of Neso, said: “The investigation’s findings are clear that there was no evidence to substantiate any of the allegations around inappropriate influence over decision-making or inappropriate record-keeping processes.
“The board will oversee the development of plans to address the issues raised in the report and ensure these are implemented as a matter of urgency.”'

records.bodyText:
A sincere thank you to Hethersgill Parish Council and residents from across the surrounding communities for welcoming North Carlisle Against Pylons and Substation (NCAPS) to our latest community meeting.
The strength of feeling was unmistakable, with residents and farmers expressing deep concerns about National Grid's proposed Cross Border Connection, the extensive pylon route and the potential North Cumbria mega-substation at Option A.
The meeting brought several important outcomes:
 Growing political recognition: We welcomed David Allen, Labour's mayoral candidate, who made clear his view that Option A was the wrong location for the proposed substation — a statement met with applause. He also committed to working with affected communities and ensuring their concerns are heard should he become Mayor.
 Strengthening the campaign: We outlined the establishment of NCAPS Community Action Limited, providing a formal structure to raise funds, secure specialist legal and technical advice, and mount an evidence-led challenge to the pylon route, its design and the proposed substation location.
 Communities working together: Continued collaboration with the North Cumbria Parish Council Alliance will help ensure communities across the affected area have a coordinated and effective voice.
 Holding Cumberland Council to account: Our petition will be presented to Full Council on 3 November, calling on the Council to take a more proactive role in assessing the cumulative impacts of these proposals and representing affected communities.
It was also encouraging to reflect that representatives from across the mayoral political parties have now engaged with our communities, with concerns about the adequacy of National Grid's consultation extending across party lines.
We are not against upgrading the electricity network. We are challenging how and where that infrastructure is being proposed, and the potentially irreversible consequences for North Cumbria.
More than a year of uncertainty is already taking its toll on residents, farmers and businesses. Continued community engagement, fundraising and support will be essential as NCAPS moves into its next phase.
Thank you again to Hethersgill for hosting us and to everyone who attended, spoke openly and offered their support.
Our greatest strength remains the collective voice of our communities. We need to keep that momentum going.
#NCAPS #NorthCumbria #Hethersgill #CrossBorderConnection #NationalGrid #CommunityVoice #Carlisle

records.title: STOP EAST LINCOLNSHIRE PYLONS
records.bodyText:
WESTON MARSH - SUBSTATION A - PLANNING COMMITTEE MEETING
I previously advised that I would be speaking as a ward member at the meeting of the planning committee tomorrow, (Wednesday 21st October at 6:30pm) being held at South Holland District Council offices in Priory Road, Spalding at 6:30pm
Unfortunately, I have been told today that as the actual substation doesn’t sit in the ward I represent, that I will not be able to speak on this item as a ward member. 
I have emailed all councillors today with what I intended to say tomorrow, which I have added below, for their consideration prior to the meeting. 
Good afternoon, Chairman and members of the planning committee.
I am sending this to all members in case any substitutions have been made for planning committee tomorrow evening. 
I had planned to speak as a ward member at the meeting but have been told that as the site itself does not sit in my ward, that it is not possible, so wanted to contact you regarding my concerns in addition to what I have already submitted which has been summarised within the agenda.
The number of resident objections, together with my request for this application to be referred to committee, is why this application is being presented to you tomorrow evening for your consideration. I think it is fair to say that this is one of the most significant applications to come before one of the final meetings of this committee under the current arrangements.
Whilst the substation itself sits outside the ward I represent, the impacts of this development, and the wider infrastructure it is intended to support, reach far beyond Weston Marsh and will be felt across South Holland and beyond, including in The Saints ward which I proudly represent.
Like many people, I recognise the importance of energy security and the need to improve our infrastructure. However, recognising that need does not mean accepting every proposal regardless of its impact on our communities and our landscape.
This application is being presented as a standalone development when, as we all know, it forms part of a much larger programme of energy infrastructure. Whilst members of the planning committee are required to determine every application on its own merits, the reality is that this is only one piece of a much larger puzzle. Officers, residents and members are effectively being asked to make a judgement without being able to take into consideration the wider picture including the multiple NSIPS and infrastructure associated with this application. 
The cumulative impact on our countryside, our communities, our agricultural land and our increasingly damaged and depleted highway network would be profound. 
As a stand alone application, this development would have a detrimental impact on Walpole Marsh and along the pylon route associated with it. 
I have been contacted by farmers, residents and business owners who all have real and valid concerns about their land, property values and impact on their lives and businesses associated with this application alone. This application would change the very character of rural South Holland for generations to come.
In particular, the associated infrastructure, including extensive pylon networks and transmission connections, would permanently alter the flat, open Fenland landscape that our district is renowned for. 
This landscape is one of South Holland's defining characteristics. It is part of our identity. Once these structures are introduced on this scale, it’s impossible for them to simply be screened away, planted over or undone in the future.
What is being proposed is, in effect, the industrialisation of our open countryside. The impact on our landscape will be irreversible and, in my view, detrimental not only to the character of the area but also to the residents who live, work and enjoy this unique part of Lincolnshire.
I am also deeply concerned about the continued industrialisation of our open countryside. This is a significant development on Grade 1 agricultural land, the very best farmland in the country. At a time when food security is becoming an increasingly important national issue, the continued loss of productive agricultural land should not be dismissed lightly.
Flood risk and drainage remain equally important concerns. South Holland exists because of careful and effective water management. Our residents understand better than most the importance of resilient drainage systems, and I am not convinced sufficient certainty has been provided regarding the long-term resilience of these proposals or their impact on existing infrastructure.
Likewise, I remain concerned about ecological impacts and the significant disruption that residents, businesses and road users would experience during what would be a lengthy construction period.
These concerns are not mine alone. They have been raised repeatedly by residents, parish councils and consultees throughout the life of this application. People are worried about what this development, and those that will inevitably follow it, mean for the future of the area they call home.
As we all know, planning is about balance. It is about weighing benefits against harm. Whilst I acknowledge the national benefits put forward by the applicant, I do not believe it has been satisfactorily demonstrated that the environmental, landscape and community impacts on South Holland have been fully addressed.
I would ask members to ask themselves whether the irreversible industrialisation of our countryside, the permanent change to our landscape and the cumulative impact on our communities are harms that can genuinely be justified in this location.
For those reasons, I strongly object to this application, and on this occasion, I do not agree with the officer's recommendation for approval.
I believe there are material planning considerations that could justify refusal of this application should members of the committee be minded to do so, and in my opinion the harm outweighs the benefits. I therefore ask you, on behalf of those residents who have taken the time to engage in this process, to give those concerns the serious weight they deserve when reaching your decision tomorrow evening.
Thank you for your consideration in this.
Kind regards,
Laura 
Laura Eldridge 
District Councillor for ‘The Saints Ward’ - Gedney Hill, Sutton St James, Sutton St Edmund & Throckenholt

records.bodyText:
THIS IS WHAT THEY CALL SAVING THE PLANET. WATCH THE VIDEO.
Apparently, destroying the countryside is perfectly acceptable — provided you call it GREEN.
In May 2024, a hillside at Upper Kergord in Shetland gave way, sending a torrent of peat down the landscape during construction work on the Kergord–Gremista electricity connection.
This wasn't construction of the Viking wind farm itself. It was associated grid infrastructure. And that distinction makes the wider question even more important.
How much environmental destruction are we prepared to tolerate in the name of environmental protection?
Peatlands take centuries, sometimes thousands of years, to develop. They are natural carbon stores, valuable habitats and part of Britain's irreplaceable landscape.
Yet we are repeatedly told that the industrialisation of our countryside is necessary to save the environment.
What a staggering contradiction.
Politicians celebrate renewable capacity. Developers announce investment. Energy companies talk about sustainability.
But who accounts for the damaged land, disturbed peat, construction impacts and the consequences for local communities?
You cannot claim to be protecting the environment while treating the countryside as expendable.
We need proper scrutiny of the full environmental consequences of these developments, not just the electricity they might generate.
And we need politicians who understand the difference between genuinely protecting nature and simply meeting a government target.
The industry calls it progress. The countryside pays the price.

MILLIONS WASTED IN THE PURSUIT OF RENEWABLES — AND WHO PAYS THE PRICE?
Millions of pounds paid to turn down wind farms because the grid cannot handle their electricity. Peatlands disturbed, water pollution concerns and communities left questioning where the promised benefits have gone.
Our latest investigation into Shetland's Viking Wind Farm reveals over £20 million in constraint payments during 2025 and part of 2026 alone.
Meanwhile, the companies report substantial profits, and ordinary households continue paying the bills.
How much more countryside must we sacrifice, and how many more millions must consumers pay, before Parliament demands a proper assessment of the true costs?
We are not asking for miracles. We are demanding accountability, transparency and evidence.
